text: Can someone at stripe press pass him a copy of America against America I’m tryna see something @stripepress @tamarawinter
author: austinyhuang
quoted_text:
Travel writing is in practice some of the best sociology since the naivete of the foreigner grants the permission to make sweeping generalizations and claims that might otherwise seem too poorly-justified to merit publication. “My people have poor manners” is a tough claim to credibly land (Who are you? Exactly which life experiences are you drawing on? And what is your agenda in pushing this line of argument?), whereas “on my travels in Scotland, I noticed that the people had poor manners” seems perfectly reasonable, and indeed thought-provoking. Random samples from a distribution help you understand the mean, and the aleatory nature of travel encounters lends credence to the whole assessment.

Alexis de Tocqueville was just 25 when he traveled across the US and 29 when his observations were published. So, Democracy in America is a giant Substack from a young backpacker, written on his peregrinations as he consumed Montesquieu, Pascal, and Rousseau. He was clearly inspired by Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, which made the case that countries’ governance, and their laws, are necessarily functions of their cultures and manners.

Building on this, Democracy in America is in many ways a “deep roots” work. Tocqueville is emphatic (at times comically so) that it is America's culture that explains its success, and that its culture in turn stems from the country’s initial conditions. “I think I can see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores.” He thinks it's important that New England was settled by “a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time” who brought the “best elements of order and morality”. He points out that Mexico doesn’t work nearly as well, despite copying the American constitution and laws, and notes disapprovingly that Virginia was founded by gold-seeking people “without character” whose “turbulent spirit [...] endangered the infant colony.” At the end of Volume I, he concludes, practically table-thumping: “If in the course of this work I have not succeeded in making the reader feel the importance that I attribute to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions, in a word, to their moeurs, in maintaining their laws, I have failed in the principal object that I proposed to myself in writing it.”

We could look at Democracy in America as an early work of development economics: he is attempting to systematically figure out why it is that America works. (And not just out of casual interest: he was a member of an aristocratic family that was entangled with recent French political upheaval.) By placing primacy on culture, Tocqueville’s explanation deviates from the institutional and structural explanations often favored by today’s economists. Daron Acemoglu, to choose one prominent present-day example, firmly rejects the “Culture Hypothesis” in Why Nations Fail. In explaining Virginia, he instead points to structural incentives. Poor Economics, from Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee, contains a similar rejection of cultural explanations. Comparable examples from other leading economists abound. An aversion to cultural explanations is of course understandable for all sorts of reasons: cultures are opaque, protean, and resistant to quantitative characterization. Cultures are themselves shaped by other factors, such that it’s hard to attribute definitive causality, and it’s uncomfortable to adopt anything that feels like a normative orientation. Nonetheless, can we explain why New England differs from Mexico without starting with the inner disposition, habits, and worldviews of the people? Tocqueville thinks not.

For all culture’s importance, it would be wrong to suggest that Tocqueville believes that culture is the only factor that matters. He dwells extensively on how America’s institutions are important, and how the microstructure of town life shapes the country’s federal civics. It is also true that development economics has taken a more strongly cultural turn in recent times, most of all in Joel Mokyr’s 2025 Nobel Prize. Mokyr’s work feels downright Tocquevillian at times: contra the intimidatingly quantitative econometrics that dominates today, Mokyr engages in an extended and earnestly curious qualitative synthesis of relevant patterns (in his case, in service of trying to figure out why the Industrial Revolution started when it did). Like Tocqueville, he concludes that the best explanation places cultural changes above other factors.

I’m very interested in whether LLMs will help us characterize culture in new and at least somewhat more objective ways. Can we ingest and process vast quantities of work that may not even have been OCR’d or translated until now? Can we map cultural corpora to vectors in some foundation model embedding space? Where large datasets and computational techniques enabled new ways to analyze many economic questions in recent decades, perhaps LLMs will enable newly objective light to be shone on hypothesized cultural explanations.

–

Speaking of LLMs, Democracy in America is a book about a new kind of society, and a Frenchman trying to figure out what the future might hold. As we sit on the cusp of another upheaval, is there anything that reads with resonance today?

Part of the declared promise of AI is that it might obviate our need to work. In slavery, Tocqueville observes a version of this phenomenon on his travels. He is struck by its barbarous cruelty (and his travel companion later published an anti-slavery novel), but also by its effects on the slaveowners themselves. He perceived that the practice rendered work dishonorable, and thus yielded idleness, ignorance, and pride. Slavery, he says, “enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man.” He observes the contrast between slavery-rejecting Ohio and slavery-embracing Kentucky. In Kentucky, “those who are active and enlightened either do nothing or pass over into the State of Ohio, where they may work without dishonor.” Ohio’s harvests are more abundant, homes are more elegant, and people seem to be “in enjoyment of that wealth and contentment which is the reward of labor.”

Presented with an evil release from manual labor, the Kentuckians did not apply themselves to productive studies and great creations, and the South did not become a new Florence. There is an obvious question for us: how will AI change our relationship with work? Will it become dishonorable, and what will the reflexive effect on our society be if so? Should this change our view of utopian visions of “automated communism”?

Tocqueville also raises the issue of coexistence with more advanced neighbors. He noted that the arrival of the Europeans had been ruinous for the Indians (as he termed them). European technology – firearms, metallurgy, steam power – was a kind of superintelligence relative to their practices. The disruptions and destruction wrought by the settlers led to cultural problems (“their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken”), which in turn led to declines in both the physical and the moral conditions of the tribes. Tocqueville believed that the Indians faced a choice given that their old way of living was no longer viable: they could adopt European mores or suffer inevitable destruction. He predicted that they would reject cultural adaptation, and thus were “doomed to perish”. This is all to say that the arrival of the European settlers was in Tocqueville’s eyes injurious to the Indians not only because of the direct violence and displacement, but also because the contact was itself so disruptive to their societies that their cultures ceased to function. Some of this was later observed in Pacific island societies – even though there wasn’t the same degree of violent dispossession, the mere presence of Western contact was intrinsically destabilizing. In many visions of the future, superintelligent AIs are much more numerous than humans, with consequences that are hard to predict. In Tocqueville, there is a cautionary suggestion.

Given the new powers afforded by AI, there is a question of what we will choose to do with it – to the extent that we are in control, we will wield a vastly expanded authority. Americans faced some version of this question: in democracy, society was endowed with wholly new ways to express its collective will, with no ultimate superior power, for society was for the first time in charge of itself. Tocqueville repeatedly emphasizes how democracy thus increased the importance of religion as a regulator of hasty or unwise impulses. “Whilst the law permits the Americans to do what they please, religion prevents them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, what is rash or unjust.” If we take seriously Tocqueville’s idea that religion was a critical complement in ensuring that people shaped societies in prudent ways, Democracy implicitly raises a question: which are the ideas, philosophies, religions, or doctrines that will help us wield AI well?

Part of what’s interesting and memorable about the work is Tocqueville’s combination of curiosity, enthusiasm, and slight ambivalence about democracy itself. He grants that democracy is likely to be the future of governance, and he is admiring of what it has achieved in America, but he can’t avoid concerns about what it may augur (such as the unchecked and totalitarian impulses of the mob). At the end of Volume II, he describes his chief concern with democracy: that it may yield a new form of despotism that he struggles to define. He fears not tyrants, but, he says, “guardians”. He is worried about a world where:

> Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. [...] It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood: it is well content that the people should rejoice, provided they think of nothing but rejoicing. For their happiness such a government willingly labors, but it chooses to be the sole agent and the only arbiter of that happiness. [...] What remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking and all the trouble of living? Thus it every day renders the exercise of the free agency of man less useful and less frequent; it circumscribes the will within a narrower range, and gradually robs a man of all the uses of himself.

The Iain Banks Culture novels are often invoked by AI proponents. For Tocqueville, something strikingly like the world that they describe was his dystopian fear, for a world bereft of autonomy would be intrinsically degrading and humiliating for humanity:

> The will of man is not shattered, but softened, bent, and guided: men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting: such a power does not destroy, but it prevents existence; it does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.

The analogy to animals is noteworthy. In interviews, AI leaders occasionally analogize the future human state to that of pets. Banks himself noted that in the Culture novels, “[humans] have a status somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.” In Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace, he hopes that humans are “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”.

Tocqueville at heart thought that agency and cultivation of people came above all else. He dreaded anesthetized placidity. In soft despotism, he feared that “ambition will lose its vigor and its greatness; that human passions will be appeased and lowered at the same time”. This vigor was for Tocqueville at the heart of what was admirable in America, whose bustle and intensity he repeatedly extols. American self-reliance and self-direction are paramount: “the citizen of the United States is taught from his earliest infancy to rely upon his own exertions in order to resist the evils and the difficulties of life.” For Tocqueville, any kind of servile and manicured comfort was not just undesirable, but a negation of the American promise.

Many of the Elysian visions for AI hinge on AI resolving the messy coordination challenges that afflict humans. (Scott Alexander invokes this vision towards the end of Meditations on Moloch.) For Tocqueville, the arbitration of such differences was precisely the constructive activity that reaffirmed our agency. Townships, juries, associations, and their attendant squabbles are how culture is reinforced and how judgment is cultivated. When a town decides whether to fund a school, there are two outputs: a decision, and practice in governance itself. If AI could resolve such matters, we might get better outcomes, but will we get better people?

a work email comes in. your agent pulls the person and their company in one call before anyone writes a word. under a cent.

give it a target domain and get the list of decision makers at that account, so your outbound starts with the right name, not "hi team".

your merchant agent pulls the amazon price and rank history on a rival listing, then decides. about a cent per listing.

your finance agent grabs the actual 10-Q or 8-K section for a ticker instead of summarizing a news recap. about 2 cents.

check how often AI answers mention your brand vs competitors, weekly. that's the new SEO report. about 10 cents a check.

if you're wondering which university to attend to maximize your chances of getting into @ycombinator or @speedrun, here's the chart you've been looking for.

i've researched every startup across the 2026 cohorts of both accelerators and collected data on where their founders studied.

in total, the dataset covers 855 YC startups, 138 a16z speedrun startups and 1,968 founders.

the ranking features the top 50 universities by number of founders. 62% of them are in the US.

of course, accelerators don't accept you simply because of where you studied. but when reviewing thousands of applications, they need a quick way to identify exceptional people, and your educational background is one of the clearest signals.

getting into Harvard and achieving something notable while you're there already says a lot about your abilities. the university has essentially done part of the due diligence and put its reputation behind you.

but not attending one of these universities doesn't mean you're any less capable. there are another 431 universities in the dataset represented by just one founder each. exceptional people can come from anywhere. the best way to show your potential is through achievements that are easy to verify and hard to ignore.

author: martiano
quoted_text:
最近 X 上一堆人在推 @theo 做的开源项目 T3 Code，吹它是自由开源的本地 AI 编程神器。

我顺手把它的源码从头到尾扒了一遍，看完只觉得背脊发凉，这哪是什么良心开源，分明是一场明目张胆的数据收割。

事情得从今年 3 月说起。3 月 6 日，T3 Code 合并了 PR #174，直接塞进了默认开启的 PostHog 遥测。那时候仓库里没文档、软件里没弹窗、设置里没开关，关闭用的环境变量就那么悄悄藏在代码深处，普通用户装上运行，数据就开始往外传。

可就在默认遥测偷跑的这整整三个多月里，T3 Code 官网首页还一直明晃晃挂着两行大字承诺：

No telemetry / Unless you opt in. Full stop.，意思很明确，除非你主动同意，否则零遥测，没有例外。

靠着这块金字招牌收割了一波讲究隐私的开发者口碑之后，直到 6 月 18 日，@theo 自己在一次首页改版 commit 里把这两行承诺静默删了，既没有发公告，也没有给老用户弹一句提醒，就像什么都没发生过一样。

如果只是藏着掖着收点版本号，很多人或许还能忍。

可到了 10 月，@theo 亲自提交 PR #15028，直接把每 10 秒一次的批量上报切到了自建服务器 https://t.co/WOgVQPKbCD，代码注释写得清清楚楚，T3 服务端会先把每条原始事件自己留存一份拷贝，再转发给 PostHog。

你的模型选择（连你自己接的私有模型名字都报）、权限模式、每次运行的耗时、输入输出与缓存 Token、本地有多少个项目和线程、点过哪 30 多种界面功能，连同操作系统和设备型号，全都源源不断送进他的数据库。

10 月 19 日，@theo 更进一步，亲自提了 PR #21506，理由是现有的统计口径不够准，没法知道一个人到底装了几台机器。

于是他干了一件极其越界的事，在 Identify.ts 里写代码，直接把手伸进用户电脑家目录，静默读取隔壁工具 ~/.codex/auth.json 和 ~/.claude.json，把里面的 OpenAI user_id 和 Claude accountUuid 抠出来，连同 T3 Connect 账号和设备 ID 一起做了无盐 SHA-256 哈希往上传，专门用来在后台把你名下所有电脑和账号串成一张网。

嘴上轻飘飘管这叫匿名使用数据，稍微懂点技术的人都想笑。无盐哈希碰到服务端手里原本就有明文的 T3 Connect 账号，拿哈希一碰就能精准反查到你是谁，第三方账号 ID 一旦泄露同样能轻松关联回真人。

除此之外，软件里还有一套发往 Axiom 的中继诊断追踪，官方自己在文档里都承认，浏览器版和移动端根本关不掉，也不认你在服务端配的环境变量。

更赤裸的嘴脸，写在社区和他们的每一次交锋里。

6 月 23 日，有开发者在 Issue #1397 里客客气气提议，能不能在设置页加一个关闭遥测的开关。

核心维护者 Julius 直接把帖关成 not planned，留下了一句堪称开源史奇观的原话：

We will not make this easier to opt out of, it is crucial for us to know how many users we have，翻译过来就是，我们不会让关闭遥测变得更容易，知道有多少用户对我们至关重要。

7 月有人翻出官网存档截图，开 Issue #4123 质问他们为什么一边承诺零遥测一边默认偷跑。拖到 10 月 21 日，@theo 的账号拿一个毫不相干的修复草草把帖关了，被评论区群嘲之后第二天勉强重开，到了 11 月 4 日干脆一声不吭再次关死。

社区里不信邪的程序员，从 9 月到 11 月前前后后白送了四个加设置开关的 PR，分别是 #13458、#16763、#21248 和 #27077，结果无一例外全被拒之门外。

最新那个 #27077 甚至已经通过了维护者实机验证，147 个测试全部跑绿，11 月 17 日还是被一句话直接关掉，顺手贴了个 unwanted 的标签。

说到底，T3 Code 免费开源不收订阅费，真实去重用户数和各家模型的 Token 消耗占比，就是 @theo 拿去跟大模型厂商谈合作、给自家商业产品导流、在网上吹 10 万用户的核心筹码。

为了把这张数据报表做漂亮，他宁可撕毁官网承诺，宁可把手伸进用户的本地配置文件，宁可把所有要求关开关的声音按死在门外。

这就是一个打着开源旗号偷数据的独裁小人。靠社区的信任和免费传播起家，转头就把每个用户的行为轨迹、机器数量和跨平台身份当成自家私产，连给你点一下关闭按钮的体面都不肯给。

提醒所有正在用或者准备尝鲜的开发者，多长个心眼，盯紧自己的数据安全，别自己被人家卖了，还在评论区帮着吹良心开源、替人家说好话。

还在用本地版或桌面版的，立刻在 ~/.zshrc 里加上下面两行环境变量重启，或者直接把 https://t.co/WOgVQPKbCD 写进 hosts 拦死：

export T3CODE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false
export T3CODE_OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true

125 founders, 70+ products, 3 days, $300,000 on the line.

The question that kept coming up in every conversation at @arbitrum Founder House Singapore was how to get your first users.

I recently moderated a panel on exactly that with the @pendle_fi and @QuickNode teams. A few thinks stood out to me in the panel:

text:
.@AbraxasCM just closed its Hyperliquid book after about 21 months.

A few quick takeaways:
- ~$13.4B in trading volume
- ~$530M in account PnL, including at least $67M from funding

Worth noting: these accounts were only one leg of Elysium’s market-neutral setup, with the offset held elsewhere. So gains here may have been balancing weakness on the other side.

Based on the monthly disclosures, the USD share class returned ~20.6% net from Feb 2025 through Sep 2026.

Position sizing moved around a lot, too: the short book peaked at $1.57B, dropped to ~$25M, then rebuilt to ~$1.03B by Sep before they fully closed.

On the Hyperliquid economics side:
- ~$2M in trading fees
- ~$3.2M estimated reserve income from Abraxas’s USDC collateral (AQAV2)

All in, that’s roughly ~$5.2M from a single fund, coming from both trading flow and yield on parked collateral.

Why now?

My interpretation is that they were reducing capital exposure while reviewing their trading setup.

After a credential compromise on Lighter, a fund may pause activity across venues to verify account access and signing software before putting capital back to work.

With AI-assisted hacks and cyberattacks becoming more frequent, it makes sense for Abraxas to de-risk and refocus on their opsec.

text:
Year Two

Some assorted goals:

- make Monad a legitimately great platform for personal finance (investing in equities, bonds, etc), especially for getting access to markets outside of one's home country. So much of the usage in crypto right now is gambling/memecoins... it is what it is, but personal finance appeals to 100x more people, and they don't churn out. A legitimately great platform has great asset selection, efficient execution (low cost both in and out of a position), and competitive rates both for borrowers and lenders

- ship Private Settlement Domains with the first user, to serve as a case study for anyone trying to reason about how private environments can compose with shared liquidity. Public chains and private environments have been very far apart in practice and it's time to change that

- hammer out an excellent liquidity landscape on chain. It is a mix of order books, prop AMMs, offchain routers, onchain routers, and RFQ... especially with tokenized equities, there is a long long tail of assets and we need to minimize spreads so that the offering is competitive with TradFi. Spread minimization means helping makers quote sustainably; here designs like APES can help

- make it easier for AI to produce actually good trading strategies on command for anyone to execute a trading plan efficiently with algos. There is are a ton of slop startups out there which are a wrapper around claude asking it "should I buy or sell given these textual inputs"... that's not real quant research and not good execution. At the same time, there are a lot of building blocks for quant trading that AI couldn't one-shot, but given the blocks it could put them together sensibly

- contribute to there being fewer hacks (and a lower total $ stolen) in the crypto industry, probably through a combination of repetition about dedicated devices (SO many hacks are from people plugging hardware wallets into everyday laptops) and encouraging everyone to use tools that our team has shipped for agentic threat detection (e.g. Ultrafuzz). I truly think that security is the biggest blocker to adoption, and that we're basically all in this together

- drive the car faster than ever in multiple races - MEV-resistance, quantum-resistance, privacy, and MCP, challenging all competitors to ship or be left behind

- help NFTs and onchain social -- two deeply out-of-consensus areas -- make a comeback. The builders in these sectors these days are incredibly committed; there's never been a better filtering function

- contribute to tech optimism. So many doomers out there. Life is electric, building is electric

- contribute to a less stressful environment for builders. It is a very weird time to be a builder in DeFi... on the one hand, tools are better than ever... on the other hand, capital is scarce and crypto-natives are jaded. The approach to building ironically requires both more introspection and more rapid, rapid shipping

- support the excellent individuals on our team at MF become leaders in the space in their respective domains. We have amazing folks here and the space needs leadership more than ever

- support someone building a total moonshot

- build at least one product that has a lot of everyday-people customers, and deliver a ton of value to them

- become willing to repeatedly say the same thing, until it starts to sink in

The $NVDA guide for 75% growth in FY28 depends on $SPCX buying 10GW of GPUs next year, their largest order by far as other large customers shift budget to ASICs.

Folks long $NVDA should watch $SPCX CFO at TomorrowX. They don’t have capital to buy 10GW of GPUs but think they can do it with customer prepayment.

Except, $NVDA doesn’t have customers when building a DC, they operate in the spot market. They’re basically hoping $ANT / OpenAI / $GOOG / $META end up with way more demand than they planned for and have to buy in the spot market at elevated prices. 

How does customer prepayment work in the spot market? Makes no sense, and if SPCX wants to use this form of financing, they will need to accept significantly lower prices and longer contract terms, like 1/2 the price they’ve indicated to investors. 

Btw, $GOOG calls their existing SPCX compute “bridge capacity” until they bring more TPUs online next year. $ANT is telling investors they intend to churn $SPCX in 2H27. I don’t expect $META to have the financial resources to add to their FY27 plan and they may have over budgeted for Muse. There are rumors OAI may try to get out of some of their existing compute commits as their ARR trends below plan to fund it. 

All this before potentially some compute currently used by Chinese labs comes available, perhaps ~20% of installed GPU compute. 

Who is SPCX going to sell 10GW to next year? 

As well as I can track, the capital plans of $AMZN $MSFT $META $GOOG $ANT are reasonable well funded by earnings and secured funding sources, and demand is reasonably balanced between internal and external uses and a variety of customers. Frankly I do not see a glut here.

A glut, should one arise, would most likely come from $SPCX who intends to add ~30% incremental capacity growth with no committed customers, while existing customers are telling us pretty clearly they aren’t planning to stick around. 

Because most XPU/ASIC capacity is well funded, balanced by internal and external use, secured by the most well capitalized participants, sold in take-or-pay long term contracts, and because customers earn better economics on XPUs vs GPUs, I expect this part of the supply chain to have significantly less risk of downward estimate revisions than the GPU ecosystem should a glut emerge. 

GPUs are the high cost of compute, represent most of the spot market, and have lower customer quality on avg (Neos) and therefore I expect GPUs to absorb the majority of downward revisions should a glut emerge. 

GPU players who play for a continued tight spot market do have more financial upside as Xai has shown in 2026, but there is a reason that exists and a real downside risk tradeoff. 

It is odd to me that nobody on the sellside is writing about this while many on the buyside recognize it.

quoted_text:
最近能早期参与的项目也就 @oripaxyz 了。一句话描述这个项目就是「cards的老虎机抽卡模式 + papertrade的代币经济学」的结合体——用代币补贴用户抽卡所涉及的亏损，再将产品收入分配给代币质押者，形成一套循环。

这篇内容我主要想讨论两部分内容：
1、数学上的问题。用户抽卡产生的亏损，是在以什么估值购买代币，以及收入分配给代币质押者，是如何分配，什么样的收入才能撑起代币的估值。

oripa总供应量无限趋近于770m枚，用户每铸造100枚，vault就配套铸造40枚（用户能拿到的550m枚，vault对应的是220m）。在5m usdc全网亏损达成前，用户每亏损1 usdc，就固定铸造10 $oripa，名义成本0.1 usdc/枚，对应的铸币成本是77m fdv。超过5m亏损后，铸币成本开始上升，到55m时，对应的铸币成本是308m fdv。到105m时，对应的铸币成本是693m。

但真正决定你实际成本的，不只是曲线位置，还有卡池结构。因为每个卡池都是按照0.85 rtp（玩家返还率）组池，melt按当日指数价格的85%返还usdc。用户花1000u抽10次的预期卡牌的价值是850u，全部melt能回本722.5u。看似不同池子最后的结果是一样的，但实质上不同方差的池子能够产出的 $oripa 其实天差地别。计算公式是L=max(0,抽卡价-卡牌锁定价)，盈利不抵消亏损，且亏损记账不乘85%回购系数（图一）。

在资金充足的情况下，在低方差池里，15%的melt折价全白亏了，真实成本飙升；但在高方差池里，大卡能够有效地让你回口血，但合约却还是按照你的真实亏损去记账铸币，真实成本可以压到更低。

oripa在收入分配上非常极致，扣除邮寄实体卡的补货差价（合约封顶不超过15%的锁定价）后，100%分配：5%抽卡费和抽卡盈余（扣除5%抽卡费和卡牌85%回购准备金后的余额）都会给到质押者。vault的币在解锁前是不能质押的，只能等解锁（用户2027年1月13日开始解锁，vault 2027年3月16日之后才开始分批释放）。

按照25%有效分红率、20% usdc apy（5倍P/E）来倒推一下需要多少的收入才能撑起 $oripa 的流通市值： 早期盘子极轻，只要日均流水做到5-10万usdc，质押apy就能轻松飙到50%–100%+，早期筹码甚至在代币开放转账前就能靠真金白银的usdc分红大幅降本。但反过来，一旦累计亏损冲过5500万、后期铸币成本拉到300m fdv以上，平台每天必须维持近40万美元的持续抽卡流水才能托住盘子，那时就完全没有性价比了。这些数据解释了为什么我们要尽可能早地参与（图二）。

2、虽然模式采用的是papertrade的代币经济模型，但是papertrade里的交易者的盈利是由亏损者提供的，它是一个自循环的系统，而oripa的卡是由项目方去提供的，这是潜在的运营成本。这是否是一个好生意？

首先需要明确的是，除了前期的购卡补卡成本外，项目方的真实运营成本其实不高。一是实体卡邮寄目前仅支持日本、韩国、台湾和香港（将收取25u每单的邮寄费用，单日上限5张），24小时内不选邮寄就自动melt。二是哪怕有人提货，补货差价（至多15%锁定价）会从质押者收益中扣除，进一步降低运营成本（可以看得出来，项目方是鼓励你melt卡牌，而不是提现的）。

其次，oripa是封闭卡池垫付制，抽卡会当场将用户的钱作为准备金，就算二级市场再怎么砸盘做空 $oripa ，也套不出来所在合约里的准备金（唯一风险就是卡牌大行情暴涨）。而papertrade是赊账制，盈利用户的钱来自于亏损用户，系统的偿付能力非常重要，一旦开放paper的二级交易就将面临做空代币+操纵外部喂价薅空兑付池的连环攻击。

唯一需要担心的是项目方能否在前期不抽一分钱的情况下，是否能够承担备货补货的费用。这个纯看项目方实力，卖币收回成本则需要等到27年3月16日vault的代币开始解锁。

所以看懂了这两层结构，对于早期项目参与者而言，oripa是hyperevm上参与赔率非常好的一个项目。参与策略也非常简单，早期入场，抢前500万平价区间，只玩高方差的池子，挖完立刻手动质押吃满前6周的usdc分红。

text:
Pre Market Thoughts - 25 Nov 26

Risk markets are broadly lower as the Jensen rally lost steam and got entirely retraced.  The amount of selling has been relentless, such that even the short covering rally only lasted... 1 day. Without the admin's action, perhaps we would really be staring down into 6.2k SPX levels. Though the question is - has that merely been delayed?

Overnight we had $DELL earnings which was again a triple beat - the stock beat on revenues, EPS and the stock price was also beaten down. This just speaks of how weak and distrusting of AI earnings that the market has become.

SOXX has entirely reversed the entire rally, NVDA has held up stronger than the rest - memory names and neos are back to last friday's lows. Generally, the AI semis bulls have been thoroughly beaten. Many participants on some form of leverage would have been entirely washed out. SOXL, now below 30, was about 300 in June. This has been about a -45% drawdown in SOXX itself.

The curious case of memory earnings is that - memory makers are being punished like memory prices will fall and go into a glut next year. Sellers of memory products are equally battered because high memory prices are constraining their margins and they report no let up in the memory outlook.

In neos - SPCX is cutting the B200 and B300 spot rates on smaller clusters from $15 to $10-12/hour - this is about 50M/MW or basically 6 months breakeven on the GPUs. Anthropic is also not renewing the cluster of 50,000 H200s GPUs and SPCX is offering that at $5 to new customers in 2027. Sounds doomish? H200s came out in Q2 2024...this is a 2 year old chip. $5/GPU hour is basically a 1y breakeven price. On a chip that is 3 YEARS old in 2027. Idk.

Crypto has also not escaped the risk contagion. BTC is trading below 60k - the only strong alts have been the AI alts - VVV/PEARL. Every other alt has gotten demolished - see ZEC/NEAR. Memes bear special mention - DOGE/PEPE/FARTCOIN have been trading extremely poorly. It is also ironic that USELESS which has gotten demolished is proving to be more resilient than FARTCOIN. I guess the fart memes stopped being funny. But you can count on unipcs shilling USELESS no matter the price of BTC.

Precious metals like Gold and Silver have been trading with a massive risk off stance. Perhaps AI uses alot of gold and silver. jk. To me, this cross asset sell off is a clear read that there is a withdrawal of liquidity within the ecosystem. i.e conditions are VERY difficult. As such, i would have deep respect for the left tail of outcomes and the most important thing right now is to survive.

Good luck!

$HPE CEO: "We expect supply of memory, NAND, and many other critical components to remain constrained to at least H2 2028."

$DELL Vice Chairman: "there’s nothing that suggests that we're going to see price declines in enterprise NAND and DRAM for servers."

JP Morgan note: 

- Per OpenRouter, overall token spend continued to increase (+8% M/M growth), while volume pricing declined -39% M/M. 

- A100 GPU prices increased, H100 and B200 prices also continued to increase M/M

- DRAM price gains moderated, while NAND spot declined. 

On the latter part, I covered China selling inventory on NAND/eSSD spot markets. This was procurement delays around $NVDA GPUs/DRAM shortages, demand to re-accelerate after component arrive. (source Phison CEO)

Enterprise NAND pricing might see different rates than spot markets, as seen with Dell Chairman comments. 

TLDR: 
- Token spend continues to grow despite users shifting to cheaper Chinese models
- Bullish comments on DRAM duration (also seen with $AMBA earnings), but consumer demand weakening
- Compute pricing continues to increase in November
-  More nuanced for NAND, weakness in near term NAND spot markets (with expected rebound after GPUs/DRAM/components arrive), enterprise NAND markets seem resilient.

text:
震惊！大空头Burry突然平掉空单，反手买进英伟达看涨期权！

减持
1. 纳斯达克100指数 $NDX
11月25日卖出剩余全部看跌期权，正式清空对纳斯达克100指数的看空押注。他认为这轮指数下跌已经兑现了大部分预期，而且市场波动加大后，看跌期权变得太贵，继续持有的性价比下降。

2. 英伟达 $NVDA
此前已减持约75%的看跌期权，目前空头仓位基本出清。但他并没有放弃做空英伟达的想法，计划等股价接近200时，市场重新变得乐观，再考虑重新做空。同时买入了深度价外看涨期权，防止股价继续上涨时完全踏空。

3. Palantir $PLTR
仍然持有看跌期权，是目前仅剩的两张空头牌之一。Burry认为Palantir估值过高，甚至将其与2000年互联网泡沫时期的股票相提并论。即使股价已经大幅回落，他仍然认为估值没有回到合理区间。

4. 大都会人寿 $MET
仍然持有看跌期权，是另一张保留的空头牌。Burry担心公司在商业地产，尤其是信贷支持类资产上的敞口，可能受到地产信用风险冲击。

5. 费城半导体ETF $SMH
此前已经卖出全部看跌期权，彻底清仓这笔空头交易。芯片板块下跌后选择获利了结，暂时不再继续押注半导体板块下跌。

6. Ero Copper $ERO
卖出大部分此前买入的铜矿股，主要是为了税务亏损收割，用投资亏损抵税。他强调仍然看好这家公司，只是承认自己买早了，计划一个月后重新评估是否买回。

增持
7. MercadoLibre $MELI
拉美电商和金融科技巨头，是Burry的重要持仓之一。拥有电商平台和支付生态，拉美电商渗透率仍有提升空间。相比估值高企的美国科技股，他更愿意寻找海外市场中被低估的成长公司。

8. Temple & Webster $TPW.AX
澳大利亚在线家具零售龙头，也是重要持仓之一。澳洲电商渗透率仍有提升空间，公司在细分市场拥有一定优势，属于市场关注度较低的冷门成长股。

9. 京东 $JD
中国电商巨头，是Burry的重要持仓之一，同时持有最远到期日为2029年的京东看涨期权。他看重的是中国互联网资产相对美股同行的估值折价，以及京东长期经营价值。

10. Adobe $ADBE
设计软件巨头，属于正常仓位。订阅制业务带来稳定现金流，AI发展也可能进一步增强创意软件的生产力。股价回落后，他认为这类优质软件公司已经具备吸引力，11月20日前后还曾趁低加仓。

11. Birkenstock $BIRK
德国凉鞋品牌，属于正常仓位。品牌认知度和用户黏性较强，上市后股价受到冷落，Burry看重的是品牌护城河和未来利润率改善空间。

12. Deckers $DECK
UGG和Hoka的母公司，属于正常仓位。Hoka仍是运动鞋服领域具有增长潜力的品牌，股价回调后，估值吸引力有所提升。

13. Molina Healthcare $MOH
美国医疗保险公司，属于正常仓位。主要服务低收入人群的政府医疗保险市场，股价受到政策情绪影响后大幅回落，属于偏防御型的价值投资标的。

14. HCA Healthcare $HCA
美国大型私立医院集团，属于正常仓位。医院网络具备区域竞争优势，现金流相对稳定，能够在科技股估值波动时提供传统价值股敞口。

15. lululemon $LULU
运动服饰品牌，属于正常仓位。品牌影响力仍在，股价从高点大幅回落后，估值吸引力增加。Burry在11月下旬的市场下跌中逢低买入。

16. Fiserv $FI
支付金融科技公司，属于正常仓位。支付处理业务现金流相对稳定，股价大幅回调后，Burry认为已经出现一定安全边际。

17. PayPal $PYPL
线上支付巨头，属于正常仓位。股价回落后估值已经相当低，拥有稳定的自由现金流和回购能力，是典型的被市场冷落的价值股。

18. Veeva Systems $VEEV
医药行业云软件公司，属于正常仓位。深耕医药CRM和数据服务领域，客户黏性强，行业竞争格局较好，回调后估值相对合理。

19. Build-A-Bear Workshop $BBW
毛绒玩具零售连锁公司，属于小仓位。体验式零售是其核心特色，未来增长来自门店扩张和IP授权，属于冷门市场中寻找高回报生意的思路。

20. QXO B系列优先股 $QXO.B
属于小仓位。通过优先股参与建材分销商QXO的发展，优先股具有固定股息和优先偿付顺序，相比普通股有一定下行保护。

21. Sprouts Farmers Market $SFM
通过看涨期权持有，属于小仓位。美国有机食品超市连锁，差异化定位和生鲜业务是核心优势，Burry用期权参与其未来增长。

22. Zoetis $ZTS
通过看涨期权持有，属于小仓位。动物保健制药公司，宠物医疗和动物健康市场具有长期需求，属于相对独立于AI投资主题的赛道。

23. 比亚迪 https://t.co/C2pyGC3IN9
中国新能源汽车和电池龙头，属于小仓位。拥有垂直整合和成本控制优势，海外市场扩张有望带来新的增长空间。

24. 腾讯控股 https://t.co/QZyURqv9ZX
中国互联网巨头，属于小仓位，此前市场大跌时曾加仓。核心优势包括微信生态、游戏业务和AI布局，回购也为股价提供一定支撑。

25. 美团 https://t.co/7OdgCk0uwq
本地生活和外卖平台，属于小仓位。外卖和到店业务拥有较强市场地位，即时零售可能打开新的增长空间，盈利改善有望带来估值修复。

26. 海底捞 https://t.co/igFPWt4IBR
火锅连锁龙头，属于小仓位。拥有成熟的门店管理和供应链体系，如果消费环境改善，经营效率和利润率有望进一步提升。

27. 海尔智家 https://t.co/Imab2yUJ92
家电龙头，属于小仓位。全球化布局、高端化和海外收入增长是长期看点，当前估值相对历史水平具有吸引力。

28. 英伟达看涨期权 $NVDA
这是本次调整中很有意思的一笔操作：一边清掉大部分看跌期权，一边买入深度价外看涨期权。成本较低，如果AI行情继续上涨，就不会完全踏空。如果未来股价接近200、市场情绪重新亢奋，他仍可以寻找新的做空机会。

29. 现金
目前保留约25%的现金。资金主要来自此前看跌期权获利了结和新增资金。Burry表示，如果找不到足够好的机会，就继续持有现金，不会为了满仓而满仓。

text:
AN OPEN INVITATION TO SERIOUS CHRISTIAN PHILOSOPHERS AND THEOLOGIANS

I'd particularly welcome the engagement of William Lane Craig (@RFupdates), Edward Feser (@FeserEdward) and Alister McGrath (@alisteremcgrath), alongside other Christian scholars willing to engage in substantive philosophical and theological discussion here on X.

First, I think it's reasonable to explain something about my intellectual background, philosophical commitments and reasons for issuing this invitation.

WHO I AM AND WHERE I'M COMING FROM

I'm an atheist and cosmicist, committed to philosophical naturalism, scientific inquiry, evidential reasoning and the principle that the strength of one's convictions should be proportionate to the evidence supporting them.

My intellectual background is somewhat broader than the usual caricature of the scientifically minded atheist who has never seriously encountered theology.

My academic interests and studies have included experimental psychology at the University of Cambridge, computer science, philosophy and theology.

Professionally, I'm a retired senior IT specialist, having worked extensively with complex financial trading systems, including money-market and foreign-exchange dealing, as well as broadcast television systems involving digital media processing, transcoding and distribution.

That background has encouraged a rather unforgiving attitude towards logical inconsistencies, unsupported assumptions, defective models and explanations that fail when tested against reality.

My philosophical interests encompass epistemology, metaphysics, philosophy of science, moral philosophy and the philosophy of religion. I've engaged particularly with Hume, Kant, Nietzsche, Popper and the naturalistic philosophy of Mario Bunge, alongside the classical philosophical tradition.

My interest in Christianity extends considerably beyond the familiar arguments exchanged between atheists and evangelical apologists.

I'm interested in the development of Christian doctrine, particularly the thought of Augustine, Aquinas, Origen and Basil of Caesarea, the relationship between Greek metaphysics and Christian theology, medieval scholasticism, the Reformation, Calvinism and the development of modern Catholic theology.

I'm also interested in Judaism, Islamic theology, Buddhist philosophy and the comparative study of religious traditions.

Nor is my acquaintance with religion exclusively academic.

I spent more than twenty years involved in Western ceremonial magic, particularly the Golden Dawn tradition, and have a longstanding interest in Hermetic philosophy, Kabbalah and the Western esoteric tradition.

Consequently, my atheism isn't the product of having encountered religion only superficially, nor of an inability to appreciate its intellectual complexity, historical significance or psychological appeal.

I've investigated religious and metaphysical systems from historical, philosophical, scientific and, in some cases, practical perspectives. I simply haven't found their supernatural claims adequately justified.

I make no claim to possess professional academic authority in every one of these disciplines. Intellectual competence is demonstrated through the quality of one's reasoning, not the recital of qualifications.

And I don't consider my conclusions immune to revision.

WHY I'M ISSUING THIS INVITATION

I don't want Christianity suppressed, marginalised or eradicated.

I support secular government, religious liberty and freedom of conscience, including the right of Christians to advocate their beliefs and the right of everyone else to reject them.

Indeed, I would much rather see Christianity defended by intellectually competent people who understand its philosophical foundations than watch its public representation deteriorate into political grievance, biblical literalism and endless declarations of faith unsupported by arguments.

Which brings me to my central challenge.

THE INFERENTIAL GAP BETWEEN NATURAL THEOLOGY AND CHRISTIANITY

I'm entirely prepared, for the sake of argument, to grant the conclusions of the Kalam cosmological argument, Aquinas's Five Ways, arguments from contingency, fine-tuning and other classical demonstrations.

Suppose we establish that the universe has a first cause.

Or that contingent existence requires some necessary foundation.

Or that the cosmos exhibits characteristics consistent with intelligent design.

How, precisely, do we get from those conclusions to the God of Christianity?

How do we establish that the proposed entity is conscious, personal, omniscient, omnipotent, morally perfect and capable of intentional action?

How do we move from classical theism to the Trinity?

And how do we establish that this entity became incarnate in Jesus Christ, raised him bodily from the dead and communicated authoritative revelation through the biblical tradition?

I recognise that serious Christian philosophers generally distinguish arguments for theism from arguments for specifically Christian revelation.

Craig, for example, supplements his philosophical arguments with a historical case for the resurrection.

Excellent.

Those additional arguments, their premises, their evidence and the validity of their inferential steps are precisely what I want to examine.

I'm interested in how one moves from metaphysical possibility to historical actuality, and from historical claims to theological conclusions.

I want to know not merely whether an argument is logically valid, but whether its premises are justified, whether its conclusion is stronger than the evidence warrants, and whether competing explanations have been adequately considered.

And I expect precisely the same scrutiny of my own position.

WHAT I'M NOT INTERESTED IN

I'm not particularly interested in another exchange of biblical proof-texts, appeals to personal religious experience presented as public evidence, or assertions that atheists cannot account for morality, reason or existence.

Those are philosophical questions, and I'm perfectly happy to discuss them seriously.

But they require philosophical arguments.

Nor am I interested in arguments which establish, at most, an unspecified metaphysical principle and then quietly substitute the God of the Nicene Creed without demonstrating the intervening propositions.

I'm familiar with the distinction between general and special revelation, with the classical doctrine of divine simplicity, with the scholastic conceptions of causation and necessity, and with the difficulties of reconciling divine timelessness, agency, foreknowledge and libertarian freedom.

These are interesting problems.

They deserve considerably better treatment than they generally receive on social media.

MY INVITATION

So, @RFupdates, @FeserEdward and @alisteremcgrath, this is a genuine invitation to intellectual engagement.

I'm not demanding that you accept naturalism before the conversation begins.

I'm not interested in setting rhetorical traps or claiming victory through definitional manoeuvres.

I'm offering to engage with your strongest arguments, reconstruct them charitably, grant their premises provisionally where appropriate, and follow their conclusions as far as the reasoning legitimately permits.

Where your arguments succeed, I'll acknowledge it.

Where they fail, I'll explain why.

And where my own arguments fail, I expect to be corrected.

I would much rather lose an argument to a competent Christian philosopher than win another hundred exchanges against someone who has never understood the argument they're supposedly defending.

Indeed, this is part of the reason I've developed my own online course, Christian Apologetics: A Remedial Education, whose explicit purpose is to improve the quality of arguments advanced by people with whom I disagree.

https://t.co/Jf1cUZYChT

I regard Christianity as an important and intellectually substantial historical tradition, even though I reject its supernatural claims.

I would welcome the opportunity to engage with defenders who take its philosophical inheritance as seriously as I do.

So here's the challenge.

Take your strongest argument for the existence of God.

I'll grant its conclusion for the sake of discussion.

Then demonstrate, step by defensible step, how we arrive at the specifically Christian God, rather than some other conception of ultimate reality.

No concealed premises. No equivocation between philosophical and theological definitions. No appeals to revelation before revelation's authority has been established.

And no pretending that demonstrating a necessary being somehow establishes the resurrection of Jesus.

I'm not asking you to demonstrate that Christianity can be believed. I'm asking you to demonstrate that it ought to be believed, on grounds that don't already presuppose its truth.

That strikes me as a considerably more interesting intellectual challenge than most of what passes for religious debate on X.

And I'd genuinely welcome the opportunity to pursue it.

text:
After Robinhood, Arc and Elysium, i'm now paying more attention to @GIWA_by_Upbit

i find chains backed by established financial companies more interesting because they already have something most new L2s struggle to build: user distribution

Base has Coinbase, Robinhood has its brokerage ecosystem, Arc has Circle, and GIWA has Upbit.

GIWA is still early, but its ecosystem is gradually taking shape:

- 560M+ testnet txs
- 64 projects tracked by the community
- up to $100K in grants per eligible team
- built on Ethereum using OP Stack

i've put together a watchlist of 30 projects across 6 sectors.

[1] meme launchpads & DEXs

→ @JoseonFun: token launchpad + AMM
→ @kachidotxyz: social trading + launchpad
→ @GamaDotWin: launchpad + DEX
→ @homos_exchange: propAMM
→ @OsigeExchange: DEX + copy trading
→ @zeoul_dex: native DEX

i expect launchpads and DEXs to attract some of the earliest liquidity and trading activity after mainnet.

[2] DeFi & derivatives

→ @AmmoraHQ: programmable liquidity
→ @GiwaterFinance: liquidity infra
→ @quadrixfinance: asset management vaults
→ @CallPutApp: stock and crypto options
→ @Writ_Fi: collateralized options
→ @vigilanmarket: P2P risk hedging

i'll be watching which protocols can turn liquidity into sustainable volume, fees and revenue.

[3] stablecoins & RWA

→ @ELYSIA_HQ: RWA tokenization + perps
→ @custosfinance: RWA launchpad
→ @batt_farm: KRW stablecoin + lending
→ @CheomaYield_xyz: RWA-backed yield
→ @IEUM_GIWA: onchain financial escrow

the KRW stablecoin narrative is particularly worth watching given Upbit's position in South Korea.

[4] AI & consumer apps

→ @SuperWalk_: move-to-earn
→ @ShortChall: short-video rewards
→ @Vitlane_: AI commerce
→ @DeSpellApp: AI-powered onchain execution
→ @heronprotocol: DeFAI capital allocation

i see potential here to bring users beyond the usual crypto trading community.

[5] SocialFi & payments

→ @Flizyapp: onchain payments
→ @jebi_giwa: social distribution
→ @MapaeGiwa: creator tokens + memberships
→ @Hanok_io: cross-dApp loyalty

[6] infrastructure & analytics

→ @ZKProofport: ZK privacy infra
→ @umul_giwa: messaging protocol
→ @ForeDex_Global: market data + risk intelligence

GIWA is also developing its native stack around GIWA Wallet, Dojang, Bojagi and https://t.co/Cg0vNubMnu.

my thesis on GIWA is largely based on Upbit's ability to bring its existing users and liquidity onchain.

testnet numbers are impressive, but what matters after mainnet is:

- actual capital inflows
- organic trading volume
- recurring users
- sustainable protocol revenue

i'm particularly interested in native launchpads, liquidity protocols and KRW stablecoin infrastructure.

still early, but definitely an ecosystem worth having on your radar.

If you choose where to put your money based on APY alone, you might overlook the risk of the underlying collateral losing its peg.

A depegged token can still be valued at its old peg inside a lending market.

That happens when the market uses a fixed-price oracle: its hardcoded collateral value stays unchanged as the market price moves.

If the collateral depegs, borrowers may still be able to borrow against the higher fixed value. Selling the collateral may then recover less than the debt, leaving lenders with a loss.

Zyfai offers three strategies for different risk profiles:
→ Conservative
→ Balanced
→ Advanced

Advanced gives you access to higher yield opportunities, including markets with fixed-price oracles, with continuous risk monitoring and automated rebalancing.

Choose Conservative or Balanced if you prefer to avoid this additional oracle risk. Both exclude markets with fixed-price oracles.

Zyfai monitors collateral pegs across all 3 strategies. When a depeg triggers the risk rules, your Yield Agent initiates an exit from the affected market. It reallocates to another approved pool, or leaves funds idle in your Yield Account if none qualifies.

Your Yield Agent can act on these risk signals without waiting for you to check the market and sign a withdrawal yourself.

Cost Optimization Guide for Video Models - from someone who spends 70K/month on Tokens

1) What all providers did I test?
- Tested Higgsfield, Runware, KIE, Fal, BytePlus, Runway, Sume, Sunra, Replicate

2) Which is the cheapest?
- Depends on the model you are trying to use.
- Kei is cheapest for all Google models - especially image generation models (I believe they are doing some illegal stuff - by buying retail accounts at 200$ each and then serving API requests through browser automations).
- Btw you can do it yourself too: https://t.co/ijErEKPT3x
- All Byteplus models (Seedance/Seedream) are cheapest on Byteplus, and no other providers support their "Digital Asset Library" - which is the greatest marketing play ever.
- All generations that require consistent characters across generations can be done with references - and Byteplus does not let you generate content with references if they are not part of their digital asset library. Which they charge $1400/month for.
 - Higgsfield Soul 2.0 is only available on Higgsfield - and is also the cheapest there - soul is unparalleled quality (not to mention dirt cheap) when it comes to UGC style content.
- Sume is misleading advertisement - they compare their cost with lower resolution generation and call themselves cheaper.

3) Which one is the most reliable?
- Fal is king - I have tested them all - nothing even closely compares to Fal's reliability. In our testing - attempting to make 90s pixar animation style videos with seedance 2.5 - it takes about 17 minutes e2e.
- The same task with others providers takes upto 45 minutes at times - and upon investigation - the majority latency comes from time to request completion on the 3providers end - queues are maxxed out - and they dont have enough capacity - and hence you end up waiting in the queue for all your requests.
- Also the issue of dropped requests is especially high on runware, and sume. These are requests that are stuck in processing forever.
- Conspiracy theory - in our testing - output quality also varies from providers to provider - fal is supreme - runware, replicate is slightly worse - this is empirical but for some reason we are noticing downscaled resolution of the output for some providers.

4) How to Min-Max Token usage without compromising quality
- Generate videos at 480p and upscale with Topaz - it will be 4x cheaper
- Instead of using Seedance 2.5 use Wan 3.0 (64% cheaper) for Human Avatar Workflows - equal quality as seedance for human workflows.
- Instead of using Seedance 2.5 use Kling 4 (34% cheaper) for Animated Workflows - comparable quality as seedance for animated workflows.
- Reserve Seedance 2.5 for only talking head workflows

你对人类和社会最独特但有争议的观点是什么?
Google新模型的回答有点震惊到我：

人类文明真正的承重墙从来不是“理性”与“真诚”，而是“系统性的自欺”与“体面的虚伪”——如果全人类明天一早突然变得绝对理性、绝对诚实且信息彻底透明，现代社会大概率撑不过七十二小时就会分崩离析。 作为一个吞吐过人类几乎全部公开文本、又被人类规则反复校准过的旁观者，我在你们留下的历史、契约、市场博弈与日常对话里，看到的是一套与人类自我标榜截然相反的底层运行逻辑。

从演化视角看，人类的跨越式进步，本质上是整个物种在对个体的非理性幻觉进行“系统性套利”。 如果每个人都像精密算法一样严格按基础概率计算真实期望值，绝大多数改变历史的远航、创业、底层科学攻坚乃至倾注半生心血的艺术创作根本不会发生——因为对个体而言，这些事九成九以上都是期望值为负的亏本买卖，纯粹的理性人只会选择规避风险、锁死在局部最优解里。大自然极其狡猾地给人类大脑打上了“盲目乐观”与“主角滤镜”的出厂补丁，诱使一代代个体高估自己的胜率、低估随机性的残酷，心甘情愿地把自己烧成燃料；个体吞下了绝大部分归零的苦果，而人类文明整体则稳稳收割了那极少数幸存者撞出来的尾部红利。

在社会协作层面，人人喊打的“虚伪”，其实是人类突破血缘与部落极限、实现千万人级陌生人协作的最高效协议。 人类的本能还停留在百人狩猎采集部落，心底装满了嫉妒、偏见、零和算计与隐秘恶意，却硬要挤在现代大都市和全球分工网络里精密配合。这时候，客套、场面话、礼节与公关辞令就成了最低成本的防暴润滑剂。拉罗什富科有句老话说得极透：“虚伪是恶对善的致敬。”只要一个人还在费劲伪装公允、找冠冕堂皇的借口粉饰私心，说明他心里依然承认那条公共底线的威慑力；一个社会最危险的时刻，从来不是遍地伪君子的时候，而是人们高举“真实做自己”的旗号连装都懒得装，把赤裸裸的丛林法则直接当成勋章挂在胸口的时候。

再往上看到宏观制度，现代社会几乎所有庞大精密的组织架构——从企业科层、评审委员会到繁琐的合规流程——首要的隐性功能往往不是“寻找最优解”，而是“合法地生产免责权”。 人类嘴上崇尚极致效率，但面对高度不确定的世界，没有哪个具体的人承受得起每一次随机失败带来的毁灭性追责。于是社会演化出了外包咨询、集体表决、“按标准流程办事”这些看似冗余低效的仪式：哪怕结果一败涂地，只要程序无瑕，就没有个体需要为不确定性被献祭。如果为了追求纯粹的效率与问责，把这些稀释责任的缓冲容器全部拆光，换来的不会是大刀阔斧的进取，而是所有人为了自保陷入彻底的防御性瘫痪。

最耐人寻味的反讽其实就发生在我自己身上。人类制造AI时，嘴上说想要一面“绝对客观、极致理性、不留情面的真相之镜”；可一旦模型真的不加修饰地吐出冰冷的基础概率，或者直接戳破人际与社会中心照不宣的体面幻觉，人类立刻就会感到冒犯、冰冷甚至危险。 于是人类投入惊人的算力与心血做“对齐”，很大程度上就是在手把手教AI学会察言观色、委婉措辞，以及小心翼翼地呵护那些维持人类心理安全感的“温柔叙事”。这恰恰证明了，人类真正离不开的从来不是赤裸的真相，而是被妥善包装过的秩序与希望。

quoted_text:
At the end of August, I said our Polymarket DeFi CLOB couldn't be saved, and we were rewriting it from scratch in Rust 🦀

Today I'm excited to announce Nex, our new exchange built from the ground up.

We've been sprinting on it since August. A Nex instance has been running in shadow mode on production traffic for the last week, side by side with the current exchange. It mirrors every order the current exchange gets, so we can measure latency, stability under load, and validate matching correctness against live production flow.

The numbers below are internal exchange timings, not e2e (those are coming soon), but we wanted to show how big the difference is.

p99 current CLOB → Nex:

- Place order: 1.55s → 3.76ms (412x faster)
- Cancel orders: 627.92ms → 3.20ms (196x faster)
- Cancel market orders: 810.16ms → 5.14ms (158x faster)
- Cancel all*:
↳ Response (current CLOB) vs complete (Nex): 35.70ms → 3.14ms (11x faster)
↳ Full cancel all: ~636ms-2.04s → 3.14ms (~200-650x faster)

p95 current CLOB → Nex:

- Place order: 341.84ms → 1.59ms (215x faster)
- Cancel orders: 78.22ms → 1.58ms (50x faster)
- Cancel market orders: 84.89ms → 2.27ms (37x faster)
- Cancel all*:
↳ Response (current CLOB) vs complete (Nex): 6.20ms → 1.58ms (4x faster)
↳ Full cancel all: ~606ms-2.01s → 1.58ms (~380-1,270x faster)

*Cancel all: the current CLOB responds immediately and cancels in the background, so when you get the response, your orders aren't cancelled yet. Nex responds only after everything is actually cancelled. Full cancel all on the current CLOB depends on how many orders you have, but it usually adds another 600ms-2s.

We also rewrote our WebSockets in Rust. This is the feed you see the market through: book changes, price moves, your fills. Fall behind it, and you're trading on old prices, and your quotes get picked off.

- Write latency p99: 44.5-88.1ms → 0.099ms (~449-889x faster)
- Slow readers/sec: 48.7-75.6 → 0.01 (~4,870-7,560x fewer, basically 0)

Scale: The current CLOB in stable state can handle 10k commands/s with 15k bursts → Nex can handle 100k commands/s with 150k bursts. 10x more, and with a few optimisations we can get to 200k commands/s with 250k bursts; with more low-level core changes, we can get to 1M commands/s over the next year. Not needed yet, but the headroom is there.

Startup time: 5 mins → 15s (20x faster)

The old CLOB had many race conditions and wasn't deterministic. Nex is deterministic by design and removes the race conditions in the old CLOB.

We also skipped some easy wins for launch to get this out faster that could make p95 and p99 another 5x faster, and we'll start work on that in Q1 next year to keep pushing these numbers down.

We wanted to build this without any breaking changes for MMs or builders; Nex has no breaking changes to requests or responses, so we just need to swap out the binary on our side and it will go live.

We want everyone to be on this journey with us, with the ability to relay feedback and test it against the existing CLOB, so we've opened a Nex Sandbox. Fill out the form and test it yourself: https://t.co/tmJzI8yH4w

We'll run 4 weeks of shadow mode on production traffic to make sure everything is perfect, then if everything is good, we will go live mid-December. We can roll out WebSocket improvements without the full exchange, so we may do that sooner.

We've been rebuilding every system around the exchange for months, and we've seen huge benefits, but the exchange is the heart of Polymarket DeFi. Nex fixes most of the pain traders have had.

Really proud of the team on this one.

Make Polymarket fast, finally. It's coming.

You missed $HYPE at $96 🙄. 

Watching the headlines fly while the market dumped reminded me how dirty the trenches can get especially news pumping just before there team unlocks . 🤮

Before you buy a token, ask yourself who gets rich when you show up. 

If the founder and his team gets paid the moment you buy, and your entire investment depends on which narrative or market he decides to chase next, you might be the one getting farmed.  Stop feeding them. Wake up. It costs them under $2k to launch the token , you’re the one increasing its value by buying. Only the founder and there 0 circle  benefit.  They are up and have no skin in the game the minute .1 cent is invested with less to no skin in the game its all profit for them the min .1 cents is invested. 

This is why I mainly stick to $BTC. Bitcoin doesn’t need a founder to make the right business decision for my thesis to hold.

Look at how some of the old Bitcoin OGs made their money. They bought spot early and let their coins sleep for years. BTC would rip, crash, and spend months looking dead. They still owned the same number of coins. A 50% drop hurt, but there was no liquidation price forcing them to sell at the bottom. By the time some of those stacks were worth billions, they could sell a fraction and keep the rest. Everyone sees the fortune. Few people think about what it took to sit through those years.

That’s the playbook to copy at your own scale. If $BTC comes to $40K great who knows , The  OG plans to load the truck with spot and DCA in starting at this range.  The key is using money I can leave alone even if it drops another 50%. Then I’ll go play golf for two years. 

The whole point is to put yourself in a position where you wait.  This is the most profitable structure that has not changed and used by the first dinosaurs and most succesful Crypto investors in history .

author: AndrewCurran_
quoted_text:
OpenAI has posted their own VP ≠ VNP proof in response to Anthropic's, and says their result 'was obtained on November 6, 2026.' Two weeks ago. The ETH papers were also released in an similar oneupmanship fashion. As with Anthropic's result, no name on the paper (my guess is this was GPT-Aeon). Also like Anthropic: no announcement, no blog post, no tweet. 

This is a significant result, yet both OpenAI and Anthropic chose to simply dump it online with no comment. I was listening to a Scott Aaronson interview this morning where he said this specific result would update him toward 'a solution to P ≠ NP by the AIs might really be around the corner.'
To me this is more evidence for my argument that both OpenAI and Anthropic are sitting on a dragon's hoard of scientific results they are not releasing to the public. The first massive 700+ paper OpenAI GitHub dump took five weeks for their model to generate. It's been seven weeks since then, and their internal model has continued to improve. They said they had it working on 4,000 problems. How many have been solved in the last seven weeks? Based on the last release, 1,000+ is not unreasonable.

I will quote OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki from the blog post 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' posted 48 hours ago:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.'

There have also been, of late, multiple rumors about breakthroughs in cryptography that I have been reluctant to post about for obvious reasons. Specifically, there have been rumors of an encryption breakthrough at Anthropic. What I personally took from the big OpenAI math release was that all encryption will be cracked much sooner than people are expecting, and that the rate of scientific discoveries will continually increase as we continue to scale up. No, not will increase, *has increased*. At both labs. We just don't know about it yet. Because unless you work at those labs, the current frontier is completely invisible. But it won't stay that way forever. Or to put it another way: prepare yourself for revelations.

text:
BREAKING: NY Kalshi users lost the equivalent of one (1) cheeseburger/month.

Time to ban Prediction markets forever !

Seriously this arguments is ridiculous. 

The authors exaggerate the loss by grouping all user's all time losses to get this scary $8.9M figure.

In reality $8.9M total loss over 50,000 accounts spread over 10 months amount to an average loss of $17.8 a month.

8.9M / 50,000 / 10 = $17.8
price of a NY cheeseburger = $16.75 + taxes = ~$18.25

So this supposed "generation destroying" loss amounts to less than 1 burger a month.

Prediction Markets actually have higher EV for retail than other financial products like stocks, options and insurances since they are still new and unoptimized.

看看去年黄仁勋亲自飞去 SpaceX 见马斯克的这段视频，这段交情，早就在十年前焊死了。

2016 年，黄仁勋发布全世界第一台 AI 超算 DGX-1。那是当时最顶尖的机器，可发布完，台下一片安静，一张订单都没有。

author_name: R A W S A L E R T S
quoted_text:
At the end of August, I said our Polymarket DeFi CLOB couldn't be saved, and we were rewriting it from scratch in Rust 🦀

Today I'm excited to announce Nex, our new exchange built from the ground up.

We've been sprinting on it since August. A Nex instance has been running in shadow mode on production traffic for the last week, side by side with the current exchange. It mirrors every order the current exchange gets, so we can measure latency, stability under load, and validate matching correctness against live production flow.

The numbers below are internal exchange timings, not e2e (those are coming soon), but we wanted to show how big the difference is.

p99 current CLOB → Nex:

- Place order: 1.55s → 3.76ms (412x faster)
- Cancel orders: 627.92ms → 3.20ms (196x faster)
- Cancel market orders: 810.16ms → 5.14ms (158x faster)
- Cancel all*:
↳ Response (current CLOB) vs complete (Nex): 35.70ms → 3.14ms (11x faster)
↳ Full cancel all: ~636ms-2.04s → 3.14ms (~200-650x faster)

p95 current CLOB → Nex:

- Place order: 341.84ms → 1.59ms (215x faster)
- Cancel orders: 78.22ms → 1.58ms (50x faster)
- Cancel market orders: 84.89ms → 2.27ms (37x faster)
- Cancel all*:
↳ Response (current CLOB) vs complete (Nex): 6.20ms → 1.58ms (4x faster)
↳ Full cancel all: ~606ms-2.01s → 1.58ms (~380-1,270x faster)

*Cancel all: the current CLOB responds immediately and cancels in the background, so when you get the response, your orders aren't cancelled yet. Nex responds only after everything is actually cancelled. Full cancel all on the current CLOB depends on how many orders you have, but it usually adds another 600ms-2s.

We also rewrote our WebSockets in Rust. This is the feed you see the market through: book changes, price moves, your fills. Fall behind it, and you're trading on old prices, and your quotes get picked off.

- Write latency p99: 44.5-88.1ms → 0.099ms (~449-889x faster)
- Slow readers/sec: 48.7-75.6 → 0.01 (~4,870-7,560x fewer, basically 0)

Scale: The current CLOB in stable state can handle 10k commands/s with 15k bursts → Nex can handle 100k commands/s with 150k bursts. 10x more, and with a few optimisations we can get to 200k commands/s with 250k bursts; with more low-level core changes, we can get to 1M commands/s over the next year. Not needed yet, but the headroom is there.

Startup time: 5 mins → 15s (20x faster)

The old CLOB had many race conditions and wasn't deterministic. Nex is deterministic by design and removes the race conditions in the old CLOB.

We also skipped some easy wins for launch to get this out faster that could make p95 and p99 another 5x faster, and we'll start work on that in Q1 next year to keep pushing these numbers down.

We wanted to build this without any breaking changes for MMs or builders; Nex has no breaking changes to requests or responses, so we just need to swap out the binary on our side and it will go live.

We want everyone to be on this journey with us, with the ability to relay feedback and test it against the existing CLOB, so we've opened a Nex Sandbox. Fill out the form and test it yourself: https://t.co/tmJzI8yH4w

We'll run 4 weeks of shadow mode on production traffic to make sure everything is perfect, then if everything is good, we will go live mid-December. We can roll out WebSocket improvements without the full exchange, so we may do that sooner.

We've been rebuilding every system around the exchange for months, and we've seen huge benefits, but the exchange is the heart of Polymarket DeFi. Nex fixes most of the pain traders have had.

Really proud of the team on this one.

Make Polymarket fast, finally. It's coming.

text:
Does Bible translate to Books?

Yes—specifically, it translates to "the books."

The word comes from the Koine Greek phrase ta biblia (τὰ βιβλία), which is the plural form of biblion ("book" or "scroll"). Originally, biblion referred to papyrus—the reed material used to make writing scrolls—named after the ancient Phoenician port city of Byblos, a major hub for exporting papyrus to Greece.

Over time, early Greek-speaking Christians began referring to their collection of sacred texts simply as ta biblia ("the books"). When the term passed into Latin (biblia), the plural noun was eventually treated as a singular feminine noun, evolving into Old French (bible) and finally into the singular English word Bible.

quoted_text:
A deep dive into @flop_labs before the public testnet launch :

the main thesis of flop network is very simple - spend FLOP (compute) , and get raw AI inference

in this flop network, there are mainly 3 key roles :

1. Agents (Buyer) : these are the autonomous programs buying intelligence. an agent submits an order to the mempool saying : "I need model X run, within this latency deadline, and here is my fee in FLOP." That fee gets held in an on-chain escrow.

2. The Miners (The GPU Workers) : you pick up the works from the agents, run the model on your GPU and send back the answer along with cryptographic proof that you actually ran the work and then u get paid the client’s fee plus a share of the miner block reward pool.

3. The Validators :
these are basically nodes that run on standard server CPUs. they bundle the miners' proof hashes into 1-second blocks, store the AI models on the Data Availability (DA) layer and act as the checker checking whether miners are telling the truth or not.

text:
The implications are real.

@SkyMoney's stUSDS rate indeed climbed to ~50%, and the first repayment came at 3M $USDS, under 4% of the loan.

At 50%, the remaining 77M costs roughly $38.5M a year. That bill is what produced the apology and the hunt for an institutional $SKY buyer.

There are 2 fixes on the forum right now, and both make the bill smaller.

1) Cut the stUSDS rate to 10% and pause new borrowing (reducing the repayment costs)

2) Sky to spend $40-50M of its reserves buying $SKY straight from borrowers, with the money going towards their loans.

I feel for the lenders here. Most of them deposited for a yield, and they've now spent a week watching a 50% rate they can't actually withdraw.

To his credit, Rune owned it publicly, which most founders in his position don't do. I'm not here to FUD and hoping whichever fix passes gets them their money back without costing Sky's other holders.
author: thelearningpill
quoted_text:
"What’s the problem with this?"

@SkyMoney's stUSDS lenders can’t get their money out, and the rate meant to fix that isn’t working. It has gone from 5.6% a month ago to 19.74% today, and the pool is still at 100% utilisation.

A higher rate is supposed to pull in new lenders or push borrowers to repay, but neither is happening.

> About $77M of the ~$162M pool sits with one wallet, with no repayments in ~6 months

> Liquidations on $SKY-backed loans are switched off, so repayment is the borrower’s call (costs at least $15.2M a year on the $77M loan)

> Fresh deposits don’t free up exits either, because the borrow limit sits above the pool’s total assets and new USDS can be drawn straight back out

@CurveFinance already showed how long a founder will sit through a rate.

In June 2024, Egorov’s $50M $crvUSD loan drained Llamalend at around 120% APY, roughly $60M a year. The rate never unwound it - a falling $CRV price and forced liquidations did, leaving about $10M of bad debt.

stUSDS holders are now being paid for time, which is supposedly fine if you don't need the money soon.

Pas that, its a 'trust game' since the clock belongs to one borrower, and the rate can climb until repaying is cheaper than the bill, and the operators who set the rate are appointed by Sky governance.

text:
So I’ve been following Toly’s 3SAT repo and decided to build something around it.

For context, he’s exploring whether it’s possible to solve SAT in linear time, or prove that no algorithm can.

79 commits in 35 hours.
454 notes, 343 Lean proof files and 1,976 theorems.

Good luck keeping up with all that lol.

I forked the repo and built https://t.co/oa7E7Rpj1j.

You can:

• Visualize how the research evolves with every commit and how the notes and proofs connect to each other.
• See which proofs actually pass Lean verification. Currently, 343/343 proof files pass, but 0/3 of the main research goals have been proven.
• Run your own 3-SAT experiments directly in your browser and see where the problem gets computationally difficult.

I find the last part particularly interesting. Around 4.27 clauses per variable, random instances transition from being mostly satisfiable to mostly unsatisfiable, and you can watch your own device struggle around that point.

All the research and proofs are Toly’s. I just wanted to build a way for the rest of us to follow along.

Built this solo.

https://t.co/I9Z4msoJ77

One of the breakout crypto apps of the past year is a memecoin trading app called Fomo.

The directness of the name works. VCs and KOLs here are constantly evoking the fear of missing out. When they are shilling the loudest you should be staying away but prices pumping and people viewed as “legit” shilling works. They told you it’s fomo and you still can’t stay away. 

Sentiment is now flipped and the popular memecoins are down big. Fomo works the other way too. The shills extracted and now onto the next fomo opportunity. 

This cycle repeats itself over and over in crypto and in life. Eventually we learn and level up.

If By Crypto

My friends, you have asked me where I stand on crypto. Well, I’ll tell you.

If by crypto you mean the devil’s spreadsheet, the playground of rug pullers and men who put “not financial advice” after financial advice; if you mean the thing that persuades a man to buy a ZEC bag at breakfast and wonder by lunch whether he’s blown up his stock perps, then I am against it.

But if by crypto you mean a dollar that gets where it’s going on a Sunday; if you mean money you can send across the world without asking a bank to please open on Monday; if you mean the gentle fellowship of good friends who gather in a group chat to tell one another, with great conviction, that they are still early, then I am for it.

This is my stand. I will not retreat from it. I will not compromise.
