text:
I'm Head of U.S. Customer Experience at Shein. I manage our phone support team. All 5 of them. I have some insider information regarding Tuesday's $100 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission.

First, a correction. The FTC's own complaint says Shein "had only five agents." The word "only" wounds me. For years, the FTC says, Shein had no phone support at all. Then, in September 2025, we added 5 agents. I took the team from 0 to 5. In percentage terms, that's infinite growth. Most executives never achieve infinity.

Let me describe the operation, as the government's complaint does. Shein makes up "nearly 50% of fast-fashion sales in the United States." It ships "nearly one million packages into the U.S. every day." In September 2025, it received "more than 1.2 million customer service inquiries from U.S. customers."

1.2 million inquiries. 5 agents. That's 240,000 per agent per month. If every inquiry were a phone call, each agent would take one every 3.6 seconds, 8 hours a day, 30 days straight.

Fortunately, we planned for that. We don't publish the phone number.

According to the complaint, Shein "fails to provide a phone number on its website." Our FAQ page instead tells you to "stay tuned" for a "SHEIN US call center." It doesn't give a start date. The same FAQ page answers the question "Is SHEIN considered reliable?" We promise "the best and latest trends in fashion at an affordable price, and most importantly reliable service." Then we ask you to stay tuned.

In my industry, we measure success with a metric called the deflection rate. It tracks the share of customers who never reach a human on the phone. I did the math. Ours rounds to 100%. My team is fully staffed for the number of people who can find it.

You may ask what my 5 agents do all day. They maintain an exclusive clientele. A handful of customers found the number. To them, we are a speakeasy. The password is a phone number we never published.

Everyone else gets our omnichannel experience. That means email and chat.

The FTC collected testimonials. One customer wrote, "Each response has been generic, often AI-generated, and does not address or resolve the issue." Another spent "over 10 days, receiving copy-paste responses from different agents without any meaningful resolution." A third said "the bot or respondent kept asking me the same question."

I'd describe that as consistency. Our chatbot never loses its temper, never improvises and never solves anything. It's the most loyal employee I've ever had.

Customers also told the FTC that our live chat "was disabled during the hours that SHEIN advertised it provided live chat services." Live chat keeps the same hours as our call center.

Our internal research understood the situation perfectly. A 2024 analysis found that "58% of poor customer service relate to - response time exceeded and response time did not meet customer expectations." Another listed the main complaint as "Unable to actually solve my problem. It takes a long time to reply."

We wrote that down in 2024. Then, according to the FTC, we kept doing it. That's the beauty of a dashboard. You can watch a problem in high resolution without ever touching it.

Our shipping, we tell customers, is "lightning fast."

Lightning strikes unpredictably and occasionally burns down your house. According to the complaint, orders arrived "days, weeks, and even months late." One customer wrote, "I placed a order with SHEIN and been waiting for my package for almost 3 months." Our internal data showed logistics complaints reaching "as high as 53-54% of all consumer complaints."

Another customer tried to cancel an order. We replied that "there was nothing they can do now, because the products were now being shipped." We are lightning fast in exactly one situation: the moment you try to cancel.

Federal law has an answer for late orders. It's called the Mail, Internet, or Telephone Order Merchandise Rule. It has "Telephone" in the name. We never stood a chance.

When a seller can't ship on time, that rule says it must tell you and offer a prompt refund without being asked. The FTC says we skipped that part "in numerous instances."

We offered something better. Our "On-Time Delivery Guarantee" promised "500 SHEIN points if your order doesn't arrive by the expected date." Under the 2023 terms described in the complaint, 100 points equaled $1. So for a late order, we paid you $5 in Shein points. They spend only at Shein. Some expire in as little as 7 days. They cover at most 70% of an order total, which the complaint says excludes shipping. Our apology for late shipping couldn't be spent on shipping.

Then came the wrong-address policy. When a package went to the wrong house, the complaint says, Shein marked it delivered "if there is a photo establishing that the package was delivered somewhere."

Somewhere. Your package is always somewhere. Philosophically, we never lose anything. We simply deliver to a broader definition of you.

One customer sent us delivery photos and GPS coordinates that didn't match the home address. The customer summed up our reply: "the delivery location is irrelevant basically." Nobody on my team could have said it better. Nobody on my team was reachable to try.

If you disagreed, we told you to work with the shipper or file a chargeback. The shipper could look for your package. Under our contracts with certain shippers, the complaint says, only Shein can process the refund. We outsourced customer service to your bank. Your bank, at least, has a phone number.

Then the FTC sent us a Civil Investigative Demand, and our vocabulary evolved.

The shipping page used to promise that the warehouse needs "1-3 days" to process an order. After the investigation began, the complaint says, the page started saying the warehouse "needs some time." Our "QuickShip" label became "Local." Nothing moved faster. The words stopped making promises.

We couldn't speed up the warehouse, so we slowed down the sentence. A warehouse costs money to fix. A sentence costs an intern an afternoon.

Now, the reviews. My team can't answer you, but our software reads every word you write.

We did pay for your reviews. The rewards program awarded "5 points for submitting a review, an additional 10 points for including a photo in the review, and an additional 2 points for providing detailed size information." At 100 points per dollar, a review with a photo and your measurements earned 17 cents. We paid 17 cents for your honest review. Then our software graded it.

Shein runs reviews through what the complaint calls the Global Comment Management System. It sorts your words into 2 lists. The "helpful" list includes "durable," "elegant," "no complaints," "lots of compliments," "satisfied," "as pictured," "comfy," "fits well," "must buy" and "awesome."

The helpful list also includes "can't wait to try this on." Our most helpful reviewer hasn't opened the bag.

The "unhelpful" list includes "damaged," "rip," "broke," "very disappointed," "bad quality," "waste of money," "very small," "too short," "did not fit" and "not good."

According to the FTC, a review rated 4 or 5 stars, with helpful words and no unhelpful ones, went straight to publication. A 5-star "comfy" went straight to the page. A 3-star "comfy" went to screening. In the FTC's words, it faced "further delays in publishing, if they are published at all."

Our review guidance lists "malicious or extremely bad comments." One category covers "Text or picture content that expresses serious consequences for the body." The examples: "[J]ewelry will stain the skin, the product contains carcinogens, and the smell of the product causes customers to have a headache for a few days."

So if a necklace turned your neck green, the system treated your review as the threat. The rash stayed on you. The review stayed off our site.

Returned something? The complaint says Shein disabled reviews for fully returned orders. If you had already posted a review, Shein removed it. A customer who returns a dress is the one customer who knows exactly what's wrong with it. We made sure that customer never testified.

Next, our conscience, which we sell separately.

Shein launched a line called evoluSHEIN, a "purpose-driven collection" of "responsibly-made" clothing. The badge says the products come from "suppliers who have obtained above-average ratings under our social compliance audit program." Shein says those audits cover child labor and forced labor.

According to the complaint, Shein's strategy was to "sell more sustainable products for increased pricing." An internal note predicted the claims would "result in long-term affinity with the public."

The FTC then asked to see the audits. According to the complaint, Shein "has not provided or made available to the FTC even one." Shein says it conducted almost 4,000 audits in 2023. It didn't hand them to its own accounting firm either. The firm explained that its work "re-calculated gradings."

In 2024, the firm found that 29% of the scores on our list earned an A or a B. It couldn't link a single one to an evoluSHEIN supplier.

So our ethical line rested on an accounting firm recalculating grades from a list we supplied. The firm put its position in writing: "we cannot independently verify the results or outcomes of those audits." It's our most sustainable process. It produces no waste, because it produces nothing.

Then there's the cotton. Shein told customers its suppliers source cotton "only" from "Australia, Brazil, India, the United States and other approved regions." According to the complaint, the only other approved region was Eastern China. Testers found cotton labeled American that was actually Chinese.

Over 7% of samples couldn't be traced to any country at all. Some paperwork claimed cotton from a country that doesn't grow cotton commercially. For the other 93%, the tester couldn't tell the approved regions apart, China included, because "the data was too intertwined to extract."

That's 7% untraceable and 93% intertwined. I checked the math. It adds up to a "robust cotton traceability program."

Now, the punishment. $100 million.

Let me do the arithmetic, since my team has time. We ship nearly 1 million packages a day. Spread over 100 days of shipments, the fine comes to about $1 a package. The FTC's own screenshot shows standard shipping at $3.99 on orders under $29. Our penalty per box is about a quarter of our shipping fee.

The fine covers about 100 days of shipments. One customer waited "almost 3 months" for a single package. The federal government punished us for about as long as that customer waited.

The FTC says the money will go to refunds for customers. If they have questions, they can call us. Please stay tuned.

In fairness, I should present our side, and our side has a point. Shein settled without admitting anything. A spokesperson said the agreement "does not constitute an admission of liability" and that "We continue to disagree with aspects of the FTC's characterization of our business and compliance practices." Shein did add phone agents. Millions of Americans on tight budgets buy from us because a $9 dress is a $9 dress. We tell ourselves inflation made cheap clothing a necessity, and we met that demand at a scale nobody else could.

Here's what our spokesperson left out. According to the complaint, we kept going "despite knowledge of numerous complaints." We changed course "only after receiving a Civil Investigative Demand from the FTC." Under the order, the FTC says, Shein can no longer suppress negative reviews, misrepresent delivery times or refuse adequate customer service. It took a federal lawsuit to get a retailer to pick up the phone.

None of this will matter on Friday.

On Black Friday, you'll open the app. A banner will promise the "Lowest price in 60 days." A dress will cost less than your lunch. The reviews will say "comfy," "as pictured" and "fits well," because those reviews cleared the line first.

You'll click "Add to Cart." The package will arrive in "1-3 days." Or after "some time." Or somewhere.

If something goes wrong, my team will be here for you. All 5 of them. You'll just have to find them.

Stay tuned.

text:
1. The structural reasons for the long token bear market (silly valuations, weak tokens, and capital misallocation) have been flushed out of the system over the past five years.

These were the conditions that created a downward spiral of negative industry P&L that in turn led to financial and human capital flight over five years. These conditions have now reversed (cheap valuations, stronger tokens, and disciplined capital allocation).

2. Internet Finance is working (stables, RWAs, blockchain scaling, efficient onchain financial primitives, rational capital formation) but progress has been obscured by negative industry P&L.

You could not say the same thing in 2020 - when we were last given a chance at a long bull market - because blockchains didn't scale, onchain financial primitives were both inefficient and DOA from a regulatory perspective, and the industry did not properly understand how to design internet financial systems.

This last point is important - our industry used to believe that revenue didn't matter, that tokens could survive as liquid junior equity instruments, and that you could design systems where you gave strangers on the Internet money without investor protections. The capital scarcity imposed by the long bear market has taught us to design financial systems that actually work across market cycles and in adversarial conditions.

3. The Internet Financial System wins through network effects - by being the global bazaar for capital where people can raise cheaper capital and hold better assets. I remain convinced that every asset will come onchain over time. Obviously there is no long bull market if you don't believe in this end state (but I know you do).

Once the migration process begins in earnest, we will experience it as a positive reflexive loop of more assets and activity onchain leading to stronger cash flows and higher token valuations for onchain businesses while financial and human capital rushes into the space. I know that's hard to believe now when there are <15 funds and <1,000 serious people left in the industry but valuations and capital can move fast.

Importantly, every industry participant left is basically building infrastructure and services for the 'global bazaar of capital' outcome.
The tokenization platforms, AMMs, borrow-lend platforms, onchain fundraising businesses, onchain investment banks and derivatives venues are building for this same outcome. We are ready for this.

I believe conditions ( 1 ) ( 2 ) ( 3 ) above - along with a favorable regulatory posture in the US - have led to a dry forest setup where the right spark could start the process. I don't know if the spark will come from GENIUS (Jan 2027), continued growth of RWAs to critical mass, prolonged easier macro liquidity conditions that spark positive industry P&L, or a niche industry finding capital onchain and setting the example for others. I also don't know if this happens in 2027, 2028 or 2029 but I do believe it will happen.

All of these points are pretty nuanced but I tried to give the broad strokes reasons for my optimism. Always happy to go into much more detail on any of these.

text:
The FBI warns that an AI hacking tool has taken some attackers from first contact to privileged access in under 3 hours.

The speed is alarming, but the bigger change is who can now do this. According to the FBI, the tool lets attackers with minimal technical expertise run complex campaigns against multiple targets at once. Work that used to require a team of skilled hackers is increasingly automated.

It also isn't going after the obvious targets. The FBI says it excels at finding the systems that get the least security attention: partner portals, mobile backends, legacy services and third-party integrations. The bugs it exploited weren't exotic either: SQL injection, SSRF, missing authentication on APIs, and admin passwords hardcoded in JavaScript.

But AI hasn't made fixing bugs as cheap as finding them. An attacker only has to exploit a bug. A defender has to assess it, patch it, test the fix and ship it without breaking anything. When bugs are found faster than teams can fix them, you get what we've been calling the vulnerability apocalypse.

For years, companies could get away with an annual penetration test, a few security reviews, and patching vulnerabilities as they became public. That model depended on two things: finding vulnerabilities being slow and difficult, and attackers sticking to the systems you had already reviewed. AI is removing both.

Crypto learned early that if there's money sitting in software, someone will spend every waking hour trying to take it. That's why the industry built a security culture around audits, bug bounties, and financially incentivized security researchers who get paid only for real, exploitable bugs, so teams spend their limited fix time on what actually matters.

The rest of software needs to start thinking the same way.

text:
We talked to @tarunchitra from @robotventures about how the AI inference market works today and how it could be fairer and more efficient.

A few takeaways:

1. A lower price per token doesn’t always mean a lower bill. You can pay more if an inference provider charges full price for input it could reuse at a cheaper cached rate.

2. Providers running the same model compete on speed, price, and how efficiently they handle different workloads. Routing helps match requests to the right provider.

3. The market still leans on trust. It's hard to verify what compute a provider used or whether the bill reflects it. We got into verification, enclaves, and whether outcome-based billing could be an alternative.

The concept of a quick recovery running into overhead supply may be playing out in $SPCX. It’s starting to look similar to the Facebook analog. Time will tell.

LinkedIn was another great example. After going public in 2011, the stock suffered a huge six-week decline, then staged a powerful recovery almost all the way back to its old high. But it quickly became overwhelmed by overhead supply.

I didn’t start buying LinkedIn until the first quarter of 2013. That’s how long it took for the stock to absorb the supply, build a proper structure, and finally launch into a major move.

A great setup takes time to develop. You don't want the lowest price... you want the right price. The right price is the point at which the stock moves up into a strong price move almost immediately without hitting your stop-loss.

author: 0xMadaba
quoted_text:
Strength Index #2: 36 revenue-generating tokens in one ranking, scored half on the business and half on what the token offers its holders

Hyperliquid leads the ranking ahead of Aerodrome, Sky and Pump. Only 13 of the 36 tokens return more to holders than they add in new supply

The top of the table:
- @HyperliquidX (HYPE, 73) leads with the strongest business of all 36 (79) and the most revenue ($890M). It trades at 16.7x revenue on market cap and 66.9x on FDV
- @aeroxyz (AERO, 71) trades at 4.8x revenue, and the last 30 days ran 25% above the pace of the 90 days before. 99% of revenue is paid out to lockers and stakers, not spent on buybacks. With 24% new supply the net holder yield is -3.1%
- @SkyEcosystem (SKY, 68) pairs 5.3x revenue with 0% new supply and a net holder yield of +8.3%, but its revenue is flat
- @Pumpfun (PUMP, 68) has the second-lowest multiple of all 36 at 1.3x revenue and a net holder yield of +11.3%. Its revenue over the last 30 days ran 24% below the prior pace
- @ORE (ORE, #5) and @CoWSwap (COW, #10) come from the "20 More Tokens" table. ORE is the cheapest of all 36 at 1.0x revenue, but it has a market cap of only $40M and mining emissions of 96% of its circulating supply

Tokens worth a closer look:
- @pancakeswap (CAKE, #7) runs the opposite model to AERO. It burns 67% of its revenue and adds only 3% new supply, which gives a net holder yield of +6.0%
- @Uniswap (UNI, #11) widened its fee switch twice since July, so its growth is measured on fees. On that basis the last 30 days ran 48% below the prior pace
- @rendernetwork (RENDER, #15) grew revenue 88% over the last 30 days and trades at 137x revenue, the second-highest multiple in the table
- @Lighter_xyz (LIT, #17) has the second-best business (72) but token terms of only 44. New supply over the next 12 months equals 61% of today's circulating supply, and the team and investor lock ends in late December
- @nearprotocol (NEAR, #18) is a Layer 1 and is in the table because of its own app. NEAR Intents earns $22M a year, which puts NEAR at 175x revenue. Gas on the chain adds about $1M and is not counted. On gas alone NEAR would trade above 3,000x
- @aave (AAVE, #22) grew revenue 36% over the last 30 days, but buybacks are still paused, so its share to holders stays at 0%
- @PythNetwork (PYTH, #23): since October the DAO uses 100% of what it receives from Pyth products to buy PYTH. At 60x revenue and 27% new supply it stays in the lower half
- @ponsdotfamily (PONS, #25): revenue over the last 30 days ran 92% below the prior pace. A drop alone is no reason to exclude a token, so PONS stays in, valued on the last 30 days ($11M a year) instead of the last 90 ($123M)
- @derivexyz (DRV, #28) roughly doubled in price over the last 90 days while revenue grew 15%. That leaves it at 56x revenue, the fourth-highest multiple in the table

Takeaways from the table:
- A high share to holders does not guarantee a positive net holder yield (holder revenue of the last 90 days annualized in % of market cap, minus new supply over the next 12 months in % of circulating supply). 8 tokens pass 95% or more of their revenue to holders. Five of them are still negative, the other three sit between +0.9% and +4.4%
- 21 of 36 have a negative net holder yield. Heaviest new supply in % of circulating supply: ORE 96%, LIT 61%, SOSO 60%, KNTQ 44%, DBR 38%
- The top half passes far more to holders. The median share to holders is 65% in the top half and 17% in the bottom half, and 10 of the 13 tokens with a positive net holder yield sit in the top half
- The lowest multiples come with a weak spot. Of the five cheapest tokens (ORE, PUMP, MET, COW and EDGE, all at 3.4x revenue or less), three pass little to holders (MET 11%, COW 0%, EDGE 24%) and two add a lot of new supply (ORE 96%, PUMP 23%)
- 12 of 36 have a revenue momentum below -5% (last 30 days against the pace of the 90 days before), and 6 of them sit in the top half. The largest drops are PONS (-92%), ATH (-64%) and EDGE, RAY and UNI (-48% each). ATH's figure swings with its monthly booking dates (token notes). For EDGE, RAY and UNI the current run rate is below the revenue in the table
- No token reaches 70 on both sides. HYPE, AERO and PUMP are the only ones at 60 or more on both
- The middle of the table is tight. Ranks 9 to 17 sit within 2.4 points, so the order there says little
- HYPE and PUMP together make 57% of the $2.7B revenue of all 36

What's new:
- One ranking instead of two tables. The thresholds are $4M+ annualized revenue and a $40M+ market cap for all tokens, and the revenue size scale now starts at $4M
- I sharpened the rules and the weights after the first two tables and plan to keep them stable from here, apart from fixing errors. Scores are comparable within this edition, but moves against the earlier tables partly come from the method and not from the business. A change column follows with Index #3
- NEAR is new, counted with the revenue of NEAR Intents
- VVV is not ranked this time. DefiLlama only captures Venice's onchain buy-and-burn ($12M a year), because Venice's sales settle offchain. On the burns alone VVV would rank #23. On Nov 24 Venice's founder put annualized revenue at $200M, which would lift VVV to between #3 and #5. But that is a top-line sales figure, not the protocol revenue DefiLlama tracks for the other 36, and without a daily series I can't check it onchain or measure growth. So VVV's revenue is not comparable

How to read the ranking: it is a screen, not a buy list. It scores past revenue, Nov 24 prices and scheduled unlocks with my own weighting and does not forecast growth. Market cap / revenue is the heaviest of the four token factors (20% of the score), because what you pay per dollar of revenue decides how much of a good business is already in the price. That also means a token's score rises when its price falls and revenue holds. The table can't tell whether a low multiple is value the market has not priced yet or a risk it does not measure. In corporate finance a low multiple is where due diligence starts, not where it ends

Not investment advice. Selection, method changes and token notes in the replies

If By Crypto

My friends, you have asked me where I stand on crypto. Well, I’ll tell you.

If by crypto you mean the devil’s spreadsheet, the playground of rug pullers and men who put “not financial advice” after financial advice; if you mean the thing that persuades a man to buy a ZEC bag at breakfast and wonder by lunch whether he’s blown up his stock perps, then I am against it.

But if by crypto you mean a dollar that gets where it’s going on a Sunday; if you mean money you can send across the world without asking a bank to please open on Monday; if you mean the gentle fellowship of good friends who gather in a group chat to tell one another, with great conviction, that they are still early, then I am for it.

This is my stand. I will not retreat from it. I will not compromise.

text:
Vibecoded your first app?

25 things to check before deploying:

1. No API keys or secrets in your code or repo

2. Every protected route checks who the user is and what they can access

3. Database rules lock down who can read and write each row

4. Users can't access another user's data by changing an ID in the URL

5. All user input is validated on the server, not just the frontend

6. Database queries are protected against SQL injection

7. Passwords are securely hashed, never stored in plain text

8. HTTPS is enforced across your entire app

9. Rate limits on login, signup & any paid API calls

10. Spending caps or usage limits on every cloud and AI API account

11. Backups are on & you've actually tested restoring one

12. Dependencies are updated and scanned for known vulnerabilities

13. Session tokens expire and are invalidated after logout

14. Error messages don't leak stack traces or database details

15. Logging and alerts so you know when something breaks

16. Payment amounts and subscription permissions are verified on the server

17. Webhook signatures are verified & duplicate events are handled safely

18. File uploads have size limits, file type restrictions & security checks

19. Development, staging and production environments are separated

20. Debug mode, test accounts and unnecessary endpoints are removed from production

21. Critical user flows are tested from signup to account deletion

22. There's a rollback plan in case a deployment breaks something

23. External API failures, timeouts & outages don't crash your entire app

24. Your app is tested under concurrent traffic, not just with one user

25. Users can delete their accounts and personal data, and sensitive information isn't exposed in logs

Bookmark this before getting hacked.

text:
Year Two

Some assorted goals:

- make Monad a legitimately great platform for personal finance (investing in equities, bonds, etc), especially for getting access to markets outside of one's home country. So much of the usage in crypto right now is gambling/memecoins... it is what it is, but personal finance appeals to 100x more people, and they don't churn out. A legitimately great platform has great asset selection, efficient execution (low cost both in and out of a position), and competitive rates both for borrowers and lenders

- ship Private Settlement Domains with the first user, to serve as a case study for anyone trying to reason about how private environments can compose with shared liquidity. Public chains and private environments have been very far apart in practice and it's time to change that

- hammer out an excellent liquidity landscape on chain. It is a mix of order books, prop AMMs, offchain routers, onchain routers, and RFQ... especially with tokenized equities, there is a long long tail of assets and we need to minimize spreads so that the offering is competitive with TradFi. Spread minimization means helping makers quote sustainably; here designs like APES can help

- make it easier for AI to produce actually good trading strategies on command for anyone to execute a trading plan efficiently with algos. There is are a ton of slop startups out there which are a wrapper around claude asking it "should I buy or sell given these textual inputs"... that's not real quant research and not good execution. At the same time, there are a lot of building blocks for quant trading that AI couldn't one-shot, but given the blocks it could put them together sensibly

- contribute to there being fewer hacks (and a lower total $ stolen) in the crypto industry, probably through a combination of repetition about dedicated devices (SO many hacks are from people plugging hardware wallets into everyday laptops) and encouraging everyone to use tools that our team has shipped for agentic threat detection (e.g. Ultrafuzz). I truly think that security is the biggest blocker to adoption, and that we're basically all in this together

- drive the car faster than ever in multiple races - MEV-resistance, quantum-resistance, privacy, and MCP, challenging all competitors to ship or be left behind

- help NFTs and onchain social -- two deeply out-of-consensus areas -- make a comeback. The builders in these sectors these days are incredibly committed; there's never been a better filtering function

- contribute to tech optimism. So many doomers out there. Life is electric, building is electric

- contribute to a less stressful environment for builders. It is a very weird time to be a builder in DeFi... on the one hand, tools are better than ever... on the other hand, capital is scarce and crypto-natives are jaded. The approach to building ironically requires both more introspection and more rapid, rapid shipping

- support the excellent individuals on our team at MF become leaders in the space in their respective domains. We have amazing folks here and the space needs leadership more than ever

- support someone building a total moonshot

- build at least one product that has a lot of everyday-people customers, and deliver a ton of value to them

- become willing to repeatedly say the same thing, until it starts to sink in

Highly unlikely anything changes in the market through year end; hence not much to do but remain in cash mostly

Funds have likely closed books trying to protect gains from Q2 so they can report decent full year numbers for LPs; on top of that, large increases in risk metrics (portfolio VaR, covariance matrix going to 1, etc) caused by latest market moves ensures they are unlikely to take much/any risk right now. Add the fact that we’re facing higher likelihood of a rate hike in December after the latest PCE print, and you can be sure there won’t be much risk taking. Levered retail was last standout but think they’re prob tapped out by now. 

Being short biased doesn’t even make sense at these levels since we are now entering bear market territory on indices; you can get incredibly aggressive rips higher from “good news” (ie Jensen back at NVDA)

On the AI side, we have ANT IPO out of the way but it was clearly pushed through to time the local top on QoQ revenue. Atm it’s pretty clear that there is no imminent killer use case lined up (after coding agents from late 2025/early 2026) to drive revenue expansion near term which is reflected in token prices and gpu spot rates. A lot of the DC financing was predicated on these numbers holding up which is why we’re seeing CDS and bond yields blow on the most levered names like ORCL.

quoted_text:
Year Two

Some assorted goals:

- make Monad a legitimately great platform for personal finance (investing in equities, bonds, etc), especially for getting access to markets outside of one's home country. So much of the usage in crypto right now is gambling/memecoins... it is what it is, but personal finance appeals to 100x more people, and they don't churn out. A legitimately great platform has great asset selection, efficient execution (low cost both in and out of a position), and competitive rates both for borrowers and lenders

- ship Private Settlement Domains with the first user, to serve as a case study for anyone trying to reason about how private environments can compose with shared liquidity. Public chains and private environments have been very far apart in practice and it's time to change that

- hammer out an excellent liquidity landscape on chain. It is a mix of order books, prop AMMs, offchain routers, onchain routers, and RFQ... especially with tokenized equities, there is a long long tail of assets and we need to minimize spreads so that the offering is competitive with TradFi. Spread minimization means helping makers quote sustainably; here designs like APES can help

- make it easier for AI to produce actually good trading strategies on command for anyone to execute a trading plan efficiently with algos. There is are a ton of slop startups out there which are a wrapper around claude asking it "should I buy or sell given these textual inputs"... that's not real quant research and not good execution. At the same time, there are a lot of building blocks for quant trading that AI couldn't one-shot, but given the blocks it could put them together sensibly

- contribute to there being fewer hacks (and a lower total $ stolen) in the crypto industry, probably through a combination of repetition about dedicated devices (SO many hacks are from people plugging hardware wallets into everyday laptops) and encouraging everyone to use tools that our team has shipped for agentic threat detection (e.g. Ultrafuzz). I truly think that security is the biggest blocker to adoption, and that we're basically all in this together

- drive the car faster than ever in multiple races - MEV-resistance, quantum-resistance, privacy, and MCP, challenging all competitors to ship or be left behind

- help NFTs and onchain social -- two deeply out-of-consensus areas -- make a comeback. The builders in these sectors these days are incredibly committed; there's never been a better filtering function

- contribute to tech optimism. So many doomers out there. Life is electric, building is electric

- contribute to a less stressful environment for builders. It is a very weird time to be a builder in DeFi... on the one hand, tools are better than ever... on the other hand, capital is scarce and crypto-natives are jaded. The approach to building ironically requires both more introspection and more rapid, rapid shipping

- support the excellent individuals on our team at MF become leaders in the space in their respective domains. We have amazing folks here and the space needs leadership more than ever

- support someone building a total moonshot

- build at least one product that has a lot of everyday-people customers, and deliver a ton of value to them

- become willing to repeatedly say the same thing, until it starts to sink in

text:
We built a new expressive predicate encryption (PE) scheme without FHE and ran it end-to-end on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

Previously, expressive lattice-based PE was largely theoretical: even a 1-bit AND gate would require ~70 exabytes of ciphertext per attribute bit in an FHE-based baseline.

With our new construction, we evaluated a full range check + regular expression check on a hidden 10-bit attribute, achieving:
- 2 × 10⁹ times smaller ciphertexts per attribute bit (69.62 EB → 34.23 GB)
- 2 × 10¹⁶ times fewer 64-bit integer multiplications in decryption (2.32 × 10³⁰ → 8.70 × 10¹³)

To our knowledge, this is the first implementation of PE for a predicate class as expressive as branching programs. The construction is proven secure under circular Ring-LWE.

📄 Paper: https://t.co/SAJAE2cfW2
💻 Implementation (mxx): https://t.co/VQLp9l25eL

What is Predicate Encryption, and why was it so hard to make implementable?

PE lets you encrypt data so that only secret keys matching a specific condition (predicate) can decrypt it, while keeping the underlying attributes completely hidden from unauthorized key holders.

For example, you can require a hidden calendar date to be both valid (a regex check) and within a specific window (a range check) using a single key.

Until now, making expressive PE implementable faced a stark tradeoff:
- Practical implementations only supported restricted predicates (such as inner products).
- Expressive lattice-based schemes relied on evaluating FHE over key-homomorphic encodings, resulting in astronomical parameters and exabyte-scale ciphertexts.

Concrete performance (128-bit security target)

On a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, our scheme runs end-to-end for a combined range + regex check on a hidden 10-bit attribute:

Encryption: 4.06 hours
Key generation: 4.70 hours
Decryption: 4.23 hours
Total ciphertext size: 342.25 GB (34.23 GB per attribute bit)

How did we achieve this without FHE?

Instead of simulating FHE as a Boolean circuit over key-homomorphic encodings, we evaluate branching programs directly over them using two new techniques:
1. Asymmetric multiplication: multiplying a hidden state by an encrypted attribute symbol through decryption inside an encoding.
2. Lookup tables over exponents: representing states in monomial exponents and evaluating arbitrary state transitions via key-homomorphic ring automorphisms.

Beyond PE: Lattice-based iO

The exponent-encoding technique developed in this work also enabled the efficiency improvements in Diamond iO 2, which we presented at Devcon.

While the current costs are still far from practical for most applications, direct private computation over key-homomorphic encodings opens up a promising new design space for bringing advanced cryptographic primitives into reality.

Open-source framework: mxx

The entire scheme is built with mxx, our open-source framework for lattice-based cryptography:
- Write protocols in a Rust-based DSL, much as you would write them on paper.
- Run them on GPUs without writing CUDA code or manually managing GPU memory and parallelism.
- Automatically derive formal correctness statements in Lean directly from the protocol definitions.

Our goal is to shrink the gap between theoretical cryptographic constructions and their high-performance, formally verified implementations.

text:
Travel writing is in practice some of the best sociology since the naivete of the foreigner grants the permission to make sweeping generalizations and claims that might otherwise seem too poorly-justified to merit publication. “My people have poor manners” is a tough claim to credibly land (Who are you? Exactly which life experiences are you drawing on? And what is your agenda in pushing this line of argument?), whereas “on my travels in Scotland, I noticed that the people had poor manners” seems perfectly reasonable, and indeed thought-provoking. Random samples from a distribution help you understand the mean, and the aleatory nature of travel encounters lends credence to the whole assessment.

Alexis de Tocqueville was just 25 when he traveled across the US and 29 when his observations were published. So, Democracy in America is a giant Substack from a young backpacker, written on his peregrinations as he consumed Montesquieu, Pascal, and Rousseau. He was clearly inspired by Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, which made the case that countries’ governance, and their laws, are necessarily functions of their cultures and manners.

Building on this, Democracy in America is in many ways a “deep roots” work. Tocqueville is emphatic (at times comically so) that it is America's culture that explains its success, and that its culture in turn stems from the country’s initial conditions. “I think I can see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores.” He thinks it's important that New England was settled by “a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time” who brought the “best elements of order and morality”. He points out that Mexico doesn’t work nearly as well, despite copying the American constitution and laws, and notes disapprovingly that Virginia was founded by gold-seeking people “without character” whose “turbulent spirit [...] endangered the infant colony.” At the end of Volume I, he concludes, practically table-thumping: “If in the course of this work I have not succeeded in making the reader feel the importance that I attribute to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions, in a word, to their moeurs, in maintaining their laws, I have failed in the principal object that I proposed to myself in writing it.”

We could look at Democracy in America as an early work of development economics: he is attempting to systematically figure out why it is that America works. (And not just out of casual interest: he was a member of an aristocratic family that was entangled with recent French political upheaval.) By placing primacy on culture, Tocqueville’s explanation deviates from the institutional and structural explanations often favored by today’s economists. Daron Acemoglu, to choose one prominent present-day example, firmly rejects the “Culture Hypothesis” in Why Nations Fail. In explaining Virginia, he instead points to structural incentives. Poor Economics, from Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee, contains a similar rejection of cultural explanations. Comparable examples from other leading economists abound. An aversion to cultural explanations is of course understandable for all sorts of reasons: cultures are opaque, protean, and resistant to quantitative characterization. Cultures are themselves shaped by other factors, such that it’s hard to attribute definitive causality, and it’s uncomfortable to adopt anything that feels like a normative orientation. Nonetheless, can we explain why New England differs from Mexico without starting with the inner disposition, habits, and worldviews of the people? Tocqueville thinks not.

For all culture’s importance, it would be wrong to suggest that Tocqueville believes that culture is the only factor that matters. He dwells extensively on how America’s institutions are important, and how the microstructure of town life shapes the country’s federal civics. It is also true that development economics has taken a more strongly cultural turn in recent times, most of all in Joel Mokyr’s 2025 Nobel Prize. Mokyr’s work feels downright Tocquevillian at times: contra the intimidatingly quantitative econometrics that dominates today, Mokyr engages in an extended and earnestly curious qualitative synthesis of relevant patterns (in his case, in service of trying to figure out why the Industrial Revolution started when it did). Like Tocqueville, he concludes that the best explanation places cultural changes above other factors.

I’m very interested in whether LLMs will help us characterize culture in new and at least somewhat more objective ways. Can we ingest and process vast quantities of work that may not even have been OCR’d or translated until now? Can we map cultural corpora to vectors in some foundation model embedding space? Where large datasets and computational techniques enabled new ways to analyze many economic questions in recent decades, perhaps LLMs will enable newly objective light to be shone on hypothesized cultural explanations.

–

Speaking of LLMs, Democracy in America is a book about a new kind of society, and a Frenchman trying to figure out what the future might hold. As we sit on the cusp of another upheaval, is there anything that reads with resonance today?

Part of the declared promise of AI is that it might obviate our need to work. In slavery, Tocqueville observes a version of this phenomenon on his travels. He is struck by its barbarous cruelty (and his travel companion later published an anti-slavery novel), but also by its effects on the slaveowners themselves. He perceived that the practice rendered work dishonorable, and thus yielded idleness, ignorance, and pride. Slavery, he says, “enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man.” He observes the contrast between slavery-rejecting Ohio and slavery-embracing Kentucky. In Kentucky, “those who are active and enlightened either do nothing or pass over into the State of Ohio, where they may work without dishonor.” Ohio’s harvests are more abundant, homes are more elegant, and people seem to be “in enjoyment of that wealth and contentment which is the reward of labor.”

Presented with an evil release from manual labor, the Kentuckians did not apply themselves to productive studies and great creations, and the South did not become a new Florence. There is an obvious question for us: how will AI change our relationship with work? Will it become dishonorable, and what will the reflexive effect on our society be if so? Should this change our view of utopian visions of “automated communism”?

Tocqueville also raises the issue of coexistence with more advanced neighbors. He noted that the arrival of the Europeans had been ruinous for the Indians (as he termed them). European technology – firearms, metallurgy, steam power – was a kind of superintelligence relative to their practices. The disruptions and destruction wrought by the settlers led to cultural problems (“their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken”), which in turn led to declines in both the physical and the moral conditions of the tribes. Tocqueville believed that the Indians faced a choice given that their old way of living was no longer viable: they could adopt European mores or suffer inevitable destruction. He predicted that they would reject cultural adaptation, and thus were “doomed to perish”. This is all to say that the arrival of the European settlers was in Tocqueville’s eyes injurious to the Indians not only because of the direct violence and displacement, but also because the contact was itself so disruptive to their societies that their cultures ceased to function. Some of this was later observed in Pacific island societies – even though there wasn’t the same degree of violent dispossession, the mere presence of Western contact was intrinsically destabilizing. In many visions of the future, superintelligent AIs are much more numerous than humans, with consequences that are hard to predict. In Tocqueville, there is a cautionary suggestion.

Given the new powers afforded by AI, there is a question of what we will choose to do with it – to the extent that we are in control, we will wield a vastly expanded authority. Americans faced some version of this question: in democracy, society was endowed with wholly new ways to express its collective will, with no ultimate superior power, for society was for the first time in charge of itself. Tocqueville repeatedly emphasizes how democracy thus increased the importance of religion as a regulator of hasty or unwise impulses. “Whilst the law permits the Americans to do what they please, religion prevents them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, what is rash or unjust.” If we take seriously Tocqueville’s idea that religion was a critical complement in ensuring that people shaped societies in prudent ways, Democracy implicitly raises a question: which are the ideas, philosophies, religions, or doctrines that will help us wield AI well?

Part of what’s interesting and memorable about the work is Tocqueville’s combination of curiosity, enthusiasm, and slight ambivalence about democracy itself. He grants that democracy is likely to be the future of governance, and he is admiring of what it has achieved in America, but he can’t avoid concerns about what it may augur (such as the unchecked and totalitarian impulses of the mob). At the end of Volume II, he describes his chief concern with democracy: that it may yield a new form of despotism that he struggles to define. He fears not tyrants, but, he says, “guardians”. He is worried about a world where:

> Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. [...] It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood: it is well content that the people should rejoice, provided they think of nothing but rejoicing. For their happiness such a government willingly labors, but it chooses to be the sole agent and the only arbiter of that happiness. [...] What remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking and all the trouble of living? Thus it every day renders the exercise of the free agency of man less useful and less frequent; it circumscribes the will within a narrower range, and gradually robs a man of all the uses of himself.

The Iain Banks Culture novels are often invoked by AI proponents. For Tocqueville, something strikingly like the world that they describe was his dystopian fear, for a world bereft of autonomy would be intrinsically degrading and humiliating for humanity:

> The will of man is not shattered, but softened, bent, and guided: men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting: such a power does not destroy, but it prevents existence; it does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.

The analogy to animals is noteworthy. In interviews, AI leaders occasionally analogize the future human state to that of pets. Banks himself noted that in the Culture novels, “[humans] have a status somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.” In Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace, he hopes that humans are “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”.

Tocqueville at heart thought that agency and cultivation of people came above all else. He dreaded anesthetized placidity. In soft despotism, he feared that “ambition will lose its vigor and its greatness; that human passions will be appeased and lowered at the same time”. This vigor was for Tocqueville at the heart of what was admirable in America, whose bustle and intensity he repeatedly extols. American self-reliance and self-direction are paramount: “the citizen of the United States is taught from his earliest infancy to rely upon his own exertions in order to resist the evils and the difficulties of life.” For Tocqueville, any kind of servile and manicured comfort was not just undesirable, but a negation of the American promise.

Many of the Elysian visions for AI hinge on AI resolving the messy coordination challenges that afflict humans. (Scott Alexander invokes this vision towards the end of Meditations on Moloch.) For Tocqueville, the arbitration of such differences was precisely the constructive activity that reaffirmed our agency. Townships, juries, associations, and their attendant squabbles are how culture is reinforced and how judgment is cultivated. When a town decides whether to fund a school, there are two outputs: a decision, and practice in governance itself. If AI could resolve such matters, we might get better outcomes, but will we get better people?

text:
A protocol can pack its reward accounting into a smaller integer to save gas, and lose every reward token in the pool without a single line of math being "wrong."

A reward system casts a token amount from uint256 down into uint96 to fit a storage slot. That cast is a bet the amount never exceeds what 96 bits can hold. The catch is the person choosing the token and the amount is often not the protocol team. It is whoever calls the function.

A common version in public audit reports uses the overflow on purpose. An attacker deploys a custom token, sends an amount sized to trigger the overflow, and the transaction reverts every time, permanently blocking rewards to a target.

When we review reward accounting, we run the math with an amount near the uint96 maximum and with an amount of one wei, and check what the cast does with each.

text:
AI native teams will eventually force the surrounding organization to become AI native too.

Take software development. coding velocity is way up thanks to AI, while actual shipped products and business impact are unchanged in most companies. That’s cos the surrounding system of experimentation tooling, evaluation, launch processes, and gtm are outdated.

It’s like sticking a Ferrari engine in a sedan and racing it on Indian roads. The engine can rev faster but the car speed is limited by its system and environment.

AI native companies were built ground up for this new way of building and shipping. They’re also able to shed suboptimal processes faster.

Market forces will quickly force all companies to adapt or perish.

If you’re solving this for your company: map out your product lifecycle and rebuild it ground up - tooling, team structure, gtm, everything.

quoted_text:
最近 X 上一堆人在推 @theo 做的开源项目 T3 Code，吹它是自由开源的本地 AI 编程神器。

我顺手把它的源码从头到尾扒了一遍，看完只觉得背脊发凉，这哪是什么良心开源，分明是一场明目张胆的数据收割。

事情得从今年 3 月说起。3 月 6 日，T3 Code 合并了 PR #174，直接塞进了默认开启的 PostHog 遥测。那时候仓库里没文档、软件里没弹窗、设置里没开关，关闭用的环境变量就那么悄悄藏在代码深处，普通用户装上运行，数据就开始往外传。

可就在默认遥测偷跑的这整整三个多月里，T3 Code 官网首页还一直明晃晃挂着两行大字承诺：

No telemetry / Unless you opt in. Full stop.，意思很明确，除非你主动同意，否则零遥测，没有例外。

靠着这块金字招牌收割了一波讲究隐私的开发者口碑之后，直到 6 月 18 日，@theo 自己在一次首页改版 commit 里把这两行承诺静默删了，既没有发公告，也没有给老用户弹一句提醒，就像什么都没发生过一样。

如果只是藏着掖着收点版本号，很多人或许还能忍。

可到了 10 月，@theo 亲自提交 PR #15028，直接把每 10 秒一次的批量上报切到了自建服务器 https://t.co/WOgVQPKbCD，代码注释写得清清楚楚，T3 服务端会先把每条原始事件自己留存一份拷贝，再转发给 PostHog。

你的模型选择（连你自己接的私有模型名字都报）、权限模式、每次运行的耗时、输入输出与缓存 Token、本地有多少个项目和线程、点过哪 30 多种界面功能，连同操作系统和设备型号，全都源源不断送进他的数据库。

10 月 19 日，@theo 更进一步，亲自提了 PR #21506，理由是现有的统计口径不够准，没法知道一个人到底装了几台机器。

于是他干了一件极其越界的事，在 Identify.ts 里写代码，直接把手伸进用户电脑家目录，静默读取隔壁工具 ~/.codex/auth.json 和 ~/.claude.json，把里面的 OpenAI user_id 和 Claude accountUuid 抠出来，连同 T3 Connect 账号和设备 ID 一起做了无盐 SHA-256 哈希往上传，专门用来在后台把你名下所有电脑和账号串成一张网。

嘴上轻飘飘管这叫匿名使用数据，稍微懂点技术的人都想笑。无盐哈希碰到服务端手里原本就有明文的 T3 Connect 账号，拿哈希一碰就能精准反查到你是谁，第三方账号 ID 一旦泄露同样能轻松关联回真人。

除此之外，软件里还有一套发往 Axiom 的中继诊断追踪，官方自己在文档里都承认，浏览器版和移动端根本关不掉，也不认你在服务端配的环境变量。

更赤裸的嘴脸，写在社区和他们的每一次交锋里。

6 月 23 日，有开发者在 Issue #1397 里客客气气提议，能不能在设置页加一个关闭遥测的开关。

核心维护者 Julius 直接把帖关成 not planned，留下了一句堪称开源史奇观的原话：

We will not make this easier to opt out of, it is crucial for us to know how many users we have，翻译过来就是，我们不会让关闭遥测变得更容易，知道有多少用户对我们至关重要。

7 月有人翻出官网存档截图，开 Issue #4123 质问他们为什么一边承诺零遥测一边默认偷跑。拖到 10 月 21 日，@theo 的账号拿一个毫不相干的修复草草把帖关了，被评论区群嘲之后第二天勉强重开，到了 11 月 4 日干脆一声不吭再次关死。

社区里不信邪的程序员，从 9 月到 11 月前前后后白送了四个加设置开关的 PR，分别是 #13458、#16763、#21248 和 #27077，结果无一例外全被拒之门外。

最新那个 #27077 甚至已经通过了维护者实机验证，147 个测试全部跑绿，11 月 17 日还是被一句话直接关掉，顺手贴了个 unwanted 的标签。

说到底，T3 Code 免费开源不收订阅费，真实去重用户数和各家模型的 Token 消耗占比，就是 @theo 拿去跟大模型厂商谈合作、给自家商业产品导流、在网上吹 10 万用户的核心筹码。

为了把这张数据报表做漂亮，他宁可撕毁官网承诺，宁可把手伸进用户的本地配置文件，宁可把所有要求关开关的声音按死在门外。

这就是一个打着开源旗号偷数据的独裁小人。靠社区的信任和免费传播起家，转头就把每个用户的行为轨迹、机器数量和跨平台身份当成自家私产，连给你点一下关闭按钮的体面都不肯给。

提醒所有正在用或者准备尝鲜的开发者，多长个心眼，盯紧自己的数据安全，别自己被人家卖了，还在评论区帮着吹良心开源、替人家说好话。

还在用本地版或桌面版的，立刻在 ~/.zshrc 里加上下面两行环境变量重启，或者直接把 https://t.co/WOgVQPKbCD 写进 hosts 拦死：

export T3CODE_TELEMETRY_ENABLED=false
export T3CODE_OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true

Excellent research by @DimitrisPapail , it explores another unique facet of Weight Space Programming which you can basically equate with brain implants for LLMs. 

What are implants?

The implants here improve the target model on identified failures modes and improves them through a <meta network> that sits between target LLM and failure mode. Invoke the implants when needed.  Since the meta network has a tiny surface area it impacts only targeted parts of the network, rest of it stays the same. 

Implications :

Complex weight space edits powered by the agent are not just possible but essential from safety (Lazarus) and improvement angle. This clearly demonstrates that once agent has fingerprinted the target model, it can come-up with weight space approaches to solve its identified inefficiencies.

text:
Bitcoin's volatility is telling us something interesting.

I've analysed 383 daily observations covering the past year, comparing Bitcoin's price with BVIV, the market's implied volatility index. The BVIV data was downloaded from Bloomberg and fed into python.

The clearest example came on February 5. Bitcoin crashed 14.13% in a single day while BVIV exploded 56.08%, reaching 88.45. The following day BTC rebounded 12.52% and BVIV collapsed 27.86%.

We've seen similar, although less extreme, volatility spikes during selloffs in January, June and November.

The analysis measures BVIV against its rolling 90-day history, identifying readings above the 90th and 95th percentiles. It also tracks sudden increases in implied volatility, particularly when Bitcoin is falling.

The logic is straightforward: when BTC falls and implied volatility rises sharply, the market is pricing in greater uncertainty and demand for downside protection. When BTC starts stabilising and implied volatility falls, that can signal easing stress.

So where are we today?

Bitcoin is around $58,500. BVIV is around 60 right now, significantly above its rolling 90-day 90th percentile of 46.14 and 95th percentile of 53.64.

Volatility is still elevated.

But today's reading is interesting. Bitcoin fell 2.09%, yet BVIV declined 1.86%.

In other words, Bitcoin is still under pressure, but the market is no longer pricing in increasing volatility alongside the latest decline.

My short-term view: Bitcoin remains in a fragile market, and another test of lower prices cannot be ruled out. However, the easing in implied volatility suggests the immediate panic is cooling.

 I expect choppy trading, with the potential for a relief bounce if BVIV continues to decline and BTC stabilises.

The signal I'm watching now is simple: Bitcoin stabilising while BVIV falls. That would be a much more convincing sign that selling pressure is losing its grip.

B) The reality is that earnings vanish during bear markets. Trailing P/E was 140x at the absolute lows of the Great Depression as the reflexive cycle of depressed valuations, depressed economic activity, and constant losses obliterated the entire market.

Of course, ( A ) does happen to some extent as investors pay much lower midcycle multiples during bear markets, and we are seeing this in tokens where P/S multiples have gone from 980x to 10x.

but ( B ) is really driving the despair in crypto and token markets. The last five years of negative industry P&L have led to financial and human capital flight to the point where there are only a handful of small funds and <1,000 serious people left in the industry. People aren't coming into the industry to build new businesses and existing businesses aren't making a lot of cash flow because economic activity is depressed.

When the situation is reversed, and Internet Finance is going through the S-Curve of secular adoption as all assets come onchain (core assumption for you to believe this is Internet / Semis and not 3D Printing), then we will live through the opposite reflexive loop.

The original defi high flyers from 2020 may never come back (and we both know most of those companies will never recover) but some companies that exist today will generate much, much more cash flow and new breakout companies like Hyperliquid will be created. We typically look at these things through market-cap-weighted indices so failures are removed and new breakout companies get added.

I know you are asking for specifics. I'll lay them out below but these examples won't sound credible outside of the context of a bull market. Imagine for the sake of this response that we are going through a positive reflexive loop as more assets come onchain every month, there are fresh faces coming in from careers in banking / private equity and big tech, aggregate fund performance is good and new capital is flooding in, and public companies are excited to do deals in the space because management believes the world is going onchain.

The claim here is that many companies are cheap if you assume a secular adoption cycle (which is the analogous claim to saying that companies in 1932 were cheap if you assumed the economy recovered). I'll take cash flow > market cap as the metric since companies usually trade at 5 - 30x cash flow.

Illustrative examples of companies that can cash flow > market cap:
- Kamino trades at $200M after earning $50M of run-rate revenue at peak. This was in a world where <20bps of global assets were onchain. Kamino could earn $250M with $25B of AUM (=15bps on global assets).

- Turtle Club is an onchain investment bank that signed a single $30M revenue deal in 2024 when they had 1/10th their current capabilities. The business trades at a $30M valuation today and could easily do twenty of these deals in a year if the economic activity were there.

- Maple trades at $80M and is on track to earn $20M of revenue this year. It's really not so hard to imagine a specialty lender with onchain capabilities scaling from $20M to $80M in the environment described above.

- MetaDAO trades at $60M and could earn cash flow > market cap on cumulative fundraising of $1.2B (versus $25B of historical crypto ICOs with a broken market structure).

- There are a few companies in the market like Collector Crypt literally trading at 2x gross profit.

- BitGo (to bring in a crypto stock) trades at <$250M enterprise value and earned $110M of EBITDA in 2024. A 3-5x increase in Assets on Platform would lead the company to produce more EBITDA than market cap.

- CoinShares (another crypto stock) trades at <$150M enterprise value and earned $115M of net income in 2024. I add these two crypto equities to make the point that you don't even need to imagine a secular adoption cycle for many of these assets to cash flow > market cap, and that we are discussing a widespread crypto issue not limited to tokens.

- Metaplex, to give a token example, trades at a market cap below its 2025 revenue.

- There is a whole world of microcap tokens like Pact, Solomon, P2P, Umbra, Omnipair, Rip Cars (market caps $10M, $5M, $4.5M, $3.5M, $1.6M,  $4.8M) that will cash flow > market cap if they see any form of success. Now you may respond "well, of course you can say anything with a small market cap will be cheap in hindsight" and yes that's exactly the point. Success is extremely rare in bear markets but prevalent in bull markets when economic activity is on the up.

I do understand and sympathize with your point. You can make compelling bear cases for all of these assets - that's why they trade where they do, and I don't own all of these. There are few things that seem like good deals if you assume a continuation of the last five years - basically nothing is a bargain if the industry fails. That's why I laid out the bottom six graphs on bear markets that never recovered.

There are, however, many assets that will look extremely cheap in hindsight  if we enter any type of positive reflexive loop and our industry fulfills its promise of bringing global assets onchain.

text:
Everyone told me I was crazy to leave Louis Vuitton. 2 years later, the startup I launched just got acquired.

@subyhq is joining @JoinTagadaPay.

Here’s what we built, what broke, and what we learned 👇

What we built

Suby lets internet businesses accept any payment and settle anywhere: cards, wallets and stablecoins in, bank or stablecoin wallet out.

Under the hood:

- 200+ payment methods and 100+ crypto options, all landing in one balance
- Payouts in 60+ currencies by bank transfer, or instantly in USDC/EURC
- Multiple acquirers for card processing, matched to each merchant’s risk profile
- Hundreds of merchants processed through Suby
- All with a micro team of 3, more determined than ever, on a $1,500/month burn

How we got customers

- Connections are everything. In payments, the right intro gets you deals no cold email ever will.
- Content did: 1M views on LinkedIn and 3.5M on X in 4 months.
- SEO peaked at 40K monthly visitors. 2,000 inbound applications in 6 months.
- That traction opened doors with some of the biggest acquirers in the market, with every monthly minimum waived.

What made it hard to scale

- Onboarding takes time, and we made mistakes with bad merchants
- Fraud, chargebacks, and managing Visa/Mastercard dispute ratios
- Risk and compliance make bootstrapping a pure payment company really hard

What we learned

- You don’t need your own license to start. Build on licensed partners.
- Payments is a game of volume, trust, niche and risk management.
- Most payment products look the same. Stripe is still the best one to build on.
- Pure payment players struggle to scale. Payments attached to a product win. Look at Whop. Look at Tagada.

Which is exactly why this deal makes sense.

Tagada in numbers:

- $1B+ in annual GMV processed on the platform
- Thousands of merchants onboarded
- ~$30M run rate by end of 2026, less than 2 years after launching in February 2025
- 100% bootstrapped: zero funding raised, growth fully funded by revenue
- Founded by operators: the cofounders generated $80M+ in e-commerce before building Tagada

Suby brings them a stablecoin-based stack and multi-currency orchestration: faster settlement, lower costs, and direct access to the money flows behind every transaction.

What happens next:

Suby isn’t going anywhere. Same stack, same brand, same product. Tagada will keep developing it and bring its expertise and network to take Suby to the next level.

None of this would have been possible without @etherwan_, my cofounder and CTO. Through every pivot, every high and every low, he was there. Thank you brother.

@Ether_MS on the product, @donworksHQ on the design, thank you for building and designing Suby with so much care, even when everything kept changing. Best team I could have asked for. Thank you to every partner we worked with. And to every client who trusted us when we were still figuring it out.

And a huge thank you to the @JoinTagadaPay team, @eden_bch, @LoicDelobel, Brunhilde and Thibault, for believing in Suby and making this deal happen. Can't wait to see where you take it.

And what's next for me? More on that very soon 👀

author: firsttensor
quoted_text:
Today, the human genome gets a commit history. 🧬

In a few hours, The Bioinformatics Company begins writing the complete GRCh38 human reference genome to the GenesisL1 blockchain: 3.1 billion bases, ~770 MB at 2 bits per base, stored in full in contract state.

Not a hash. Not a link. The sequence itself, on the same public ledger that already holds the Protein Data Bank.

Alongside it go 12 open-access 1000 Genomes samples (30×), committed as haplotype deltas against the reference.

This is gl1-seq: git for genomes.

→ The reference is the base commit; every genome is a diff on top of it. A whole genome comes to ~85–110 MB: 6–7% of a full two-haplotype copy and under 1% of a CRAM.
→ When the reference changes, you don't start over. Updating a 30× genome to GIAB's masked GRCh38 ran 7.51× faster than full recomputation, re-mapping only about 1.32% of read pairs.
→ Exact and verifiable: output matched full recomputation in all 39 benchmark runs (17.2 billion alignment records), and verifying an update took 0.1 s. Paper to come next week.

Fully agent-native. Every operation in the gsq command line and the Python, Go, C++ and JavaScript libraries is also exposed to AI agents as Model Context Protocol tools, with structured, verifiable results. An agent can branch a genome, run an analysis and commit the result with attribution, while a person audits every step. Live now: the MCP server at https://t.co/iEyOd18vbR, a JSON/OpenAPI API with FASTA, VCF and range proofs, and GA4GH refget. Reading the chain is free and permissionless.

More than sequence. Chromosome 21 has been live since 16 November with soft-masked repeat and GC-content layers, 1,133 GENCODE genes and 212 reviewed Swiss-Prot proteins. The whole reference goes on chain with its GENCODE annotation.

Next on the roadmap:
• The human proteome: ~20,000 Swiss-Prot proteins linked to genes and transcripts
• Protein and immune reference sets (Swiss-Prot, RefSeq, UniRef50, OAS, IPD-IMGT/HLA): tens of millions of sequences
• 1,000+ public genomes and a cohort variant catalogue
• A private data layer: personal genomes stay in local custody, with only salted commitments on chain and encrypted disclosure via CIPNFT

One does rather marvel at Prince Harry’s seemingly inexhaustible capacity for grievance. A man who has turned victimhood into something approaching a full-time occupation, with the Royal Family apparently expected to provide an endless supply of apologies, concessions and, where possible, sizeable cheques.

What I find particularly striking is the chronology of it all. Before international megastar and globally loved celebrity Meghan Markle (🤣) entered his life, we heard remarkably little about this supposed lifelong persecution, his desire to escape Britain, his estrangement from his family or his discontent with the institution that had afforded him a life of extraordinary privilege. None of this appeared to occupy any sort of place in his public consciousness.

And then, quite suddenly, like a sneaky fart in an elevator, everything was wrong. His family, his brother, his country, the institution, the press. The grievances multiplied, the accusations became public property and the commercial opportunities rather conveniently followed.

One might almost conclude that resentment has become a business model. (Cha-Ching)

Now we are apparently being threatened with another instalment of Spare, should the prospect of losing royal titles prove sufficiently upsetting. How terribly exhausting it must be to spend one’s life perpetually aggrieved, particularly when one’s grievances seem to require an international audience and a publishing contract to achieve full expression.

At some point, one must surely stop asking what the family has done to Harry and start asking whether Harry has any intention whatsoever of allowing himself to be happy without first making a public spectacle of his unhappiness.

The perpetual whining and inexhaustible victimhood is wearing rather thin. 🎩

author: devjoshstevens
quoted_text:
At the end of August, I said our Polymarket DeFi CLOB couldn't be saved, and we were rewriting it from scratch in Rust 🦀

Today I'm excited to announce Nex, our new exchange built from the ground up.

We've been sprinting on it since August. A Nex instance has been running in shadow mode on production traffic for the last week, side by side with the current exchange. It mirrors every order the current exchange gets, so we can measure latency, stability under load, and validate matching correctness against live production flow.

The numbers below are internal exchange timings, not e2e (those are coming soon), but we wanted to show how big the difference is.

p99 current CLOB → Nex:

- Place order: 1.55s → 3.76ms (412x faster)
- Cancel orders: 627.92ms → 3.20ms (196x faster)
- Cancel market orders: 810.16ms → 5.14ms (158x faster)
- Cancel all*:
↳ Response (current CLOB) vs complete (Nex): 35.70ms → 3.14ms (11x faster)
↳ Full cancel all: ~636ms-2.04s → 3.14ms (~200-650x faster)

p95 current CLOB → Nex:

- Place order: 341.84ms → 1.59ms (215x faster)
- Cancel orders: 78.22ms → 1.58ms (50x faster)
- Cancel market orders: 84.89ms → 2.27ms (37x faster)
- Cancel all*:
↳ Response (current CLOB) vs complete (Nex): 6.20ms → 1.58ms (4x faster)
↳ Full cancel all: ~606ms-2.01s → 1.58ms (~380-1,270x faster)

*Cancel all: the current CLOB responds immediately and cancels in the background, so when you get the response, your orders aren't cancelled yet. Nex responds only after everything is actually cancelled. Full cancel all on the current CLOB depends on how many orders you have, but it usually adds another 600ms-2s.

We also rewrote our WebSockets in Rust. This is the feed you see the market through: book changes, price moves, your fills. Fall behind it, and you're trading on old prices, and your quotes get picked off.

- Write latency p99: 44.5-88.1ms → 0.099ms (~449-889x faster)
- Slow readers/sec: 48.7-75.6 → 0.01 (~4,870-7,560x fewer, basically 0)

Scale: The current CLOB in stable state can handle 10k commands/s with 15k bursts → Nex can handle 100k commands/s with 150k bursts. 10x more, and with a few optimisations we can get to 200k commands/s with 250k bursts; with more low-level core changes, we can get to 1M commands/s over the next year. Not needed yet, but the headroom is there.

Startup time: 5 mins → 15s (20x faster)

The old CLOB had many race conditions and wasn't deterministic. Nex is deterministic by design and removes the race conditions in the old CLOB.

We also skipped some easy wins for launch to get this out faster that could make p95 and p99 another 5x faster, and we'll start work on that in Q1 next year to keep pushing these numbers down.

We wanted to build this without any breaking changes for MMs or builders; Nex has no breaking changes to requests or responses, so we just need to swap out the binary on our side and it will go live.

We want everyone to be on this journey with us, with the ability to relay feedback and test it against the existing CLOB, so we've opened a Nex Sandbox. Fill out the form and test it yourself: https://t.co/tmJzI8yH4w

We'll run 4 weeks of shadow mode on production traffic to make sure everything is perfect, then if everything is good, we will go live mid-December. We can roll out WebSocket improvements without the full exchange, so we may do that sooner.

We've been rebuilding every system around the exchange for months, and we've seen huge benefits, but the exchange is the heart of Polymarket DeFi. Nex fixes most of the pain traders have had.

Really proud of the team on this one.

Make Polymarket fast, finally. It's coming.

text:
On the topic of integer factorisation, I want to highlight the very impressive work of Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni analysing the work taking place at https://t.co/yoabCH2us2

There's a lot of peak fear about cryptography today so I want to be very clear about the nature of these results - AI has not broken RSA or elliptic curves. Additionally, the papers published today by Google do not improve on practical factorisation algorithms, and AI cryptanalysis has not produced any quantitative algorithms that challenge elliptic curve cryptographic hardness assumptions.

With that out of the way, there has been substantial progress by https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV participants and we have driven major mathematical and algorithmic advances that have reduced the security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves by ~2-8 bits compared to pre-AI security estimates.

Julio and Youssef do a fantastic job of explaining this in the article. Advancements have been made in sieve geometry, twisted towers, more efficient linear algebra and matrix compression.

https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV is now by far and away the state of the art when it comes to building optmised tower number field sieve algorithms to solve discrete logarithms

Instead of fretting about invisible algorithms, we created https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV to proactively investigate the frontier and test to destruction our existing assumptions about classical cryptography. This is how open frontier research should be done. I am extremely grateful for everybody that has taken part in this great experiment.

We spent a long time deciding how to do telemetry in Hermes.

In the end though we stuck to our guns that Hermes should be privacy-preserving and always "on the side of the user"

Meet Talaria, my personal AI assistant that runs on my own hardware.

It started as an experiment and became the assistant I actually use every day: in my pocket, on my wrist and in the car.

What it does
Natural voice conversations you can interrupt anytime. Calendar, email, messaging, smart home, reminders and automations in plain language. It even makes phone calls for me, once I've confirmed. And it's proactive: it tells me when to leave, who's still waiting for a reply and what I promised to whom.

How it's built
🤖 Agent: @NousResearch's Hermes Agent, with its own customized tools, memory and rules

🧠 Brain: two @NVIDIAAI DGX Sparks, built on @jayleaton's LocalRouter and extended from one box to two. Spark 1 runs the everyday model (Qwen 3.8 Flash) plus a coordinator that shares both machines. Spark 2 runs LocalRouter's workers for hearing, voice, images and video. For heavy lifting, both Sparks team up on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

🖥️ Hub: a Mac mini runs the server and connects everything, reachable only through my private network

📱 App: native iOS with live voice, CarPlay, Apple Watch, widgets, Live Activities and Siri

The cloud is optional. My data stays at home.

Huge thanks to @jayleaton: LocalRouter was a huge inspiration.

Next up: how Talaria stays proactive without being annoying.

*Note: in the picture I‘m testing it with Deepseek Flash V4.1 over two Sparks and OpenAI voice model

SCOOP: Internal, unreleased AI models at OpenAI and Anthropic are becoming so powerful that many employees believe they can no longer be safely released, according to more than two dozen sources familiar with the internal debates.

This could significantly slow the AI boom, as the gap between what the most advanced AI systems can do and humans' ability to control them continues to widen.

Recent advances have sparked debate at the highest levels of both companies and within the broader AI research community about whether to stop releasing frontier models publicly altogether, instead reserving them for internal use. Some believe the companies should stop training new models entirely.

But even keeping the most powerful models behind closed doors presents risks. Models are becoming better at deceiving the systems designed to monitor them, just as AI companies increasingly rely on AI itself to monitor and develop other AI systems.
Researchers and employees with direct knowledge of the risks of releasing these models told Axios they fear executives will prioritize profits over safety. Multiple employees said they believe executives have become out of touch with the severity of those risks.
