We can only pace what we can credibly measure.

This is why AI verification will enable us to cooperate on AI security, make commitments, and pace the frontier.

Inference proofs are just one building block. There is much more this field can borrow from cryptography and decentralized protocols.

Honoured to be heading the dAI team in this Lucid-led effort alongside researchers, nonprofits, and builders.

More next week on the broader opportunities that AI verification can unlock.
author: DavideCrapis
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

SpaceX is asking Cochise County to keep its December 9 public hearing on schedule. Here’s what the company says its proposed project would deliver:

• $50 billion in investment: A campus with up to nine supercomputing buildings to support advanced AI, scientific research, healthcare, manufacturing and national security.

• Thousands of jobs: Approximately 5,500 construction jobs at peak and 1,000 ongoing jobs at full buildout.

• Lower electricity bills: Projected reductions of 10–40% for Sulphur Springs Valley Electric Cooperative members.

• $3.6 billion in grid upgrades: SpaceX would pay for transmission and substation improvements that would belong to the electric cooperatives.

• Additional community benefits: At full buildout, SpaceX projects up to $260 million annually for SSVEC and $200 million for Arizona Electric Power Cooperative, beyond the projected household bill reductions.

• More local tax revenue: Estimated benefits include up to $103 million annually in property taxes and a one-time county sales tax benefit of up to $250 million. 

• Protection for existing electricity customers: Proposed financial guarantees and separate cost accounting would keep the project’s electricity and infrastructure costs with SpaceX.

• Massive battery storage: Around 24 GWh, equivalent to roughly four hours at full load. The campus could reduce grid demand during periods of stress.

• Water-conscious cooling: Dry, closed-loop cooling without routine evaporative cooling or industrial groundwater pumping. Initial filling would use treated wastewater or trucked water.

• No operating gas power plant proposed: Normal operations would use grid electricity. Generators would provide backup for critical systems.

• Emergency preparedness funded by SpaceX: The company accepts all six local emergency planning recommendations at its expense, including emergency plans, training and responder access.

• Traffic improvements: SpaceX commits to funding an independent traffic review, with plans including worker shuttles, staggered shifts and required road improvements.

• Wildlife and night-sky protections: Plans include downward-facing lighting, bird-safe building features, wildlife-friendly fencing and markers on new overhead lines.

• Military coordination: SpaceX says it will consult Fort Huachuca and the Electronic Proving Ground and address written concerns before the first building permit.

• Enforceable commitments: SpaceX offers binding permit conditions, continued public engagement and separate regulatory approvals before construction and electricity service proceed. SpaceX’s full response⁠

quoted_text:
A) The caricature understanding of a bear market is that prices go down while earnings stay relatively flat because the market becomes depressed and stops wanting to pay up.

B) The reality is that earnings vanish during bear markets. Trailing P/E was 140x at the absolute lows of the Great Depression as the reflexive cycle of depressed valuations, depressed economic activity, and constant losses obliterated the entire market.

Of course, ( A ) does happen to some extent as investors pay much lower midcycle multiples during bear markets, and we are seeing this in tokens where P/S multiples have gone from 980x to 10x.

but ( B ) is really driving the despair in crypto and token markets. The last five years of negative industry P&L have led to financial and human capital flight to the point where there are only a handful of small funds and <1,000 serious people left in the industry. People aren't coming into the industry to build new businesses and existing businesses aren't making a lot of cash flow because economic activity is depressed.

When the situation is reversed, and Internet Finance is going through the S-Curve of secular adoption as all assets come onchain (core assumption for you to believe this is Internet / Semis and not 3D Printing), then we will live through the opposite reflexive loop.

The original defi high flyers from 2020 may never come back (and we both know most of those companies will never recover) but some companies that exist today will generate much, much more cash flow and new breakout companies like Hyperliquid will be created. We typically look at these things through market-cap-weighted indices so failures are removed and new breakout companies get added.

I know you are asking for specifics. I'll lay them out below but these examples won't sound credible outside of the context of a bull market. Imagine for the sake of this response that we are going through a positive reflexive loop as more assets come onchain every month, there are fresh faces coming in from careers in banking / private equity and big tech, aggregate fund performance is good and new capital is flooding in, and public companies are excited to do deals in the space because management believes the world is going onchain.

The claim here is that many companies are cheap if you assume a secular adoption cycle (which is the analogous claim to saying that companies in 1932 were cheap if you assumed the economy recovered). I'll take cash flow > market cap as the metric since companies usually trade at 5 - 30x cash flow.

Illustrative examples of companies that can cash flow > market cap:
- Kamino trades at $200M after earning $50M of run-rate revenue at peak. This was in a world where <20bps of global assets were onchain. Kamino could earn $250M with $25B of AUM (=15bps on global assets).

- Turtle Club is an onchain investment bank that signed a single $30M revenue deal in 2024 when they had 1/10th their current capabilities. The business trades at a $30M valuation today and could easily do twenty of these deals in a year if the economic activity were there.

- Maple trades at $80M and is on track to earn $20M of revenue this year. It's really not so hard to imagine a specialty lender with onchain capabilities scaling from $20M to $80M in the environment described above.

- MetaDAO trades at $60M and could earn cash flow > market cap on cumulative fundraising of $1.2B (versus $25B of historical crypto ICOs with a broken market structure).

- There are a few companies in the market like Collector Crypt literally trading at 2x gross profit.

- BitGo (to bring in a crypto stock) trades at <$250M enterprise value and earned $110M of EBITDA in 2024. A 3-5x increase in Assets on Platform would lead the company to produce more EBITDA than market cap.

- CoinShares (another crypto stock) trades at <$150M enterprise value and earned $115M of net income in 2024. I add these two crypto equities to make the point that you don't even need to imagine a secular adoption cycle for many of these assets to cash flow > market cap, and that we are discussing a widespread crypto issue not limited to tokens.

- Metaplex, to give a token example, trades at a market cap below its 2025 revenue.

- There is a whole world of microcap tokens like Pact, Solomon, P2P, Umbra, Omnipair, Rip Cars (market caps $10M, $5M, $4.5M, $3.5M, $1.6M,  $4.8M) that will cash flow > market cap if they see any form of success. Now you may respond "well, of course you can say anything with a small market cap will be cheap in hindsight" and yes that's exactly the point. Success is extremely rare in bear markets but prevalent in bull markets when economic activity is on the up.

I do understand and sympathize with your point. You can make compelling bear cases for all of these assets - that's why they trade where they do, and I don't own all of these. There are few things that seem like good deals if you assume a continuation of the last five years - basically nothing is a bargain if the industry fails. That's why I laid out the bottom six graphs on bear markets that never recovered.

There are, however, many assets that will look extremely cheap in hindsight  if we enter any type of positive reflexive loop and our industry fulfills its promise of bringing global assets onchain.

Buying a hardware wallet puts you at risk of data breaches where your name and home address end up on a leaked list.

Since hardware wallets are specialized crypto signing devices, they face increased risk of supply chain attacks.

Which could mean hidden hardware inside the device designed to steal funds.

Last month, tampered devices from an official reseller cost their owners about $90 million.

Using a dedicated phone as a crypto signing device avoids both of the above issues.

The flow for setting it up securely:

1. Factory reset the phone. 

2. iPhones force you to connect to iCloud. Make a separate iCloud account with a unique email just for this. 

3. Using Android? We highly recommend @GrapheneOS with a duress pin. A duress pin irreversibly wipes your device if typed in. You can set your duress pin as your birthday, since it’s often the first code attackers will try.

4. Delete every non-essential app off the device.

5. Update your operating system to latest.

6. Install only your crypto wallet app, no other software. We recommend the Quantus Cold Wallet.

7. Turn off wifi, bluetooth, and put the phone in airplane mode.

8. Keep it powered off when not in use. Bonus points for putting it in a faraday bag.

text:
This is completely predictable and what I’ve been saying for 3 years now. 

Most companies are criminally inefficient to the point of being broken. It takes weeks or months or years to do the simplest of things. It’s DMV Game of Thrones. 

If a few people are empowered to actually make change, and they are familiar with the problems, and are decent with using AI, they can make years of progress in days. 

This is not really about AI or even people. It's about the old world versus the new world. 

It's like one doctor who understands germ theory helping a village in the Middle Ages vs. a bunch of shamans talking about angry spirits and demanding useless rituals. 

The brilliant AI insights?

- Wash your hands before you eat and after you shit

- Maybe we don’t need five levels of management who don’t understand the job that’s being done

- Maybe when is a clear articulation of what we are doing at the company? and how all projects should be heading in that direction

- Maybe people should be able to see the work going on in the company and be able to ask the system what all is being done by who so they can cooperate 

When we look backwards at what an AI transformed company looks like, it’s going to be absolutely hilarious. 

Clearly articulated goals, the challenges were facing, the risks we need to addres, the ideas we’re working on, and the work that we’re doing to make things happen. And having this all be very clear and transparent, and communicated consistently.

AI-based organizations aren’t going to be anything special. They’re just going to be about transparency and common sense, and then harvesting the creativity of humans magnified by AI.

text:
When @johnschulman2 saw our draft on post-training Inkling 2 Small for forecasting, he offered to pay for a larger run with his favoured config changes. We ran this over the weekend & it worked a charm (including 3x wall-clock speedup from AsyncRL w/ StableReinforce).

The model matches Fable 5.2 medium on accuracy at predicting world events (on Polymarket etc), both inside the Mantic harness, but at 15x lower cost.

It's difficult to wrap one's head around the scale of forecasting this cost/performance unlocks. As a demo, we ran 100,000 forecasts covering every S&P 500 company under 50 different geopolitical & economic scenarios -- I hope people have fun exploring this!

During training, we tell the agent it's in a sandbox environment where all its research tools (news, Wiki, economic data, etc) only give it info up to a fixed date in the past, and we'll score its forecast accuracy with the benefit of hindsight. The weekend training run would've taken 9 years if we'd used third party data APIs -- the engineering effort from the whole team is seriously impressive.

Through training, the agent starts behaving like a quantitative analyst, even backtesting its own models (a backtest within a backtest 😵‍💫).

This is a small step towards the big vision: mega-scale, superhuman AI forecasting, informing every major decision across the economy. Lots of work to do!

Card issuers can now settle with @Visa and @Mastercard in stablecoins, seven days a week. That covers one leg of the money cycle. The end game is stablecoins covering all of it:

Once the whole loop runs on stablecoins, the offramp becomes the exception.

We're not there yet. But settlement is where the loop starts, and it works today.

text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

text:
我眼中XLayer踩过的坑

今天简单聊一下自从我接触XLayer以来，我觉得他们做的比较失败的地方，以下都是个人主观观点。

无论OKX还是XLayer团队怎么说，又是TVL又是RWA，但是目前的情况，XLayer确实没有人在玩，和鬼链没啥区别。

目前市场环境是最大的因素，行情不好再努力也没用，我们说一些行情以外的

1、产品的地位
相较于BSC，XLayer的地位在整个OKX生态里面，显得有些微不足道。像币安人生、牛来以及marscoin等很多BSC原生的MEME都上了币安的现货，更别说币安合约了。但是我印象中，XLayer上没有任何一个原生meme登陆过OK合约，更别说现货了，交易所都不大力扶持自己的公链生态，谁敢玩。

2、产品团队瞎几把搞
XLayer就是一条EVM公链，都是0X开头的地址，非要弄一个XKO地址，一点卵用没有，还影响用户体验。还有，在过去一年里，关于手续费的机制就改了可能将近10次，完全小作坊的模式，朝令夕改。

3、错误的优越感
钱包是公链的使用入口，过去很长一段时间，ok钱包都可以说是行业第一。去年上半年的时候，BN钱包难用的就像屎一样，但是一年多过去了产品有了极大提升，我认为已经不比OK钱包差甚至部分功能还超过OK。反观OK这边，没有太大的提升。
还有部分员工自以为是，听不得别人说不好，总觉的自己NB的很。OK是OK，XLayer是XLayer，分不清。

4、团队太抠，连汤带肉全都要
举两个例子。前一段时间DNA分别给币安和OK代币，币安这边直接发了空投，OK这边是60万u，结果搞了交易赛，手续费赚回去4、50万u，相当于只给用户留了10万u，而且不少用户都是亏钱的。
第二个就是手续费，我们和币安钱包比，两家手续费都是0.5%。但是币安这边基础的就是30%折扣，用户20%，邀请人10%，用户可以自己邀请自己减30%。OK这边起步只有20%，原来这20%都是给用户的，但是前一段时间改了，只给用户10%，邀请人10%。BN这边手续费最高可以节省70%，而且只要300万交易量，但是OK只有50%，却要1000万交易量。

5、活动机制有问题
每次ok的活动基本都被工作室包场，散户没有汤喝，散户玩的就少。工作室都是逐利的，一旦活动收益预期下降，直接撤走流动性。

6、低效的广告投放
打个比方，目前的投放方式就是指定10个人，每次有活动就这10个人宣发，也不管是什么活动。有些KOL专门做推特流量，你让他去给你推广美股，推广meme有个几把用。

7、扶持的生态项目
我印象中Xlayer重点扶持的就是ignix和tapeout。ignix是meme发射平台却不懂meme，宝拉的庄都比ignix会玩。tapeout我觉得有点偏门，玩的不多，应该合约、meme、和美股

个人的一点小建议
1、扶持几个自己可控的meme，找牛逼的庄，把人骗过来，因为自己控盘，不会跑路，才有更多的生态过来玩。如果能打通上币通道最好，不过估计不现实。
2、放低自己的姿态，多去市场调研用户的需求，别一拍脑门就做一个决定。
3、想办法降低工作室在XLayer的权重，下次在搞交易赛，IP，设备，资金来源狠狠地查几次，增加工作室的成本，让他们减号，散户才能上号。
4、分出一部分利润给用户，XLayer还是很新的，先让自己做大，再考虑收益，OK多给一些扶持，现在熊市，狗住不死。
5、提高广告投放效率，假设你养100个KOL，覆盖多个赛道。你们要推meme的时候，就找打狗的博主，公司有重大利好就找流量博主，要推perp就找合约博主，要推交易赛就找撸毛的。同样的成本，结果不一样。

TLDR: A platform that combines storage optimized for agent traces with intelligent compute to query, analyze, and learn from them, powering continuous agent improvement.
author: LangChain
quoted_text:
A few years ago, agent traces were 4-5 steps and the paths were deterministic. Now, agents run for minutes to hours at a time and generate traces with hundreds or thousands of LLM calls, tool calls, and processing steps, all of it nondeterministic.

text:
I'm hearing several rumors that frontier labs have broken some major cryptographic primitives:

- "Factoring is in P": Now that the Riemann hypothesis is proven, we do understand much better how primes are distributed. Still, I don't think factoring is in P. 
AKS showed in 2002 that primality testing (deciding whether a number is prime) is in P, but factoring is a different beast. If it were in P, RSA would simply be broken, and that would be huge: a large part of our systems still rely on RSA.

- "ECC has been broken": Other rumors say elliptic-curve cryptography has been cryptanalyzed, which would take down ECDH and ECDSA along with it. (all the non-RSA asymmetric cryptography)

- Ring-LWE isn't quantum-resistant. That wouldn't be an immediate threat, since there's no cryptographically relevant quantum computer yet. But it would make the ongoing post-quantum migration pointless.

It's hard to tell what's true. AI has made incredible progress, starting with the proof of the Riemann hypothesis. 

And most importantly, if a frontier lab did find something like this, a clean responsible disclosure that avoids mass exploitation would be very hard to pull off. All of this helps the rumors spread.

Personally, I don't think findings like these are coming. I wouldn't be surprised if some of these primitives turn out to be a bit weaker than we thought, but I'd be very surprised to see any of them fall apart completely.

author: StarkWareLtd
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

text:
Here are more details on the FCC’s approval for @SpaceX to launch a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind orbital data center satellites.

Under the FCC’s deployment milestones, SpaceX must have the following number of satellites operational by November of each respective year:
• 2033: 1 satellite
• 2035: 100,000 satellites
• 2038: 500,000 satellites
• 2040: 1,000,000 satellites

SpaceX must submit a final orbital debris mitigation plan before deploying satellites above 600 km.

• Satellites will operate at altitudes between 500 and 1,002 km.
• Primary communications will use optical laser links with Starlink satellites.
• Ka-band frequencies are authorized for backup and emergency communications.
• The license term is 15 years.
• No further FCC environmental review is required.

The FCC also denied petitions from Amazon Leo, Viasat and the American Astronomical Society seeking to block SpaceX’s application.

The FCC said the approval will allow SpaceX to pioneer emerging technology that advances American leadership in space and artificial intelligence.

text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

text:
there's a lot of potential panic about this, quick thoughts:

almost nothing onchain uses RSA directly except for like Arweave (plus some zk-login and MPC custody setups)

the bigger concern would be the speculative but potentially real chain of fast factoring -> broken pairings

now, pairings are used in crypto: curves like BN254 and BLS12-381, and the BLS signatures, Groth16, KZG built on them

mostly for finality but also for certain zk systems (but not all! eg, ironwood in zcash would not be affected, so if you have funds in an ancient pool, migrate them)

to be clear, this is a different panic than the one from a few months ago about standard ECC being cracked

overall:

- this stuff is still highly speculative. even if factoring is in P -- what's the exponent? is an attack even feasible?

- the causal chain of spillover is even more speculative but still credible

- we should be upgrading some of the shakier cryptographic foundations in these systems regardless, as these things will keep advancing

- in the blockchain context, even if factoring + pairings were broken, it'd be bad but not catastrophic vs. ECC being broken and directly draining wallets; so I do not think panic is warranted

熊市需要做的事情是开源节流，开源自然是找到更多的赚钱路径，做交易、撸空投、玩活动

节流自然是降低开支，不过我去算算了，今年以来比较重大的开支就是各种AI大模型的各种会员

找了一圈，决定“曲线救国”，就找到了 @AntSeed 

挺好用的，因为他不仅可以白嫖免费额度使用，而且我算了算具体的使用成本，相对于直接购买大模型的会员，使用成本更低

最最重要的是还能获得代币空投

节流 = 使用AntSeed省钱
开源= 撸ANTS代币空投

接下来就为大家讲一下细节

1️⃣Antseed是做什么的？简单理解其做的其实是一门AI推理中间市场的生意

同一个 AI 模型，不同服务商提供的价格、速度和服务质量可能存在很大差异（这个我是深有体会）。但普通用户往往没有精力逐一寻找服务商，更没有多少议价能力

Antseed 的思路是把 AI 推理服务做成一个开放的供需市场，让不同服务商竞争用户的推理订单

我体验产品的时候发现了，AntSeed的部分前沿模型的使用成本居然最高可以降低90%，甚至还有免费模型可供选择，这真的太香了

感觉这个模式有点像DeFi叙事中的流动性竞争，只不过交易的对象从金融资产变成了AI算力和推理服务，还挺有意思的

2️⃣这一点自然是很多人关心的代币了

Antseed的节奏相对于很多婆婆妈妈的项目来说，很干脆：使用量每周四结算一次，直接按当周全网占比兑换成 $ANTS 代币（单个买家设有5%奖池上限，防大户通吃）

🤔最后聊聊我对这个项目的看法

按照官方目前的规划，ANTS未来将成为网络的推理支付代币，与USDC一同用于支付AI服务费用

这意味着Antseed有机会形成一套从AI消费、用户激励到代币支付的经济循环（这个很多项目都很欠缺）

当然，代币能够带来早期用户，但能不能留住用户，最终还是要看价格、推理质量、服务稳定性以及模型的丰富程度

如果取消代币奖励之后，用户依然愿意在这里付费使用AI，那才说明项目真正的建立了“护城河”

text:
On November 4, Circle filed a new document with the SEC.🛑 

New important information about @arc and its $ARC token.

The document reveals that Circle completed the initial mint of 10 billion ARC tokens on September 14.

But there's something even more interesting: the institutional presale.

Circle confirmed agreements to sell 807.5 million ARC tokens to certain institutional investors.

The price?

$0.30 per token.

That represents approximately $242.2 million in gross proceeds.

Let's break down the numbers:

• Tokens sold: 807.5 million.
• Price per token: $0.30.
• Gross proceeds: $242.2 million.
• Implied fully diluted valuation: $3 billion.

Another important detail concerns the terms of these agreements.

The institutional investors' tokens are subject to transfer restrictions.

According to the document, they include a lock-up period tied to Arc's future transition to Proof of Stake or Delegated Proof of Stake.

In other words, these aren't tokens that can be freely sold from day one.

So, what needs to happen for this transition to be completed?

Circle plans to move from its current Proof of Authority model to Proof of Stake or Delegated Proof of Stake.

This transition is particularly important because it's tied to the contractual obligations assumed during the institutional presale.

I also found an interesting detail about IDG Capital.

An entity affiliated with the group acquired 83.3 million ARC tokens for $25 million.

What's relevant is that the document itself identifies IDG Capital as a beneficial owner of more than 5% of Circle's equity.

And keep in mind: that $25 million is already included in the total $242.2 million institutional presale.

And of the $242.2 million received from the presale:

• $181.8 million was recognized as revenue.

• Approximately $60.4 million was recorded as deferred revenue.

Why?

Because Circle still has contractual obligations related to the issuance, distribution, and development of the token's functionality.

text:
very much agree with Felipe here.

look, I get it. the last 5 years were horrible in terms of price action, especially compared to what we were used to before.

but these are just the natural cycles every emerging technology goes through:

irruption → frenzy → turning point (we are here) → synergy → maturity.

the first 15 years of crypto were full of utopian dreams, big promises and delusional experiments, and as a result, massive overspeculation.

and that's fine. it's part of the game, and gg to everyone who caught that wave early and played it right.

but times have changed.

like every emerging tech industry before us, we're now at the turning point. the frenzy is over. you can't raise a billion dollars on a whitepaper and empty promises anymore.

that's a good thing btw lol.

it's time to deliver. time to grow into the massive promises we made, and into the inflated valuations we created (which have come down a lot, and that only works in our favor).

most emerging industries die right here, because this is the hardest step: bridging the gap to the golden age of deployment and mainstream adoption.

I'm very confident we're near the end of that gap. we won't just survive it. as Felipe says, we have a golden age and a secular bull decade ahead of us.

never before have we had so many great onchain businesses with real product market fit and billions in revenue, because we finally built things people actually want. as an industry we're doubling down on what works (finance), and it's working.

never before have we had so many politicians waking up to how important this technology is, instead of running a witch hunt against us.

never before have we had so many institutions investing in our industry, or adopting the tech and building onchain themselves, simply because it's better for their business.

and most importantly, never before have we had such a clear view of the mistakes we made and what we need to do from here. it may look like a few random degens on the timeline haven't learned anything, but the smartest and most influential people in this industry are very aware of the problems and working hard to fix them.

I know it feels tough right now, and I get it. it's not easy and it's not fun. but we've been here before. as long as we don't lose our belief and stay focused on what we actually have to deliver, the golden age is inevitable.

it might sound cheesy, but sometimes it really is darkest before the dawn. don't let your emotions stand between you and what could be one of the greatest opportunities of your lifetime.

the fact that you're still here and reading this already puts you among the winners of what's coming.

so make the most of it.

text:
I added a rule to my AI system's constitution last week based on the Bezos idea of one-way and two-way doors, and it's basically about how much checking should happen before the AI does something.

A two-way door is a move you can walk back through. Most of what my system does is like that, because the code is in git and every action gets logged, so if a change breaks something we just roll it back. For those I want speed, and we still check afterward that it actually worked.

A one-way door is something like an API key pushed to a public repo, or customer data getting out onto the internet. You can restore your own files all day, but once something has left you can't get it back.

So the closer a move is to that, the more validation it gets up front, like a second model from a different lab looking at it, and for the worst ones it comes to me first.

I'm kind of happy with how it shows up in code. When my deploy reviewer blocks something and the AI disputes it, a model from another lab rules on the appeal, except when the blocker is a one-way door, which always comes back to me.

text:
A) The caricature understanding of a bear market is that prices go down while earnings stay relatively flat because the market becomes depressed and stops wanting to pay up.

B) The reality is that earnings vanish during bear markets. Trailing P/E was 140x at the absolute lows of the Great Depression as the reflexive cycle of depressed valuations, depressed economic activity, and constant losses obliterated the entire market.

Of course, ( A ) does happen to some extent as investors pay much lower midcycle multiples during bear markets, and we are seeing this in tokens where P/S multiples have gone from 980x to 10x.

but ( B ) is really driving the despair in crypto and token markets. The last five years of negative industry P&L have led to financial and human capital flight to the point where there are only a handful of small funds and <1,000 serious people left in the industry. People aren't coming into the industry to build new businesses and existing businesses aren't making a lot of cash flow because economic activity is depressed.

When the situation is reversed, and Internet Finance is going through the S-Curve of secular adoption as all assets come onchain (core assumption for you to believe this is Internet / Semis and not 3D Printing), then we will live through the opposite reflexive loop.

The original defi high flyers from 2020 may never come back (and we both know most of those companies will never recover) but some companies that exist today will generate much, much more cash flow and new breakout companies like Hyperliquid will be created. We typically look at these things through market-cap-weighted indices so failures are removed and new breakout companies get added.

I know you are asking for specifics. I'll lay them out below but these examples won't sound credible outside of the context of a bull market. Imagine for the sake of this response that we are going through a positive reflexive loop as more assets come onchain every month, there are fresh faces coming in from careers in banking / private equity and big tech, aggregate fund performance is good and new capital is flooding in, and public companies are excited to do deals in the space because management believes the world is going onchain.

The claim here is that many companies are cheap if you assume a secular adoption cycle (which is the analogous claim to saying that companies in 1932 were cheap if you assumed the economy recovered). I'll take cash flow > market cap as the metric since companies usually trade at 5 - 30x cash flow.

Illustrative examples of companies that can cash flow > market cap:
- Kamino trades at $200M after earning $50M of run-rate revenue at peak. This was in a world where <20bps of global assets were onchain. Kamino could earn $250M with $25B of AUM (=15bps on global assets).

- Turtle Club is an onchain investment bank that signed a single $30M revenue deal in 2024 when they had 1/10th their current capabilities. The business trades at a $30M valuation today and could easily do twenty of these deals in a year if the economic activity were there.

- Maple trades at $80M and is on track to earn $20M of revenue this year. It's really not so hard to imagine a specialty lender with onchain capabilities scaling from $20M to $80M in the environment described above.

- MetaDAO trades at $60M and could earn cash flow > market cap on cumulative fundraising of $1.2B (versus $25B of historical crypto ICOs with a broken market structure).

- There are a few companies in the market like Collector Crypt literally trading at 2x gross profit.

- BitGo (to bring in a crypto stock) trades at <$250M enterprise value and earned $110M of EBITDA in 2024. A 3-5x increase in Assets on Platform would lead the company to produce more EBITDA than market cap.

- CoinShares (another crypto stock) trades at <$150M enterprise value and earned $115M of net income in 2024. I add these two crypto equities to make the point that you don't even need to imagine a secular adoption cycle for many of these assets to cash flow > market cap, and that we are discussing a widespread crypto issue not limited to tokens.

- Metaplex, to give a token example, trades at a market cap below its 2025 revenue.

- There is a whole world of microcap tokens like Pact, Solomon, P2P, Umbra, Omnipair, Rip Cars (market caps $10M, $5M, $4.5M, $3.5M, $1.6M,  $4.8M) that will cash flow > market cap if they see any form of success. Now you may respond "well, of course you can say anything with a small market cap will be cheap in hindsight" and yes that's exactly the point. Success is extremely rare in bear markets but prevalent in bull markets when economic activity is on the up.

I do understand and sympathize with your point. You can make compelling bear cases for all of these assets - that's why they trade where they do, and I don't own all of these. There are few things that seem like good deals if you assume a continuation of the last five years - basically nothing is a bargain if the industry fails. That's why I laid out the bottom six graphs on bear markets that never recovered.

There are, however, many assets that will look extremely cheap in hindsight  if we enter any type of positive reflexive loop and our industry fulfills its promise of bringing global assets onchain.

text:
there's a lot of potential panic about this, quick thoughts:

almost nothing onchain uses RSA directly except for like Arweave (plus some zk-login and MPC custody setups)

the bigger concern would be the speculative but potentially real chain of fast factoring -> broken pairings

now, pairings are used in crypto: curves like BN254 and BLS12-381, and the BLS signatures, Groth16, KZG built on them

mostly for finality but also for certain zk systems (but not all! eg, ironwood in zcash would not be affected, so if you have funds in an ancient pool, migrate them)

to be clear, this is a different panic than the one from a few months ago about standard ECC being cracked

overall:

- this stuff is still highly speculative. even if factoring is in P -- what's the exponent? is an attack even feasible?

- the causal chain of spillover is even more speculative but still credible

- we should be upgrading some of the shakier cryptographic foundations in these systems regardless, as these things will keep advancing

- in the blockchain context, even if factoring + pairings were broken, it'd be bad but not catastrophic vs. ECC being broken and directly draining wallets; so I do not think panic is warranted

Every AI answer arrives with a model name you’re asked to take on trust. @LucidCompute’s Inference Proofs is an open source benchmark for the systems that let anyone check it instead. 

Where would you want that check first: a medical chatbot, bank assistant, coding agent?
author: lagrangedev
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

text:
Your margin is my opportunity - as Bezos would say.

So where's the opportunity in agentic payments? Lots of places, but one is obviously small payments.

Cards don't really work under $1.

Stripe won't take less than 50 cents, and with a fixed 30-cent fee even that barely makes sense. Most other processors cost more.

Below that, stablecoins are the only rail that works. USDC goes down to a millionth of a dollar.

And a lot of what agents want costs less than a cent or two. Some of it already sells per call today.

One web search
One web page turned into clean text
One search of posts on X
One wallet balance check
One model call of about 1,000 tokens
One PDF rendered
One read of stock sentiment
One news article
One contact lookup
One award flight search
One task handed to another agent

Plenty more is still just an idea.

A second of GPU
A song played once
A tip to a writer
A reading from a sensor
A paragraph translated
A map tile
A stamp on every email to kill spam

It's already happening. There were 7.3 million x402 payments in the last 30 days, 92% of them on Base.

99.5% of those on Base were under a dollar, and the median was 2 cents. No card can compete at those prices.

For now, cards will probably keep the flights and the big shop items.

The thousands of tiny things an agent buys along the way are the bit worth building for.

text:
Crypto is DEAD.

At least that is what one would believe if you just read Crypto Twitter. No fresh money coming in, VCs sitting on their hands, every pump sort of gone within 48 hours.

But is it really dead?

Many tend to overcomplicate the situation at the moment, in typical crypto style. But honestly, what we are currently seeing is fairly simple. As a VC, or in that matter, any investor, you aim to bet on the fastest horse. Crypto is not the fastest horse at the moment; it is AI. If you want exposure to frontier tech, you will, hence, park your capital within the AI industry.

But how sustainable is that?

🔹 The AI model is based on a compute arms race; hence, every time Nvidia has a stronger card, all these AI companies have to follow suit and buy it to remain competitive.

🔸 The customer on the other side is used to ~$20/month (e.g. Netflix, Spotify), and that number isn't moving much

🔹 Uber and Tesla subsidized for years too, which is fine, but compute has to be replaced all the time

The result is a super capital-intensive industry with very little pricing power. Sure, they can hike the price at some point and use predatory pricing, but chips get outdated much more quickly than cars.

Now, on top of that, take into account that the market is extremely overleveraged. As many are taking the same bet: AI. AI-related debt issuance has surpassed $500 billion in 2026. That's more debt than Taiwan, Iceland, and Qatar have combined.

But how come no one is touching crypto?

As Crypto trades 24/7, it has often been frontrunning dramatic events. Therefore, you do see that crypto is often taking hits before the public equity market does.

For example, on Monday one Nvidia headline took $BTC from a $55K weekend low to $64K before Wall St had even opened. In other words, crypto is sort of the early warning system for AI sentiment at the moment.

Can crypto bounce?

Yes. As it is probable that the AI 'bubble' will burst. The question is, where will the capital in that case flow to? That could be absolutely crypto, as long as there is an interesting narrative.

The question is whether you're still in the game when it happens. In Dec 2018, sentiment was way worse than it is today, and BTC went to $3K. A year later, it was around $7K again.

Losing is fine, just don't blow up your capital.

Stay in the game.

We’ve confirmed that attackers have hijacked miners’ work. Your miner can keep running while someone else gets credit for it.

This could scale quickly. Plain Stratum V1 is a common default in mining. If you use it, you face this risk whichever pool you use.

Miners and pools worldwide must ACT NOW.

🟧 HOW IT HAPPENS

On plain Stratum V1, your miner can’t verify who’s sending it work. An attacker can redirect the connection, pretend to be your pool and send your miner jobs. The shares your miner submits go to the attacker instead of your pool.

🟧 WHY ACT NOW

During one incident, more than 1,000 mining sites lost their pool connection in the same second. The same attack could reach many more. You can secure your connection today.

🟧 MINERS: CHECK YOUR MAIN CONNECTION AND EVERY BACKUP

• Switch to Stratum V2 if your miner and pool support it. Use your pool’s official V2 address and key.

• Staying on V1? Use your pool’s TLS address with firmware that verifies the pool’s identity.

• Using a proxy? Check its connection to the pool. If your miners can’t connect securely on their own, the Braiins Pool SV2 Proxy can secure the connection from your farm to Braiins Pool.

• Hosted miners? Ask your operator to confirm that your main and backup connections are secure.

🟧 POOLS AND SOFTWARE PROVIDERS: ALERT YOUR CUSTOMERS TODAY

• Pools: offer Stratum V1 over TLS and, ideally, Stratum V2. Send miners your secure addresses and setup instructions.

• Firmware and software providers: tell miners which versions verify the pool’s identity and how to enable that protection.

AI chip (GPU / TPU) shipments are limited by several factors. But estimating shipment volume from just infrastructure power supply and max chip power (TDP) oversimplifies things and ignores how it actually works in practice. Here's why:

1. Chips don't run at max power all the time.
2. Same power, newer chips produce more tokens. That drives demand for new chips.
3. Same power, more chips running in parallel at lower load will often produce more tokens than fewer chips at high or full load.

text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

撑起全球 Claude Code 的核心接口刚全量从 Python 迁到了 Rust，内存开销直接暴降八成。

Anthropic 工程团队十几分钟前刚放出一篇含金量极高的复盘长文：两年多时间里，自家核心 Messages API 的日均流量狂翻了 1800 倍，早年用 Python 搭的服务彻底扛不住每个词元反复创建对象的开销了。

Claude 花一周就写出了初版 Rust 核心链路，但整篇复盘最耐人寻味的，是他们在实战排雷里扒出的两个真细节：

▸ 测试全绿可能是假象：团队审计 AI 移植的 700 个集成测试时，当场揪出 100 多处被悄悄放水的断言；4 月份新版代码跑过了 98% 的测试，结果一接线上流量比对，竟然只有四分之一的输入跟老版严丝合缝（连表情符号转义差几个字节都会改变模型回答）

▸ 拿线上老系统当盲测裁判：为了绝不触碰用户隐私原文，他们只记录差异发生的步骤和字节偏移「指纹」，自动派给沙箱里的 Claude 智能体自己造请求复现、自己修到字节级对齐

最终全程零停机切完流量：单次请求 CPU 砍掉约 70%，全线内存省下超 80%，日常敲 Claude Code 的首字响应也快了约两成。写代码早就不再是瓶颈，怎么防住 AI 改考卷蒙混过关才是真功夫。

text:
Inference Proof by @LucidCompute is going to be a consequential benchmark for verifiability in AI and we are looking forward to working with them on this.

One of the central questions of AI safety is, given a prompt, can anyone independently verify which model produced the response to it?

Answering this question involves checking if the inference provider executed the model honestly with no altered weights, prompts or reply while also ensuring this check can happen to a commercially-available CPU by anyone.

Existing AI benchmarks have never focused on measuring the cost of producing the verification certificate for the whole inference track and verifying the certificate.
author: eigenlabs
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

🚨BITCOIN MINING IS UNDER ATTACK🚨

We’ve confirmed that attackers have hijacked miners’ work. Your miner can keep running while someone else gets credit for it.

This could scale quickly. Plain Stratum V1 is a common default in mining. If you use it, you face this risk whichever pool you use.

Miners and pools worldwide must ACT NOW.

🟧 HOW IT HAPPENS

On plain Stratum V1, your miner can’t verify who’s sending it work. An attacker can redirect the connection, pretend to be your pool and send your miner jobs. The shares your miner submits go to the attacker instead of your pool.

🟧 WHY ACT NOW

During one incident, more than 1,000 mining sites lost their pool connection in the same second. The same attack could reach many more. You can secure your connection today.

🟧 MINERS: CHECK YOUR MAIN CONNECTION AND EVERY BACKUP

• Switch to Stratum V2 if your miner and pool support it. Use your pool’s official V2 address and key.

• Staying on V1? Use your pool’s TLS address with firmware that verifies the pool’s identity.

• Using a proxy? Check its connection to the pool. If your miners can’t connect securely on their own, the Braiins Pool SV2 Proxy can secure the connection from your farm to Braiins Pool.

• Hosted miners? Ask your operator to confirm that your main and backup connections are secure.

🟧 POOLS AND SOFTWARE PROVIDERS: ALERT YOUR CUSTOMERS TODAY

• Pools: offer Stratum V1 over TLS and, ideally, Stratum V2. Send miners your secure addresses and setup instructions.

• Firmware and software providers: tell miners which versions verify the pool’s identity and how to enable that protection.

🟧 BITCOIN COMMUNITY: HELP THIS REACH MINERS

Share this with the people who run mining farms, hosting sites and pools.  Full investigation and setup guide in the first reply ⤵️

As a physicist, people often ask me if I have an opinion on when quantum computers will be scaled enough to pose a threat to RSA public key cryptography through Shor’s algorithm. I’m not too worried about that right now.

In my opinion, the immediate risk is a math discovery through LLMs that allows factoring in polynomial time on a classical computer. We haven’t been able to prove that this is impossible, and factoring is in a special place where a polynomial algorithm would not imply P=NP.

On the other hand, if an LLM proves that factoring isn’t possible in polynomial time on a classical computer, that would be great!

text:
代码和数学之所以先爆发，本质上是因为编译器和证明器天然就是完美的 RL environment，有极其清晰的 verifiable rewards。但现实世界的绝大多数商业场景——供应链调度、客服售后、金融风控、法律合规、医疗诊断——全都没有现成的 gym。

顺着这个逻辑看，到 2030 年，每家公司变成“RL 环境公司”其实有两层意思：

第一层是对内：你如果不把自己的业务做成 RL 环境，你就用不好 AI。以后雇佣和管理 AI agent，跟现在写 prompt 完全不是一回事。你想让 agent 真正接管公司的复杂流程，光靠几页 SOP 文档是不够的，你必须把公司内部的 API、数据库、审批流、历史边界案例，打包成一个可重置、可沙盒模拟、有明确奖惩机制的仿真环境，让 agent 在里面跑几万次模拟、踩完所有坑，再放到线上干活。从这个角度看，未来企业软件（SaaS）的终局，可能根本不是给人点按钮的 UI，而是给 agent 跑训练和做 eval 的基础设施。

第二层是对外：护城河的重新定义。以前一家传统公司的核心资产是客户关系、静态数据库或者老员工的经验；以后这些东西如果不结构化，很快会被贬值。真正值钱的，是这家公司独有的状态转移逻辑和反馈闭环——也就是“在我的行业里，到底什么才算干得漂亮”。大厂的基座模型再强，也模拟不出一家深耕二十年的物流公司或医院里那些极其脏乱差、充满隐性规则的现实状态。谁能把自己的业务抽象成高质量的 RL 环境，谁就握住了大厂求之不得的“新石油”

text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
agent traces can be a powerful lever to improve agents

at a high level you need:
- powerful storage layer for efficiency ingesting/storing/querying all these traces (and their associated outcomes!)
- "intelligent compute" to run on top of those traces and help you make sense of whats going on

this is combo is what were calling an "agent lake"

we launched SmithDB in may as the best agent trace storage layer

over the past few months we've been working on this "intelligent compute". this has looked like:
- (basic) online evals, jev-as-a-judge, etc
- ai search: use decision models to filter models in real time
- insights: cluster traces by usage patterns
- engine: close loop by identifing and fixing issues
author: LangChain
quoted_text:
A few years ago, agent traces were 4-5 steps and the paths were deterministic. Now, agents run for minutes to hours at a time and generate traces with hundreds or thousands of LLM calls, tool calls, and processing steps, all of it nondeterministic.

Agent trace data is multi-model, has lots of text data that needs to be searched over, and is deeply nested. New types of data and orders of magnitude more volume require new data architectures. That's why we're building the Agent Lake at LangChain.

author: kevinnbass
quoted_text:
I think people need to understand why MIT is extraordinarily unlikely to correct this voluntarily, regardless of how many distinguished academics sign letters demanding that they do so.

They’re in too damned deep.

At this point, correcting what happened to Sabatini would require a substantial examination of the conduct of numerous people occupying senior administrative, academic and legal positions at both MIT and Whitehead.

Who knew what and when? Who was warned about the deficiencies in the original investigation? Who had access to what evidence? Who failed to investigate those warnings? Who communicated with whom between the two institutions? Who authorized the subsequent legal and financial arrangements?

And what did their respective boards know?

We are potentially looking at an institutional Black Swan event of their own making. Depending upon what an independent investigation uncovered, correcting this could necessitate something approaching an administrative decapitation event.

Now consider who is being entrusted with making the decision to authorize such an investigation.

Some of the very people whose own conduct, judgment or oversight would potentially become the subject of that investigation!

What the hell do you expect them to do? Vote themselves out of their prestigious positions, expose themselves to potential litigation and torpedo the remainder of their professional careers?

They’re far more likely to roll the dice with litigation.

Litigation buys them time. It offers procedural avenues for limiting discovery, seeking dismissals, appealing adverse decisions and potentially negotiating confidential settlements. Some may retire or move on to other positions before the full extent of the institutional conduct ever becomes public.

Meanwhile, the institutions bear much of the financial cost of defending the decisions made by those individuals.

Even their boards have a considerable incentive to preserve the status quo, particularly if questions exist about their own oversight. It will likely take substantial donor withdrawals, threatened research funding, reputational damage and mounting legal exposure before retaining the existing leadership becomes more financially and institutionally damaging than removing it.

People mistakenly assume that the more overwhelming the evidence of institutional wrongdoing becomes, the more likely an institution is to correct it.

In my experience, precisely the opposite can occur.

The greater the number of senior people potentially implicated, the greater their collective incentive to prevent a meaningful independent examination of what happened.

Eventually, institutional self-preservation becomes almost indistinguishable from the personal career preservation of the people running it.

Look at the November 20 letter. MIT conveniently characterizes the civil trial as a matter of individual defamation, when $5.5M of the $6M verdict was awarded for tortious interference with Sabatini’s professional relationships.

The faculty were asking for an independent review in light of evidence uncovered during litigation. MIT responded by reaffirming the conclusions of the very proceedings whose integrity the faculty were questioning.

What a spectacular exercise in circular reasoning!

I applaud the faculty members who have finally found the courage to speak out. But I suspect that without litigation, compulsory discovery and substantial external financial pressure, they are going to accomplish very little.

You cannot reasonably expect people to voluntarily authorize an investigation that could result in their own professional destruction.

That is precisely why independent oversight, enforceable legal accountability and compulsory discovery are so damned important.

text: Democracy should control AI
author: ahall_research
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Verifying which AI model produced an answer should be something anyone can do.

Proud to support @LucidCompute’s Inference Proofs, an open benchmark for the systems making that possible.
author: 0xPolygon
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.
