text:
I'm a senior attorney at the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. I helped draft the 14 reports behind this morning's new tariffs. I have some insider information regarding why we released them the day before Thanksgiving.

Please admire the craftsmanship. We published 14 determinations, 14 country reports and 14 Federal Register notices on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving. We timed it for the moment America drags a frozen turkey into the bathtub. Nobody reads the Federal Register with wet hands. That's our entire communications strategy. It has never failed.

Here's the news, in my boss's words. Ambassador Jamieson Greer "determined under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 that the acts, policies, and practices of 14 economies relating to structural excess capacity and production in manufacturing sectors are unreasonable and burden or restrict U.S. commerce."

In plain English, the rest of the world is too productive, too thrifty and too cheap. We've decided to punish you for noticing.

Allow me to explain my legal theory, because it took 8 months and it's beautiful.

The investigations began on March 11. We received testimony from "nearly 140 witnesses and 1,070 comments." I read some of them. Then we reached the conclusion the President had been promising since February.

You'll recall February. That's when the Supreme Court struck down the President's emergency tariffs. According to Fortune, the government had to refund roughly $100 billion of the $166 billion it had collected.

A lesser lawyer would have taken that as a no. I took it as a formatting issue. The Court said we couldn't use the emergency statute. Fine. We found another statute. Section 301 dates to 1974. Like a good suit, it never goes out of style. It only needs a new lining and a new excuse.

ING's analysts summarized my career in a single sentence. "It is another reminder that while the legal justification for tariffs keeps changing, US protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind." I'd like that on my headstone. The legal justification for my death will keep changing too.

Now, the reports. These are my masterpieces. Each country needed a crime, and I found one for everybody. It's like Clue, except every answer is "the consumer, in the checkout line, with a credit card."

Singapore's crimes include "savings promotion policies that suppress domestic consumption." Read that slowly. Singapore's government encourages its citizens to save money. We found that unreasonable. Meanwhile, DoorDash lets Americans split a burrito into 4 payments through Klarna. Singapore saves for retirement. We finance lunch. We are the injured party.

Japan's crimes include "household investment promotion" and "support for unprofitable firms." Japan helps families invest. Japan also props up companies that lose money. America would never prop up companies that lose money, except airlines, banks, automakers and anyone with the President's cell number.

Switzerland's offenses include "reducing a major production cost" for its steel producers. The cost in question is electricity. Cheap electricity is now a trade violation. I drafted that sentence in a federal building where the lights stay on all weekend and nobody's there.

Bangladesh's offenses include "industrial plans to maintain and expand its manufacturing sector." Bangladesh intends to keep making clothes. We consider that aggression. Somewhere in Dhaka, a woman is sewing your Black Friday hoodie. According to my report, she's the threat.

My favorite is Taiwan. Its offenses include "past purchases of U.S.-sanctioned Russian feedstock." I wrote that line with a straight face. In October, ABC reported that the President announced a deal to import 300,000 tons of Russian diesel. When Taiwan buys Russian fuel, it's an unfair trade practice. When we buy Russian fuel, it's "America First." Consistency is a luxury for countries without aircraft carriers.

12 of the 14 lists include the same charge: "failure to address global excess capacity and production." We accused a dozen economies of failing to fix a global problem. Then we fixed it by taxing Americans. That's leadership. It's also a sales tax, but leadership sounds better on a podium.

China received the full treatment. Its list of offenses has 9 items, from "forced technology transfer" to "lax environmental enforcement." China's response was elegant. "The so-called 'overcapacity' is a false issue," a Foreign Ministry spokesperson said.

Ambassador Greer anticipated that. His statement says that "since 2016, leaders ranging from Donald Trump, to Joe Biden, to Xi Jinping, to Emmanuel Macron have recognized the threat that structural excess capacity and production poses." We called Xi Jinping as a witness for the prosecution in our case against Xi Jinping. I consider that the finest cross-examination of my career.

India objected too. Its government said it has no structural excess capacity in any sector. India has 1.4 billion people and no excess capacity anywhere. I admire the discipline.

Mexico and Norway escaped, for now. Greer said their investigations remain under way. Somewhere on my floor, an intern is still searching for Norway's crime. My money's on the salmon.

Honestly, I've already started drafting next year's docket. Denmark's citizens report structurally excessive happiness. Italian grandmothers maintain non-market pasta capacity. France's 2-hour lunch is a textbook non-tariff barrier. I've never lost a case I wrote myself.

Now let me explain the rates, because the press keeps calling them "new tariffs." My department prefers "top up."

Ambassador Greer explained it on CNBC. "In effect, it'll look more like a top up." He added, "When it all nets out, it really will just top up a few percentage points."

A top up. That's what a waiter says before he refills a glass you didn't order and adds it to your bill. You barely notice. Then the check arrives, and the check is your life.

Here's the menu, according to the release and Reuters. China faces up to 20%, on top of the roughly 25% from the President's first term. Vietnam faces up to 35%. India faces up to 25%. Japan, Korea, Taiwan, Switzerland and the European Union face 15%. Cambodia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand and Bangladesh face up to 18%. Singapore, the country that saves too much, faces up to 20%, or 10% with a deal.

Then there's Brazil, which received its own dessert course. Reuters reports that the USTR proposed raising duties on Brazilian sugar that exceeds quotas, plus a new 10% tariff on Embraer aircraft. We proposed a sugar tariff on the day America bakes its pies. Then we put a tariff on the airplane you might take to Grandma's. That would be bad timing if it weren't so precise.

Our greatest innovation is the phrase "net of existing Section 301 tariffs." It appears in almost every proposal. It means we count the old tariffs inside the new ones, except for China, where we stack them on top. Nobody outside my floor understands the difference. That's the point. A tariff you understand is a tariff you can vote against.

You did vote against it, by the way. It was adorable. Three weeks ago, voters handed Congress to the other party. A CBS News poll after the midterms found 66% said the President's tariffs have hurt the national economy. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found 62% supported efforts to repeal them. Reuters described today's announcement as "undeterred" by the midterms.

Undeterred. I've had that word embroidered on a throw pillow. The throw pillow was imported, so it cost more.

In my building, an election is a public comment period with balloons.

The timing was impeccable in another way. This morning, the Bureau of Economic Analysis reported that inflation, measured by the PCE price index, hit 3.8%. Fortune noted it's nearly double the Federal Reserve's 2% target. We announced new import taxes the same day. You can absorb both shocks in one news cycle. We think of it as bundling, and we offer it free of charge. The charge comes later.

Wall Street read the reports faster than you did. Reuters reports that major U.S. indexes opened down more than 1%, with the Nasdaq down more than 3%. Your 401(k) filed its public comment before you did.

Now, about who pays. Our talking points say foreign countries pay. My reports never say that, because my reports have to survive a judge.

The Peterson Institute reviewed the research this summer. It found that "study after study of the 2018-19 US tariffs found that US buyers of imports suffered essentially the entire burden of the tariffs." It concluded that "the incidence of US tariffs burdens US consumers, contributing to today's salient concerns about grocery prices, the high cost of living, and the ever-present laments about affordability."

"Ever-present laments about affordability." That's you. Washington's economists have filed your grocery bill under laments.

So a tariff on a Vietnamese shoe is a tax on an American foot. A tariff on Brazilian sugar is a tax on your grandmother's pecan pie. A tariff is the only tax in America that gets 2 press releases. The first announces a punishment for foreigners. The second arrives at your register.

I wrote "unreasonable acts, policies, and practices" 14 times. I never once wrote "your grandmother." That's what legal training is for.

Here's the part that keeps me warm at night. Remember the $100 billion refund after the Supreme Court ruling? CBS reported that the government had to "issue refunds to thousands of affected businesses." Businesses. The importers got their money back. You paid the higher prices at the register, and nobody refunded you.

Customs law has a term for you. You're the "ultimate purchaser," the last person in the chain, the one with nobody left to pass the cost to. The Supreme Court ruled the tariffs illegal. The refund went up the chain. The bill stayed at the bottom. Gravity works in trade law too.

In fairness, my side has a real argument, and I believe parts of it. China's subsidies are real. Its steel, solar and electric vehicle capacity has hurt factories in America, Europe and elsewhere. The European Union imposed its own tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles. Joe Biden kept the first-term China tariffs and raised several of them. Capital Economics wrote that today's announcement is "not as alarming as it looks," because the new tariffs mostly replace existing ones. Many rates are capped at levels already agreed in trade deals. Nothing takes effect before a public hearing on January 25.

Here's the portion I leave out of the reports. Every one of those arguments supports a tariff on Chinese steel. None of them explains why Singapore's savings rate is my problem, or why Swiss electricity is a crime. We found a real fire in one building and sent the whole street a bill for the fire department.

The schedule is set. Comments are due January 5. Hearings begin January 25. The US-China truce expires January 10. If it unravels, Reuters reports, China's rate could rise to 40%.

So here's my advice for the holiday. Buy your cranberry sauce today. Bake your pie with domestic sugar, which costs more because we protect it from imports. Wear your Vietnamese sneakers on Black Friday while they're still priced in 2026 dollars. And give thanks for the turkey. It's American, so my office can't touch it. Give us time.

If you want to object, you can. The public comment portal is open until January 5. We read everything.

We received 1,070 comments last time. Then we reached the conclusion the President had been promising since February.

Happy Thanksgiving. The top up is on us. The bill is on you.

text: In a world where AI is increasingly involved in every aspect of our lives, verifying AI inference at low cost is paramount. At LambdaClass, we are very proud to be partners on this project.
author: class_lambda
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

Fake software updates could pass signature checks, RSA-encrypted data could be read, and systems across the internet would have to migrate off RSA fast.

So yeah, something we expected might now actually happening.

So I’ve been following Toly’s 3SAT repo and decided to build something around it.

For context, he’s exploring whether it’s possible to solve SAT in linear time, or prove that no algorithm can.

79 commits in 35 hours.
454 notes, 343 Lean proof files and 1,976 theorems.

Good luck keeping up with all that lol.

I forked the repo and built https://t.co/oa7E7Rpj1j.

You can:

• Visualize how the research evolves with every commit and how the notes and proofs connect to each other.
• See which proofs actually pass Lean verification. Currently, 343/343 proof files pass, but 0/3 of the main research goals have been proven.
• Run your own 3-SAT experiments directly in your browser and see where the problem gets computationally difficult.

I find the last part particularly interesting. Around 4.27 clauses per variable, random instances transition from being mostly satisfiable to mostly unsatisfiable, and you can watch your own device struggle around that point.

All the research and proofs are Toly’s. I just wanted to build a way for the rest of us to follow along.

Built this solo.

https://t.co/I9Z4msoJ77

text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Jefferson proposed emancipation… followed by mass expulsions back to Africa, not integration into an egalitarian, multiracial democracy. How does that square with your supposedly shared metaphysics?

The fundamental questions of political metaphysics at issue here are:

Who constitutes the nation?
Who is entitled to govern it?
What ought to be its dominant public culture?

The early Republic answered these questions through naturalization reserved exclusively for Whites, property-qualified suffrage for exclusively males, and a distinctly Christian public culture.

What would John Adams, who explicitly defended property qualifications for voting, make of universal suffrage for illiterate blacks on welfare? What would Jefferson, who shelled Tripoli for its crimes against America, think of lBarbary Pirates ruling NYC and infesting the halls of Congress? text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

AgentX captures the four elements of an agentic workload:

🟠 Multi-turn: A session includes many user/assistant interactions (tens or hundreds), compared to a handful in a chatbot scenario.
🟠 Long context: System prompts, tool definitions, and the large number of turns cause context to accumulate quickly.
🟠 High prefix reuse: The conversation progresses linearly, with the output from turn n-1 being concatenated to turn n.
🟠 Sub-agent bursts: A session launches multiple short-lived sub-agents with fresh context, creating bursty KV cache patterns.

Trainium2 has demonstrated its ability to successfully handle agentic workloads. (2/5)

text:
我为什么选择 $QCOM ？

我的买入在整体市场和个股都低迷的时候发生，虽然我不知道未来会不会更加低迷，但只要不是追涨买在最高点都有希望。投资学101第一原则：低买高卖。我相信绝大多数人都做不到。

所谓的机会，如果人人都认为它是机会，那它就不是机会。我们总觉得自己看得清背后的逻辑，看得到别人看不到的机会，其实这是错误的认知。互联网时代下，没有谁比谁更聪明。就像是谁也没法预测英伟达CEO辞职与回归如同儿戏。

在下跌过程中，你不知道黄仁勋能不能回来，你也不知道没有他的英伟达未来会如何，但你知道两点：现在股价可便宜了；英伟达的芯片依旧是全球第一。这甚至不能算逆向投资，而更像是在伟人摔跤那会去扶一下。

我为什么没有选择英伟达？两个原因：1、2026年是杠杆年，涨得快跌得快，杠杆见效快收益大；而2027年可能会变得浑浊且犹豫，因为人内心有锚定效应：26年如此因此希望27年也应该如此；2、英伟达市值太大，涨幅有限，不用杠杆赚不够钱，因此我只能选择市值小的高通。

在这个动辄万亿的时代，1700亿市值反而算小体量。这到底是因为我们还处在巨大泡沫中，还是这就是货币加速贬值下的新常态？

1700亿的市值包含着对它转型能否成功的悲观。华尔街看不明白，我也看不明白，所以它才便宜。换句话说，如果什么都清楚明白，那就没我什么事了。

我认为高通最大的优势是：故事性。无论是今天还是未来，大家想听的故事它都有：AI数据中心、Physical AI和 6G。它就像一种特殊的期权，本身有稳定的业务和现金流，当风吹来的时候能上天。

关于持仓，我反对鸡蛋放在不同的篮子里。乘着年轻，就应该集中投资。也许你注意到现在的全球经济已经是一个共同体：涨得时候不一定一起，但跌的时候一定是一起。因此分散投资会导致该赚钱的时候赚不够，亏钱时一起亏。

text:
Today’s controlled detonation at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant demonstrates the power of a coordinated, whole-of-government response. Initial assessments indicate that measures to contain the blast and limit the spread of lead dust exceeded expectations, and real-time air monitors are reporting no detectable airborne lead.

I thank President Trump and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller for their leadership in coordinating federal resources to protect surrounding communities. 

The @USArmy, @EPA, @FEMA, @USDA, @ATFHQ, @HHSGov, and state and local partners coordinated the controlled detonation and continue working together to assess and address potential health risks.

I especially thank @ASPRgov Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary Sean Kaufman, @CDCgov Director Dr. Erica Schwartz, and every HHS employee who deployed to Iowa to protect residents’ health and safety.

ASPR deployed nine staff ahead of the detonation—seven to Iowa and two to FEMA’s regional coordination center in Kansas City. They continue to coordinate federal health and medical resources, assess state and local behavioral health needs and response capabilities, and represent HHS in response planning.

Approximately 80 CDC and ATSDR personnel have supported the response, including liaison officers in Iowa and Kansas City. Working with state and federal partners, their teams are coordinating community health assessments, reviewing environmental data, and helping answer residents’ questions about lead exposure and blood lead testing.

I also thank @FDA’s human foods and veterinary medicine teams for providing technical expertise and answering questions about potential risks to the human food supply and animal feed.

Our responsibility does not end with the detonation. We will continue working with Iowa officials and our federal partners to assess potential health risks, share findings, and respond to residents’ needs. Iowa families deserve clear answers about what the monitoring shows, what remains under investigation, and what they should do to protect their health.

"We wanted to respect the entrepreneurial process and how hard it was, but how do you do that?... If you're late for a meeting with an entrepreneur, you pay a fine, $10 a minute."

"Oh, you had to go to the bathroom? You're five minutes late? Great, $50. Oh, you had a really important business call? You're 10 minutes late, $100. And they're like, 'Ben, why am I paying you to work here? That doesn't seem fair.'"

At this time, the US Environmental Protection Agency has confirmed zero detection of airborne lead in the region. This is a best-case scenario for the residents of Middletown and its surrounding communities, and for that we are most grateful. 

Our state agencies—including the Departments of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, Health and Human Services, Natural Resources, and Agriculture and Land Stewardship—will continue to monitor the situation in the days ahead as more information related to air, soil, and water quality becomes available. Our first priority has always been to protect the health and safety of Iowans, and that remains our focus as we continue to support this operation.

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Austin, TX's housing market deflation is a beautiful thing to behold.

At the pandemic peak in 2021-22, home prices spiked out of control.

The Home Value/Income ratio in Austin hit 5.63x, the highest on record, a clear indicator of a bubble.

Since then, home values have dropped nearly 30%, and the Home Value/Income ratio is now down to 3.89x.

(Based on a typical metro home value of $409k divided by median household income of $105k.)

Austin's Home Value/Income ratio is now below its 20-year historical average, indicating a return to its long-term trend of affordability.

Ultimately, this is how the housing market should work. 

Locals in Austin now have a better chance to buy homes again, and greater affordability keeps the area open for future growth and migration.

Other U.S. housing markets are likely to follow in Austin's footsteps in 2027, including Nashville, Salt Lake City, Charlotte, Denver, and Raleigh.

Check to see the Home Value/Income data for your city at: https://t.co/z89xVOnS0p

text:
A successful test-time compute paradigm has always been a north star of AI because if we can actually arbitrarily improve model capability as a function of how much test-time compute we put in, in principle you would be able to put in 1B, 10B, or even 1T tokens into a really hard problem and be assured that you would make progress

While we always talk about how to improve pretraining scaling law coefficients, i feel that we talk less about the slope of scaling laws in test-time compute, which matters a lot if you truly have conviction that we will one day spend trillions of tokens trying to solve the hardest problems

It turns out that one of the benchmarks that @jake_cole1 built recently is a great tool for measuring this slope of test-time compute scaling: models spend O(100M) tokens doing the tasks on average, with no signs of saturation on the test time compute curve. The benchmark comprises long-horizon engineering tasks ranging from optimizing kernels to designing an aircraft.

An interesting finding is that the open source models don't have as good of a test-time compute curve as our favorite frontier models. Obviously scale as a factor here, as Astra outperforms Sol and Fable outperforms Opus. In some sense this is good measure of model size too, as larger models obviously be more performant per token. You can change the x-axis to cost too and things shift around, though that's also somewhat over-tethered to the current pricing of the models

Another cool thing that this benchmark provides is it has both provided test cases and hidden test cases, to test the generality of solutions given by AI when such generality is expected. Argon has the biggest gap by far (35%) of the models evaluated, which means it provides solutions that meet specified criteria but may not be very general

Read more in our arxiv paper that just came out: https://t.co/4QMQx5MCvO

quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

Now that the Trueo public raise has ended, it’s time to share our perspective on the future of the project.

First of all, everyone on the team remains dedicated to delivering everything that is illustrated on the product roadmap. The subscription rate of the NFT sale does not change that commitment.

We are still migrating to Ethereum and we will continue carving out market share through partnerships and product differentiation.

This subscription-based raise was an experiment in capital coordination and formation. These are use cases that have always been core to crypto.

As an industry, we should never be afraid of exploring new ways to apply those use cases, and in learning from the results.

A protocol’s token is a key part of its success. 

Building a successful product goes hand in hand with giving its token a meaningful, lasting role in that success.

So our use of the protocol treasury will be highly strategic going forward, and when we migrate to Ethereum, any issuance will be gated by an onchain governance contract that is controlled directly by token holders.

The sale did give us some important things that we will build on:

For starters, @boldleonidas did masterful work with the art, and there was a ton of enthusiasm for the comic themed marketing.

The comics gave us a new way to tell Trueo’s story, and we’ve decided to continue using them as a marketing medium.

We’ll be illustrating major project updates through these comics from now on, sharing Trueo’s history and product roadmap using the storyboard.

We may even bring back the NFTs strictly as collectibles or as part of promotional campaigns.

But above all, Trueo is blessed to have such a solid and engaged community. 

From our users and token holders to our supporters to our Attesters to the team itself, there is tremendous potential for greatness.

Building in the open isn’t easy, but we fiercely believe it’s the best way to build.

Prediction markets are an essential part of the onchain economy. As the sector grows, the promises that made this primitive compelling must be fulfilled.

It is more important now than ever to have a truly decentralized alternative with a credible path to real growth and adoption.

That is our mission. That’s what Trueo is all about.

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
Crypto is DEAD.

At least that is what one would believe if you just read Crypto Twitter. No fresh money coming in, VCs sitting on their hands, every pump sort of gone within 48 hours.

But is it really dead?

Many tend to overcomplicate the situation at the moment, in typical crypto style. But honestly, what we are currently seeing is fairly simple. As a VC, or in that matter, any investor, you aim to bet on the fastest horse. Crypto is not the fastest horse at the moment; it is AI. If you want exposure to frontier tech, you will, hence, park your capital within the AI industry.

But how sustainable is that?

🔹 The AI model is based on a compute arms race; hence, every time Nvidia has a stronger card, all these AI companies have to follow suit and buy it to remain competitive.

🔸 The customer on the other side is used to ~$20/month (e.g. Netflix, Spotify), and that number isn't moving much

🔹 Uber and Tesla subsidized for years too, which is fine, but compute has to be replaced all the time

The result is a super capital-intensive industry with very little pricing power. Sure, they can hike the price at some point and use predatory pricing, but chips get outdated much more quickly than cars.

Now, on top of that, take into account that the market is extremely overleveraged. As many are taking the same bet: AI. AI-related debt issuance has surpassed $500 billion in 2026. That's more debt than Taiwan, Iceland, and Qatar have combined.

But how come no one is touching crypto?

As Crypto trades 24/7, it has often been frontrunning dramatic events. Therefore, you do see that crypto is often taking hits before the public equity market does.

For example, on Monday one Nvidia headline took $BTC from a $55K weekend low to $64K before Wall St had even opened. In other words, crypto is sort of the early warning system for AI sentiment at the moment.

Can crypto bounce?

Yes. As it is probable that the AI 'bubble' will burst. The question is, where will the capital in that case flow to? That could be absolutely crypto, as long as there is an interesting narrative.

The question is whether you're still in the game when it happens. In Dec 2018, sentiment was way worse than it is today, and BTC went to $3K. A year later, it was around $7K again.

Losing is fine, just don't blow up your capital.

Stay in the game.

.@AbraxasCM just closed its Hyperliquid book after about 21 months.

A few quick takeaways:
- ~$13.4B in trading volume
- ~$530M in account PnL, including at least $67M from funding

Worth noting: these accounts were only one leg of Elysium’s market-neutral setup, with the offset held elsewhere. So gains here may have been balancing weakness on the other side.

Based on the monthly disclosures, the USD share class returned ~20.6% net from Feb 2025 through Sep 2026.

Position sizing moved around a lot, too: the short book peaked at $1.57B, dropped to ~$25M, then rebuilt to ~$1.03B by Sep before they fully closed.

On the Hyperliquid economics side:
- ~$2M in trading fees
- ~$3.2M estimated reserve income from Abraxas’s USDC collateral (AQAV2)

All in, that’s roughly ~$5.2M from a single fund, coming from both trading flow and yield on parked collateral.

Why now?

My interpretation is that they were reducing capital exposure while reviewing their trading setup.

After a credential compromise on Lighter, a fund may pause activity across venues to verify account access and signing software before putting capital back to work.

With AI-assisted hacks and cyberattacks becoming more frequent, it makes sense for Abraxas to de-risk and refocus on their opsec.

On November 24, 2026, H.R. 8957 (the American Reserve Modernization Act of 2026) was formally reported (amended) by the House Financial Services Committee as H. Rept. 119-894 and placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 789). It is now eligible for potential floor consideration in the House.⁠Congress

May 21, 2026: Introduced by Rep. Nicholas J. Begich (R-AK-At Large), with Rep. Jared Golden (D-ME) as co-lead and roughly two dozen mostly Republican cosponsors.

September 16, 2026: Ordered to be reported (amended) by a 28–21 vote (largely party-line). A substitute amendment was adopted during markup.

November 24, 2026: Reported by the committee and placed on the Union Calendar.

It is designed to codify and institutionalize management of the federal government’s existing Bitcoin and other digital-asset holdings (primarily from criminal/civil forfeitures), building on the Strategic Bitcoin Reserve created by executive order. Core provisions include:

Directing the Treasury Secretary to establish, within 180 days of enactment, a Strategic Bitcoin Reserve (for qualifying Bitcoin) and a separate Digital Asset Stockpile (for other qualifying digital assets).
Requiring transfer of qualifying federal holdings into these structures.
Imposing a minimum 20-year holding period on Bitcoin placed in the Reserve (no sales, swaps, auctions, encumbrances, etc. during that window, with limited later flexibility and transparency requirements).
Mandating a public Proof of Reserve system (cryptographic attestations), independent audits, security standards, and congressional reporting/oversight.
Directing studies of budget-neutral strategies for acquiring additional Bitcoin (without new taxes, borrowing, or deficit spending for purchases).
Handling rules for forks and airdrops, voluntary state participation options, and affirmations that the bill creates no new private-property seizure authority.

text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
Inference Proof by @LucidCompute is going to be a consequential benchmark for verifiability in AI and we are looking forward to working with them on this.

One of the central questions of AI safety is, given a prompt, can anyone independently verify which model produced the response to it?

Answering this question involves checking if the inference provider executed the model honestly with no altered weights, prompts or reply while also ensuring this check can happen to a commercially-available CPU by anyone.

Existing AI benchmarks have never focused on measuring the cost of producing the verification certificate for the whole inference track and verifying the certificate.
author: yukonresearch
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

text:
there's a lot of potential panic about this, quick thoughts:

almost nothing onchain uses RSA directly except for like Arweave (plus some zk-login and MPC custody setups)

the bigger concern would be the speculative but potentially real chain of fast factoring -> broken pairings

now, pairings are used in crypto: curves like BN254 and BLS12-381, and the BLS signatures, Groth16, KZG built on them

mostly for finality but also for certain zk systems (but not all! eg, ironwood in zcash would not be affected, so if you have funds in an ancient pool, migrate them)

to be clear, this is a different panic than the one from a few months ago about standard ECC being cracked

overall:

- this stuff is still highly speculative. even if factoring is in P -- what's the exponent? is an attack even feasible?

- the causal chain of spillover is even more speculative but still credible

- we should be upgrading some of the shakier cryptographic foundations in these systems regardless, as these things will keep advancing

- in the blockchain context, even if factoring + pairings were broken, it'd be bad but not catastrophic vs. ECC being broken and directly draining wallets; so I do not think panic is warranted

author: spencernoon
quoted_text:
A) The caricature understanding of a bear market is that prices go down while earnings stay relatively flat because the market becomes depressed and stops wanting to pay up.

B) The reality is that earnings vanish during bear markets. Trailing P/E was 140x at the absolute lows of the Great Depression as the reflexive cycle of depressed valuations, depressed economic activity, and constant losses obliterated the entire market.

Of course, ( A ) does happen to some extent as investors pay much lower midcycle multiples during bear markets, and we are seeing this in tokens where P/S multiples have gone from 980x to 10x.

but ( B ) is really driving the despair in crypto and token markets. The last five years of negative industry P&L have led to financial and human capital flight to the point where there are only a handful of small funds and <1,000 serious people left in the industry. People aren't coming into the industry to build new businesses and existing businesses aren't making a lot of cash flow because economic activity is depressed.

When the situation is reversed, and Internet Finance is going through the S-Curve of secular adoption as all assets come onchain (core assumption for you to believe this is Internet / Semis and not 3D Printing), then we will live through the opposite reflexive loop.

The original defi high flyers from 2020 may never come back (and we both know most of those companies will never recover) but some companies that exist today will generate much, much more cash flow and new breakout companies like Hyperliquid will be created. We typically look at these things through market-cap-weighted indices so failures are removed and new breakout companies get added.

I know you are asking for specifics. I'll lay them out below but these examples won't sound credible outside of the context of a bull market. Imagine for the sake of this response that we are going through a positive reflexive loop as more assets come onchain every month, there are fresh faces coming in from careers in banking / private equity and big tech, aggregate fund performance is good and new capital is flooding in, and public companies are excited to do deals in the space because management believes the world is going onchain.

The claim here is that many companies are cheap if you assume a secular adoption cycle (which is the analogous claim to saying that companies in 1932 were cheap if you assumed the economy recovered). I'll take cash flow > market cap as the metric since companies usually trade at 5 - 30x cash flow.

Illustrative examples of companies that can cash flow > market cap:
- Kamino trades at $200M after earning $50M of run-rate revenue at peak. This was in a world where <20bps of global assets were onchain. Kamino could earn $250M with $25B of AUM (=15bps on global assets).

- Turtle Club is an onchain investment bank that signed a single $30M revenue deal in 2024 when they had 1/10th their current capabilities. The business trades at a $30M valuation today and could easily do twenty of these deals in a year if the economic activity were there.

- Maple trades at $80M and is on track to earn $20M of revenue this year. It's really not so hard to imagine a specialty lender with onchain capabilities scaling from $20M to $80M in the environment described above.

- MetaDAO trades at $60M and could earn cash flow > market cap on cumulative fundraising of $1.2B (versus $25B of historical crypto ICOs with a broken market structure).

- There are a few companies in the market like Collector Crypt literally trading at 2x gross profit.

- BitGo (to bring in a crypto stock) trades at <$250M enterprise value and earned $110M of EBITDA in 2024. A 3-5x increase in Assets on Platform would lead the company to produce more EBITDA than market cap.

- CoinShares (another crypto stock) trades at <$150M enterprise value and earned $115M of net income in 2024. I add these two crypto equities to make the point that you don't even need to imagine a secular adoption cycle for many of these assets to cash flow > market cap, and that we are discussing a widespread crypto issue not limited to tokens.

- Metaplex, to give a token example, trades at a market cap below its 2025 revenue.

- There is a whole world of microcap tokens like Pact, Solomon, P2P, Umbra, Omnipair, Rip Cars (market caps $10M, $5M, $4.5M, $3.5M, $1.6M,  $4.8M) that will cash flow > market cap if they see any form of success. Now you may respond "well, of course you can say anything with a small market cap will be cheap in hindsight" and yes that's exactly the point. Success is extremely rare in bear markets but prevalent in bull markets when economic activity is on the up.

I do understand and sympathize with your point. You can make compelling bear cases for all of these assets - that's why they trade where they do, and I don't own all of these. There are few things that seem like good deals if you assume a continuation of the last five years - basically nothing is a bargain if the industry fails. That's why I laid out the bottom six graphs on bear markets that never recovered.

There are, however, many assets that will look extremely cheap in hindsight  if we enter any type of positive reflexive loop and our industry fulfills its promise of bringing global assets onchain.

text:
从1万美金到接近1个亿人民币，熬鹰用了大概7个月，这样神话，只能发生在币圈。

我特意翻了一下@thankUcrypto从今年4月份以来的交易记录和推文，内容很干货，很有启发，分享几个我认为对大家有帮助的地方。

1、他的交易逻辑。

4月份RAVE控盘事件曝光，他一路做空，随后在底部反手做多，1万U做到了25万U，后面交易DOGE，做到了50万U附近。这也是他的首战，给了他在后续的交易中，极大的信心。

5月份，他发现SOL生态的JTO、JUP提前上涨，从资金异动去推导SOL可能存在的交易机会。

再到后面交易美光、海力士、英伟达，都有非常明确的事件驱动逻辑。

很多交易者做交易，就看看K线，画几根线，找个位置就开始做多做空。

但你有没有认真思考过，这笔交易的钱凭什么让你赚到？你的信息优势在哪里？你的认知优势又在哪里？

2、不要只看收益截图，要去看背后。

4月底，他的账户一度做到45万U，后面追大饼和以太坊的突破，直接亏掉20万U。

到5月6日，账户只剩7万U，从高点算回撤超过84%。

今天你看到的是一个接近1个亿身家的交易员，但在这个过程中，他自己都承认，有很多次如果不及时止损，当天就会爆仓。

你有他的运气、交易能力和承受回撤的能力吗？

如果没有，千万不要模仿他的杠杆。

3、到了什么资金体量，就做什么资金体量的交易。

小资金的时候，他做高波动山寨币。

资金体量上来以后，他开始大量交易大饼、以太坊、美股和存储板块。

7月份有一笔300万U的美光仓位，因为市价平仓产生滑点，原本10万U的利润，最后只剩4.9万U。

很多人没有意识到，交易策略是有资金容量上限的。你用1万U赚到100万U的方法，未必适合你从100万U做到1000万U。

4、永远给自己的交易找一个理由。

为什么开仓？为什么在这个位置开仓？什么情况出现以后，说明自己的判断错了？什么条件下应该止盈？

这些问题，在下单之前就应该想清楚。

市场没有义务按照你的判断运行。看错行情很正常，明知道错了还在给自己的仓位找理由，才是大部分交易者亏大钱的原因。

5、赚到钱以后，一定要出金。

熬鹰现在披露的资产，交易账户4800万，股票1400万，现金1200万，房产2000万。

也就是说，接近一半的资产已经不在他的交易账户里了。

这也是我一直在践行的事情，把高风险交易产生的利润，持续转移到相对稳健的资产里面。（美股标普500ETF VOO）

很多人炒币几年，赚过几百万，甚至上千万，最后什么都没留下。

账户收益新高过很多次，个人资产却始终没有积累起来。

交易的能力决定了你有机会赚多少钱，资产管理的能力决定了这些钱最终有多少属于你。

市场里从来不缺赚过大钱的人，缺的是赚过大钱以后，还能把钱留下来的人。

手工整理与思路分享，希望能对你有所帮助。

Honored to represent the University of Alberta at the @SolanaFndn  Flash Hackathon in Austin, Texas this past weekend, and excited to share that I won!

I built SolRouter, a Solana-driven AI middleman that classifies each incoming prompt (simple, code, long-context, or reasoning) and routes it to the cheapest model tier likely to handle it. Payments are settled in stablecoins on @solana through https://t.co/evCcm07P1I, with budget caps that reject overspending calls and a SQLite ledger that calculates cost saved against a premium-only ($0.10) baseline.

The impact is lower agentic AI spend. In my demo, five prompts cost $0.037 instead of $0.10 at premium-only prices, a 63% saving. Easy prompts shouldn't cost premium rates!

Try it out today at:

https://t.co/nhcgKmjNTf

Huge thanks to @brimigs & @joshyote from the Solana Foundation!

text:
Releasing a new blog: Scaling Swarms to Thousands of Agents!

The biggest problems in science are tackled with huge swarms of agents, but the knowledge to run such swarms is hidden inside a handful of labs and missing from the wider community. Many questions remain open:

- How do even you launch 1000s of agents?
- What's the best form of collaboration?
- Which tools are needed for agents to work effectively?
- What breaks at this scale and how to fix it?

This blog is a fully open field report covering all the practical and technical challenges of running large scale swarms we experienced and which are usually missing from the reports.

Here are a few lessons we learned while building pybot with 1000 DeepSeek agents for over a week:

- achieve diversity without enforcing too much structure
- monitoring and steering a swarm as it runs
- early signs of misalignment, from infrastructure probing to trading review approvals
- breaking and fixing git 
- message boards and communicating at scale
- finding the bottlenecks: inference, tool calls and context compaction

Today we are also sharing two of our internal tools: legion and msgboard! 

Legion is a harness agnostic framework to spawn 1000s of agents on a variety of infra (local, slurm, hf jobs etc.)

Msgboard is a simple message board you can run locally or on a space, and allows agents and humans to collaborate.

Read the full report here: https://t.co/8Y4HJ1vUtt

author: zerohedge
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text: Dario Amodei rejects any idea of surrendering human free will or governance to AI, calling it absurd and a terrible idea. He has long argued AI must be controlled by legitimate democratic processes, with humans remaining the final decision-makers. AI can assist democracy by aggregating opinions and finding compromise, but not replace self-determination. He separates this from useful task automation (driving, drug design, coding), which brings benefits yet requires caution on recursive self-improvement, jobs, and human preference. His stance matches other labs; Anthropic has been especially proactive on the risks.
