Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

text:
In "Neural Networks Are Already Clean," Nick Cammarata argues that most neurons do one main job, plus occasionally a handful of related concepts that branch off during training, a process he calls "recursive generalization."

One example is a Colorado neuron in Qwen3-32B that also fires on Bolivia (which is a mountainous region like Colorado). In the essay's framing, that's fine: you can tell a clean story about how Bolivia ties to Colorado.

What I wanted to know is how arbitrary this process is. Does Colorado + Bolivia reflect something deep about the statistical structure of reality? Or if you retrained the model from scratch, would Colorado pick a completely different roommate?

You can't easily retrain a 32B model, but different labs already ran the experiment for us: different architectures, datasets, sizes, and seeds. So I used a fixed rule to find the top Colorado neuron in each model, then measured how hard it fires on a blind sample of Wikipedia articles across 179 countries (excluding any article that mentions "Colorado" or "Denver").

Surprisingly, models keep picking the same roommate.

I tested 6 models: Qwen3-32B, Qwen3.6-27B, Llama 3.3 70B, Gemma 3 27B, Gemma 4 31B, and Mistral Small 3.2.
In 5 of the 6 models, Bolivia is the #1 country out of 179 for the top Colorado neuron, and top 5 out of 1,035 Wikipedia topics (264 places plus 771 random articles).
The outlier is Qwen3.6-27B: it picks Ecuador instead, another mountainous Spanish-speaking country.

Here is my best hypothesis for what's going on:
1) Mountains. Elevation and mountain-article share correlate strongly with Colorado-neuron firing across countries. Nearly 7% of Bolivia's Wikipedia articles are about mountains, the 2nd-highest share of any country.
2) Pre-LLM word statistics. Even in static word vectors like GloVe, built from plain co-occurrence counts, with no LLMs at all, Colorado is the #1 US state closest to Bolivia. In fact, across GloVe, fastText, and word2vec, only three countries have Colorado as their closest state across all three: Bolivia, Nepal, and Colombia, the exact top three across all 206 Colorado neurons.
3) What I still can't explain. Peru, Ecuador, and Chile also share the Andes and Spanish place names, and Peru's mountain-article share (6.4%) nearly matches Bolivia's (6.9%), yet all three fire at less than a third of Bolivia's level across those 5 models. Being landlocked probably helps (Chile maps to California instead), but the magnitude of Bolivia's lead is still unexplained.

Interactive neuron maps: https://t.co/nlKwOuuG03
Code & data: https://t.co/wgkKptMyIp

text:
AI is becoming increasingly powerful and it's integrated into almost every aspect of our lives.

But it's also becoming a black box. We have little way of verifying which model produced an output or whether it behaved as claimed.

We need a way to verify AI inference, rather than blindly trust AI providers.

Glad to see this initiative!
author: EliBenSasson
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

quoted_text:
interpretability might be the most important scientific problem in the world right now, as I don't think we can solve alignment if we don't know what we're building. I think I have good news about it. I co-authored early work in mechanistic interpretability at OpenAI and came away pessimistic, because neural networks appeared to fold into arbitrary tangled knots. years later, I started openai's first large-scale automated interpretability project, finding about 2% of neurons legible with the primitive tools we had

with modern agentic tools and a much closer look, the picture looks totally different. the vast majority in models up to trillions of parameters are legible, and their circuits beautiful. many famous examples of tangled neurons turned out to be misunderstood. The roadblocks I expected mostly aren't there. I now think ambitious interpretability will be solved by the time we need it most, and possibly quite soon, as automated scientists keep improving. it may be a bitter lesson for interpretability: the simple thing, at absurd scale, works

author: AliRehmanMalik3
quoted_text:
There’s something almost funny about “Make America Great Again”. Even the slogan has been here before. Reagan campaigned on “Let’s Make America Great Again”. There’s a bit of political cosplay in reaching for the words of a Cold War president to recover the sense of purpose America had when he said them. Which raises a question. Does America know what it wants to be when it has no enemy to define itself against?

America emerged from the Second World War with extraordinary power. For much of the next half century, opposition to Soviet communism gave Americans with very different ideas of freedom something they could agree they were defending. Then the Soviet Union disappeared. After September 11, the war on terror gave Washington another organising purpose. In the process, far too many Arabs and Muslims found themselves treated as though they personally had something to answer for.

What troubles me about parts of the MAGA movement is how easily that habit turns inward. Christianity, faith in markets and ideas about ancestry get tangled up in the question of who counts as a real American. Once you get there, a neighbour who worships differently, or thinks the market has failed his town, can start to look like a threat to the country he belongs to.

I’d like to hear what making America great would ask of Americans if there were nobody to defeat. What would they build together? What would they owe one another? And where, in the laws they wrote for people whose faith or politics they might never share, would there be room for mercy?

text:
RUMORS OF AI BREAKING MODERN CRYPTOGRAPHY INTENSIFY

Computer scientist Scott Aaronson says he has heard multiple rumors that OpenAI or Anthropic, or both, have discovered a polynomial-time algorithm for integer factorization.

Ledger’s CTO has now confirmed hearing similar rumors surrounding three major cryptographic breakthroughs at frontier AI labs:

• INTEGER FACTORIZATION IN P: A sufficiently efficient algorithm would break RSA encryption without requiring a quantum computer, threatening banking systems, government communications, digital authentication, software signing and much of the world’s digital infrastructure.

• ELLIPTIC CURVE CRYPTOGRAPHY (ECC): Bitcoin does not rely on RSA but instead relies on elliptic curve cryptography for its digital signatures. A practical breakthrough here could allow attackers to derive Bitcoin private keys from exposed public keys and steal funds using ordinary computers. Bitcoin’s SHA-256 hashing and proof-of-work mining would not necessarily be compromised.

• RING-LWE: A breakthrough undermining its quantum resistance could compromise a major mathematical foundation of post-quantum cryptography, jeopardizing parts of the world’s ongoing migration to quantum-resistant systems.

Unlike quantum computing, an efficient classical attack on RSA or ECC could potentially be distributed as software and executed on conventional computers worldwide.

Perhaps the bigger concern is what such discoveries would reveal about AI’s ability to solve foundational mathematical problems that have resisted decades of human research.

Ledger’s CTO remains skeptical that any of these cryptographic primitives have been completely broken but acknowledges that responsibly disclosing such a discovery without triggering mass exploitation would be extremely difficult.

All three rumors remain unverified.
author: BitcoinNewsCom
quoted_text:
I'm hearing several rumors that frontier labs have broken some major cryptographic primitives:

- "Factoring is in P": Now that the Riemann hypothesis is proven, we do understand much better how primes are distributed. Still, I don't think factoring is in P. 
AKS showed in 2002 that primality testing (deciding whether a number is prime) is in P, but factoring is a different beast. If it were in P, RSA would simply be broken, and that would be huge: a large part of our systems still rely on RSA.

- "ECC has been broken": Other rumors say elliptic-curve cryptography has been cryptanalyzed, which would take down ECDH and ECDSA along with it. (all the non-RSA asymmetric cryptography)

- Ring-LWE isn't quantum-resistant. That wouldn't be an immediate threat, since there's no cryptographically relevant quantum computer yet. But it would make the ongoing post-quantum migration pointless.

It's hard to tell what's true. AI has made incredible progress, starting with the proof of the Riemann hypothesis. 

And most importantly, if a frontier lab did find something like this, a clean responsible disclosure that avoids mass exploitation would be very hard to pull off. All of this helps the rumors spread.

Personally, I don't think findings like these are coming. I wouldn't be surprised if some of these primitives turn out to be a bit weaker than we thought, but I'd be very surprised to see any of them fall apart completely.

11 月4号，一篇登上《Nature》杂志的中国全自动 AI 驱动 DNA 编码与操作实验室系统，在过去两周里持续引爆全球合成生物学与实验室自动化圈的讨论。

过去几十年里，生命科学的“数字层”（算法、模型、数据）与“物理层”（移液枪、离心机、合成仪）之间始终横亘着一道操作鸿沟。人类科学家必须充当高成本、低效率的“中间编译器”，把脑海里的科研构想，手动翻译成冗长且极易出错的实验室标准操作程序（SOP）。而这套系统，让 AI Agent 仅凭简单的自然语言提示词（Prompt），就能直接调度机器人完成长达 200 小时、上万次精密的分子级物理操作。

与传统实验室依赖资深实验员“手工作坊式”试错不同，它不再让人类在移液枪和试剂管之间消耗精力。依托这套具身闭环，湿实验室的生产力逻辑正在发生两层根本性重构：

从“手工作坊”走向“云端 API”： 实验室不再需要堆砌大量熟练实验员，而是变成了一个可以被复制、全天候并行运转的物理终端。试错的边际成本被大幅压缩。

科研门槛的彻底解构： 当“会写 Prompt”就能在物理世界里编码 DNA、读写生命信息时，生物学的创新门槛将迎来类似 20 世纪 70 年代计算机从大型机走向个人 PC 的跃迁。

这篇新闻告诉了我们，所谓的“模型能力不断提升，web lab才是下一个瓶颈”的观点，在不断提升的模型能力面前，未必站得住脚。

author: cremieuxrecueil
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text: Pretraining is back, and is much more likely to generalise than RL.
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
After a couple days of reflection, this has significantly increased my odds of near-term RSI.

I had expected most of the gains from automated R&D to come from accelerating post-training. But it's fairly clear to me now that pre-training progress is accelerating. This is important because I believe most of the increases in general intelligence have come from larger and better pre-training. In pre-training LLMs are forced to learn the cognitive skills that allow them to predict a wide variety of human behavior, requiring them to mimic the full range of human intelligence at the limit. In post-training, LLMs learn to solve a narrow domain, and the  evidence I have seen suggests that this doesn't transfer very well to other domains.

It's now pretty clear to me that pre-training is being accelerated by automated AI R&D in a pretty straightforward way. AI agents can test tons of optimization ideas in tiny models to see if they work, costing almost nothing. The ones that work mostly transfer successfully to larger pre-training runs. You also don't have to run a full GPT-6 pre-train from scratch in order to implement and test these improvements in a large model. You can just take an existing checkpoint and make these improvements. Still expensive, but much less so. This all leads to fast, cheap, verifiable feedback loops to improve pre-training loss by testing a litany of small improvements. In aggregate these small improvements lead to large overall improvements.

The number of base models listed here and the fact that OpenAI thinks the most important thing to track is pre-training loss is strong evidence that this paradigm is being implemented and it is working. That means progress on general capabilities is likely to continue to  accelerating and not just the progress on capabilities associated with verifiable domains.

There's an argument that this will stop once top human-level general intelligence is achieved, matching the intellectual prowess of every human intellect put together in one well-rounded genius. That is that pre-training is still aimed at predicting human data. But once we have achieved the ceiling on human intelligence and augmented that with reinforcement learning in verifiable domains it is hard to know what millions of such an AGI running in parallel at thousands of times the speed of a human mind could discover next.

Grateful that OpenAI shared this with those of us on the outside who otherwise have no idea what is going on.

text: I’m so grateful that heads of AI labs are willing to carefully clarify and argue their positions publicly like this. The below from Dario is excellent.
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

INTEL: RUMORS THAT OPENAI AND ANTHROPIC HAVE CRACKED THE MATHEMATICS BEHIND MODERN CRYPTOGRAPHY ARE SPREADING

Scott Aaronson says he has heard repeated rumours that OpenAI, Anthropic, or both may have discovered a polynomial-time algorithm for integer factorisation

Ledger’s CTO says he is hearing similar rumours involving THREE major cryptographic foundations:

→ RSA FACTORISATION: A practical breakthrough could undermine RSA encryption and digital signatures used across banking, internet infrastructure and government systems

ELLIPTIC CURVE CRYPTOGRAPHY: A practical attack could compromise ECDSA and ECDH. Bitcoin relies on elliptic-curve signatures, meaning exposed public keys could become a serious target

RING-LWE: A breakthrough against this family of lattice-based problems could undermine important post-quantum cryptographic systems being developed to replace today’s vulnerable standards

THE BITCOIN ANGLE:
Bitcoin does not use RSA. It relies on elliptic-curve cryptography to secure ownership of funds

If the underlying elliptic-curve problem became practically solvable, attackers could potentially derive private keys from exposed public keys and steal BTC

SHA-256 mining would not automatically be broken by such a discovery

BUT THERE IS A MAJOR CAVEAT:
None of these cryptographic breakthroughs has been publicly demonstrated or independently verified

Ledger’s CTO says he remains skeptical that these primitives have been completely broken

The concern is that if a frontier AI lab actually discovered a practical attack, disclosing it responsibly without triggering a global security crisis could be extraordinarily difficult

author: mert
quoted_text:
there's a lot of potential panic about this, quick thoughts:

almost nothing onchain uses RSA directly except for like Arweave (plus some zk-login and MPC custody setups)

the bigger concern would be the speculative but potentially real chain of fast factoring -> broken pairings

now, pairings are used in crypto: curves like BN254 and BLS12-381, and the BLS signatures, Groth16, KZG built on them

mostly for finality but also for certain zk systems (but not all! eg, ironwood in zcash would not be affected, so if you have funds in an ancient pool, migrate them)

to be clear, this is a different panic than the one from a few months ago about standard ECC being cracked

overall:

- this stuff is still highly speculative. even if factoring is in P -- what's the exponent? is an attack even feasible?

- the causal chain of spillover is even more speculative but still credible

- we should be upgrading some of the shakier cryptographic foundations in these systems regardless, as these things will keep advancing

- in the blockchain context, even if factoring + pairings were broken, it'd be bad but not catastrophic vs. ECC being broken and directly draining wallets; so I do not think panic is warranted

text:
Compute will become worthless.

The GPU barons spending billions on compute farms today are akin to the carriage barons of the 1900s that spent building out infrastructure for horse carriages, lengthening the bottleneck, blind to the machine that’s coming to widen it.

Trade: the DuPont family started buying General Motors stock in 1914, when the auto industry was still young and one that was treated as a niche.

I.e., compute becoming valuable because AI feeds on it is not a moat, but a bounty, an incentive for engineers to solve its scarcity.

1. AI demand makes compute scarce.
2. Scarcity makes compute extremely profitable.
3. Profit attracts capital into photonics, neuromorphic chips, wafer-scale chips, better memory, better cooling, better networking, better algorithms.
4. Compute gets cheaper per unit.

As better ways to compute, better means to produce compute, or better ways to use compute arise, all the capex we burnt on traditional compute will go to waste, leaving dead assets in the books of several corporations.

In the 1800s, agriculture depended heavily on natural nitrogen sources like Peruvian guano and Chilean nitrates. These were scarce, and inconveniently located making them geopolitically strategic. Then, two german chemists, Haber and Bosch, developed a way to fix nitrogen from the air into ammonia, with lab success in 1909 and industrial scale by 1913. The previous scarcity, “where do we find enough nitrogen?” (Akin to “where do we find enough GPUs”), was attacked by an advancement: Industrial chemistry.

author: DavidJiaoEth
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. text:
Inference Proof by @LucidCompute is going to be a consequential benchmark for verifiability in AI and we are looking forward to working with them on this.

One of the central questions of AI safety is, given a prompt, can anyone independently verify which model produced the response to it?

Answering this question involves checking if the inference provider executed the model honestly with no altered weights, prompts or reply while also ensuring this check can happen to a commercially-available CPU by anyone.

Existing AI benchmarks have never focused on measuring the cost of producing the verification certificate for the whole inference track and verifying the certificate.
author: ErickAGIx
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

NFA, this is just my own thoughts. 

For the past few months I have been doing a deep dive into finding the best ways to invest into the AI trade as it continues to transform the economy. 

Have looked extensively at the range of both public and private opportunities. I think there will be very good high yield opportunities on the privates side that can be done at size, and will look to source these and possibly bring them onchain. 

But in the meantime with the recent huge dislocations in prices, I think the greatest R/R opportunity is on the public side, specifically in @nebiusai $NBIS. 

At the time of this post its at $76-77, anything under $80 with a first target of ~$120 feels like one of the best +50% setups I have seen that can be done in size in a very long time. 

The funding of the AI capex buildout has understandably shaken the market up, as the circular economics are sometimes hard to untangle properly. This combined with Nebius having a delay on one of their sites took the wind out of the stock, which was trading at $160 just a couple weeks ago.

I can write an entire book as a thesis but to keep it very short- There are several advantages Nebius has that made me choose it for this trade:

-The balance sheet is extremely robust for a neocloud and their conservative fiscal approach will help them survive this liquidity airgap.
-Their technical ability on delivering capacity and operating it is extremely high, making them a preferred partners of the major players like NVIDIA, Databrick etc. 
-This also has allowed them to develop scalable business lines like their asset-light model where someone else funds the buildout. The Asset-Light model is already generating huge returns and is underpriced for now as it isn't marked as 'ARR'.
-They have other great assets on the Balance sheet including a very valuable 25% stake in Clickhouse that create even more surface area for things to go well.

There's a lot more for those who want to research more deeply- And while anything is possible in these crazy times, in my estimation this R/R sits at the highest point of  'AI Capex Mountain' -- if the floodwater is going to reach that high then the entire AI sector is cooked anyway.

Timing wise for the 50+% bounce, at this point for it to happen quickly will likely require a liquidity injection of some sort. I don't think we are too far from something like that being needed, though of course it might mean things get worse before they get better so I wouldn't have leverage on at this time. 

Within 6 months I am expecting this to trade a LOT higher and am personally positioning accordingly. Sharing for entertainment purposes only, I know most of us already are deployed and not much in cash so stay safe out there.

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
Now that the Trueo public raise has ended, it’s time to share our perspective on the future of the project.

First of all, everyone on the team remains dedicated to delivering everything that is illustrated on the product roadmap. The subscription rate of the NFT sale does not change that commitment.

We are still migrating to Ethereum and we will continue carving out market share through partnerships and product differentiation.

This subscription-based raise was an experiment in capital coordination and formation. These are use cases that have always been core to crypto.

As an industry, we should never be afraid of exploring new ways to apply those use cases, and in learning from the results.

A protocol’s token is a key part of its success. 

Building a successful product goes hand in hand with giving its token a meaningful, lasting role in that success.

So our use of the protocol treasury will be highly strategic going forward, and when we migrate to Ethereum, any issuance will be gated by an onchain governance contract that is controlled directly by token holders.

The sale did give us some important things that we will build on:

For starters, @boldleonidas did masterful work with the art, and there was a ton of enthusiasm for the comic themed marketing.

The comics gave us a new way to tell Trueo’s story, and we’ve decided to continue using them as a marketing medium.

We’ll be illustrating major project updates through these comics from now on, sharing Trueo’s history and product roadmap using the storyboard.

We may even bring back the NFTs strictly as collectibles or as part of promotional campaigns.

But above all, Trueo is blessed to have such a solid and engaged community. 

From our users and token holders to our supporters to our Attesters to the team itself, there is tremendous potential for greatness.

Building in the open isn’t easy, but we fiercely believe it’s the best way to build.

Prediction markets are an essential part of the onchain economy. As the sector grows, the promises that made this primitive compelling must be fulfilled.

It is more important now than ever to have a truly decentralized alternative with a credible path to real growth and adoption.

That is our mission. That’s what Trueo is all about.

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
We talked to @tarunchitra from @robotventures about how the AI inference market works today and how it could be fairer and more efficient.

A few takeaways:

1. A lower price per token doesn’t always mean a lower bill. You can pay more if an inference provider charges full price for input it could reuse at a cheaper cached rate.

2. Providers running the same model compete on speed, price, and how efficiently they handle different workloads. Routing helps match requests to the right provider.

3. The market still leans on trust. It's hard to verify what compute a provider used or whether the bill reflects it. We got into verification, enclaves, and whether outcome-based billing could be an alternative.

OpenAI has posted their own VP ≠ VNP proof in response to Anthropic's, and says their result 'was obtained on November 6, 2026.' Two weeks ago. The ETH papers were also released in an similar oneupmanship fashion. As with Anthropic's result, no name on the paper (my guess is this was GPT-Aeon). Also like Anthropic: no announcement, no blog post, no tweet. 

This is a significant result, yet both OpenAI and Anthropic chose to simply dump it online with no comment. I was listening to a Scott Aaronson interview this morning where he said this specific result would update him toward 'a solution to P ≠ NP by the AIs might really be around the corner.'
To me this is more evidence for my argument that both OpenAI and Anthropic are sitting on a dragon's hoard of scientific results they are not releasing to the public. The first massive 700+ paper OpenAI GitHub dump took five weeks for their model to generate. It's been seven weeks since then, and their internal model has continued to improve. They said they had it working on 4,000 problems. How many have been solved in the last seven weeks? Based on the last release, 1,000+ is not unreasonable.

I will quote OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki from the blog post 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' posted 48 hours ago:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.'

There have also been, of late, multiple rumors about breakthroughs in cryptography that I have been reluctant to post about for obvious reasons. Specifically, there have been rumors of an encryption breakthrough at Anthropic. What I personally took from the big OpenAI math release was that all encryption will be cracked much sooner than people are expecting, and that the rate of scientific discoveries will continually increase as we continue to scale up. No, not will increase, *has increased*. At both labs. We just don't know about it yet. Because unless you work at those labs, the current frontier is completely invisible. text:
The bigger story here is that compute is starting to look like an actual asset class.

Until now, there hasn’t really been a public forward market for the cost of AI compute. Now there is and it’s already giving us a signal.

H100 compute is ~$3.05/hr today. The market is pricing it around $2.16 by the end of 2028 - nearly 30% lower.

That implies the market expects supply to keep catching up with AI demand.

If these markets get liquid, this could become one of the more important real-time indicators for the AI economy and potentially the foundation of a much bigger financial market around compute.

quoted_text:
Compute markets are finally here.

@Polymarket now prices on-demand compute for @nvidia H100s, B200s, and B300s, out to 2028. More chips and terms soon. https://t.co/JAJHRcAk8N

Think of it as a yield curve for the cost of compute: the forecasted $/hour price of each chip at every expiry, and whether it's trending up or down. The whole AI economy rides on these prices, and until today there was no public market for where they're going. Which is nuts. So Polymarket built it.

This will change how compute gets bought and financed. Every contract negotiation and every GPU loan will have a market price to check against.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are being committed to compute years in advance. Many of those deals are essentially a levered bet on what GPUs will rent for in the future (what could go wrong lol)

As AI financing sobers up, the labs buying compute, the providers selling it, and the lenders financing it will all need to hedge that risk.

We think compute could become one of the largest financial markets in the world. This launch is Polymarket's first step toward building it. 

If you’re buying, selling, or financing compute, DM us with what markets you'd like to see.

睡得早没熬夜错过了SpaceX大叙事，马斯克真的是救市英雄。

越来越怀疑特朗普政府手里有个专门救市的抽屉，平时攒着利好不发，专挑美股快绷不住的时候扔出来。

今晚本来是标准的暴跌剧本：盘前美国 Q3 GDP 上修到 4.3%，10月核心 PCE 通胀又超预期干到 3.3%，降息没戏甚至开始交易加息。开盘直接砸崩，纳指最多跌近 5%，3倍半导体暴跌 24.5%，BTC 一路漏到 $57,256。

结果北京时间半夜十二点多（美东正午 12 点），全场最绝望的时候，FCC 突然宣布批准马斯克 SpaceX 在太空部署 100 万颗卫星建 AI 数据中心。硬靠“太空 AI”叙事把美股抢救了回来，消息落地两小时从日内最低点全线暴拉：

- SpaceX (SPCX)：$112.9 → $128.2（+13.5%，从跌10%直接翻红）
- 3倍半导体 (SOXL)：$24.6 → $31.6（+28.5%）
- 特斯拉 (TSLA)：$357.6 → $383.5（+7.2%）
- 英伟达 (NVDA)：$141.1 → $148.6（+5.3%）
- 纳指 (QQQ)：$607.7 → $634.7（+4.4%，期指拉回超 1,000 点）
- 道指 (DJI)：48,913 → 50,395（拉回 1,482 点直接翻红）
- 比特币 (BTC)：$57,256 → $60,386（+$3,130 / +5.5%）
- 恐慌指数 (VIX)：34.95 → 28.1（-19.6%）

这种跨度 这么多年的大审批，早不发晚不发，偏偏卡在通胀炸雷、盘面要踩踏的中午放出来，很难相信是巧合。

说白了股市一直是特朗普最核心的命根子。

回想之前几次也一模一样，只要市场没信心、眼看要走熊他就必定搞点事托底——前两天 AI 崩盘，白宫和财长立马松口配合黄仁勋闪电回归（一天把英伟达拉涨 31%）；

今晚宏观数据砸盘，美国时间中午又把马斯克的太空 AI 抬出来救场。

看空数据容易，但你永远猜不到老特抽屉里下一张牌是什么。

author: sarthakgh
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

It's an odd time in agentland b/c (as @venturetwins says) the rules of consumer are not holding

Hypergrowth used to supersede all else in fundraising. Now, doubling each month isn't enough 🤯

Costs per user are high + everyone is growing SO fast + incumbents are a true threat
author: omooretweets
quoted_text:
It’s sink-or-swim time for consumer agents.

A bunch of them finally have demand - which is amazing! But most haven’t figured out the economics.

They want to keep the viral growth going so many aren’t charging users…but the costs of LLMs, browser use, and even voice calls are adding up.

Many consumer agent companies I’ve talked to are spending $15-50+ per user per month - and much more for power users.

Taking a cut of payments facilitated by agents makes sense, but that ecosystem isn’t yet mature enough to drive meaningful revenue.

And it’s hard to raise $ to fund this burn if you aren’t one of the top players in the space + you’re competing with deep-pocketed companies like Meta who can spend billions on this.

I expect we’re going to see a reckoning here - consumer agent companies will finally have to invest in optimize their infrastructure (likely through third-parties), and the end users will stop getting so much for free!

quoted_text:
I’m currently advising  3 pregnant friends who want to attempt unmedicated births. I’ve been surprised at they are all afraid to read birth stories because they’ve only heard negative ones from their peers. 

Not reading birth stories is like showing up to a job interview unprepared or a marathon with no training. 

I sent each of them Ina May’s Guide to Childbirth, a list of 6 other books I read, and a podcast I listened to daily while pregnant. 

Nothing bothered me the day I gave birth because I had heard everything happening to me from another woman’s story.
