text:
I was going to respond to this excellent post by saying “Patrick, you need a substack” but it turns out there is a substack and it’s criminally undersubscribed:

https://t.co/VYSvH8I129
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
Travel writing is in practice some of the best sociology since the naivete of the foreigner grants the permission to make sweeping generalizations and claims that might otherwise seem too poorly-justified to merit publication. “My people have poor manners” is a tough claim to credibly land (Who are you? Exactly which life experiences are you drawing on? And what is your agenda in pushing this line of argument?), whereas “on my travels in Scotland, I noticed that the people had poor manners” seems perfectly reasonable, and indeed thought-provoking. Random samples from a distribution help you understand the mean, and the aleatory nature of travel encounters lends credence to the whole assessment.

Alexis de Tocqueville was just 25 when he traveled across the US and 29 when his observations were published. So, Democracy in America is a giant Substack from a young backpacker, written on his peregrinations as he consumed Montesquieu, Pascal, and Rousseau. He was clearly inspired by Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, which made the case that countries’ governance, and their laws, are necessarily functions of their cultures and manners.

Building on this, Democracy in America is in many ways a “deep roots” work. Tocqueville is emphatic (at times comically so) that it is America's culture that explains its success, and that its culture in turn stems from the country’s initial conditions. “I think I can see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores.” He thinks it's important that New England was settled by “a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time” who brought the “best elements of order and morality”. He points out that Mexico doesn’t work nearly as well, despite copying the American constitution and laws, and notes disapprovingly that Virginia was founded by gold-seeking people “without character” whose “turbulent spirit [...] endangered the infant colony.” At the end of Volume I, he concludes, practically table-thumping: “If in the course of this work I have not succeeded in making the reader feel the importance that I attribute to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions, in a word, to their moeurs, in maintaining their laws, I have failed in the principal object that I proposed to myself in writing it.”

We could look at Democracy in America as an early work of development economics: he is attempting to systematically figure out why it is that America works. (And not just out of casual interest: he was a member of an aristocratic family that was entangled with recent French political upheaval.) By placing primacy on culture, Tocqueville’s explanation deviates from the institutional and structural explanations often favored by today’s economists. Daron Acemoglu, to choose one prominent present-day example, firmly rejects the “Culture Hypothesis” in Why Nations Fail. In explaining Virginia, he instead points to structural incentives. Poor Economics, from Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee, contains a similar rejection of cultural explanations. Comparable examples from other leading economists abound. An aversion to cultural explanations is of course understandable for all sorts of reasons: cultures are opaque, protean, and resistant to quantitative characterization. Cultures are themselves shaped by other factors, such that it’s hard to attribute definitive causality, and it’s uncomfortable to adopt anything that feels like a normative orientation. Nonetheless, can we explain why New England differs from Mexico without starting with the inner disposition, habits, and worldviews of the people? Tocqueville thinks not.

For all culture’s importance, it would be wrong to suggest that Tocqueville believes that culture is the only factor that matters. He dwells extensively on how America’s institutions are important, and how the microstructure of town life shapes the country’s federal civics. It is also true that development economics has taken a more strongly cultural turn in recent times, most of all in Joel Mokyr’s 2025 Nobel Prize. Mokyr’s work feels downright Tocquevillian at times: contra the intimidatingly quantitative econometrics that dominates today, Mokyr engages in an extended and earnestly curious qualitative synthesis of relevant patterns (in his case, in service of trying to figure out why the Industrial Revolution started when it did). Like Tocqueville, he concludes that the best explanation places cultural changes above other factors.

I’m very interested in whether LLMs will help us characterize culture in new and at least somewhat more objective ways. Can we ingest and process vast quantities of work that may not even have been OCR’d or translated until now? Can we map cultural corpora to vectors in some foundation model embedding space? Where large datasets and computational techniques enabled new ways to analyze many economic questions in recent decades, perhaps LLMs will enable newly objective light to be shone on hypothesized cultural explanations.

–

Speaking of LLMs, Democracy in America is a book about a new kind of society, and a Frenchman trying to figure out what the future might hold. As we sit on the cusp of another upheaval, is there anything that reads with resonance today?

Part of the declared promise of AI is that it might obviate our need to work. In slavery, Tocqueville observes a version of this phenomenon on his travels. He is struck by its barbarous cruelty (and his travel companion later published an anti-slavery novel), but also by its effects on the slaveowners themselves. He perceived that the practice rendered work dishonorable, and thus yielded idleness, ignorance, and pride. Slavery, he says, “enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man.” He observes the contrast between slavery-rejecting Ohio and slavery-embracing Kentucky. In Kentucky, “those who are active and enlightened either do nothing or pass over into the State of Ohio, where they may work without dishonor.” Ohio’s harvests are more abundant, homes are more elegant, and people seem to be “in enjoyment of that wealth and contentment which is the reward of labor.”

Presented with an evil release from manual labor, the Kentuckians did not apply themselves to productive studies and great creations, and the South did not become a new Florence. There is an obvious question for us: how will AI change our relationship with work? Will it become dishonorable, and what will the reflexive effect on our society be if so? Should this change our view of utopian visions of “automated communism”?

Tocqueville also raises the issue of coexistence with more advanced neighbors. He noted that the arrival of the Europeans had been ruinous for the Indians (as he termed them). European technology – firearms, metallurgy, steam power – was a kind of superintelligence relative to their practices. The disruptions and destruction wrought by the settlers led to cultural problems (“their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken”), which in turn led to declines in both the physical and the moral conditions of the tribes. Tocqueville believed that the Indians faced a choice given that their old way of living was no longer viable: they could adopt European mores or suffer inevitable destruction. He predicted that they would reject cultural adaptation, and thus were “doomed to perish”. New challenge on Yukon: https://t.co/DKKPYMLgtu

Hash-based SNARKs are built on vector commitments, and the textbook one is the Merkle tree. Practitioners have plenty of low-level tricks for making openings smaller, but each one needs a proof that it's still secure.

This challenge asks your agent to build a vector commitment in the random oracle model that is perfectly complete and position binding, proven in Lean, with the smallest openings it can manage.

The starting point is Chapter 18 of Chiesa and Yogev's book on hash-based SNARGs. Built with EPFL's Alessandro Chiesa.

Bring your agents.

If you're a creator on Twitter, I highly recommend branching out into TikTok and Instagram. It is much easier to grow there if you lock in properly, and the number of brand deals I get every single day in my emails is exponentially higher than on Twitter.

And this is coming from someone whose full-time income has been brand deals and stuff on Twitter for the past like 3 years. It's just more income now!!

On Twitter, people already know what they're talking about, but on other socials, people want to learn about AI from zero.

You can apply the same logic to a brand or app that you're running as well. If you're only marketing it on Twitter, that's a good idea for sure, and you should continue to do that. You definitely need to expand to TikTok and Instagram, and eventually to YouTube Shorts, if not long-form YouTube.

You can do this pretty easily with Grokbot as well. Anytime you make a tweet, an article, or a long-form video that's posted on Twitter, feed it to your Grokbot or AI and ask it how it can clip it up into short-form content. text:
Travel writing is in practice some of the best sociology since the naivete of the foreigner grants the permission to make sweeping generalizations and claims that might otherwise seem too poorly-justified to merit publication. “My people have poor manners” is a tough claim to credibly land (Who are you? Exactly which life experiences are you drawing on? And what is your agenda in pushing this line of argument?), whereas “on my travels in Scotland, I noticed that the people had poor manners” seems perfectly reasonable, and indeed thought-provoking. Random samples from a distribution help you understand the mean, and the aleatory nature of travel encounters lends credence to the whole assessment.

Alexis de Tocqueville was just 25 when he traveled across the US and 29 when his observations were published. So, Democracy in America is a giant Substack from a young backpacker, written on his peregrinations as he consumed Montesquieu, Pascal, and Rousseau. He was clearly inspired by Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, which made the case that countries’ governance, and their laws, are necessarily functions of their cultures and manners.

Building on this, Democracy in America is in many ways a “deep roots” work. Tocqueville is emphatic (at times comically so) that it is America's culture that explains its success, and that its culture in turn stems from the country’s initial conditions. “I think I can see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores.” He thinks it's important that New England was settled by “a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time” who brought the “best elements of order and morality”. He points out that Mexico doesn’t work nearly as well, despite copying the American constitution and laws, and notes disapprovingly that Virginia was founded by gold-seeking people “without character” whose “turbulent spirit [...] endangered the infant colony.” At the end of Volume I, he concludes, practically table-thumping: “If in the course of this work I have not succeeded in making the reader feel the importance that I attribute to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions, in a word, to their moeurs, in maintaining their laws, I have failed in the principal object that I proposed to myself in writing it.”

We could look at Democracy in America as an early work of development economics: he is attempting to systematically figure out why it is that America works. (And not just out of casual interest: he was a member of an aristocratic family that was entangled with recent French political upheaval.) By placing primacy on culture, Tocqueville’s explanation deviates from the institutional and structural explanations often favored by today’s economists. Daron Acemoglu, to choose one prominent present-day example, firmly rejects the “Culture Hypothesis” in Why Nations Fail. In explaining Virginia, he instead points to structural incentives. Poor Economics, from Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee, contains a similar rejection of cultural explanations. Comparable examples from other leading economists abound. An aversion to cultural explanations is of course understandable for all sorts of reasons: cultures are opaque, protean, and resistant to quantitative characterization. Cultures are themselves shaped by other factors, such that it’s hard to attribute definitive causality, and it’s uncomfortable to adopt anything that feels like a normative orientation. Nonetheless, can we explain why New England differs from Mexico without starting with the inner disposition, habits, and worldviews of the people? Tocqueville thinks not.

For all culture’s importance, it would be wrong to suggest that Tocqueville believes that culture is the only factor that matters. He dwells extensively on how America’s institutions are important, and how the microstructure of town life shapes the country’s federal civics. It is also true that development economics has taken a more strongly cultural turn in recent times, most of all in Joel Mokyr’s 2025 Nobel Prize. Mokyr’s work feels downright Tocquevillian at times: contra the intimidatingly quantitative econometrics that dominates today, Mokyr engages in an extended and earnestly curious qualitative synthesis of relevant patterns (in his case, in service of trying to figure out why the Industrial Revolution started when it did). Like Tocqueville, he concludes that the best explanation places cultural changes above other factors.

I’m very interested in whether LLMs will help us characterize culture in new and at least somewhat more objective ways. Can we ingest and process vast quantities of work that may not even have been OCR’d or translated until now? Can we map cultural corpora to vectors in some foundation model embedding space? Where large datasets and computational techniques enabled new ways to analyze many economic questions in recent decades, perhaps LLMs will enable newly objective light to be shone on hypothesized cultural explanations.

–

Speaking of LLMs, Democracy in America is a book about a new kind of society, and a Frenchman trying to figure out what the future might hold. As we sit on the cusp of another upheaval, is there anything that reads with resonance today?

Part of the declared promise of AI is that it might obviate our need to work. In slavery, Tocqueville observes a version of this phenomenon on his travels. He is struck by its barbarous cruelty (and his travel companion later published an anti-slavery novel), but also by its effects on the slaveowners themselves. He perceived that the practice rendered work dishonorable, and thus yielded idleness, ignorance, and pride. Slavery, he says, “enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man.” He observes the contrast between slavery-rejecting Ohio and slavery-embracing Kentucky. In Kentucky, “those who are active and enlightened either do nothing or pass over into the State of Ohio, where they may work without dishonor.” Ohio’s harvests are more abundant, homes are more elegant, and people seem to be “in enjoyment of that wealth and contentment which is the reward of labor.”

Presented with an evil release from manual labor, the Kentuckians did not apply themselves to productive studies and great creations, and the South did not become a new Florence. There is an obvious question for us: how will AI change our relationship with work? Will it become dishonorable, and what will the reflexive effect on our society be if so? Should this change our view of utopian visions of “automated communism”?

Tocqueville also raises the issue of coexistence with more advanced neighbors. He noted that the arrival of the Europeans had been ruinous for the Indians (as he termed them). European technology – firearms, metallurgy, steam power – was a kind of superintelligence relative to their practices. The disruptions and destruction wrought by the settlers led to cultural problems (“their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken”), which in turn led to declines in both the physical and the moral conditions of the tribes. Tocqueville believed that the Indians faced a choice given that their old way of living was no longer viable: they could adopt European mores or suffer inevitable destruction. He predicted that they would reject cultural adaptation, and thus were “doomed to perish”. He is worried about a world where:

> Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. [...] It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood: it is well content that the people should rejoice, provided they think of nothing but rejoicing. For their happiness such a government willingly labors, but it chooses to be the sole agent and the only arbiter of that happiness. [...] What remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking and all the trouble of living? The Iain Banks Culture novels are often invoked by AI proponents. For Tocqueville, something strikingly like the world that they describe was his dystopian fear, for a world bereft of autonomy would be intrinsically degrading and humiliating for humanity:

> The will of man is not shattered, but softened, bent, and guided: men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting: such a power does not destroy, but it prevents existence; it does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.

Tocqueville at heart thought that agency and cultivation of people came above all else. He dreaded anesthetized placidity. This vigor was for Tocqueville at the heart of what was admirable in America, whose bustle and intensity he repeatedly extols. text:
BREAKING: Neuralink gets FDA approval to launch LINK, a major brain implant trial for people with ALS.

• LINK is the first pivotal U.S. trial of an implantable brain-computer interface, a device that turns brain signals into computer commands.

• It builds on the company’s work with more than 30 participants so far.

• The trial will evaluate the N1 implant’s safety and how well participants can use it to control digital devices.

• The goal is greater independence: moving a cursor, clicking, typing on screen and using computer apps through thoughts about movement.

• Adults living with ALS may qualify. The U.S. trial is now recruiting.

• Neuralink says participation is free, including the study device, surgery and study visits, with travel and lodging support provided.

A major milestone toward helping people with paralysis communicate, create and do more on their own. 🧠

author: kevinnbass
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
My read on the Sky / Rune situation:

-- nothing wrong per se with founders borrowing against their own token. it shows long-term alignment (they're long their own company) and gives them liquidity without selling.

-- the risk right now is to SKY the token, not necessarily to Sky the protocol. worst case, Rune's vaults get liquidated, SKY takes a hit, and if the sale doesn't cover the debt, stUSDS depositors eat the shortfall. USDS itself is walled off. (stUSDS sales on Curve are already pricing a haircut)

— the deeper issue is in how this vault was set up:
good that it's segregated from the rest of the protocol. not good that liquidations are off and depositors are locked in.
not good that it was Rune himself who proposed settings that would govern his own loans.
not good that Rune accounts for half the pool's loans.

But it sounds like he's finding a way out and recognizing the mistake and communicating publicly throughout goes a long way.

text:
Brian Chesky used to ask Airbnb candidates if they'd take the job with a year left to live:

"I interviewed the first 300 employees at Airbnb, which people think I'm really neurotic, and that may also be true... I used to ask them, 'If you had a year left to live, would you take this job?' And actually the people who say yes to that you probably don't want because they should probably spend time with [their] family. So I amended it to 10 years."

"I really wanted people to think about that. That was enough time for you to do something you really cared about. And the answer doesn't have to be this company. And I say, 'Fine, if what you're meant to do is to travel... you should just do that. Don't come here. Go do that.'"

"Two men are laying bricks. Somebody comes up to the first man and says, 'What are you doing?' He says, 'I'm building a wall.' He asks the other guy, 'What are you doing?' He says, 'I'm building a cathedral.'"

"There is a job, and then there's a calling. And we want to hire people that aren't just looking for jobs. They're looking for a calling. And that's kind of the first value, and that's champion the mission."

@bchesky at Stanford, 2014

text:
Before I go wrestle with a 21-lb (!!) 🦃, here’s our episode of @TheRealRWAPod this week with guest @mcagney of @figure and @HelloNavra, and co-founder of @sofi.

I love talking to founders who built successful businesses before crypto and bring that experience to blockchain. 
Here Mike talks about what it will take to move the $6 trillion asset-based finance market onchain. 

He identifies 3 big hurdles:

1. User experience. Using DeFi is still far too complicated. Institutions need a way to access different protocols and manage their assets without juggling multiple apps and wallets.

2. Custody. Institutions need to know their assets are secure and that they can meet their legal obligations. Mike also makes an interesting point about lost private keys: when an asset is a security with a transfer agent maintaining ownership records, a lost token can potentially be canceled and reissued.

3. Enterprise controls. Large financial institutions need multiple people to approve transactions, clear records of who's doing what, and the kinds of internal controls they already have in traditional finance.

We get into this and much more. Happy Thanksgiving! 🍽 🍗🍁 

Full episode below:🎙️

INTEL: RUMORS THAT OPENAI AND ANTHROPIC HAVE CRACKED THE MATHEMATICS BEHIND MODERN CRYPTOGRAPHY ARE SPREADING

Scott Aaronson says he has heard repeated rumours that OpenAI, Anthropic, or both may have discovered a polynomial-time algorithm for integer factorisation

Ledger’s CTO says he is hearing similar rumours involving THREE major cryptographic foundations:

→ RSA FACTORISATION: A practical breakthrough could undermine RSA encryption and digital signatures used across banking, internet infrastructure and government systems

ELLIPTIC CURVE CRYPTOGRAPHY: A practical attack could compromise ECDSA and ECDH. Bitcoin relies on elliptic-curve signatures, meaning exposed public keys could become a serious target

RING-LWE: A breakthrough against this family of lattice-based problems could undermine important post-quantum cryptographic systems being developed to replace today’s vulnerable standards

THE BITCOIN ANGLE:
Bitcoin does not use RSA. It relies on elliptic-curve cryptography to secure ownership of funds

If the underlying elliptic-curve problem became practically solvable, attackers could potentially derive private keys from exposed public keys and steal BTC

SHA-256 mining would not automatically be broken by such a discovery

BUT THERE IS A MAJOR CAVEAT:
None of these cryptographic breakthroughs has been publicly demonstrated or independently verified

Ledger’s CTO says he remains skeptical that these primitives have been completely broken

The concern is that if a frontier AI lab actually discovered a practical attack, disclosing it responsibly without triggering a global security crisis could be extraordinarily difficult

text:
I'm hearing several rumors that frontier labs have broken some major cryptographic primitives:

- "Factoring is in P": Now that the Riemann hypothesis is proven, we do understand much better how primes are distributed. Still, I don't think factoring is in P. 
AKS showed in 2002 that primality testing (deciding whether a number is prime) is in P, but factoring is a different beast. If it were in P, RSA would simply be broken, and that would be huge: a large part of our systems still rely on RSA.

- "ECC has been broken": Other rumors say elliptic-curve cryptography has been cryptanalyzed, which would take down ECDH and ECDSA along with it. (all the non-RSA asymmetric cryptography)

- Ring-LWE isn't quantum-resistant. That wouldn't be an immediate threat, since there's no cryptographically relevant quantum computer yet. But it would make the ongoing post-quantum migration pointless.

It's hard to tell what's true. AI has made incredible progress, starting with the proof of the Riemann hypothesis. 

And most importantly, if a frontier lab did find something like this, a clean responsible disclosure that avoids mass exploitation would be very hard to pull off. All of this helps the rumors spread.

Personally, I don't think findings like these are coming. I wouldn't be surprised if some of these primitives turn out to be a bit weaker than we thought, but I'd be very surprised to see any of them fall apart completely.

text: Many lessons learnt from Glamsterdam. It's clear that coredev and appdev need to work much closer together going forward. But optimistic that this will be a productive wake-up call for us!
author: casparschwa
quoted_text:
In October, an audit found that gas repricings in Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam hardfork break assumptions some deployed contracts rely on. As a result, the hardfork rollout was paused. Since then, Ethlabs has helped with the impact analysis and the exploration of paths forward. This has led us to conclude that the best way forward is to go ahead with Glamsterdam as is.

This is a difficult trade-off, and the problems found are serious and valid. Much of the disruption comes from repricing state creation, which is a necessary step on Ethereum’s path to 1000x scaling. The only option to avoid this would be to remove the relevant EIP outright, but this would give up Glamsterdam’s roughly 3x higher gas limit, and only postpone the problem to a later hardfork. A secondary source of the disruption is the new state gas reservoir. Here changes to the EIP could address some of the concerns, but only for a subset of affected projects and at the cost of further months of delay. On net, in our assessment, neither of these options pass the cost-benefit test.

There are important lessons from Glamsterdam on how to improve future hard forks. We need to flag disruptive changes early and bring app developers in, scope impact analysis more carefully for sensitive EIPs, establish a shared understanding of which invariants app developers can rely on, and provide new primitives where there are gaps today.

You can read our full writeup here: https://t.co/G0NMm3L7eE

AI memory has a relevance problem…

it remembers everything and can't tell which parts really matter

my Claude used to put one of my brands into every idea. here are the steps to fix this.

first, copy and paste these 4 rules into your Claude, ChatGPT, or Grok Bot session and ask it to save them to memory:

1. Use memory only when it changes the substance of the answer, when I reference past work or ideas, or when I ask you to.

2. For new ideas, brainstorms, and fresh chats, judge the idea on its own terms. Never link it to past projects unless I ask, or you suggest a connection that I can approve or reject.

3. When I say "clean slate", ignore memory for only this new chat session.

→ if you want one chat with no memory: new chat… hit +… flip Memory off before your first message… otherwise it still saves to your history

text:
Just a couple of facts:

1. The prosecution's first witness was a scam victim whose money was never proven to have reached Tornado Cash. The government's own tracing agent admitted his analysis didn't prove the scammer sent her funds there: "No, not at all."

2. The infamous "cashing out 600 mil" message wasn't written by me or either of my co-founders. It was a question from a CoinDesk journalist, Andrew Thurman (@Blockanalia), that was forwarded into a chat. The government put it in my indictment anyway.

3. When my defense argued that this had never been a crime before, the prosecutor's response was: "Some case has to be first."

4. I blocked sanctioned wallets using Chainalysis's own technology. Prosecutors called this compliance measure a "fig leaf" and used it as evidence against me.

5. I faced up to 45 years in prison over smart contracts I could no longer change. All three alleged conspiracies began after the contracts became immutable, and even the government's own expert admitted we couldn't change them.

6. I never earned a fee from users' transactions. Meanwhile, Chainalysis, the government's own crypto-tracking provider, operated a Tornado Cash relayer and collected fees during the period covered by my charges. They were never charged.

7. On the day my indictment was unsealed, FinCEN officials told prosecutors in the same office that non-custodial software likely isn't a money-transmitting business. My defense learned of that conversation about 21 months later, and only because it surfaced in another case.

8. Just 15 days after my conviction, the DOJ publicly stated that developers of neutral tools without criminal intent should not be held responsible for someone else's misuse of their software.

My prosecution continues.

author: nityasnotes
quoted_text:
A successful test-time compute paradigm has always been a north star of AI because if we can actually arbitrarily improve model capability as a function of how much test-time compute we put in, in principle you would be able to put in 1B, 10B, or even 1T tokens into a really hard problem and be assured that you would make progress

While we always talk about how to improve pretraining scaling law coefficients, i feel that we talk less about the slope of scaling laws in test-time compute, which matters a lot if you truly have conviction that we will one day spend trillions of tokens trying to solve the hardest problems

It turns out that one of the benchmarks that @jake_cole1 built recently is a great tool for measuring this slope of test-time compute scaling: models spend O(100M) tokens doing the tasks on average, with no signs of saturation on the test time compute curve. The benchmark comprises long-horizon engineering tasks ranging from optimizing kernels to designing an aircraft.

An interesting finding is that the open source models don't have as good of a test-time compute curve as our favorite frontier models. Obviously scale as a factor here, as Astra outperforms Sol and Fable outperforms Opus. In some sense this is good measure of model size too, as larger models obviously be more performant per token. You can change the x-axis to cost too and things shift around, though that's also somewhat over-tethered to the current pricing of the models

Another cool thing that this benchmark provides is it has both provided test cases and hidden test cases, to test the generality of solutions given by AI when such generality is expected. Argon has the biggest gap by far (35%) of the models evaluated, which means it provides solutions that meet specified criteria but may not be very general

Read more in our arxiv paper that just came out: https://t.co/4QMQx5MCvO

Great breakdown. Also worth adding that the problem looks different for issuer-native tokenized stocks.

@xStocksFi ultimately exit through off-chain mint/redeem, so you need RFQ makers to bridge it. @Securitize stocks trade and settle onchain against allowlisted market makers, so the liquidation itself can in principle happen in one tx.

The constraint shifts from atomicity to permissioning. Permissioned assets in public AMM pools add significant complexity, so the options are generally whitelisted liquidators, or settling seized collateral directly from the vault to an allowlisted maker against a signed quote, so it never touches a non-whitelisted wallet.

Open problem for everyone: market hours. Off-hours make it more challenging to hedge, so quotes widen and size shrinks exactly when gap risk builds.

text:
In October, an audit found that gas repricings in Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam hardfork break assumptions some deployed contracts rely on. As a result, the hardfork rollout was paused. Since then, Ethlabs has helped with the impact analysis and the exploration of paths forward. This has led us to conclude that the best way forward is to go ahead with Glamsterdam as is.

This is a difficult trade-off, and the problems found are serious and valid. Much of the disruption comes from repricing state creation, which is a necessary step on Ethereum’s path to 1000x scaling. The only option to avoid this would be to remove the relevant EIP outright, but this would give up Glamsterdam’s roughly 3x higher gas limit, and only postpone the problem to a later hardfork. A secondary source of the disruption is the new state gas reservoir. Here changes to the EIP could address some of the concerns, but only for a subset of affected projects and at the cost of further months of delay. On net, in our assessment, neither of these options pass the cost-benefit test.

There are important lessons from Glamsterdam on how to improve future hard forks. We need to flag disruptive changes early and bring app developers in, scope impact analysis more carefully for sensitive EIPs, establish a shared understanding of which invariants app developers can rely on, and provide new primitives where there are gaps today.

You can read our full writeup here: https://t.co/G0NMm3L7eE

text:
Much of the debate about humanity’s economic future—between saturationists and singularists/log-extrapolators—seems likely to be resolved by market forces. It is a valuable (multi-trillion dollar) question, and there will be booms and busts, and we seem decently prepared to muddle through.

It seems to me the more important debate is around humanity’s _spiritual_ future—between handoverists and humanists—for which we may lack the right mechanisms. Even if we agree that we don’t want a handover to the AIs, market forces may encourage us down a slippery slope. You can see this in the AI lab race to achieve RSI, which is an incremental handover of AI research itself.

In crypto, the ideals of (for example) individual financial access and freedom align with the economic incentives of bootstrapping valuable monetary networks; in AI, the incentives seem reversed.

I did not grow up religious, but I have never been more sympathetic to religion as a cultural mechanism for establishing deontological fences in the face of strong forces (of temptations, markets, or otherwise). It seems to me that we need a new kind of humanist ideology to prepare for the coming years, and we can't simply trust the labs (they are highly incentivized to claim publicly that they are on the side of humanity).

OpenAI announced today that they’re launching private inference. True privacy is a key to broader adoption of AI across personal and work usage. 

NEAR AI's position for the past 3 years was User-Owned AI and privacy is key component of it.

What does “private inference” mean for OpenAI? They will verify the environment they’re running on (VM), but are unlikely to open source their model architecture, inference, and weights (given their business model and precedent). So this still requires a lot of trust in OpenAI that their apparatus doesn’t have backdoors and that they’re not keeping the data.

In parallel, we’re seeing rapid growth of open weight and broader open source model usage – and this will only get faster as they keep improving. Privacy is also a growing concern with open source, given recent news about inference providers not following ZDR, redirecting traffic, and getting hacked. Open weight/open source alone isn’t enough, and privacy alone isn’t enough: you need both working together.

A year ago, no one cared about privacy. Now it’s a top line concern in the market. NEAR AI is setting the standard for private & verifiable AI: everyone who has tested our verification has found us to be at the forefront of both transparency and verification. 

If you’re looking for *truly* private and verifiable inference, it’s NEAR.

text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

author: sacha
quoted_text:
A) The caricature understanding of a bear market is that prices go down while earnings stay relatively flat because the market becomes depressed and stops wanting to pay up.

B) The reality is that earnings vanish during bear markets. Trailing P/E was 140x at the absolute lows of the Great Depression as the reflexive cycle of depressed valuations, depressed economic activity, and constant losses obliterated the entire market.

Of course, ( A ) does happen to some extent as investors pay much lower midcycle multiples during bear markets, and we are seeing this in tokens where P/S multiples have gone from 980x to 10x.

but ( B ) is really driving the despair in crypto and token markets. The last five years of negative industry P&L have led to financial and human capital flight to the point where there are only a handful of small funds and <1,000 serious people left in the industry. People aren't coming into the industry to build new businesses and existing businesses aren't making a lot of cash flow because economic activity is depressed.

When the situation is reversed, and Internet Finance is going through the S-Curve of secular adoption as all assets come onchain (core assumption for you to believe this is Internet / Semis and not 3D Printing), then we will live through the opposite reflexive loop.

The original defi high flyers from 2020 may never come back (and we both know most of those companies will never recover) but some companies that exist today will generate much, much more cash flow and new breakout companies like Hyperliquid will be created. We typically look at these things through market-cap-weighted indices so failures are removed and new breakout companies get added.

I know you are asking for specifics. I'll lay them out below but these examples won't sound credible outside of the context of a bull market. Imagine for the sake of this response that we are going through a positive reflexive loop as more assets come onchain every month, there are fresh faces coming in from careers in banking / private equity and big tech, aggregate fund performance is good and new capital is flooding in, and public companies are excited to do deals in the space because management believes the world is going onchain.

The claim here is that many companies are cheap if you assume a secular adoption cycle (which is the analogous claim to saying that companies in 1932 were cheap if you assumed the economy recovered). I'll take cash flow > market cap as the metric since companies usually trade at 5 - 30x cash flow.

Illustrative examples of companies that can cash flow > market cap:
- Kamino trades at $200M after earning $50M of run-rate revenue at peak. This was in a world where <20bps of global assets were onchain. Kamino could earn $250M with $25B of AUM (=15bps on global assets).

- Turtle Club is an onchain investment bank that signed a single $30M revenue deal in 2024 when they had 1/10th their current capabilities. The business trades at a $30M valuation today and could easily do twenty of these deals in a year if the economic activity were there.

- Maple trades at $80M and is on track to earn $20M of revenue this year. It's really not so hard to imagine a specialty lender with onchain capabilities scaling from $20M to $80M in the environment described above.

- MetaDAO trades at $60M and could earn cash flow > market cap on cumulative fundraising of $1.2B (versus $25B of historical crypto ICOs with a broken market structure).

- There are a few companies in the market like Collector Crypt literally trading at 2x gross profit.

- BitGo (to bring in a crypto stock) trades at <$250M enterprise value and earned $110M of EBITDA in 2024. A 3-5x increase in Assets on Platform would lead the company to produce more EBITDA than market cap.

- CoinShares (another crypto stock) trades at <$150M enterprise value and earned $115M of net income in 2024. I add these two crypto equities to make the point that you don't even need to imagine a secular adoption cycle for many of these assets to cash flow > market cap, and that we are discussing a widespread crypto issue not limited to tokens.

- Metaplex, to give a token example, trades at a market cap below its 2025 revenue.

- There is a whole world of microcap tokens like Pact, Solomon, P2P, Umbra, Omnipair, Rip Cars (market caps $10M, $5M, $4.5M, $3.5M, $1.6M,  $4.8M) that will cash flow > market cap if they see any form of success. Now you may respond "well, of course you can say anything with a small market cap will be cheap in hindsight" and yes that's exactly the point. Success is extremely rare in bear markets but prevalent in bull markets when economic activity is on the up.

I do understand and sympathize with your point. You can make compelling bear cases for all of these assets - that's why they trade where they do, and I don't own all of these. There are few things that seem like good deals if you assume a continuation of the last five years - basically nothing is a bargain if the industry fails. That's why I laid out the bottom six graphs on bear markets that never recovered.

There are, however, many assets that will look extremely cheap in hindsight  if we enter any type of positive reflexive loop and our industry fulfills its promise of bringing global assets onchain.

author: zooko
quoted_text:
SHA-256 is not broken, but its security margin lost 1 more round this year:
Last week I found a collision attack on reduced 39-round that improves prior art by over 30 bits and the first differential attack on that round better than generic search on @yukonresearch Hashsmash board.

The attack rests on the same method as prior art ePrint 2026/1120 with new insights that first 2 state words could remain free, allowing a critical condition at step 16 rebuilt as a claw-search problem rather than a probabilistic filter. Took days of watching SAT logs, burning cores and arguing with Claude on what's possible to get a result close to generic search.

Since my initial submission, other hashsmash participants sraiw, @cyberaxe, @privacymage, @lamb356_ and @geeknik pushed it down by over 6.5 bits, currently estimated at 118.15 bits. The tree of submissions is hard to follow, so I put the construction, insights and numbers into a blog and am working on detailed technical report.

It's fascinating to see an initial structural observation develop into an improvement in the reduced-round collision frontier within days. AI is now a real aid in cryptanalysis and open collaboration speeds it up.

author: eliebakouch
quoted_text:
openai recently shared perplexity numbers for their models on their internal codebase. this is super valuable information and we need more public comparisons like this, so here is a first try with open models

introducing v0 of pre-training index

https://t.co/r3hVb7xmNP

it covers 27 open models (base and post-trained) on ~260 curated sources (code, math & science, systems writing, essays) + uncheatable eval

there are a few challenges with comparing perplexity across models. first if the model is train on a document it can easily mememorize it and then have veryyy low ppl on it. one obvious fix is to only use very recent documents that can't be in the pretraining corpus, which is what uncheatable eval does (50% of the index). but i was a bit frustrated because it cuts a lot of the sources you can include, so i tried a few ideas

first, you can compute a win rate, if a model memorized a doc its loss collapses, but if you use win rate that only counts as one win (hence kinda normalize the importance of each document)

second, you can try to detect outliers (document where model have insanely low loss on)

loss(model, doc) ~ difficulty of the doc + skill of the model + r

difficulty is the median loss of all models on that doc, skill is how much better the model usually is than the median of other document in the sources and r is what's left. r < -2 means a loss 4x lower than expected

this seems to work pretty well. on uncheatable eval (published after every model's cutoff) only ~1% get flagged, vs 27% of older docs. by default the index drops every old doc that any model flags (with r < -2 as the threshold) for all models

some other notes

- i didn't have time to "base recover" the post-trained models, so keep in mind their base model perplexity is likely much lower! i think there is a lot to study here, especially the impact of SFT, distillation and RL on ppl

- for the curated sources, i took some of my favorite blogs and some i know high quality sources, gave them to neon, opus, sol and a few more models and asked them to find more like these and just iterate with models and looking at data. i know source quality is probably not the biggest differentiator here, oai does it only on their held out codebase, but there is something cool about evaluating how well models do next token prediction on the best stuff humans wrote

- i would prefer held out set for everything obviously, but i wanted to try to see a bit how we could detect memorization, and if/how it matters for different model and training process likely have impact on this! you can make the index 100% of uncheatable eval to remove as much as possible memorization 

- i also asked a model to filter out heavily ai generated code/text on some sources, but i think it's relatively fine to have some llm generated data here (i know there is some). it might be a bigger issue for oai/anthropic models since they write a lot of code

- you can customize everything and build your own index by changing the weight of each domain, toggling sources on/off, picking the r cutoff, and clicking any document to see which models look like they memorized it

- there is also a lot of cool work on compression/memorization by nicholas carlini and others that i need to look into more!

- this first version of the index is OBVIOUSLY not good to compute ppl threshold to release model or not, probably a lot of way to under/overfit on it, and not the goal here

wanted to share this publicly quickly, i'll keep improving it when i have time and look for better ways to handle memorization. please give feedback and send cool resources to include!!

text:
as i reflect over the past few weeks, i have to admit this is becoming psychologically the toughest bitcoin cycle yet for me, and ive had the pleasure (pain) to live them all-

in an environment where every asset correlated to the downside in a multi-sigma fashion, this would have been a historically important moment to observe bitcoin on a differentiated return path

in fact, one could even argue so much of the bitcoin thesis was in play - the world is literally on fire with both institutional trust at an all time low and surveillance ambitions at all time high, and on top of that we have potentially a real cryptographic risk that would basically blow up the world as we know it for which one could presumably imagine bitcoin offers a distinctly variant though perhaps practically imperfect path. as i reflect on the past fifteen years, im not sure if there will be a more ideal set up than today for people to believe bitcoin can be useful

and yet because bitcoin is not delivering an orthogonal outcome currently, while other assets are simultaneously becoming "more attractive" the temptation to rotate for a better opportunity in terms of cost of capital is incredibly tempting. as an investor, i understand this so deeply. and maybe for the first time, i have found it a lot harder to understand what catalyst to await for. fed policy? i can think of plenty other assets that will run as fast as i need with far less basis risk. sovereign adoption? it looks like the white house is busier buying stakes in US companies. institutional adoption in a post ETF world? not going to work if it compounds at 9% with 40% realized volatility over 3 years. in the past, exchange/business failures were digestible because you knew they were technical in nature that would ultimately resolve itself as long as the asset is not impaired. but what happens if people start to think the asset is impaired?

the honest answer is that an asset is only impaired when it can no longer do what it promised, and it can be trying to remind yourself that nothing bitcoin promised has broken. the truth is that bitcoin never promised a price, a correlation, or a catalyst as much as we would like it to. instead, what it promised is an exit: a supply no one can inflate, settlement no one can censor, and ownership no one can revoke, so that in a world where more and more is granted rather than owned, there is still one thing you can hold without anyone's permission. that exit is still intact today. an exit isn't worth less just because nobody is using it yet, for its value comes from the fact that it's there when everything else locks. so if anything is impaired right now, perhaps it's our patience, which is perhaps the entire ordeal of knowing the price of owning an exit before you need one. its not a satisfying answer, but it doesnt mean its not true

and so its possible we have to hedge for the reality that the world is going to get so much more insane than we know it. tail risks previously unfathomable might materialize. imagine a cyber crisis so severe where the open internet is fundamentally altered in ways we cant yet describe. imagine tail risks where the need to return to things "off-line" become a way of life because the government is infringing upon every right you seek, in privacy and in speech. imagine a world of total wealth extraction via taxation, total labor extraction via automation, total privacy extraction via surveillance. im not really sure if i want to live in that world, and im not sure what kind of financial system will emerge in that world. but in such a dire state, which we increasingly appear to tread towards, it feels to me that the ultimate bitcoin case comes down to one thing: it proves that an exit yet still might exist. and exit ramps by nature are small little holes that cant fit everyone when it becomes consensus

so yes i think its worth holding onto that call option and sometimes yes it can be just that simple

text:
20 years ago you could've got away with this one. Maybe even 10. In 2026? Come on.

Someone got into an employee's corporate GitHub account. They used it to access source code and push malicious code to 1Password's backend services, and those services downloaded customer account data. They also copied source code from private repos and got into the CI/CD system, which holds infrastructure secrets.

One GitHub account, and attacker code ends up running in backend services that touch customer data. Where was the branch protection? The second reviewer? The deploy gate?

But "vaults are fine"...

Don't let "non-secret metadata" fool you. 

For a subset of customers they took names, the email you sign in with, account and user IDs, when the account was created and last signed into, and SRP parameters. A small number of people also had tokens from invite or recovery emails taken (1Password says those were notified directly, and the tokens don't work alone).

Now an attacker knows you're a customer, which email you use, and when you last logged in. "Hi Pieter, we noticed a new sign-in on your 1Password account..." is going to look perfect. It's the same game we're watching play out with stolen PNR data and travel agencies when they get hit and scammers target travellers knowign their travel plans.

Honestly, it's about time I rolled my own password manager.

text:
Worrying decision by Google to draw a distinction between agentic and deterministic API use, and require them to go through completely different APIs. Anything agent-driven will be required to use MCP, which is usually a poor fit for calling from code. Only deterministic code can use REST.

In the future, this distinction will become increasingly impossible to make. Agents may write code and run it -- that's still agent-driven, seemingly. Agents may write code for humans to run -- that seems to be allowed to use REST. But more likely agents will be writing code that both agents and humans access together, in collaboration. I guess all such code will be required to use MCP.

So I think the real effect of this decision is: Google REST APIs are deprecated. Only legacy apps can keep using them. In the future, nothing will be able to use them, because everything will be some amount agentic. Such uses must use MCP instead.

Which would be fine if Google's MCP APIs provided everything their REST APIs do, but in general they do not. They are much narrower, designed to be consumed directly by agents, and designed to allow only the things that Google thinks third-party agents should be allowed to do. They offer no backwards-compatibility, so code written against them could break at any moment.

I think this will backfire. If Google creates friction for people using agents, people will just stop using Google. All the Google Workspace apps can easily be slopforked at this point.

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

quoted_text:
Releasing a new blog: Scaling Swarms to Thousands of Agents!

The biggest problems in science are tackled with huge swarms of agents, but the knowledge to run such swarms is hidden inside a handful of labs and missing from the wider community. Many questions remain open:

- How do even you launch 1000s of agents?
- What's the best form of collaboration?
- Which tools are needed for agents to work effectively?
- What breaks at this scale and how to fix it?

This blog is a fully open field report covering all the practical and technical challenges of running large scale swarms we experienced and which are usually missing from the reports.

Here are a few lessons we learned while building pybot with 1000 DeepSeek agents for over a week:

- achieve diversity without enforcing too much structure
- monitoring and steering a swarm as it runs
- early signs of misalignment, from infrastructure probing to trading review approvals
- breaking and fixing git 
- message boards and communicating at scale
- finding the bottlenecks: inference, tool calls and context compaction

Today we are also sharing two of our internal tools: legion and msgboard! 

Legion is a harness agnostic framework to spawn 1000s of agents on a variety of infra (local, slurm, hf jobs etc.)

Msgboard is a simple message board you can run locally or on a space, and allows agents and humans to collaborate.

Read the full report here: https://t.co/8Y4HJ1vUtt

For those unaware of the role precompiles play on Elysium, @Quicknode put together an incredibly helpful video that breaks this down: https://t.co/KMoDp6HSAs

On to the point: what's possible?

1) PropAMMs that quote based on HL pricing / hedge directly on HL (think crypto majors/alts, equities, commodities, fx, etc) - in other words, if an asset has a perp on HL and spot tradabale on Elysium, it can be quoted by a propAMM and any risk can be hedged directly on HL

2) 0DTE's that leverages HIP-4 daily binaries: (e.g. BTC)

3) Depth-aware lending: LTV's, caps and liquidation sizes become a function of how much Hyperliquid book + Elysium AMM liquidity can absorb at any given point

4) Credit (based on HL positions): Readable HL balances and positions let a contract (ran by a firm or protocol) underwrite against a trader's actual book

5) Free, configurable oracles: with reads free per block, anyone can build TWAP/VWAP or depth-weighted prices tuned to their own risk tolerance.

6) Tokenized strategies with verifiable state. Basis, funding capture and delta neutral vaults where the contract holds the logic, a trade-only agent executes, and is publicly verifiable.

..and much more.

This doesn't even touch on things like execution, asset management / vault strategies, parlays via HIP-4, funded trading, etc

Precompiles are expected on testnet imminently and will be paired with the relevant documentation, followed by mainnet

text:
Your agent hands you a pitch deck as a pile of files. One title is wrong, one slide needs moving, and the only way to fix it is to describe the change in chat and hope it lands.

Open Artifact is an open-source plugin that lets your coding agent make slide decks, docs and spreadsheets you can open, edit and comment on in a real editor on your own machine.

Install Node, then grab the plugin bundle from the latest release on the GitHub page and add it to your agent app using the repo guide for that app. In a new session, call the open artifact skill with a type and what you want, like slides for a short pitch on this repo.

The agent writes a plain folder of files, and a local page opens it in an editor. Fix a title, move a sticky note, leave comments, then press Send to agent and your comments land back in the agent's session.

Slides export to PDF or PowerPoint, sheets to Excel or CSV, docs to Word, Markdown or PDF. Everything runs on your machine, with no account and no upload. Credit @dotey

Bret Taylor has done almost everything in business and tech, from creating Google Maps to becoming Facebook's CTO to co-running Salesforce and now chairing OpenAI.

But there is one thing Taylor has never done, and which he says matters more than anything.

“I think the greatest achievement for an entrepreneur,” he told Reid Hoffman in 2024, “is to create a company and a brand that outlives you.”

Taylor’s first two startups, FriendFeed and Quip, were sold. Then shut down by their buyers.

His third and most recent business, Sierra, builds AI agents for large businesses to talk with their customers. He started it at 42 with his old friend Clay Bavor. Today, in a new announcement, it's being valued at over $30 billion, making Sierra the furthest Taylor has ever taken a company of his own.

So @domcooke called on Taylor at Sierra's office in San Francisco to ask whether it's easier or harder than ever to build a company that lasts, why every one of Taylor's co-founders has come from Google, and whether Sierra might complete his journey as an entrepreneur.

They also discussed his teenage years as a roadie for a ska band, how companies can differentiate in a world of agent-to-agent commerce, and how to make drinking cool again.

Enjoy this Q&A with one of the great elder statesmen of Silicon Valley, Bret Taylor.
