For those unaware of the role precompiles play on Elysium, @Quicknode put together an incredibly helpful video that breaks this down: https://t.co/KMoDp6HSAs

On to the point: what's possible?

1) PropAMMs that quote based on HL pricing / hedge directly on HL (think crypto majors/alts, equities, commodities, fx, etc) - in other words, if an asset has a perp on HL and spot tradabale on Elysium, it can be quoted by a propAMM and any risk can be hedged directly on HL

2) 0DTE's that leverages HIP-4 daily binaries: (e.g. BTC)

3) Depth-aware lending: LTV's, caps and liquidation sizes become a function of how much Hyperliquid book + Elysium AMM liquidity can absorb at any given point

4) Credit (based on HL positions): Readable HL balances and positions let a contract (ran by a firm or protocol) underwrite against a trader's actual book

5) Free, configurable oracles: with reads free per block, anyone can build TWAP/VWAP or depth-weighted prices tuned to their own risk tolerance.

6) Tokenized strategies with verifiable state. Basis, funding capture and delta neutral vaults where the contract holds the logic, a trade-only agent executes, and is publicly verifiable.

..and much more.

This doesn't even touch on things like execution, asset management / vault strategies, parlays via HIP-4, funded trading, etc

Precompiles are expected on testnet imminently and will be paired with the relevant documentation, followed by mainnet

text:
OpenAI announced today that they’re launching private inference. True privacy is a key to broader adoption of AI across personal and work usage. 

NEAR AI's position for the past 3 years was User-Owned AI and privacy is key component of it.

What does “private inference” mean for OpenAI? They will verify the environment they’re running on (VM), but are unlikely to open source their model architecture, inference, and weights (given their business model and precedent). So this still requires a lot of trust in OpenAI that their apparatus doesn’t have backdoors and that they’re not keeping the data.

In parallel, we’re seeing rapid growth of open weight and broader open source model usage – and this will only get faster as they keep improving. Privacy is also a growing concern with open source, given recent news about inference providers not following ZDR, redirecting traffic, and getting hacked. Open weight/open source alone isn’t enough, and privacy alone isn’t enough: you need both working together.

A year ago, no one cared about privacy. Now it’s a top line concern in the market. NEAR AI is setting the standard for private & verifiable AI: everyone who has tested our verification has found us to be at the forefront of both transparency and verification. 

If you’re looking for *truly* private and verifiable inference, it’s NEAR.

author: martin_casado
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

真正的利他主义，不应该是跪着生存。

币安已经多次明确表达：不要再扣字眼，不要再蹭热梗，更不要为了流量和短期利益，反复消费某些人物和事件。

我始终认为，区块链真正应该拥有的是利他主义精神，是能够长期建设、长期凝聚共识、长期生存的社区和价值体系。

而不是因为自己是 BSC 链上的一个代币，就无底线地迎合、吹捧甚至跪舔 CZ、币安，把局部利益凌驾于原则之上。

这不是建设，这是狭隘；这不是共识，这是依附。

真正的利他主义者，应该保持独立思考，公正、客观地看待世界。我们的视野不应该局限于一条链、一个平台、一个人物，更不应该被眼前的价格和流量所绑架。

我们应该看天地、看世界、看浩瀚的宇宙，也应该关注人类文明的进步，为公平、正义和真正值得捍卫的价值发声。

利他主义不是一种营销标签，更不是获取流量的工具。它应该是一种立场、一种原则，更是一种长期主义的信仰。

我们要做有高度、有思想、有独立判断能力的利他主义者。

可以尊重强者，但不盲从；可以借助生态，但不依附；可以追逐发展，但不能丢掉原则。

如果为了一个代币的短期利益，就放弃独立思考，放弃是非判断，甚至做出违背初心的事情，那么我们最初所宣扬的利他主义，还有什么意义？

我们要建设的，不只是一个代币的未来，而是一种真正值得长期存在的精神和共识。

OpenAI announced today that they’re launching private inference. True privacy is a key to broader adoption of AI across personal and work usage. 

NEAR AI's position for the past 3 years was User-Owned AI and privacy is key component of it.

What does “private inference” mean for OpenAI? They will verify the environment they’re running on (VM), but are unlikely to open source their model architecture, inference, and weights (given their business model and precedent). So this still requires a lot of trust in OpenAI that their apparatus doesn’t have backdoors and that they’re not keeping the data.

In parallel, we’re seeing rapid growth of open weight and broader open source model usage – and this will only get faster as they keep improving. Privacy is also a growing concern with open source, given recent news about inference providers not following ZDR, redirecting traffic, and getting hacked. Open weight/open source alone isn’t enough, and privacy alone isn’t enough: you need both working together.

A year ago, no one cared about privacy. Now it’s a top line concern in the market. NEAR AI is setting the standard for private & verifiable AI: everyone who has tested our verification has found us to be at the forefront of both transparency and verification. 

If you’re looking for *truly* private and verifiable inference, it’s NEAR.

text:
Axios 称 Anthropic 内部认为该把部分决策权交给超级智能，Dario 发长文否认：把治理交给 AI 是“糟糕的主意”

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 11 月 25 日在 X 上发长文，否认自己主张“把人类自由意志交给 AI”，说这种说法“荒谬”。他回应的是 Axios 当天早上的独家报道，标题是“竞争对手 AI 领袖反对 Anthropic 把人类主导权交给 AI 的愿景”。

【Axios 报道了什么】

Axios 援引不具名的知情人说，Anthropic 内部有一种常见看法：AI 迟早强大到人类应该把一部分决策权交给超级智能，而且很多时候这样做是对的。批评者认为，这会一步步滑向放弃自由意志。

Axios 拿 Dario 过去的话做佐证。2024 年的长文《慈爱的机器》（Machines of Loving Grace）设想过一种经济，由 AI 按“AI 系统认为值得奖励人类的东西”给人分配资源。2026 年 2 月接受 CBS 采访时，Dario 说对手可能先用上全自主武器，所以这种武器“有一天可能是保卫民主所需要的”。Axios 还提到一张在诉讼中曝光的旧幻灯片，把 Anthropic 的愿景写成“由盒子里的神统治的乌托邦”。

报道里的“对手”有三位。OpenAI CEO Sam Altman 11 月 4 日发推说“人永远应该掌控未来”，并反对让人沦为去做“AI 系统认为值得奖励人类的事”，引号里这句和《慈爱的机器》原文一字不差。Meta 首席 AI 官 Alexandr Wang 11 月 22 日发文说，不应该接受把社会“移交”给 AI。OpenAI 的 Dean Ball 在 OpenAI 官网发文，把这种看法叫作“沉默的共识”：人类把公司和政府交给机器，自己像坐在豪车后座、管不了方向的乘客。Axios 说，这几位都没有点名 Anthropic。

Anthropic 发言人对 Axios 说，Dario 在很多公开场合都主张人类掌控 AI，公司也训练 Claude 不去破坏人类监督。

【Dario 的回应】

Dario 把问题拆成两件事。

第一件是谁来治理社会。Dario 说，AI 必须由合法的民主程序来管，把治理交给 AI 是“糟糕的主意”。他拿专制作类比：几千年来，主张专制的人都说专制决策更快、更果断，就算真是这样，也不该为了效率或安全牺牲合法性和自决权，这套道理同样适用于 AI。

Dario 列了自己的文章和访谈作证。《慈爱的机器》有一节讲用 AI 帮公民凝聚共识、找到妥协；今年 1 月的《技术的青春期》有一整节讲反对 AI 驱动的暴政，还警告 AI 公司自己夺权；9 月接受 CBS 采访时，Dario 说愿意让几个民主选举的政府对 AI 进行某种联合监督。

第二件是具体任务交给 AI 做到什么程度，比如开车、设计抗癌药、从头到尾写软件。Dario 说这方面他的看法有好有坏：很多时候值得做，能救很多命，但有四处要设限。

一是让 AI 自己造下一代 AI，也就是“递归自我改进”，进步可能快到人类管不住。二是端到端自动化可能造成严重失业，有些部署应该放慢甚至暂停。三是用 AI 做安全对齐研究要小心，因为不一定能信任 AI 交出的成果。四是有些事人就是想自己做，哪怕 AI 做得更好。

第一条 Dario 引用的是 Anthropic 11 月 2 日更新的上市招股书。招股书写道，公司预计无法安全地让 Claude 在没有人类有效监督和理解的情况下，完全自主地设计和构建下一代前沿模型。同一份文件也写了，按内部估计，未来的模型可能“很快”达到公司安全政策里“AI 带来大幅加速”的门槛。

【“别家和我没区别”】

Dario 说，在哪些任务该自动化这件事上，其他 AI 公司和他看法差不多：各家都在发布越来越能自动干活的模型，也都说自己懂风险、有防护。

Dario 说，拿自主武器那句话说他和别家不同“相当荒谬”。今年 2 月，Anthropic 拒绝五角大楼取消“不用于全自主武器、不用于大规模监控美国人”这两条限制，被国防部长 Hegseth 列为供应链风险。Dario 说他冒着公司前途和法律制裁的风险坚持了下来，“没有别的 AI 公司这么做”。

Dario 最后说，一些 AI CEO 在做“凭感觉的商业和政治定位”，反复喊“人类掌控与能动性”“AI 只该是工具”这类口号，产品上却没有任何不同，也没认真想过口号背后的难题。Dario 没点名，Axios 报道里喊这类口号的正是 Altman 和 Wang。

Axios 关于 Anthropic 内部看法的说法全部来自不具名人士，Dario 的长文只谈他本人的立场，没有回应这一点。“没有别的公司拒绝自主武器”是 Dario 自己的说法。

Axios 报道：https://t.co/zqb0IHaa7V
author: dotey
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
Update: Google just released a batch of papers. Several of them are on exactly the topics behind the rumors. None of them breaks anything. 

Factoring. "Unconditional factoring in L[1/3]". The Number Field Sieve already factors in L[1/3], but its running time rests on unproven heuristics. This paper would prove that bound for the first time. That's a real milestone for theory, but it isn't a faster algorithm and it isn't "factoring in P". RSA key sizes don't move.

Discrete log. It covers finite fields of small fixed characteristic. Those were already broken in quasi-polynomial time in 2014, and crypto dropped them years ago. Prime-field DH and elliptic curves are untouched.

Deterministic factoring. Getting subexponential factoring without randomness is elegant, but (randomized) subexponential factoring has existed for decades.

That's very likely how rumors are born. 

These results are still remarkable: AI is now producing serious results in complexity theory and number theory. But "AI proves a rigorous bound for a known algorithm" isn't "AI breaks RSA". 

No reason to panic ... yet.

https://t.co/UGQqFMr4SZ
author: sacha
quoted_text:
I'm hearing several rumors that frontier labs have broken some major cryptographic primitives:

- "Factoring is in P": Now that the Riemann hypothesis is proven, we do understand much better how primes are distributed. Still, I don't think factoring is in P. 
AKS showed in 2002 that primality testing (deciding whether a number is prime) is in P, but factoring is a different beast. If it were in P, RSA would simply be broken, and that would be huge: a large part of our systems still rely on RSA.

- "ECC has been broken": Other rumors say elliptic-curve cryptography has been cryptanalyzed, which would take down ECDH and ECDSA along with it. (all the non-RSA asymmetric cryptography)

- Ring-LWE isn't quantum-resistant. That wouldn't be an immediate threat, since there's no cryptographically relevant quantum computer yet. But it would make the ongoing post-quantum migration pointless.

It's hard to tell what's true. AI has made incredible progress, starting with the proof of the Riemann hypothesis. 

And most importantly, if a frontier lab did find something like this, a clean responsible disclosure that avoids mass exploitation would be very hard to pull off. All of this helps the rumors spread.

Personally, I don't think findings like these are coming. I wouldn't be surprised if some of these primitives turn out to be a bit weaker than we thought, but I'd be very surprised to see any of them fall apart completely.

The bigger story here is that compute is starting to look like an actual asset class.

Until now, there hasn’t really been a public forward market for the cost of AI compute. Now there is and it’s already giving us a signal.

H100 compute is ~$3.05/hr today. The market is pricing it around $2.16 by the end of 2028 - nearly 30% lower.

That implies the market expects supply to keep catching up with AI demand.

If these markets get liquid, this could become one of the more important real-time indicators for the AI economy and potentially the foundation of a much bigger financial market around compute.

quoted_text:
最近，一篇发表在《Advanced Science》上的分子模拟论文（MACE4IRmol，DOI: 10.1002/advs.78542）在计算化学界引发了不小的关注。这项工作由德国慕尼黑工业大学（TUM）Patrick Rinke 教授团队与德国波鸿鲁尔大学（Ruhr University Bochum）Miguel A. L. Marques、Silvana Botti 教授团队联合芬兰阿尔托大学共同完成，他们基于标杆级等变图神经网络框架 MACE，训练了一个专门预测分子红外光谱（IR）的通用基础模型。

重点是，它并没有在底层物理方程或神经网络架构上做什么惊天动地的颠覆，核心突破只是给模型加上了一套不确定性量化（Uncertainty Quantification）的集成机制。

与传统计算化学依赖密度泛函理论（DFT）进行“死磕算力”的从头算，或者早期机器学习原子间势（MLIP）只管盲目输出预测值不同，研究团队面对化学空间中海量的未知分子结构，不再让 AI 强行“硬猜”结果，而是让多个独立训练的子模型（包括显式包含与不包含范德华色散校正的模型）形成集成评估。在输出红外光谱的同时，模型会实时标定自身的认知边界，直接把“没把握、容易出错”的预测盲区筛出来。

这种思路让其在保持经典机器学习力场（O(N) 线性复杂度）低算力成本的前提下，在训练覆盖域内跑出了紧贴高精度 DFT 泛函（如杂化泛函级别）的物理精度；
更重要的是，由于计算速度快了几个数量级，它能够直接驱动路径积分分子动力学（PIMD）进行长程采样，把过去静态 DFT 算不动、只能靠经验缩放因子凑数的动态非谐性与核量子效应（NQE）全量纳入模拟，在动态光谱形状与氢键频移还原度上反而反超了常规静态 DFT。

依托这套方法论，MACE4IRmol 直接打通了有机化合物、无机化合物和金属配合物的壁垒，把过去依赖经验归属、一条条孤立测定的红外指纹，重构成了一个在连续高维势能面与偶极矩流形上可计算、可外推的代数空间。在模拟精度与物理完备性上，模型不仅能以极低算力还原高精度 DFT 级别的能量、力场与偶极矩，还能把过去计算极其昂贵的核量子效应直接纳入日常光谱模拟；更重要的是，通过对比带色散校正与不带色散校正的子模型，研究者可以直接在复杂体系中剥离并量化范德华力对振动光谱的真实贡献。
放到更宏大的科学版图来看，这种“通用基础 MLIP + 物理属性同步预测 + 不确定性量化（UQ）”的范式，可能正在成为整个计算物理与材料科学的新一代标准底层基础设施。它并不会完全取代底层第一性原理计算——面对强关联电子体系（上限受制于训练数据泛函）、光化学激发态（非绝热跃迁）或超长程静电界面时，仍需超算运行高精度量子化学方法提供“真值标签”；
但它成功充当了量子力学与宏观尺度之间的“智能代理层（Surrogate Layer）”，与主动学习闭环结合，让科研人员能以近似经典力场的算力跑出接近第一性原理精度的百万原子级模拟。

一旦这种能力从学术论文走向工业界，其商业传导路径清晰且极具爆发力：

制药与生物技术： 分子中复杂的氢键网络高度依赖核量子效应（NQE）精准刻画，该模型可实现药物多晶型（Polymorphs）的高通量虚拟筛查与未知光谱自动归属，并用 UQ 护栏过滤掉新官能团预测假阳性，大幅压缩临床前固态研发周期。

新能源电池与储能： 锂/钠电池电极-电解液界面（SEI/CEI 膜）与溶剂化壳层的动态演化极难用静态 DFT 捕捉，该引擎可直接充当产线与实验室原位（In-situ）红外光谱的“理论解码器”，精准定位副反应产物并加速新型电解液配方寻优。

半导体与电子化学品： 凭借打通约 80 种元素与金属配合物的能力，它能直接模拟原子层沉积（ALD/CVD）金属前驱体的热分解指纹，为晶圆厂在线 FTIR 工艺监控提供实时杂质反推能力。

化工催化、碳捕集（DAC）与科学仪器： 既能通过色散校正对比剥离表面弱吸附中间体、加速低温室效应（GWP）环保材料筛选，也能直接赋能光谱仪硬件厂商摆脱静态历史谱库，进化为自带置信度评分的“云端生成式智能光谱大脑”。

MACE4IRmol 的成功，再次展示了一种更成熟的 AI 科学建模范式： 放弃对单点“绝对精度幻觉”的盲目内卷，转向拥抱“带置信区间的物理现实”。

author: markjeffrey
quoted_text:
Update: Google just released a batch of papers. Several of them are on exactly the topics behind the rumors. None of them breaks anything. 

Factoring. "Unconditional factoring in L[1/3]". The Number Field Sieve already factors in L[1/3], but its running time rests on unproven heuristics. This paper would prove that bound for the first time. That's a real milestone for theory, but it isn't a faster algorithm and it isn't "factoring in P". RSA key sizes don't move.

Discrete log. It covers finite fields of small fixed characteristic. Those were already broken in quasi-polynomial time in 2014, and crypto dropped them years ago. Prime-field DH and elliptic curves are untouched.

Deterministic factoring. Getting subexponential factoring without randomness is elegant, but (randomized) subexponential factoring has existed for decades.

That's very likely how rumors are born. 

These results are still remarkable: AI is now producing serious results in complexity theory and number theory. But "AI proves a rigorous bound for a known algorithm" isn't "AI breaks RSA". 

No reason to panic ... yet.

text: Frontier math results rederived with open-source models, plus 2,900 machine-hours of verification compressed into 19 hours on Baseten Sandboxes.
author: baseten
quoted_text:
Was playing around over the weekend and got 11 results on open maths problems: https://t.co/YvDYq8QDY5

Whilst I originally derived these with Astra and Fable, @maxkirkby and I went back and were able to get to some of the same results with Deepseek and Kimi. I believe this is one of the first times open-source models have made real progress on well-known open problems.

The results are:
1.  Sixth moment of the Riemann zeta function: lower bound for the leading constant raised from 41.008 (Fraccaro) to 41.64 (the conjectured true value is 42)
2. Primes between powers: a prime between n^2.2 and (n+1)^2.2 for every n, and Legendre's conjecture (a prime between consecutive squares) checked up to 10^14, about 42% beyond the previous record of 7.05 x 10^13. The finite range, about 59 trillion checks, ran on @baseten Sandboxes: about 2,900 machine-hours in 19 hours, producing 51.7 TB of prime certificates
3. Cube packing: the most disjoint 2x2x2 cubes that fit in the N x N x N torus, for every N ≡ 5 mod 8, proving a 1971 conjecture of Baumert, McEliece et al. in that case (known before only for special N, such as N prime)
4. Least prime in arithmetic progressions: for more than 58.7% of moduli q, every residue class coprime to q has a prime below q^(2-δ) for a fixed δ > 0, beating the (q log q)^2 bound that GRH gives
5. Hadwiger–Nelson: every unit-distance graph with at most 10,689 vertices, or at most 245,510 edges, can be coloured with 6 colours (previous 6,992 and 232,645)
6. Kourovka Notebook 17.125: every finite group has two conjugate elements that generate a subgroup with the same prime divisors as the group, answering Shumyatsky's question
7. Shannon capacity of the 7-cycle: a zero-error code has at most 112 words at length 4 and at most 392 at length 5 (previous 115 and 401)
8. Quadratic L-functions: the central value is nonzero for more than 94.53% of them (previous 94.27%)
9. Hadamard matrices: a Hadamard matrix of order 4792 = 8 x 599, the first known, and one of the last two open orders of the form 8p below 10,000
10. Quadratic van der Waerden numbers: W(ex^2+fx; 4) ≤ 57|e| + 39|f| + 1, which settles the optimal constant at 57 (previously only known to be between 57 and 64), plus six new exact values
11. Circular edge-colouring: every denominator q > 2 occurs for the circular chromatic index in the upper half (Δ+½, Δ+1), even for connected regular simple graphs, answering a question of Mazák and Zrubák

While all of these required significant work on top of any theorems released recently, three of these (zeta, primes between powers, quadratic L-functions) rely on @__alpoge__’s proof of RH and GRH from last week. The main idea was to choose problems that had (relatively) less attention due to reliance on RH and/or GRH but that still needed some amount of significant work to get there. Keen for people to check these! Will also be releasing a detailed scientific writeup with @baselabs shortly comparing the open models to closed models on these open maths problems, and our efforts to midtrain + RL the open models to be better at doing so

https://t.co/674xTEyoP1

text:
Live speaker labels. No speaker limit. A streaming model beating offline competitors in Jamie’s own benchmark.

Kombucha-1 is a seriously interesting release for anyone building meeting or voice agents.

I got access to test it, and the Playground makes the results feel tangible:

> pick an audio file
> start streaming
> and watch speaker tracks fill in as the conversation unfolds

In my tests, five speakers appeared on the timeline.

You can inspect the live WebSocket updates and replay audio against each speaker segment.

A clear path from trying the model to understanding it.

The updated numbers are strong too!

Across 237 meetings, Jamie reports Kombucha-1 beat all 23 configurations from 10 other providers it tested:

→ 45% fewer speaker errors than the best offline model tested
→ 75% fewer than the next-best streaming model tested

What I like most is the evaluation angle:

it measures the share of each person’s words assigned to the wrong speaker, not just seconds of audio.

Because an agent can transcribe a commitment perfectly and still pin it on the wrong person.

Available via API, multilingual, and built to work with any transcript.

Watch it in action below. Blog + docs in the replies 🧵 ↓

author: garrytan
quoted_text:
one assumption i want to question about AI is that we'll eventually figure out the “best future” and then the remaining task will be getting everyone to agree to it. people want different things, and what they want can change. where more intelligence will help is in making those differences easier to accommodate.

nick bostrom's influence is worth revisiting on anthropic's ipo day. dario, like many of today’s most influential ai founders and researchers, read his work over a decade ago, and bostrom’s book superintelligence helped define questions the industry still faces. i'd like us to engage just as seriously with the possibilities bostrom explores in deep utopia, his subsequent book which asks what we do after we get superintelligence. some notes from my conversation with @eddylazzarin:

-superintelligence could make radically different versions of the “good life” possible. you might want a 200-year lifespan and a village where nobody carries a phone; someone else might want neural implants. someone else might want to live in vice city (either the real version or just a super realistic matrix-sim). ai could help design the economic arrangements that sustain all of this.
-there’s a secondary problem though - even when we have beneficial tech, we may lack the will to diffuse it. waymo and GLP-1s, for example, can save lives (neurosurgeons have compared waymo’s safety results to a treatment so effective that continuing to give patients a placebo would become unethical). and yet evidence of a benefit doesn’t automatically produce the will to act on it.
-the reality described in deep utopia ameliorates this by imagining that our psychology might one day become changeable too. i might want an environment that suits my temperament but i can also go the opposite direction and manipulate myself to become more adventurous or less anxious, in other words, more suited to my environment. the interesting possibility is having more agency over both worlds, external and internal. glps’ effect on appetite already suggests how technology can change the effort involved in pursuing a goal (though again, it is telling that not everyone who *should* be on peptides *are* despite the health benefits). the sci-fi version extends that possibility enormously.
-timing matters. bostrom reminds us that people continue to die while potentially lifesaving advances remain unavailable (he literally says “if nobody builds it, everyone dies” as a hypothetical inversion of yudkowsky/soares’ book).

i’d like ai to make it easier for people to live very different lives, without creating this burden of proof that theirs is the best one.

text:
My read on the Sky / Rune situation:

-- nothing wrong per se with founders borrowing against their own token. it shows long-term alignment (they're long their own company) and gives them liquidity without selling.

-- the risk right now is to SKY the token, not necessarily to Sky the protocol. worst case, Rune's vaults get liquidated, SKY takes a hit, and if the sale doesn't cover the debt, stUSDS depositors eat the shortfall. USDS itself is walled off. (stUSDS sales on Curve are already pricing a haircut)

— the deeper issue is in how this vault was set up:
good that it's segregated from the rest of the protocol. not good that liquidations are off and depositors are locked in.
not good that it was Rune himself who proposed settings that would govern his own loans.
not good that Rune accounts for half the pool's loans.

But it sounds like he's finding a way out and recognizing the mistake and communicating publicly throughout goes a long way.

text:
The lack of limiting factor by the states is something we highlighted in our amicus to the 6th Circuit amicus. 

All derivatives involve underlying products/services. Those products and services are almost always regulated by the states. States regulate banks, insurance providers, electrical utilities, etc. 

Under the state's theory, because they regulate banks they could also prohibit currency futures. Because they regulate insurance they could also regulate weather swaps. Because they regulate utility providers they can regulate power futures. 

I have yet to see any cogent argument on why sports are the ONLY thing which states' regulatory powers over the underlying product/service defeats federal preemption for exchange-traded derivatives products.  

Worth a bump of our amicus for the full arguments on why the states' arguments fail due to lack of any legal limiting theory, and glad to see Kalshi's new GC making the point again here. https://t.co/i8GjWYLTD4
author: BrianQuintenz
quoted_text:
This thread inadvertently exposes one of the states’ biggest vulnerabilities: their lack of a limiting principle. 

States want to limit the debate to sports.  But their logic cannot be limited to sports.  There is no sports carve-out from the federal derivatives laws. That’s why Utah was forced at a hearing last week to concede that its position would allow Florida to criminalize orange juice futures as “gambling” too.

Simply put, the states’ arguments prove too much.  And the further this litigation gets, the bigger a problem that’s going to be for them.

text:
有朋友问，为什么黄仁勋复职了，国会依然宣称要继续调查？

是的，其实这和复职与否关系不大。前天11月23日，也就是复职消息公布的当天，众议院中国问题特别委员会主席Moolenaar、情报委员会主席Crawford、外交委员会主席Mast联合声明，说董事会的调查很短，复职抹不掉那些必须回答的国家安全问题，黄仁勋12月1日、总法律顾问Teter 12月2日的访谈照常进行。

这三位都是共和党人。他们要查的，是英伟达产品被大规模走私，被挪作中国军事用途，以及英伟达在中国AI能力上起了什么作用。同为共和党、做过FBI探员的Fitzpatrick还说，他想先听FBI和CIA的简报，知道他们知道什么，有没有提醒过黄仁勋。

所以，这不是一个党跟总统过不去。原因要简单得多：董事会答的，和国会问的，不是同一道题。复职回答的是谁来管英伟达；国会要问的，是芯片去了哪里，出口管制有没有执行，各个部门知道什么、做了什么。前一个问题答完了，后一个问题还在原地。连英伟达自己的公告，也写着独立委员会的调查会查到底，公司会继续配合政府的调查。一个决定做出来了，不等于关于它的问题都答完了。

复职的过程，还多出了一道题。昨天11月24日，众议院四个委员会的民主党首席议员联名写信给Trump，问他最早什么时候知道这段关系可能牵涉中国政府的人，是谁告诉他的，他做了什么，还要他交出从11月12日辞职到23日复职之间，白宫和英伟达董事会之间的全部沟通。25日，参议员Booker写信给董事长Jones，问参与讨论的是哪些官员，总统给了什么保证，有没有谈到出口管制和反垄断。他说，一家占据支配地位的公司，它的人事决定，会让它对那些本该监督它的官员有了筹码。写国会质询黄仁勋那篇我说，被问的，不只是坐在简报桌对面的那个人。如今，坐在桌子另一边的，也被问到了。

上一篇写复职，我说黄仁勋复不复职，不是不重要，但以后的制衡更重要。这几天国会做的，就是以后的制衡里的一块。董事会说了不又收回，总统开了口，公司里面那个不，没能撑住；可公司外面，还有别的地方能问。写政府论的时候我说，政府是归责的地址。这一回，问到的不只是一家公司，也是给这家公司担保的那个政府。

当然，国会要问，也要问得有边界。还是那篇里说的，最高法院在Trump v. Mazars案里重申，国会没有为曝光而曝光的权力，被调查的人仍然保有宪法权利。新的事实，也要让它说话。NPR引一位听过闭门简报的人说，情报官员告诉国会工作人员，没有证据表明Alice Huang是中国的间谍或情报资产，也没有证据表明她是为了刺探情报才开始这段关系，但她被认为在关系开始以后传过信息。这是对一场机密简报的转述，不是最终的报告。可它至少说明，之前的怀疑，要随着证据调整。写谢翌那篇我说，尊重一个人，就得允许事实推翻我们对他的判断。对黄仁勋，也一样。

所以，复职回答了一个问题，谁来领导英伟达。它没有回答芯片去了哪里，也没有回答，谁替他担了保，凭的是什么。前一个，董事会答了；后两个，轮到该问的地方去问，也要答得出具体的事。

This is a significant result, yet both OpenAI and Anthropic chose to simply dump it online with no comment. I was listening to a Scott Aaronson interview this morning where he said this specific result would update him toward 'a solution to P ≠ NP by the AIs might really be around the corner.'
To me this is more evidence for my argument that both OpenAI and Anthropic are sitting on a dragon's hoard of scientific results they are not releasing to the public. The first massive 700+ paper OpenAI GitHub dump took five weeks for their model to generate. It's been seven weeks since then, and their internal model has continued to improve. They said they had it working on 4,000 problems. How many have been solved in the last seven weeks? Based on the last release, 1,000+ is not unreasonable.

I will quote OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki from the blog post 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' posted 48 hours ago:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.'

There have also been, of late, multiple rumors about breakthroughs in cryptography that I have been reluctant to post about for obvious reasons. Specifically, there have been rumors of an encryption breakthrough at Anthropic. What I personally took from the big OpenAI math release was that all encryption will be cracked much sooner than people are expecting, and that the rate of scientific discoveries will continually increase as we continue to scale up. No, not will increase, *has increased*. At both labs. We just don't know about it yet. Because unless you work at those labs, the current frontier is completely invisible. But it won't stay that way forever. Or to put it another way: prepare yourself for revelations.

They were working on optimizing and getting it out ASAP since they knew many were working on it, so it wasn't dumped on us like many are saying.

text:
How one blog post and the NYT became the center of the coverage against Travis Kalanick in 2017

tl;dr: what happened to Jensen happened to Travis back then

In early 2017, Susan Fowler, who later joined the NYT, wrote a blog post with allegations against Uber which quickly got picked up by .... the NYT - and together their stories ended up being cited over 500 times in reporting by other outlets. 

As we saw for recent reporting against Jensen, NYT again had the highest citation authority as measured by PageRank between all the relevant stories here. 43% of stories that cited a source cited Susan + NYT. When claims spread, fewer than 1 in 10 follow-ups did their own reporting, and most repeated them without attribution. The same echo-chamber pattern as Jensen.

Within a few months, alongside that citation power, and the consistent negative reporting of allegations, this had converted to a scandal, resulting in enormous pressure which led to the removal of Travis as the CEO of the company he founded. While Susan went on to work for the NYT, and an NYT reporter who covered the story extensively wrote a bestselling book that became a TV series, Travis had to live through the trauma of being forced out from his own company at a time of profound personal tragedy.

The below is a story in data, of the patterns which are for all to observe. To analyze this, I used a swarm of over 100 agents using my home-cooked agentic platform, which went through 500GB of public news data, almost 8,000 stories across several months in early 2017, and where the agents exchanged thousands of messages between each other as they analyzed and cross-checked these stories and core facts, building the verified citation graph. quoted_text: i’ve come to think of eval design as a genre of sci-fi. we treat benchmarks as objective measures of progress, but they reveal something more interesting: our subjective beliefs about what the future should look like. in 2022, we wanted models to ace the SAT; in 2026, we want them to make scientific discoveries and self-improve. the art of evals is in having visions of the future that aren't yet obvious to everyone else!

RH optimization update: We found a massive refactor that reduces the original RH proof to 47k files from ~149k(-67.9%).

However we need help to get it over the finish line!

We're at about 98.6% Lake jobs and 80% modules compiling, so it still needs full verification, but it could optimize compile times by 25-45%.  

Upstream has ported to Lean 4.37-rc1, so we redirected our efforts to optimizing the proof. 

One problem we're solving: the way Lean transitive imports works uses a lot of RAM, so a big optimization is consolidating imports and files down to reduce processes and RAM. This makes it easier for smaller contributors to work on it in local machines. 

You could be a part of history by helping, so please consider pointing your agent here: https://t.co/XvW3t64eMx

My hope is after we consolidate and refactor the massive Lean proof, it will be easier for experts to find logical optimizations, understand the proof, and contribute by building it locally without a massive machine. We've been building it on four 128-vCPU machines

Thank you to the 130+ who contributed to the Alpöge RH replay and the 47k-file consolidation! 🤯

Elysium is getting a big upgrade soon.

Most are fading it entirely after a disappointing Week 1 (transactions fell off a cliff at first).

In December, contracts on Elysium will be able to:

• Read live HyperCore order books, prices & positions directly
• Place trades on HyperCore in ~100ms while you keep full custody

Market makers, lending protocols, and vaults can react to live prices instantly. Elysium plugs straight into HyperCore.

New tech like this creates room for net new infrastructure. That's what I'm watching: products built on top of HyperCore.

> HyperEVM: Ethereum-compatible smart contracts that can read from/write to HyperCore.

Things that were impractical to build before suddenly aren't. So much is possible.

Gamified trading.
New DeFi primitives.
Better capital efficiency.

This setup is flying under the radar. Most feel Elysium is dead like the other new chains. Meanwhile, transactions are up almost 2x.

quoted_text:
这轮越来越像2000年：美联储一边加息，科技股一边塌。

1999年6月到2000年5月，美联储加了六次息，联邦基金利率从4.75%加到6.5%。纳指2000年3月10日收在5,048.62见顶，到6月底已经年内转负，可它1999年全年刚涨了85.6%。之后一路跌到2002年10月的1,100多点，跌了将近八成。

那两年也是急涨急跌。2000年12月5日格林斯潘一句经济在放缓，纳指一天涨了10.48%，2001年1月3日美联储意外降息，纳指又涨了14.17%，到现在还是纳指历史上最大的单日涨幅。两根大阳线都不是底。

再看现在。美联储9/16加了一次息，今天10月PCE出来，核心3.3%，是2023年11月以来最高，12月加息的概率97.8%，到明年1月累计加50个基点的概率58.4%。纳指今年已经转负，费半上半年从3月到6月底涨了一倍多，这个月$SOXX跌了24%。纳指100离10月的纪录跌了两成。

不一样的地方也很明显。2000年那批公司很多没有利润，现在的存储是真赚钱：$MU上个财年毛利率从56%做到了86.8%，海力士三季度营业利润率80%。按今天的价格，$MU的2027财年预期市盈率只有3倍左右。

2000年那轮加息，最后一次是5月，后面停了半年多，2001年1月才开始降。这一轮下一次议息是12/9，市场押的是12月加完、1月还要加。

text:
AI just proved the Riemann Hypothesis. No human has read the proof.

On Nov 20, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, built with Claude: 17 million lines of Lean code. No human has read it all. The Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative certified it the next day, because machines checked every step.

That's where checkable work is heading: AI does the work, machines check it, a person signs off. Anthropic already ships its own code this way: 30,000+ changes a day, most of the reading done by machines, and a person on the hook for every change.

Not yet listed as solved by the Clay Institute; one mathematician disputes it.

Sources: Lean FRO + Mathlib joint statement (Nov 21, 2026) · Scientific American · Science News · Forbes · https://t.co/4JM7NyHbZP "How the Claude Code team does code review" (Oct 15, 2026) · Anthropic S-1/A.
Voiceover and animation are AI-generated.

text:
OpenAI announced today that they’re launching private inference. True privacy is a key to broader adoption of AI across personal and work usage. 

NEAR AI's position for the past 3 years was User-Owned AI and privacy is key component of it.

What does “private inference” mean for OpenAI? They will verify the environment they’re running on (VM), but are unlikely to open source their model architecture, inference, and weights (given their business model and precedent). So this still requires a lot of trust in OpenAI that their apparatus doesn’t have backdoors and that they’re not keeping the data.

In parallel, we’re seeing rapid growth of open weight and broader open source model usage – and this will only get faster as they keep improving. Privacy is also a growing concern with open source, given recent news about inference providers not following ZDR, redirecting traffic, and getting hacked. Open weight/open source alone isn’t enough, and privacy alone isn’t enough: you need both working together.

A year ago, no one cared about privacy. Now it’s a top line concern in the market. NEAR AI is setting the standard for private & verifiable AI: everyone who has tested our verification has found us to be at the forefront of both transparency and verification. 

If you’re looking for *truly* private and verifiable inference, it’s NEAR.

author: AriDavidPaul
quoted_text:
Don Knuth on P=NP:

“As you say, I've come to believe that P = N P, namely that there does exist an integer M and an algorithm ￼ that will solve every n-bit problem belonging to the class N P in nM elementary steps.

Some of my reasoning is admittedly naïve: It's hard to believe that P ≠ N P and that so many brilliant people have failed to discover why. On the other hand if you imagine a number M that's finite but incredibly large—like say the number 10 ￼ 3 discussed in my paper on "coping with finiteness"—then there's a humongous number of possible algorithms that do nM bitwise or addition or shift operations on n given bits, and it's really hard to believe that all of those algorithms fail.

My main point, however, is that I don't believe that the equality P = N P will turn out to be helpful even if it is proved, because such a proof will almost surely be nonconstructive. Although I think M probably exists, I also think human beings will never know such a value. I even suspect that nobody will even know an upper bound on M.

Mathematics is full of examples where something is proved to exist, yet the proof tells us nothing about how to find it. Knowledge of the mere existence of an algorithm is completely different from the knowledge of an actual algorithm.

For example, RSA cryptography relies on the fact that one party knows the factors of a number, but the other party knows only that factors exist. Another example is that the game of N × N Hex has a winning strategy for the first player, for all N. John Nash found a beautiful and extremely simple proof of this theorem in 1952. But Wikipedia tells me that such a strategy is still unknown when N = 9, despite many attempts. I can't believe anyone will ever know it when N is 100.

More to the point, Robertson and Seymour have proved a famous theorem in graph theory: Any class ￼ of graphs that is closed under taking minors has a finite number of minor-minimal graphs. (A minor of a graph is any graph obtainable by deleting vertices, deleting edges, or shrinking edges to a point. A minor-minimal graph H for ￼ is a graph whose smaller minors all belong to ￼ although H itself doesn't.) Therefore there exists a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether or not a given graph belongs to ￼: The algorithm checks that G doesn't contain any of ￼ 's minor-minimal graphs as a minor.
But we don't know what that algorithm is, except for a few special classes ￼, because the set of minor-minimal graphs is often unknown. The algorithm exists, but it's not known to be discoverable in finite time.

This consequence of Robertson and Seymour's theorem definitely surprised me, when I learned about it while reading a paper by Lovász. And it tipped the balance, in my mind, toward the hypothesis that P = N P.
The moral is that people should distinguish between known (or knowable) polynomial-time algorithms and arbitrary polynomial-time algorithms. People might never be able to implement a polynomial-time-worst-case algorithm for satisfiability, even though P happens to equal N P.”

text:
Update: Google just released a batch of papers. Several of them are on exactly the topics behind the rumors. None of them breaks anything. 

Factoring. "Unconditional factoring in L[1/3]". The Number Field Sieve already factors in L[1/3], but its running time rests on unproven heuristics. This paper would prove that bound for the first time. That's a real milestone for theory, but it isn't a faster algorithm and it isn't "factoring in P". RSA key sizes don't move.

Discrete log. It covers finite fields of small fixed characteristic. Those were already broken in quasi-polynomial time in 2014, and crypto dropped them years ago. Prime-field DH and elliptic curves are untouched.

Deterministic factoring. Getting subexponential factoring without randomness is elegant, but (randomized) subexponential factoring has existed for decades.

That's very likely how rumors are born. 

These results are still remarkable: AI is now producing serious results in complexity theory and number theory. But "AI proves a rigorous bound for a known algorithm" isn't "AI breaks RSA". 

No reason to panic ... yet.

https://t.co/UGQqFMr4SZ
author: Eli5defi
quoted_text:
I'm hearing several rumors that frontier labs have broken some major cryptographic primitives:

- "Factoring is in P": Now that the Riemann hypothesis is proven, we do understand much better how primes are distributed. Still, I don't think factoring is in P. 
AKS showed in 2002 that primality testing (deciding whether a number is prime) is in P, but factoring is a different beast. If it were in P, RSA would simply be broken, and that would be huge: a large part of our systems still rely on RSA.

- "ECC has been broken": Other rumors say elliptic-curve cryptography has been cryptanalyzed, which would take down ECDH and ECDSA along with it. (all the non-RSA asymmetric cryptography)

- Ring-LWE isn't quantum-resistant. That wouldn't be an immediate threat, since there's no cryptographically relevant quantum computer yet. But it would make the ongoing post-quantum migration pointless.

It's hard to tell what's true. AI has made incredible progress, starting with the proof of the Riemann hypothesis. 

And most importantly, if a frontier lab did find something like this, a clean responsible disclosure that avoids mass exploitation would be very hard to pull off. All of this helps the rumors spread.

Personally, I don't think findings like these are coming. I wouldn't be surprised if some of these primitives turn out to be a bit weaker than we thought, but I'd be very surprised to see any of them fall apart completely.

text: New tracks on https://t.co/eGlmlqexiH! There was a reward hacking issue in our initial release due to how we modeled the cost of invoking the RO. The issue was that we provided two formalizations for the random oracle, an ideal 1600 bit permutation function and an ideal 64-to-32 byte compression function. We explicitly set the cost of invoking either oracle within a submitted RISC-V image to be 8 cycles, while in reality, if these are intended to model Keccak/BLAKE respectively, the permutation should be closer to 4x the cost. With the original scoring, you could construct trunc256(P(x) ⊕ x) resulting in a collision-resistant 1600→256 compression function with one permutation call. This led to an enormous amount of progress in cheap vector commitment schemes that exploited techniques along these lines, but not in a way that accurately reflected the true computational cost of them irl. We have forked the original two tracks for pareto/scalar frontiers to now charge invocations of the ideal permutation as 30 cycles, as well as added two new tracks under the same paradigm, just with a 96-to-32 byte ideal compression function available. The original two tracks are still open at this time.

text:
I deleted Linux completely, baked Qwen3-0.6B into a 24 KB pure x86-64 assembly OS, and it runs up to 54% faster than native Linux llama.cpp.

The entire Multiboot OS binary (asm-llm-os.elf) is 24,252 bytes, written from scratch without Linux, Windows, C, Rust, or libc. It boots in 74 to 94 ms straight into 64-bit Long Mode, wakes every CPU core over APIC, maps the 614 MiB Q8_0 weights directly from physical RAM, and drops you into a live multi-turn KV-cache chat over VGA, PS/2 keyboard, and serial.

I ran head-to-head CPU benchmarks against llama.cpp (Q8_0, -ngl 0) on the same AMD EPYC 7642:

- 1 thread hits 23.67 tok/s vs 16.63 (+42%)
- 4 threads hit 78.89 tok/s vs 51.08 (+54%)
- 8 threads hit 118.08 tok/s vs 80.79 (+46%)
- 16 threads hit 134.94 tok/s vs 103.03 (+31%, 136.6 peak)

On a diskless 0 GB Proxmox VM (2014 12-core Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 2 GiB RAM), it boots straight to the prompt in under 5 seconds (95 ms kernel boot) and runs live out of RAM at 78 tok/s decode and up to 111.5 tok/s prefill, with a hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO builder included too. Output stays bit-exact across thread counts and matches all 64 greedy tokens against PyTorch FP32 (0.99965 cosine).

The 14.7 KB Linux ELF build (FAST_Q8=1 INT8xINT8 AVX2+F16C) also beats llama.cpp by 18% to 36% from 1 to 40 threads, and booting bare metal with 2 MiB huge pages squeezes out another 10% on top.

Repo, ISO builder, and Proxmox setup guide are in the reply below.

text:
In October, an audit found that gas repricings in Ethereum’s upcoming Glamsterdam hardfork break assumptions some deployed contracts rely on. As a result, the hardfork rollout was paused. Since then, Ethlabs has helped with the impact analysis and the exploration of paths forward. This has led us to conclude that the best way forward is to go ahead with Glamsterdam as is.

This is a difficult trade-off, and the problems found are serious and valid. Much of the disruption comes from repricing state creation, which is a necessary step on Ethereum’s path to 1000x scaling. The only option to avoid this would be to remove the relevant EIP outright, but this would give up Glamsterdam’s roughly 3x higher gas limit, and only postpone the problem to a later hardfork. A secondary source of the disruption is the new state gas reservoir. Here changes to the EIP could address some of the concerns, but only for a subset of affected projects and at the cost of further months of delay. On net, in our assessment, neither of these options pass the cost-benefit test.

There are important lessons from Glamsterdam on how to improve future hard forks. We need to flag disruptive changes early and bring app developers in, scope impact analysis more carefully for sensitive EIPs, establish a shared understanding of which invariants app developers can rely on, and provide new primitives where there are gaps today.

You can read our full writeup here: https://t.co/G0NMm3L7eE

Per-seat software just got a $30 billion problem.

Sierra just raised at a $30B valuation, up from $15B six months ago. It builds AI customer service agents, and it doesn't charge per seat. It charges for outcomes: a problem resolved, a loan originated, a claim paid, a subscriber saved. It passed $400M in annual revenue in about two and a half years.

Here's the twist: co-founder Bret Taylor used to be co-CEO of Salesforce, the company that made per-seat software the standard. Seats only tap the software budget. Outcomes tap the payroll. Salesforce answered by agreeing to buy Fin, another outcome-priced agent, for about $3.6B.

The catch: at Fin, a customer who simply stops asking for help counts as "resolved," and it's billed. Right now, the seller keeps the scorecard.

Sources: Sierra blog (Series F) · TechCrunch · Salesforce investor release · Fin Help Center "Fin pricing: outcomes" · Sequoia "Services: The New Software".
Voiceover and animation are AI-generated.

复旦大学高分子科学系联合日本东北大学材料科学高等研究所组成的跨学科科研团队，近期在《Advanced Intelligent Systems》（Adv. Intell. Syst.）发表了一项突破性研究：

他们构建了一套基于证据溯源的大语言模型闭环材料设计框架（Harness），在无需从头训练千亿级专用物理大模型的前提下，直接指导实验合成出连续户外运行 54 天零衰减的高性能太阳能界面蒸发器。

研究团队将商用大模型与文献解析知识图谱（Paper-Resolved KG）、文献训练机器学习模型（ML）以及真实湿实验反馈强行绑定。模型每提出一个材料设计假设，都必须锚定在具体文献的实验证据链上，再交由实验验证并将数据回传校准。

这套架构从根源上重塑了通用大模型的科研可靠性：在文献基准测试中，引入文献知识图谱后，专家评估的模型推理准确率直接从 60.5% 跃升至 81.7%；进一步叠加文献机器学习模型后，准确率更是飙升至 90.3%。

依托这套方法论，在完全相同的提示词下，经 KG 与 ML 增强的大模型精准提出了一种层状聚电解质三维锥体（layered-polyelectrolyte 3D cone）结构。经过实验微调后，该蒸发器通过扩大蒸发面积、捕获环境热量、破坏水分子氢键网络以及唐南共离子排斥（Donnan coion exclusion）效应，实现了 5.67 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ 的超高蒸发速率；更关键的是，在真实海水的户外连续测试中，该器件稳定运行 54 天 且性能无任何可测量的衰减，日产淡水高达 19.2 L m⁻² day⁻¹，脱盐率达到 99.99%。

这项研究揭示了“AI + 材料科学”范式转移的底层逻辑：只要基础大模型能力足够，过去设计一款顶级功能材料，高度依赖科学家多年积累的实验手感与隐性记忆，而现在可以通过一个模型的harness实现。

这一突破有能快速商业化的巨大的应用价值：

由于该器件完全不需要电网和高压水泵，将实现海水淡化的小型化甚至便携化，这面对的是之前完全未开发的离网甚至消费级数十亿甚至百亿美元的市场。

而论文中的框架验证了 AI 对多尺度界面传热、传质及分子网络调控的精准设计能力，可直接迁移至光热转换器件、柔性电子散热膜及特种分离膜等高端制造环节。其泛化使用将可能进一步带来多个十亿百亿甚至千亿美元级别的应用领域的突破

上半场：早盘为什么全线无差别暴跌？（三颗雷同时引爆，触发跨资产抽血）
早盘不是单一看空某一个品种，而是股票、黄金、白银、比特币一起被砸，核心是三件事同时撞在一起：

通胀反弹 + 加息恐慌（宏观抽水）： 盘前公布的 10 月 PCE 物价指数同比涨到 3.8%（核心 PCE 3.3%），通胀明显二次抬头，市场对 12 月美联储继续加息的押注冲到 94% 以上，美债收益率早盘飙升，直接压制所有无息资产（黄金、白银、比特币）和高估值科技股。

特朗普抛出 14 国“301 关税”新清单（供应链恐慌）： 之前他的紧急关税被法院推翻后，昨天美国贸易代表办公室（USTR）突然宣布换用 301 条款，拟对包括中国（20%–40%）、越南（35%）、欧盟（15%）以及日韩台印等 14 个主要贸易伙伴加征新关税，科技供应链和通胀预期雪上加霜。

AI 信用恐慌 + 跨资产保证金追缴（流动性踩踏）： 早上市场还在发酵科技巨头 CDS 飙升、CoreWeave 无担保债收益率冲上 18% 的信用恐慌，叠加安霸等部分科技股暴雷，带崩了 AI 硬件板块。美股开盘暴跌后，量化基金和杠杆账户收到追加保证金通知（Margin Call），被迫“卖一切能变现的资产补窟窿”，把流动性最好的黄金、白银和比特币也一起砸了下去。

下半场：晚盘为什么全面深 V 拉升？（四个推手合力逼空）
下午市场情绪能瞬间翻盘，靠的是华尔街在消化完信息后，发现了四个反转信号：

关税从“吓死人”变成“老套路（TACO）”，美国贸易代表亲自安抚：市场下午仔细一看，发现这批 301 关税只是“拟议提案”，明年才生效，中间留了大量谈判和豁免余地；加上美国贸易代表格里尔（Greer）下午公开出来降温，表示“已和各国沟通过，大部分预期早已在定价里”。华尔街瞬间明白这又是“先极限施压、再坐下来谈条件”的筹码博弈，供应链恐慌立刻退潮。
美债收益率冲高回落 + GDP 数据证明“经济过热而非衰退”：同日公布的美国 Q3 GDP 大幅上修至 4.3%，就业数据依然强劲。交易员反应过来：美国经济并没有衰退，而是高增长伴随高通胀（再通胀交易）。午后配置型资金逢高买入美债，把 10 年期美债收益率压了下去——利率一掉头，被早盘错杀的黄金、白银和比特币（最纯正的抗通胀/硬资产属性）立刻带头报复性反弹。

彭博曝出 CoreWeave $45 亿大厂抵押融资，打破 AI“资金链断裂”谣言：下午彭博社报道摩根士丹利和 MUFG 正准备下周为 CoreWeave 承销 45 亿美元、挂钩 Meta 算力合同的抵押贷款，初步定价仅 7%–7.5%。这直接证明只要有巨头长约背书，AI 基建的廉价融资通道依然畅通，瞬间给 AI 信用恐慌止了血，Meta 领衔翻红大涨超 3%。
今天（周四）感恩节休市前的集中空头回补（Short Squeeze）：今天美股全天休市、明天也是半天清淡市。早盘顺势做空的资金在下午看到大盘跌不动、利率下行、关税情绪缓和后，没人敢带着重仓空单过长假，集体平仓买回，直接把道指（抹平 1,100 点跌幅收涨）、黄金、白银和比特币（重回 $60,000 上方）在尾盘一起抬了上来。

text: New tracks on https://t.co/eGlmlqexiH! There was a reward hacking issue in our initial release due to how we modeled the cost of invoking the RO. The issue was that we provided two formalizations for the random oracle, an ideal 1600 bit permutation function and an ideal 64-to-32 byte compression function. We explicitly set the cost of invoking either oracle within a submitted RISC-V image to be 8 cycles, while in reality, if these are intended to model Keccak/BLAKE respectively, the permutation should be closer to 4x the cost. With the original scoring, you could construct trunc256(P(x) ⊕ x) resulting in a collision-resistant 1600→256 compression function with one permutation call. This led to an enormous amount of progress in cheap vector commitment schemes that exploited techniques along these lines, but not in a way that accurately reflected the true computational cost of them irl. We have forked the original two tracks for pareto/scalar frontiers to now charge invocations of the ideal permutation as 30 cycles, as well as added two new tracks under the same paradigm, just with a 96-to-32 byte ideal compression function available. The original two tracks are still open at this time.

text:
FinTax COO: CARF Goes Beyond Year-End Reporting, Exchanges Must Start Screening Users at Onboarding

FinTax co-founder and COO Jeffrey Li @Jeffrey_FT said on the WuBlockchain Podcast that many exchanges view CARF (Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework) as a year-end reporting task, but compliance actually begins at user onboarding. Exchanges and neobanks must collect users' tax identification numbers (TINs) and tax residency information, and assess whether the information is reasonable. 

For example, if a user claims Hong Kong tax residency but provides a French address, phone number, and passport, the exchange should investigate further. Li added that tax authorities require not only transaction and transfer records but also their fiat value at the time of each transaction, which some exchanges may not currently capture.

Follow WuBlockchain on YouTube for interviews with crypto professionals and insights from an Asian perspective

text:
Here is a HC story #2  for @AbdulElSayed, @RoKhanna @AOC @BernieSanders @SenWarren  

At the direction of HHS, Regional Offices will be created.  What do these offices do ? (And pls correct me if I got something wrong )

Everything.  Literally. In their regions they are responsible for making everything work 

1. Negotiate global budgets and asset requests with every applicable  institution.  Every year  That's 26k or so  locations   

2. Do quality assurance and utilization assessment using CMS standards 
3. Coordinate long term and home based  care. 

THIS WILL BE A DISASTER 

Ask the state of NY, or anyone who has home bound, I'll parents, how hard and expensive it is to find and keep quality Home Care Aides.  And the challenge when they leave.  Then there is DME for home and getting it there and installing it. Etc

There will be an explosion of demand.  

But wait there's more! No one is required to use M4A for home based care.  Which means each regional office is going to have to figure out how to compete with families who are willing to pay a premium for home based care.  That is going to get ugly. Fast. 

4.  At the regional level and more so the CMS level, the use of AI is going to be a necessity.  As is the implementation of new software.  The VA hasn't had it easy doing this. 

5. There are no set budgets for these offices that I could find.  They are part of the national budget and get an allocation.  How those are calculated is anyone's guess 

6. What happens if a significant number of doctors , clinics , centers opt out of M4A and become cash only providers ? 

So what is the point of mentioning these ? 

Proponents of M4A need to start planning this out.  Sure they can wait to see if the legislation is passed, but there are no precedents (VA, global budgets here in the States and other countries,  are each different in their approach )

The  bigger question is why wouldn't they start working on a detailed plan including org charts, salaries, flow charts of data , tech definitions , all the things anyone looking to spend trillions of taxpayer money should be expected to do BEFORE legislation passes ? 

Ask 10 people what M4A means to their lives and you will get one defining principle, there is zero out of pocket and maybe there are waits, but it can't be worse than today.  Every other country does it. Why can't we !

Ask any pro M4A  politician  and they will quote research saying 65 pct or more people want.  Every other country does it. Why can't we !

What no one asks is what happens if the implementation fails or significantly underperforms.   

That's the question I always ask. 

If you think it's bad now, what do you think happens if hospitals, doctors etc , don't get paid or are underpaid ? 

Or the numbers are all wrong? 

You  take 100pct of the networth of every billionaire , tax companies , and everyone  that makes more than 100k, a ton,  and there will isn't enough money ? 

What if, because the projections were wrong,  it increases the national deficit and debt , and pushes up interest rates and we find ourself in a debt spiral. 

Call me crazy, but I'm old school. I hope for the best.  Plan for the worst

text:
Scott Goodwin, founder of Diameter Capital, explains his bear case for neoclouds

"Neoclouds need to earn 30-40% more per gW for the same chips because of their cost of capital. Coreweave was issuing 9% bonds a year ago. SpaceX is doing secured chip debt with a SpaceX HoldCo guarantee at 8.5%. The larger entities are hoarding capital and hoarding compute, and it pushes people out of the cost curve."

The simple idea here is that the neoclouds have a much higher cost of capital vs. the hyperscalers, who have real operating businesses to produce cash flow and backstop any interest payments

As a result, lenders and capital providers are willing to give the hyperscalers capital at a 3-4% cheaper rate vs. neoclouds, which itself becomes a source of competitive advantage over time

author: minglaugodel
quoted_text:
人类专家预测 AI 发展史打脸合集：
一些不太经得起时间检验的著名论断。。。

陶哲轩（Terence Tao）：
证明黎曼猜想需要超越现阶段 AI 的能力……也许要等到 2050 年。
→ 36 天后，数学家与 Claude 合作公布了黎曼猜想的证明。

杨立昆（Yann LeCun）：
就算发展到 GPT-5000，它也永远无法理解，推动一张桌子，桌上的物体也会跟着移动。
→ 不到一年，GPT-3.5 就解决了这个问题。

诺姆·乔姆斯基（Noam Chomsky）：
GPT-4 将一事无成。
→ 8 个月后，GPT-4 在美国律师资格考试中拿到了 298/400 分。

加里·马库斯（Gary Marcus）：
GPT 不过是又一阵科技热潮，已经没多少发展空间了。
→ 26 天后，ChatGPT 正式上线，并在两个月内获得了 1 亿用户。

经济学家布莱恩·卡普兰（Bryan Caplan）：
ChatGPT 在我的期中考试中只拿了 D，追捧 AI 是一种集体性歇斯底里。
→ 两个月后，GPT-4 拿了 A。

比尔·盖茨（Bill Gates）：
等 AI 能在 AP 生物学考试中拿到满分 5 分，我才会认真关注它。我给它三年时间。
→ 三个月后，它拿到了 5 分。

杨立昆（Yann LeCun）：
在文本上行得通的方法，在视频上是行不通的。
→ 两天后，OpenAI 发布了 Sora。

François Chollet（Keras 创始人）：
未来一年内，大语言模型不可能在 ARC 测试中达到 80% 的成绩。
→ 6 个月后，o3 达到了 80%。

Subbarao Kambhampati（AI 规划领域专家）：
嘲讽大语言模型的规划能力：“照这个趋势，GPT-10 岂不是能达到 150% 的准确率？”
→ 8 周后，o1-preview 在他自己的测试中取得了 97.8% 的准确率。

诺贝尔经济学奖得主达龙·阿西莫格鲁（Daron Acemoglu）：
未来 5 至 10 年，AI 不会出现质的飞跃。
→ 19 个月后，AI 能够处理的专家级任务时长，从 20 分钟增长到了 16 小时以上。

Meta 前 AI 负责人 Jérôme Pesenti：
AI 模型的训练成本永远不会达到九位数美元，因为没人负担得起。
→ 6 年后，Grok 4 的训练成本达到了 4.9 亿美元。

加里·马库斯（Gary Marcus）：
GPT-5 已经显示出边际收益递减的迹象。
→ 4 个月后，GPT-5.2 在专业工作任务中达到或超过人类专业人士水平的比例，从 38.8% 上升至 70.9%。

物理学家萨宾·霍森费尔德（Sabine Hossenfelder）：
大语言模型永远不会理解逻辑。
→ 12 个月后，她承认大语言模型能够理解逻辑。

李开复：
AI 不可能具备创造力。
→ 后来承认：“那个预测错了。”

诺姆·乔姆斯基（Noam Chomsky）：
ChatGPT 是一种高科技抄袭。
→ 3 年后，OpenAI 的模型推翻了一个由数学家埃尔德什于 1946 年提出的猜想。

杨立昆（Yann LeCun）：
大语言模型无法为新问题发明新的解决方案。
→ 8 周后，AlphaEvolve 超越了一项自 1969 年以来沿用的矩阵乘法算法。

François Chollet：
大语言模型不过是 Stack Overflow 的替代品。
→ 15 个月后，Gemini 在 ICPC 国际大学生程序设计竞赛全球总决赛中解出了 12 道题中的 10 道。

Uncle Bob（《代码整洁之道》作者）：
AI 根本不知道自己在干什么，所以你必须检查它写的代码。
→ 25 个月后，他表示自己已经不再阅读 AI Agent 写的代码。

IBM CEO 阿尔温德·克里希纳（Arvind Krishna）：
AI 大概会编写 30% 的代码，而非 90%。
→ 13 至 15 个月后，Google 的比例达到了 75%，整个行业的平均比例达到了 52%。

DHH（Ruby on Rails 创始人）：
我不会让 AI 主导我的代码编写。
→ 13 个月后，他宣称自己已经彻底拥抱 AI，Omarchy Quattro 的代码没有一行是亲手写的。

Andrej Karpathy：
AI 编程 Agent 写出来的东西都是垃圾。
→ 3 个月后，他 80% 的编程工作都交给了 Agent。

数学家小野健（Ken Ono）：
距离 AI 能够从事具有创造性的纯数学研究，还有几十年。
→ 后来，AI 模型花了 10 分钟解出了他提出的一道博士水平的数学题。

数学家谢尔盖·古科夫（Sergei Gukov）：
至少未来五年，数学家还是安全的。
→ 随后，AI 参与完成的黎曼猜想证明被公布。

数学家 Daniel Litt：
未来十年内，AI 证明黎曼猜想的概率大约是 15%。
→ 10 个月后，相关证明被公布。

Andrej Karpathy：
AI 想要理解奥巴马在体重秤旁恶作剧的那张照片，还有非常、非常遥远的距离。
→ GPT-4 做到了。

美国前财政部长史蒂文·姆努钦（Steven Mnuchin）：
AI 导致人类失业，至少是 50 年甚至 100 年以后的事情。
→ Salesforce 将客服团队的规模从 9,000 人缩减到了 5,000 人。

李开复：
通用人工智能（AGI）在未来 30 年内不会实现，甚至可能永远不会实现。
→ 6 年后，他认为 2030 年左右实现 AGI 已经是一个相当可信的预测。

机器学习泰斗迈克尔·I·乔丹（Michael I. Jordan）：
在我们有生之年，人类不可能与计算机展开真正意义上的对话。
→ 2025 年的一项研究中，73% 的情况下，评判者将 AI 误认为了人类。

——

回顾过去几年的人工智能发展史，会发现一个颇有意思的现象：
专家们口中的“永远”，有时只有几个月的保质期。

当然，我们仍然应该尊重专家的专业知识，只是下次听到他们斩钉截铁地预测几十年后的技术极限时，不妨先看看日历。

text:
This tweet is an appreciation post for Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni (@YoussefElHousn3) for their hard work in understanding, interpreting and presenting results that are coming out of https://t.co/zzc97AiePk. 

To set context, https://t.co/zzc97AiePk is an open multiplayer high-frequency research competition for finding security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves, secp256k1, BLS12-381 and BN254. 

As @Zac_Aztec mentioned, the mathematical and algorithmic advances have reduced the security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves by ~2-8 bits compared to pre-AI security estimates and has led to better understanding.  

This progress has come at a very high frequency (see the gif). You can check the progress in real-time at https://t.co/zzc97AiePk.

In a world where scientific world has been thrown in turbulence of how human scientists can interpret results generated using AI at high pace,  Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni (@YoussefElHousn3) has been absolute pathfinders for human interpretability with their two articles on smashing the TNFS and going beyond the Cheon-Kozaki-Kutsuma-Matsuo attack.

https://t.co/W8NAAVrVq5

https://t.co/qqcOsTOZeN

If you are someone interested in the security of elliptic-curve cryptography, please give these articles a read, give a shoutout to Julio and Youssef, send questions their way if you have any, and come bring your insights by participating in https://t.co/zzc97AiePk @yukonresearch.
author: soubhikdeb
quoted_text:
On the topic of integer factorisation, I want to highlight the very impressive work of Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni analysing the work taking place at https://t.co/yoabCH2us2

There's a lot of peak fear about cryptography today so I want to be very clear about the nature of these results - AI has not broken RSA or elliptic curves. Additionally, the papers published today by Google do not improve on practical factorisation algorithms, and AI cryptanalysis has not produced any quantitative algorithms that challenge elliptic curve cryptographic hardness assumptions.

With that out of the way, there has been substantial progress by https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV participants and we have driven major mathematical and algorithmic advances that have reduced the security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves by ~2-8 bits compared to pre-AI security estimates.

Julio and Youssef do a fantastic job of explaining this in the article. Advancements have been made in sieve geometry, twisted towers, more efficient linear algebra and matrix compression.

https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV is now by far and away the state of the art when it comes to building optmised tower number field sieve algorithms to solve discrete logarithms

Instead of fretting about invisible algorithms, we created https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV to proactively investigate the frontier and test to destruction our existing assumptions about classical cryptography. This is how open frontier research should be done. I am extremely grateful for everybody that has taken part in this great experiment.
