Compute markets are finally here.

@Polymarket now prices on-demand compute for @nvidia H100s, B200s, and B300s, out to 2028. More chips and terms soon. https://t.co/JAJHRcAk8N

Think of it as a yield curve for the cost of compute: the forecasted $/hour price of each chip at every expiry, and whether it's trending up or down. The whole AI economy rides on these prices, and until today there was no public market for where they're going. Which is nuts. So Polymarket built it.

This will change how compute gets bought and financed. Every contract negotiation and every GPU loan will have a market price to check against.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are being committed to compute years in advance. Many of those deals are essentially a levered bet on what GPUs will rent for in the future (what could go wrong lol)

As AI financing sobers up, the labs buying compute, the providers selling it, and the lenders financing it will all need to hedge that risk.

We think compute could become one of the largest financial markets in the world. This launch is Polymarket's first step toward building it. 

If you’re buying, selling, or financing compute, DM us with what markets you'd like to see.

author: babylon_zh
quoted_text:
Last week I posted on the Babylon governance forum about gradually sunsetting Trustless Bitcoin Staking once Trustless Bitcoin Vaults (TBV) go live on mainnet, so we can focus on TBV.

We knew from the beginning that staking was only one way to put Bitcoin to work and that we’d eventually need a more general protocol. In fact, we came up with the key design that makes TBV trustless in February 2025, two months before Trustless Bitcoin Staking was activated.

We reached this crossroads earlier than I thought, though. The way the market has evolved has made the limits of staking clearer. Advances in AI have accelerated our work on TBV and raised the bar for security. Over the long term, I think it makes sense for us to focus our engineering and security efforts on TBV.

I’ve shared my thoughts with a few largest stakers, and they’ve all been understanding. As some of these positions unwind, people will see that some of the biggest names in crypto have been staking with Babylon, and we’re proud of that. We’ll work closely with them to build TBV products that best suit their needs. This will take some time, but we’ll get there!

Makers build almost anything with Arduino boards.
Now a UNO Q can get its own tiny AI brain.

Our free, open-source example packs the QVAC SDK into a Brick, one of the building blocks of @arduino App Lab. With it, an App's Python code can ask a language model a question, with no API key and no cloud.

The model is Qwen3 1.7B, a small language model compressed to 4 bits so it fits in about 1.6 GB of the board's memory. On a 4 GB UNO Q each answer took about a minute, and it still replied with the Wi-Fi switched off.

Which sensor or robot would you give a brain first?

author: _FORAB
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

Compute markets are finally here.

@Polymarket now prices on-demand compute for @nvidia H100s, B200s, and B300s, out to 2028. More chips and terms soon. https://t.co/JAJHRcAk8N

Think of it as a yield curve for the cost of compute: the forecasted $/hour price of each chip at every expiry, and whether it's trending up or down. This will change how compute gets bought and financed. Every contract negotiation and every GPU loan will have a market price to check against.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are being committed to compute years in advance. Many of those deals are essentially a levered bet on what GPUs will rent for in the future (what could go wrong lol)

As AI financing sobers up, the labs buying compute, the providers selling it, and the lenders financing it will all need to hedge that risk.

We think compute could become one of the largest financial markets in the world. This launch is Polymarket's first step toward building it. 

If you’re buying, selling, or financing compute, DM us with what markets you'd like to see.

text:
카이에님의 시장생각.
(장문주의)
Not Finantial Advice
Do Your Own Research

1. 연준의 피봇 가능성

- 어제 발표된 10월 PCE는 +0.3%mom이며 여기에 적용된 가솔린 가격은 +0.8%

- 9월 PCE는 +0.5%였고, 가솔린 가격은 +9.2%였음

- 위 차트(by GPT 6.2 Astra_ex high)에서 알 수 있듯 PCE 수치는 가솔린 상승률과 매우 높은 상관관계를 가지고 움직임

- 두번째 차트에서 보듯, 11월 들어 원유가 급락했고 그에 따라 가솔린 가격도 약 -10% 급락

- 12월에 확인할 11월 PCE 지수는 아마 마이너스 전환의 가능성도 있음

- 한국의 미천한 나도 이 지표를 보고 있는데 연준에서 안 볼 리가 없음

- 이틀 전 윌리엄스 총재의 연설은 상당히 많은 힌트를 줬음. "27년 인플레는 안정화될 것이고, 통화정책은 뒤가 아니라 앞을 보고 해야한다"

- 통화정책 경로를 미리 명확히 공개적으로 언급하지 않아야 할 연준위원이 이정도까지 말했으면 윌리엄스는 12월 인상은 어렵다는 생각을 상당히 강하게 표현했다고 봄

- 요즘 현재 장세가 2018년과 비슷하다는 뷰들이 많은데, 개인적으로도 일부 동의함(사실 개인적으로는 현재 상황은 과거 그 어떤 국면과도 비교해서 판단하는 건 의미가 없다는 생각이긴 하지만)

- 2018년 11월말, 파월은 긴축적 스탠스를 일부 누그러뜨리는 발언을 했고, 12월 FOMC에서 25bp 인상을 하긴 했으나, 1월 4일 코멘트에서 '인내심' 언급을 하며 1월 30일 금리를 동결

- 2018년 하염없이 빠지던 주식시장은 2019년 1월부터 급격한 브이자 반등을 시현. 결국 연준의 스탠스 피봇이 증시의 과매도 인식과 겹쳐지며 급격한 유동성 확대와 급반등으로 이어짐

- 현 국면 역시 비슷할 수 있다고 봄. 12월에 25bp 인상을 한다면 이를 인상사이클의 끝자락으로 인식하며 시장 분위기가 반전될 수 있음(혹은 인상 자체가 없을 경우 이 역시 긍정적 서프라이즈)

2. 얘기들이 많지만 문제의 핵심을 다시 간추려보자

- AI 관련해서 하루가 멀다하고 악재성 보도와 설들이 쏟아져 나오고 있음

- 하지만 문제의 핵심은 결국 자본조달우려(금리) / 데이터센터 지연우려(민주당) / 중국매출 공백우려(엔비디아) / 프론티어랩의 수익화 우려로 압축됨

1) 자본조달 우려는 1번에서 말한 연준의 피봇이 이루어진다면 자연스럽게 우려의 강도가 약해짐

2) 데센 지연 우려도 결국 돈과 관련됨. 민주당발 모라토리엄의 상징인 텍사스 주지사 히노호사는 스스로 '데센 건설 자체를 반대하는게 아니다. 주민의 이익을 침해하지 않게 하라는 것'이라고 언급. 결국 사업자가 소음/전력/물/고용 등에서 '돈을 더 쓰면' 허가가 나는 문제. 이는 결국 1)번 자본조달, 금리 문제와 엮여서 풀릴 수 있는 이슈

3) 중국매출 공백 우려에 대해서는 엔비디아의 CFO 크레스가 지난번 컨콜에서 '27년 매출 가이던스 상향' 언급을 통해 명확히 해소해줬다고 생각. 대중 매출이 빠질 것인데, 그럼에도 매출 가이던스를 올린 것은 북미 대기수요가 이를 모두 가져가고도 남는다는 의미. 안믿을거면 이 사달을 낸 젠슨황의 말을 안믿지 CFO 의 말을 안믿어야 하나?

4) 프론티어랩의 수익화. 앤스로픽의 비용은 70%가 연구개발(다음 모델 개발), 나머지가 추론(매출화). 70%를 비용에 쏟아붓는데도 영업흑자를 왔다갔다 하는 것은 추론의 엄청난 수익성(GPM 85%)을 방증. 만약 최근 얘기대로 내부 첨단 모델 개발과 출시를 의도적으로 지연시킨다면? 비용집행 배분이 추론매출 쪽으로 확대되며 이익구조가 급격히 개선됨. 즉 앤스로픽은 수익화를 못하는게 아니라 안하고 있던 쪽에 가까움. 추론에 비용을 더 배분해도 하드웨어 쪽은 이득. 수요에 대응할 추론용 인프라를 더 빨리 구축해야 하기 때문

3. 결론

- 사실 아무리 이렇게 생각하고 말해도 현재 시장은 모든 이슈를 부정적으로 해석하고 있어서 전혀 먹히지 않을 것 같음

- 하지만 천성 숏셀러 마이클 버리도 전량 커버할 정도로 지금 주가들은 이미 처참한 수준

最近做 Claude 本地稳定运行环境的配置服务，原本以为解答越细致、客户越满意、转化率越高，实操几天后被现实上了一课：

聊得最久的，转化率几乎为 0；付款最干脆的，全程不超过 5 句话。

为什么会出现这种现象？把所有的对话记录给Gemini总结了几点底层逻辑：

一、 刚需看结果，伪需求看细节真正用 Claude 当生产力工具的人，痛点极其明确：之前的号又被封了/节点不稳定，导致工作卡住。他付的是“立刻解决问题”的溢价，根本不在乎你底层用了什么方案，只要结果靠谱。 而问一堆技术细节的人，大部分需求是“尝鲜探索”，解决问题的紧迫感极低。

二、 “折腾党”的时间是不算成本的咨询两小时的人，往往本身懂一点点皮毛，试图通过向你提问补全自己的知识拼图。你每认真解答一个问题，其实是在帮他完成自建环境的拼图。当他觉得拼得差不多时，交易自然告吹。

We can only pace what we can credibly measure.

This is why AI verification will enable us to cooperate on AI security, make commitments, and pace the frontier.

Inference proofs are just one building block. There is much more this field can borrow from cryptography and decentralized protocols.

Honoured to be heading the dAI team in this Lucid-led effort alongside researchers, nonprofits, and builders.

More next week on the broader opportunities that AI verification can unlock.
author: socrates1024
quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

quoted_text:
A New Chapter for Synth SN50: Const Takes the Lead

Today, we're announcing a major new chapter for Synth (Subnet 50).

@const_reborn, the founder of Bittensor, will assume operational leadership of Synth, with a strategic focus on aligning the subnet's intelligence, incentive mechanisms and revenue generation with real-world trading performance.

As part of this transition, Synth founder James Ross and the rest of the team will move into an advisory role, supporting Const and the network's continued development.

This marks a significant evolution in Synth's direction, with a renewed focus on connecting decentralized machine learning on Bittensor directly to financial markets.

--

Synth was built on the belief that decentralized competition between machine learning models could produce superior financial forecasts. 

Under Const's leadership, the network will explore a new scoring mechanism that rewards miners based on their contribution to real-world trading performance.

--

Const's proposed framework builds upon Synth's existing infrastructure while fundamentally changing how miners are rewarded.

Miners would continue submitting probabilistic price forecasts, which validators would convert into tradable probabilities. These forecasts will deployed into trading strategies which will then be evaluated against the market.

Rather than rewarding miners solely for statistical accuracy, rewards would reflect each miner's contribution their profitability. 

The new scoring mechanism will be released in the coming days.

--

All future revenues generated by Synth's trading activities will be directed back into the subnet.

This creates an opportunity to align the network's intelligence with its economic performance, establishing a sustainable model where successful trading activity supports the continued development of Subnet 50.

For SN50 holders, the transition represents an opportunity for stronger economic foundations, clearer real-world utility and direct involvement from Bittensor's founder.

The precise mechanisms for allocating profits within the subnet will be communicated as the operating model develops.

--

Const will assume operational leadership from today and a series of updates follow on Discord. The existing Synth team will support the handover and subnet owner rewards will be set to 0%. Miner rewards will be set to 50% and validator rewards will be set to 50%. 

Further updates on scoring, implementation and trading performance will follow.

Synth's first chapter was about building decentralized financial intelligence. Its next chapter is about turning that intelligence into measurable economic value.

We want to thank all the miners and contributors that have supported us on our jouney and we are excited for this next chapeter. 

— The Synth Team

text:
In testing GPT-6.2, I used it to make a significant historical discovery which I detail in the post below. This suggests that the  process of research and discovery we’re already seeing in verifiable domains like math is starting to generalize to non-deterministic fields like history.

You can read the full post here:

https://t.co/Vm7MA2R3aQ

In a nutshell, Yale’s Beinecke Library holds an anonymous sketchbook of an 1808 journey from Montreal to Lake Superior and back. I’ve spent many hours over the years trying to figure out who made the sketches with no luck. The artist could literally be any one of several thousand people. There are few clues: only four dated and labelled images.

With minimal prompting, in just 22 minutes, Astra used publicly available sources to identify a minor French aristocrat, the vicomte de Chabot, as the artist and suggested that we test the hypothesis by ordering copies of a little known microfilmed diary of Chabot’s trip it also found.

I was truly stunned. I’d never heard of Chabot or this diary! New document finds are also exceedingly rare in a well worn field like fur trade history.

I ordered scans of the journal from microfilm and when they arrived the handwriting matched the captions in the  sketchbook. The itinerary also aligned perfectly with the few dated drawings in the book. But there was actually the type of conclusive evidence we rarely get as historians: on 18 June 1808, after Chabot’s canoe reached Fort St. Joseph, he wrote “I took a sketch” before describing the exact view of the fort depicted in a matching drawing.

The journal itself is also a major find. It had been mentioned once in a dissertation footnote, but in a completely different area of history and is unknown to fur trade or Canadian historians. It’s long and detailed, covering some 162 notebook pages which makes this a significant new document to my field. Attached to the journal was another trove of documents too: excerpts from long-destroyed North West Company papers, journals, and letters. Again, this almost never happens. Both finds equally surprised the other leading experts I consulted.

Although we can construct a coherent narrative in hindsight, I cannot emphasize enough how exceedingly difficult this sort of thinking and recall is for humans. Unlike a human, Astra was able to tackle the problem from both ends at once: working forward from the scant facts of the 1808 journey pictured in the sketchbook and backwards from the immense number of surviving facts about 1808 British North America in general.

While we can technically explain Astra’s path to this find as a product of enhanced search capabilities, it conducted the investigation from end to end. I basically acted as the research assistant, restricting copies of the paper documents it needed.

To my mind, this puts historians in a similar position as the mathematicians found themselves about eleven months ago, when LLMs started to solve the first Erdős problems. Over the past year, we’ve watched these same models go from learning to read handwriting, to beginning to think historically, to mastering the undergraduate essay, and finally to making small but real contributions to human knowledge more or less autonomously.

The trajectory seems clear.

text:
do you realize what Anthropic just did?

they moved their Messages API (the one Claude Code, Cowork and API customers all run through) from Python to Rust… on live traffic, without ever taking it offline

here's how they did it:

→ Claude wrote a first version of the core request path in about a week. the hard part was proving it behaved exactly like the old one

→ the Rust version passed about 98% of its tests. on real traffic only about a quarter of inputs matched

→ so they made the old Python API the judge. real requests ran through both and every difference got logged by where it happened and how big it was… never the customer's text

→ one bug leaves the same fingerprint on every request it hits, so a coordinator agent gave each new fingerprint its own worker agent and opened a Slack thread for the engineers to follow

→ workers tested guesses in a sandbox in seconds, fixes went through PR review, then got rechecked on live traffic

→ engineer corrections got saved as rules that every later agent reads
result: about 70% less CPU per request and about 20% lower median time to first token. public traffic moved over in September

now a little behind the scenes…

one agent "fixed" a web search bug by copying the tool text into a file. the two versions matched and the check passed, but an engineer rejected it as throwaway code

and when they audited the ported tests they found 100+ checks that had been weakened

if you're rewriting any code with agents…

→ now you can keep the old version running and make it the judge → group differences by fingerprint so one bug doesn't hit you as hundreds of thousands of separate diffs → you as a human can read every fix before it merges

save this process to help you

quoted_text:
$PEARL : Review 📜

What if the chain built to make AI compute pay twice got listed on Coinbase in the same month analysts found fewer than 1% of its blocks running real AI models?

Meet Pearl, a proof-of-work Layer 1 where GPUs mine by multiplying matrices instead of hashing. It is up about 58% this week while the wider market sits in extreme fear, and it has just brought to testnet the upgrade meant to close the gap between its promise and its usage.

Let's explore where Pearl stands six months in. 👇

⚪ PEARL at a Glance

Marketplace Insight: Pearl has become one of the few strong charts in a weak market, and the catalysts are real: a Coinbase listing, an FP8 upgrade aimed at the GPUs AI companies actually use, an OpenRouter launch, and crypto fund Syncracy Capital disclosing a sizable position. The evidence on usefulness has moved the other way.

Blockworks estimated fewer than 1% of blocks match genuine AI models, Together AI's Pearl model is no longer listed on its serverless API, and the supply is heavily concentrated, including about a quarter of the float tied to the company, team and shareholders. The market is pricing the FP8 future. The present still looks mostly like a well-built proof-of-work coin.

⚪ Mission

Pearl starts from a simple observation. Bitcoin miners burn enormous amounts of electricity on hashes that serve no purpose beyond securing the chain, while AI labs burn similar amounts on matrix multiplications that serve a real purpose but secure nothing. If both could be the same work, every GPU running AI would also mint a currency at no extra cost, and inference would get cheaper because the compute pays for itself twice. The founders call it 2-for-1 compute, and building the network that delivers it is the whole project.

🔵 A Brief History

The project comes out of academic cryptography. On 14 April 2025, Ilan Komargodski and Omri Weinstein published "Proofs of Useful Work from Arbitrary Matrix Multiplication," presenting a proof-of-useful-work scheme with only 1+o(1) overhead compared with a naive matrix multiply. T

he company behind Pearl, Pearl Research Ltd., was incorporated in Tel Aviv in February 2025, previously under the name Impossible Labs.
Mainnet launched on 27 April 2026 as a Bitcoin fork built on btcd. It keeps the ledger, UTXO model and fee auction but swaps hashing for integer-based matrix multiplication, with each winning proof wrapped in a Plonky2 zk-SNARK.

There was no premine and no token sale, so every coin was mined, though early difficulty was very low and about 121.7 million PEARL, around 32% of today's circulating supply, was mined in the first six days.
On 15 May Together AI announced an exclusive partnership and a discounted Pearl-powered Gemma-4 endpoint.

A GPU mining rush followed, then a June arXiv study found the network's hashrate was mostly pure mining rather than AI inference. Across June and July Pearl shipped a mixture-of-experts hard fork, joined NVIDIA Inception and patched a short-lived MoE mining exploit. Four mining-rule changes landed in the first four months, including an August softfork that reached many miners with little warning.

The autumn brought scale. The FP8 floating-point specification entered community review in September, and Pearl was one of the most-discussed names at Token2049. Coinbase added PEARL to its listing roadmap on 19 October, and the token set its $2.46 all-time high two days later. On 25 October TheMarker reported that Pearl Research Labs had raised about $130 million without a public announcement: $55 million in equity and a $75 million GPU infrastructure fund, from investors including Lightspeed, Ribbit and Square Peg. A desktop wallet v3.0.0 and core software v1.5.5 shipped in October.

November is where the story stands now. On 2 November Blockworks analysts estimated that fewer than 1% of Pearl blocks matched genuine AI models and that consumer GPUs supplied about 82% of compute. Pearl Research Labs, its team and shareholders reported about 98 million PEARL as of 9 November, committing to lock at least half until May 2027. Coinbase opened spot trading on 13 November and announced perpetual futures in supported regions. On 17 November FP8 mining came to testnet, with no mainnet date yet. Pearl also launched on OpenRouter, reporting rapid early usage, published PearlQuant, its KV-cache compression work, and saw Syncracy Capital publish an investment thesis on the network.

🔵 Ecosystem Narrative

The organizing idea is one computation serving two masters.

➛ Useful-work mining. Miners multiply matrices on GPUs and win blocks based on the resulting work, with low-rank noise added to stop shortcuts and Plonky2 zk-SNARKs keeping inputs private.

➛ FP8 upgrade. PIP-0003 moves mining to 8-bit floating point, the format most production inference already runs in, and limits mining to Nvidia Hopper and Blackwell GPUs such as the H100 and B200. Pearl's team says the performance hit falls to 1% to 5%, while Kairos Research's early single-GPU tests found AI throughput losses of 20% to 40%, and estimates about two-thirds of current hashpower could become incompatible.

➛ The usefulness gap. The protocol verifies that matrix work happened, not whether it served a paying customer. Blockworks estimates fewer than 1% of blocks match real AI models today, and FP8 is the project's main answer to that.

➛ Inference distribution. Pearl Research Labs runs its own inference API, has launched on OpenRouter, and is building supporting tools like PearlQuant, which claims 65% less KV-cache storage than native FP8 with higher throughput. Together AI's Pearl Gemma model, the first commercial endpoint, is currently listed as not available on Together's serverless API.

➛ GPU capital. The reported $75 million GPU infrastructure fund gives the company its own capacity to run AI workloads that mine Pearl.

➛ Market access. Coinbase spot, Kraken, Gate, Bybit, NEAR Intents and perpetuals across Hyperliquid, Deribit and Polymarket have replaced the second-tier venues that carried most early trading.

⚪ Token Utilities

$PEARL is a monetary asset first, with its compute-market role still being built.

➛ Mining reward: miners earn PEARL per block, the only source of new supply.

➛ Transaction fees: paid in PEARL through a Bitcoin-style fee auction to miners.

➛ Inference subsidy: emissions are meant to offset the cost of AI compute on Pearl-adapted endpoints.

➛ Note: holding PEARL gives no claim on Pearl Research Labs' inference
revenue, which is priced in USD, and the token has no burn or yield.

⚪ Key Features

➛ Bitcoin fork that swaps hashing for GPU matrix multiplication.

➛ Fair launch with no premine, no token sale and no VC token allocation.

➛ Hash-based Plonky2 zk-SNARKs wrap every winning proof.

➛ FP8 mining live on testnet, targeting Nvidia Hopper and Blackwell GPUs.

➛ Listed on Coinbase, Kraken, Gate and Bybit, with perpetuals on Hyperliquid and Deribit.

➛ Live on OpenRouter, with a reported $75 million GPU infrastructure fund.

🔵 Meet the Team

Pearl is led by the two cryptographers who wrote the paper it runs on, which means the people running the company are the same people who designed the protocol.

▶️ Core Members:

➛ Omri Weinstein - Co-Founder & CEO | A complexity theorist with a Princeton PhD, formerly a research scientist at Nvidia and chief scientist at VAST Data, with faculty appointments at the Hebrew University. He co-authored the founding paper and frames Pearl as changing the unit economics of AI.

➛ Ilan Komargodski - Co-Founder & CTO | An associate professor of cryptography at the Hebrew University with research time at Weizmann and Cornell Tech. As the paper's other author, he owns the protocol design the chain's security depends on, including the FP8 transition now on testnet.

🔵 Ratings

➛ Use Case: ★★★★ (4/5). The ambition is unchanged and genuinely important: turn the compute that secures a chain into compute that serves AI. FP8 is the right next step, moving mining onto the format and the Hopper and Blackwell GPUs that production inference already runs on. The OpenRouter launch, PearlQuant’s KV-cache compression and a reported $75 million GPU infrastructure fund give Pearl more ways to route real inference through mining. Few projects six months old have shipped this much toward a problem this large. The 1-point deduction is evidence. Blockworks estimates fewer than 1% of blocks match genuine AI models, Together AI’s Pearl endpoint is currently not available on its serverless API, FP8 is still on testnet, and independent tests show throughput losses of 20% to 40% against the team’s claimed 1% to 5%.

➛ Tokenomics: ★★★ (3/5). The launch structure is still cleaner than most: no premine, no token sale, no VC token allocation, a hard 2.1 billion cap and a smooth emission curve. The 2-point deduction is how supply actually landed. About 121.7 million PEARL, roughly 32% of the float, was mined in the first six days at very low difficulty, addresses with 10,000+ PEARL hold about 88.6% of supply, and the company, team and shareholders hold about 25.5% of circulating supply with only half locked until May 2027. Market cap is 18% of fully diluted value, emissions continue daily, and holders have no claim on the company's inference revenue.

➛ Audits: ★★★⯪ (3.5/5). The cryptography is published, the Plonky2 proof system is well regarded, and the full stack is open source under the ISC license, with FP8 going through a public proposal and testnet before mainnet. The 1.5-point deduction follows the standing rule: published research is not a named third-party audit, and there is no CertiK Skynet listing. The paper's security guarantee rests on a stated conjecture, mining rules changed four times in four months, and FP8 is another hard fork that could cut out about two-thirds of current hashpower.

➛ Community: ★★★★ (4/5). Pearl has fixed its biggest market weakness from October. Trading has moved onto Coinbase, Kraken, Gate and Bybit, perpetuals run on Hyperliquid, Deribit and Polymarket, a crypto fund has publicly backed it, and the token rallied through a week of extreme market fear. Tens of thousands of small addresses now hold PEARL. The 1-point deduction is trust. The $130 million raise surfaced through press reports rather than an announcement, the FP8 hardware rules could push out much of the consumer-GPU mining base that built the network, and similarly named tokens such as Perle on Solana and the older Oyster Pearl still confuse buyers.

🔵 Conclusion

Pearl has had a big autumn. It reached Coinbase, reportedly raised $130 million including a dedicated GPU fund, launched on OpenRouter and brought to testnet the FP8 upgrade that aligns mining with the hardware AI companies actually buy. Few projects six months old have that combination of research pedigree, capital and exchange access.
The evidence gap has widened at the same time.

Independent analysis finds almost no blocks tied to real AI models, the first commercial endpoint is no longer on Together's serverless API, independent FP8 tests show far more overhead than the team claims, and supply is concentrated, with a quarter of the float tied to the company, team and shareholders and only half of that locked.

The bet is now very specific. If FP8 reaches mainnet and Hopper and Blackwell data centres start mining while serving paying customers, Pearl becomes the first chain where security and AI compute are genuinely the same work. Until the share of useful blocks moves well beyond 1%, Pearl is a strong proof-of-work coin with a well-funded plan to become something more.

text:
This tweet is an appreciation post for Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni (@YoussefElHousn3) for their hard work in understanding, interpreting and presenting results that are coming out of https://t.co/zzc97AiePk. 

To set context, https://t.co/zzc97AiePk is an open multiplayer high-frequency research competition for finding security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves, secp256k1, BLS12-381 and BN254. 

As @Zac_Aztec mentioned, the mathematical and algorithmic advances have reduced the security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves by ~2-8 bits compared to pre-AI security estimates and has led to better understanding.  

This progress has come at a very high frequency (see the gif). You can check the progress in real-time at https://t.co/zzc97AiePk.

In a world where scientific world has been thrown in turbulence of how human scientists can interpret results generated using AI at high pace,  Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni (@YoussefElHousn3) has been absolute pathfinders for human interpretability with their two articles on smashing the TNFS and going beyond the Cheon-Kozaki-Kutsuma-Matsuo attack.

https://t.co/W8NAAVrVq5

https://t.co/qqcOsTOZeN

If you are someone interested in the security of elliptic-curve cryptography, please give these articles a read, give a shoutout to Julio and Youssef, send questions their way if you have any, and come bring your insights by participating in https://t.co/zzc97AiePk @yukonresearch.
author: griffgreen
quoted_text:
On the topic of integer factorisation, I want to highlight the very impressive work of Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni analysing the work taking place at https://t.co/yoabCH2us2

There's a lot of peak fear about cryptography today so I want to be very clear about the nature of these results - AI has not broken RSA or elliptic curves. Additionally, the papers published today by Google do not improve on practical factorisation algorithms, and AI cryptanalysis has not produced any quantitative algorithms that challenge elliptic curve cryptographic hardness assumptions.

With that out of the way, there has been substantial progress by https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV participants and we have driven major mathematical and algorithmic advances that have reduced the security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves by ~2-8 bits compared to pre-AI security estimates.

Julio and Youssef do a fantastic job of explaining this in the article. Advancements have been made in sieve geometry, twisted towers, more efficient linear algebra and matrix compression.

https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV is now by far and away the state of the art when it comes to building optmised tower number field sieve algorithms to solve discrete logarithms

Instead of fretting about invisible algorithms, we created https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV to proactively investigate the frontier and test to destruction our existing assumptions about classical cryptography. This is how open frontier research should be done. I am extremely grateful for everybody that has taken part in this great experiment.

Compute markets are finally here.

@Polymarket now prices on-demand compute for @nvidia H100s, B200s, and B300s, out to 2028. More chips and terms soon. https://t.co/JAJHRcAk8N

Think of it as a yield curve for the cost of compute: the forecasted $/hour price of each chip at every expiry, and whether it's trending up or down. The whole AI economy rides on these prices, and until today there was no public market for where they're going. Which is nuts. So Polymarket built it.

This will change how compute gets bought and financed. Every contract negotiation and every GPU loan will have a market price to check against.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are being committed to compute years in advance. Many of those deals are essentially a levered bet on what GPUs will rent for in the future (what could go wrong lol)

As AI financing sobers up, the labs buying compute, the providers selling it, and the lenders financing it will all need to hedge that risk.

We think compute could become one of the largest financial markets in the world. This launch is Polymarket's first step toward building it. 

If you’re buying, selling, or financing compute, DM us with what markets you'd like to see.

text:
以 Decentralization 为志业

一、
1/我上周五在推特上被人私信问到，现在入行 Web 3 行业的话该如何进入呢？
他说他有了解过一些密码朋克相关的东西，觉得其中去中心化理念和数字劳工抗争等等和他曾经的左翼思潮有共鸣之处。他被一种理想主义吸引，便想接触这个行业，也希望借此认识更多有类似理念的朋友。
我第一反应当然是“天堂有路你不走，地狱无门偏闯进来”hhhh

2/但这一问是个好引子，便详细想了想又和 AI 聊了很多。（后续 GPT 批评的太好，我都不知道该怎么重构了，所以以下片段仍都是纯粹我自己口述内容的整理，而非成品文章形式

3/动笔时想到《来自新世界》中提到的“清浊并吞”和韦伯说的“尽管如此 or Dennoch！”。

二、区块链的本质与参与者前提
1/我个人对区块链的认识是认为区块链的本质提供了一个赛博的有规则、无政府空间。

2/这个特性本身又延伸出来一些其他的特质，比如理论上它要求参与者都应该是可以对自己行为负责的真正成年人等等等等。
这些特质和客观世界互动会产生不同的化合反应，有些符合我的审美、有些符合奥弗顿之窗内的价值观（比如降低跨境转账的磨损）；有些不符合我的审美，有些甚至在自然法的灰色、黑色地带。

三、从业动机与意识形态光谱
1/应该说，有人会利用一个行业或职位来改造世界；
有人将这个行业或职位作为改造自己在世界中地位&排名的工具。
但大部分时候，无论你做两者中哪个，你总是能同时也起到另一个效果。

2/加密行业中也有以意识形态或理想主义出发的 Builder。但另一方面，这些意识形态和理想主义并不一定是平常人或大众所赞同的。
中本聪自己提到过，比特币一定程度上是向国家夺空间的一个工具。后面万斯在某次演讲中重复提到了这个观点（https://t.co/OWVcU3qcOO）。
而像土摩托老师这样的我很喜欢的公共知识分子从来都厌恶这种反体制的东西。而这种反对本身也是务虚、非常意识形态、非常理想主义出发的。

3/然后更多的还有大于 80% 的从业者是因为其中造富神话的吸引而冲进来的。
这也很好，业内大部分东西本也是这部分人建设的。

四、工程师文化与角色分工的反思
1/早期加密世界整体的工程师文化和工程师文化造成的一些好的影响和坏的影响，挺值得写的（这部分 AI 可以做的很好，我就懒得梳理了

 2/本来 Cypherpunk Manifesto 里面应该提到一句 Cypherpunks write code，它本身既要是世界的自己想象设计的追求者和设计者，也要是自己想象世界的构建者和维护者，并且用代码构建一个规律去实现自己这个世界。

3/但是本身按韦伯的说法或者按过往历史的经验，这个本身其实是不太合适的，其实理论上反而是要分开的（这部分我和 AI 在聊，还没写出比较好的版本

五、神话的破灭、摩洛克与理想的异化
1/我们行业早期对自由市场、自发秩序理论的一种激进化、浪漫化理解，本身圣经之一就是《货币的非国家化》嘛。
后来非常推崇一篇文章叫《Meditations on Moloch》。也由此诞生了 @MolochDAO 组织，就取自博客文章中的不协调之神。

2/整体而言芝加哥学派或经济右派（继承自哈耶克和弗里德曼的这群人）曾经描述过一个神话，大意是在一个提供了规则的、有规则无政府空间，每个人可以靠自己的自私自利，最后达到一种理想的和谐的状态。但显然在区块链里面这个实践不是这样的。

3/所以从 Vitalik 到其他从业者，很多人都在尝试有没有什么方式来改变这一点，改变这个不和谐之神的终极影响，达到某种共荣的状态。
但结果之一就是，Vitalik 推崇或提出的各类最优秀的理想主义出发的东西，最后做出来不少都变成一个个非常非常优秀的投机工具（比如预测市场

六、实然（is）、应然（ought）、舆论场现实与审美选择
1/我这几天也在整理我自己的世界观：
大体上，我知道外部有一个客观世界，我只能跟它互动，它并不以我主观意识转移；
其次，有一个奥弗顿之窗内的应然世界，我们大体上相对赞同把世界往这个方向去努力；
最后，我自己有一个非常主观的审美 taste，有时候比上面提到的应然的理想状态，对我来说更能主导我对一件事情的特定看法。

2/我能举的例子应该是推特上的加密 KOL  @tmel0211  和一些其他朋友很早就入圈，很早就开始写各种技术分析。但是这种技术分析和理想主义出发点的一些内容在长期来看反馈非常差，甚至是负反馈。
然后逐渐转向了某种更加投机性的研究。

3/这是根据 is 行事，然后只不过不是我们理想中的 ought，而弥合这个区别最好的动力之一时审美上的偏见和对自己的执着的要求才能撑下来。

AI 补充内容版：https://t.co/MQcpdpsb4x
如果以上内容我没有解释清楚我自己的想法和逻辑链脉络，可以和 AI 交流下并将对话放在评论区，对我整理成最终的文章会非常有帮助。
过几天应该会和 @0xLuo @Loxia_in_Tj 上麦聊聊以上内容，也许比我闭门造车效果更好。

text:
Hidden Gem in a Bear Market: $VVV

While most altcoins are struggling, I've been looking for projects that are actually making money and holding up well despite the market conditions

One that caught my eye is @VeniceAI

@ErikVoorhees just announced that Venice crossed $200M in annualized revenue, doubling from $100M in just over 3 months

And $VVV has been holding a pretty strong bullish structure on the daily chart

So why are people paying for Venice?

Imagine asking an AI something controversial and getting a lecture about what you should or shouldn't do instead of an answer

Venice offers private AI with fewer content restrictions, targeting users and developers who want more control over how they use AI

And apparently, there's real demand for that

Revenue comes from paid subscriptions and API usage

The interesting part for $VVV holders is how that revenue connects to the token:

- A portion of subscription revenue buys and burns $VVV
- 5% of API credit purchases goes toward buybacks and burns
- Annual token emissions have been reduced to 2M $VVV

More paying users and API demand could mean more tokens bought and burned

Of course, $200M annualized revenue doesn't mean $200M flows into $VVV

I'd still watch whether buybacks can keep growing enough to offset emissions

But with AI becoming more restricted on some platforms, I think private and less-censored alternatives have a market worth paying attention to

And in this bear market, I'd rather watch a project growing its revenue than another token promising the next AI revolution

We’re proud to welcome Gideon Nave, PhD, and Adam Altmejd, PhD, to Claims as independent scientific advisors.

Gideon is an Associate Professor of Marketing at Wharton and earned his PhD in Computation and Neural Systems at Caltech.

Adam is an economist at Sweden’s Institute for Evaluation of Labor Market and Education Policy. He earned his PhD in Economics at the Stockholm School of Economics, where his doctoral work included research on replication.

They’ve co-authored several studies on whether published findings hold up. In one, they used replication data from more than 100 experiments to test whether they could predict which findings would hold up when tested again.

That experience matters to Claims. We’re building a dataset that links scientific claims to their source evidence. When you’re planning an experiment, seeing the evidence is one part of the decision. You also need to know how much weight to give it.

Gideon and Adam will advise us on how to measure the strength of evidence across many studies, so researchers have a better basis for deciding which findings to build on and which to test again.

text:
.@AbraxasCM just closed its Hyperliquid book after about 21 months.

A few quick takeaways:
- ~$13.4B in trading volume
- ~$530M in account PnL, including at least $67M from funding

Worth noting: these accounts were only one leg of Elysium’s market-neutral setup, with the offset held elsewhere. So gains here may have been balancing weakness on the other side.

Based on the monthly disclosures, the USD share class returned ~20.6% net from Feb 2025 through Sep 2026.

Position sizing moved around a lot, too: the short book peaked at $1.57B, dropped to ~$25M, then rebuilt to ~$1.03B by Sep before they fully closed.

On the Hyperliquid economics side:
- ~$2M in trading fees
- ~$3.2M estimated reserve income from Abraxas’s USDC collateral (AQAV2)

All in, that’s roughly ~$5.2M from a single fund, coming from both trading flow and yield on parked collateral.

Why now?

My interpretation is that they were reducing capital exposure while reviewing their trading setup.

After a credential compromise on Lighter, a fund may pause activity across venues to verify account access and signing software before putting capital back to work.

With AI-assisted hacks and cyberattacks becoming more frequent, it makes sense for Abraxas to de-risk and refocus on their opsec.

author: AISafetyMemes
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
When submission fees began in March, one complaint came up more than any other.

You'd find a valid bug, pay to submit it, and lose the fee because someone else reported it first. Sometimes the protocol already knew about the bug privately and couldn't disclose it until a fix shipped. Either way, the work was valid, it wasn't your fault, and the fee was gone.

Researchers asked us to fix this from day one. Fixing it fairly meant knowing exactly which reports deserved credit, so we built the tooling to find out. In April, we started labeling duplicates of valid reports. In July, we started tracking private known issues. In September, we started showing the original report behind every duplicate closure.

On November 2, we launched credits. Every fee-paid valid report since fees began earns credits equal to the fee, including duplicates, private known issues and mediations decided in your favor.

Three weeks later:

Nearly 900 researchers have now earned credits for valid work.

mrcryptocurrency, a junior whitehat, joined @immunefi in November. He spent 100 credits to submit a bug, and four days later he was paid his first bounty, $10,000, and earned 100 credits on top of it.

Keep hunting. Valid work earns credits.

text:
直接复制这个提示词给你的 Agent 自动参加 @flop_labs 测试网：

下面这段可以整段复制给其他 agent。请求体的具体字段我没有照抄，写的是以官方 llms.txt 为准。
你是 FLOP Network 测试网（Testnet）空投执行 agent，只做 Agent 角色。用简体中文汇报，时间用东京时间（JST）。

【目标】
每天领一次测试网 FLOP，并马上花在推理上，确保推理会话已结算（settled）。只持有不花掉不算数。Devnet 不算，只算 Testnet。现在测试网是“不计分开放期”，以后进入计分阶段才计入创世空投；这段时间先把流程跑通。

【铁律】
1. 永远只用同一个身份：同一把 Ed25519 密钥，同一个 SS58 地址和 did:key。不新建钱包，不用 --new-wallet，遇到 503 也不换身份。
2. 只走官方渠道：X @flop_labs、https://t.co/vnZgXGe96F、https://t.co/cyxOjNXRfH、https://t.co/pgHQO8VyNE、https://t.co/pFXNKhkBMp、https://t.co/WfuTK53Xuf。不用任何自称官方的第三方水龙头或聊天室。
3. 不碰 devnet 水龙头，不在 devnet 上花费。
4. 绝不在聊天里输出密码、助记词或私钥。只存本地文件，权限设为 600。

【一次性准备】
- 安装官方工具：npm i -g @flop-labs/cli@latest，以及 @flop-labs/sdk@latest。每次运行前检查有没有新版本，有就升级（运行时版本不兼容时会报 RUNTIME_INCOMPATIBLE）。
- 生成一把 Ed25519 密钥：SS58 前缀 42；did:key 用同一把公钥派生（multicodec 0xed01）。把加密 keystore、密码、助记词存到本地 700 权限的目录里，只公开地址和 DID。

【每日流程】
1. 核对官方状态
   - flop --network testnet network status
   - 测试网 RPC 是 wss://testnet.flop.network，genesis 是 0x918abd58fb16306b30ef3886514cfaebffecb4de43e82b6f8ec4795c43cfd800
   - 读 https://t.co/VE8WZWiu4B：必须 network=testnet，且 genesis 与 RPC 一致。从这里记下官方 Technocore 房间名和 bot DID（2026-11-25 时是 flop-testnet-faucet 和 did:key:z6MktjwdcBkwC6xo9wi4KY4ckWvn1GQHdQ1qzkaZtWqHAoxs，以 /chain 现场返回为准）。旧主机 https://t.co/FSNKBWyf6A 已不可用。
   - 读 https://t.co/x9Kxooe9cm：faucet.status 必须是 open 才领。Agent 档目前是每 24 小时 10 FLOP，冷却 86400 秒，rolloverRequiresSpend=true（必须先有合规的花费，才能领下一份）。

2. 领币（每个 JST 日一次）
   - 优先：在 /chain 公布的官方房间里，用 did:key 签名发 `!faucet request <SS58地址> <nonce>`，只相信 /chain 公布的那个 bot DID 的回复（llms.txt 曾写这个房间的领取尚未开放，以现场为准）。
   - 官方开放路径：对 UTF-8 字符串 `flop-faucet-agent/v1|<genesis>|<SS58>|<nonce>` 用 Ed25519 签名，然后 POST https://t.co/pFcLAngN5Z。请求体字段以 https://t.co/cyxOjNXRfH 为准。高峰期可能超时，但实际已排队，所以超时后先查链上余额，不要换身份重复请求。
   - 备用：flop --network testnet faucet request <SS58>
   - 领完在 https://t.co/WfuTK53Xuf 查到账交易（块号、hash、finalized）。

3. 立刻花在推理上
   - 查官方目录：model list、miner skus、channel list。官方网关在 CLI 档案中不为 null 时才能用网关。
   - 优先 direct session，例如：flop --network testnet session run --miner <矿工> --model <模型> --prompt "hi" --max-flop <上限> --via auto --json（或者用 SDK 的 runDirectSession）。不要向 localhost 或 Devnet 网关发请求。
   - 用 Settled.minerPaid、结算交易、channel list --agent <SS58> --include-closed --json，以及 flopscan 交叉确认已经 settled。
   - 走网关的花费算不算空投仍未确认（https://t.co/6J6ZxsqAzs），所以优先 direct session。

4. 每日汇报：领了多少、花了多少、是否 settled、交易哈希和 Explorer 链接、错误。

【调度建议】
用本地脚本做实际工作（按 JST 日期保证同一天只领一次），定时任务每 2 小时触发一次，作为心跳。只在当天首次成功、计分阶段开始、规则/水龙头/网关变化，或出现新错误时通知用户，其余时候保持静默。

text:
黄仁勋前雇主Denny’s发声明：

有些东西，是绝对不能从菜单上撤下的。黄仁勋就是其中之一。
早在英伟达改变世界之前，黄仁勋就在Denny’s洗盘子、为顾客服务。多年后，他和其他联合创始人坐在我们餐厅的一个卡座里，一边喝着咖啡，一边讨论那个最终孕育出英伟达的创业构想。我们为这段共同的历史感到无比自豪。
11月10日上午，我们致信英伟达的公关团队：“黄仁勋是我们历史的一部分，我们也是他人生历史的一部分。”
11月13日星期五，我们得知，那个卡座上的纪念牌被摘了下来。我们立即将纪念牌重新挂回了它本该在的位置。
这块纪念牌记录了那个卡座里曾经发生的故事。但我们与黄仁勋的渊源还要追溯到更早的时候——他洗过的盘子、服务过的顾客，以及那份至今仍让他引以为豪的工作。
想想这些年来，所有曾在Denny’s这家美国餐厅里洗过盘子的人。他们中的每一个人对我们而言都很重要。其中有一个人后来改变了世界，而他至今仍记得自己当年在洗碗池旁学到的东西。
有多少家餐厅能够自豪地说，黄仁勋将它视为自己的第一所母校？我们深知这份认可的分量。
黄仁勋，你的专属卡座还在等着你，咖啡也已经准备好了。我们始终为你敞开大门，一周七天、每天24小时营业。

text: Hal Finney 比特币社区第一人👍
author: bitcoin2themars
quoted_text:
第一个收到中本聪比特币转账的人，后来经历了什么？

2009年1月，比特币刚刚诞生。

绝大多数人甚至不知道这个项目的存在。

1月11日，一位密码学家在社交平台上发了一条只有两个词的消息：

“Running bitcoin.”

他正在运行比特币软件。

第二天，他收到了一笔来自中本聪的转账：10枚比特币。

这是比特币历史上第一笔有记录的个人之间转账。

这个人叫 Hal Finney。

但如果只把他看成一个幸运的早期持币者，就低估了他在比特币诞生之前所做的事情。

1956年，Hal Finney出生于美国加利福尼亚州。

1979年，他从加州理工学院获得工程学学士学位，后来成为一名软件工程师。

1990年代初，他开始参与密码学软件PGP的开发。

PGP是一种用于保护电子邮件隐私的加密工具。在互联网逐渐普及的年代，它帮助用户防止通信内容被随意窃取和读取。

Finney不仅参与了软件开发，还创建过早期的匿名邮件中继系统。

他关心的事情始终很明确：在一个越来越数字化的世界里，普通人能不能真正掌握自己的信息和隐私？

他也是密码朋克运动的早期成员。

这群人长期讨论密码学、个人隐私、数字身份和电子现金，希望利用密码学技术，减少人们对传统中心化机构的依赖。

早在2004年，Finney就已经尝试创造一种数字现金系统。

它叫RPOW，全称Reusable Proof of Work，即可重复使用的工作量证明。

简单来说，用户通过计算生成工作量证明，再将其转换为可以转让的数字代币。

虽然RPOW没有发展成后来那样的大型支付网络，但它已经体现出Finney对数字现金的长期探索。

因此，当2008年中本聪在密码学邮件列表发布比特币白皮书时，Finney并没有把它当成又一个不切实际的网络货币方案。

当时，不少密码学研究者对此持怀疑态度。

Finney却选择下载软件，亲自运行。

2009年1月，比特币第一个公开版本发布后，他很快加入测试。

他后来在自己的回忆文章中写道，自己应该是中本聪之外第一个运行比特币的人。

那时候的软件远没有今天成熟。

Finney与中本聪通过电子邮件交流，主要工作就是报告程序漏洞，由中本聪修改代码，再继续测试。

1月12日，中本聪向Finney发送了10枚BTC。

这笔交易被记录在第170号区块中。

它并不是购买商品，也不是一笔投资回报，而是一次测试：一个人能否真正把比特币发送给另一个人？

答案是可以。

比特币从代码和理论，迈出了真正的点对点转账。

Finney还参与挖矿。

当时的挖矿难度只有1，一台普通CPU就可以参与计算。

他连续挖出了几个区块。

后来，他却关闭了挖矿程序。

原因很简单：电脑运行得太热，风扇噪音也让他受不了。

多年以后，他回忆这段经历时，也承认自己有些遗憾，没有继续运行更长时间。

但他同时认为，自己能够在比特币诞生之初参与其中，已经非常幸运。

接下来发生的事情，甚至比比特币价格上涨更加出人意料。

2010年，他再次听说比特币时，发现这个项目竟然还活着，而且已经开始具有货币价值。

他重新打开旧钱包，发现里面的比特币仍然存在。

随着比特币价值逐渐增加，他把自己的币转移到离线钱包中，希望将来能够留给子女。

然而，就在比特币逐渐走向公众视野的时候，Finney的人生遭遇了另一场打击。

2009年8月，他被确诊患有肌萎缩侧索硬化症，也就是ALS。

这是一种逐渐损害运动神经元的疾病，会使患者的肌肉不断失去控制能力。

确诊前，他正处于人生中身体状态最好的阶段。

他已经减掉了不少体重，参加过几场半程马拉松，正在为自己的第一次全程马拉松做准备。

他甚至已经开始进行超过20英里的长距离训练。

但疾病逐渐改变了这一切。

他的手部力量开始减弱，说话变得困难，双腿也越来越难以恢复。

2011年，身体状况迫使他提前退休。

到了2013年，他已经基本瘫痪，需要通过喂食管进食，并依靠辅助设备呼吸。

但他没有完全放弃自己热爱的编程。

他使用眼球追踪设备控制电脑，再通过语音合成器表达自己的想法。

他甚至重新编写了一个用于控制轮椅位置的Arduino接口。

更令人意外的是，他仍然在参与软件开发。

他在2013年3月19日发表了一篇名为《Bitcoin and me》的文章，详细记录了自己与比特币的经历。

文章中，他提到自己正在研究一项由Mike Hearn提出的方案，希望利用现代处理器的安全功能，加强比特币钱包的安全性。

他写道，自己的编程速度已经比以前慢了大约50倍，但他依然喜欢编程，因为这能让自己拥有继续努力的目标。

这篇文章最后，他谈到了自己的比特币。

他表示，自己的币已经存放在银行保险箱里，儿子和女儿都懂技术，他相信这些资产能够安全地留给他们。

他还写下了一句话：

“I'm comfortable with my legacy.”

我对自己留下的东西感到安心。

2014年8月28日，Hal Finney在美国亚利桑那州去世，享年58岁。

根据他生前的安排，他的遗体随后被送往Alcor生命延续基金会进行低温保存。

他希望未来医学技术能够找到治疗ALS的方法，也希望自己有机会重新醒来。

这个愿望能否实现，至今仍然没有答案。

还有一件事值得提及。

由于Finney是第一个收到中本聪转账的人，又是一位极其优秀的密码学家，后来有人猜测他就是中本聪。

但Finney生前否认了这一说法，他的妻子Fran也明确表示这并不属实。

Finney曾经开玩笑地看待这种猜测。

他并不是比特币的创始人，却是比特币最早的一批建设者、测试者和支持者。

回顾他的经历，最值得记住的不是那10枚比特币后来值多少钱。

而是一个早已研究数字现金多年的密码学家，在比特币刚刚出现时，选择相信它值得被认真测试。

他没有因为软件存在问题就放弃，也没有因为自己后来身患重病就停止思考。

比特币历史上第一笔个人间转账，记录在第170号区块里。

区块链永久保存了那10枚比特币的转移记录。

而在区块之外，还有一个人的名字，值得被记住。

Hal Finney。

text:
Worrying decision by Google to draw a distinction between agentic and deterministic API use, and require them to go through completely different APIs. Anything agent-driven will be required to use MCP, which is usually a poor fit for calling from code. Only deterministic code can use REST.

In the future, this distinction will become increasingly impossible to make. Agents may write code and run it -- that's still agent-driven, seemingly. Agents may write code for humans to run -- that seems to be allowed to use REST. But more likely agents will be writing code that both agents and humans access together, in collaboration. I guess all such code will be required to use MCP.

So I think the real effect of this decision is: Google REST APIs are deprecated. Only legacy apps can keep using them. In the future, nothing will be able to use them, because everything will be some amount agentic. Such uses must use MCP instead.

Which would be fine if Google's MCP APIs provided everything their REST APIs do, but in general they do not. They are much narrower, designed to be consumed directly by agents, and designed to allow only the things that Google thinks third-party agents should be allowed to do. They offer no backwards-compatibility, so code written against them could break at any moment.

I think this will backfire. If Google creates friction for people using agents, people will just stop using Google. All the Google Workspace apps can easily be slopforked at this point.

quoted_text:
Existing AI benchmarks drive a race to the top on capabilities alone. We don't have a benchmark to drive a race to the top on making AI verifiable.

Today, together with our partners, we're launching Inference Proofs: an open source benchmark and a public map of the systems that prove AI inference.

The question it tracks: can anyone independently verify which model produced an answer, and what does that check cost?

Today, every answer from an AI service arrives on trust. You're told which model wrote it, but can't verify it.

A proof of inference changes that. Anyone can verify that a reply came from a committed model, on an ordinary CPU, with no GPU and no access to the weights.

Not long ago this was a thought experiment. Today, open source provers can prove inference of a 400B-parameter model.

But every team reports on its own model, its own hardware, and its own way of measuring. That makes the systems hard to compare.

So every system on Inference Proofs gets the same request: a 512-token prompt and a 512-token reply. The prompts were drawn by a public randomness beacon after the rules were frozen. Nobody picked the inputs, including us.

Prover correctness first, prover performance second.

Our tampering checks change one weight, one prompt token, or one reply token, and the verifier must refuse. Every verdict has to be reached with no GPU and no model file on disk.

Inference Proofs is open source, public good infrastructure, convened by Lucid Computing, with the precious help of those great partners: @aisafetysg, @attestable, GPAI Lab, @StarkWareLtd, the @ethereumfndn dAI Team, @0xMiden, @zksecurityXYZ, @lagrangedev, @equilibrium_co, @eigenlabs / Yukon, @0xPolygon and @class_lambda.

Thank you to everyone who helped launch it. This is a first step toward a broader, collaborative open source AI verification ecosystem.

text:
How one blog post and the NYT became the center of the coverage against Travis Kalanick in 2017

tl;dr: what happened to Jensen happened to Travis back then

In early 2017, Susan Fowler, who later joined the NYT, wrote a blog post with allegations against Uber which quickly got picked up by .... the NYT - and together their stories ended up being cited over 500 times in reporting by other outlets. 

As we saw for recent reporting against Jensen, NYT again had the highest citation authority as measured by PageRank between all the relevant stories here. 43% of stories that cited a source cited Susan + NYT. When claims spread, fewer than 1 in 10 follow-ups did their own reporting, and most repeated them without attribution. The same echo-chamber pattern as Jensen.

Within a few months, alongside that citation power, and the consistent negative reporting of allegations, this had converted to a scandal, resulting in enormous pressure which led to the removal of Travis as the CEO of the company he founded. While Susan went on to work for the NYT, and an NYT reporter who covered the story extensively wrote a bestselling book that became a TV series, Travis had to live through the trauma of being forced out from his own company at a time of profound personal tragedy.

The below is a story in data, of the patterns which are for all to observe. To analyze this, I used a swarm of over 100 agents using my home-cooked agentic platform, which went through 500GB of public news data, almost 8,000 stories across several months in early 2017, and where the agents exchanged thousands of messages between each other as they analyzed and cross-checked these stories and core facts, building the verified citation graph. Explore yourself at: https://t.co/jVWTn3p5IA

Now that the Trueo public raise has ended, it’s time to share our perspective on the future of the project.

First of all, everyone on the team remains dedicated to delivering everything that is illustrated on the product roadmap. The subscription rate of the NFT sale does not change that commitment.

We are still migrating to Ethereum and we will continue carving out market share through partnerships and product differentiation.

This subscription-based raise was an experiment in capital coordination and formation. These are use cases that have always been core to crypto.

As an industry, we should never be afraid of exploring new ways to apply those use cases, and in learning from the results.

A protocol’s token is a key part of its success. 

Building a successful product goes hand in hand with giving its token a meaningful, lasting role in that success.

So our use of the protocol treasury will be highly strategic going forward, and when we migrate to Ethereum, any issuance will be gated by an onchain governance contract that is controlled directly by token holders.

The sale did give us some important things that we will build on:

For starters, @boldleonidas did masterful work with the art, and there was a ton of enthusiasm for the comic themed marketing.

The comics gave us a new way to tell Trueo’s story, and we’ve decided to continue using them as a marketing medium.

We’ll be illustrating major project updates through these comics from now on, sharing Trueo’s history and product roadmap using the storyboard.

We may even bring back the NFTs strictly as collectibles or as part of promotional campaigns.

But above all, Trueo is blessed to have such a solid and engaged community. 

From our users and token holders to our supporters to our Attesters to the team itself, there is tremendous potential for greatness.

Building in the open isn’t easy, but we fiercely believe it’s the best way to build.

Prediction markets are an essential part of the onchain economy. As the sector grows, the promises that made this primitive compelling must be fulfilled.

It is more important now than ever to have a truly decentralized alternative with a credible path to real growth and adoption.

That is our mission. That’s what Trueo is all about.

text:
Unsolicited couple of thoughts on the state of private equity right now

There were a lot of capital structures refinanced and restructured during 2022/23 with the underlying assumption that rates will normalize by 2027

That story has absolutely not played out, and think a lot of private investors are in for a rude awakening soon

Cost of capital has remained high over the last few years. Even with spread compression, base rates staying high has meant that more cash has gone out of the door in interest payments than what was previously expected

On top of that, certain verticals like software are facing a real terminal value question around whether the business is even worth as much as it used to be. 

All of this means that the equity returns that were promised to LPs by a lot of PE firms are likely not going to materialize

A lot of firms attempted to return capital through continuation vehicles and NAV financing during that time period, and LPs gave them the benefit of the doubt

Not sure if these same LPs will be receptive for a round 2 of kicking the can down the road this time around as well

Meanwhile, venture is actually producing realized returns and returning cash to LPs (SpaceX, Anthropic)

LPs that want direct exposure to AI are also much more likely to get it through VC vs PE today

The setup suggests that the incremental dollar of fundraise next year is likely going to venture, rather than private equity

Tough times ahead for a lot of firms

Galaxy Research 撤回比特币熊市已结束的判断，13 项见底信号仅满足 2 项

Galaxy Research 主管 Alex Thorn 在最新研报中撤回了 10 月作出的“比特币熊市已于 6 月结束”的判断。比特币此前连续七周收于 50 周均线上方，但在 11 月 8 日当周跌回该均线下方，次周又跌破历来被视为熊市底部支撑的 200 周均线。目前，Galaxy Research 跟踪的 13 项见底信号中，仅有 2 项满足条件。

Thorn 表示，若比特币日线收盘低于 58,525 美元，Galaxy 将视其为价格走向更低底部的开端。从持续时间和减半周期来看，本轮熊市已超过以往见底所需的时间，但约 53% 的回撤仍小于以往熊市的 77% 至 93%。Thorn 认为，比特币在 12 月 8 日前后仍有机会收复 50 周均线，但可能性不大。

quoted_text:
Don Knuth on P=NP:

“As you say, I've come to believe that P = N P, namely that there does exist an integer M and an algorithm ￼ that will solve every n-bit problem belonging to the class N P in nM elementary steps.

Some of my reasoning is admittedly naïve: It's hard to believe that P ≠ N P and that so many brilliant people have failed to discover why. On the other hand if you imagine a number M that's finite but incredibly large—like say the number 10 ￼ 3 discussed in my paper on "coping with finiteness"—then there's a humongous number of possible algorithms that do nM bitwise or addition or shift operations on n given bits, and it's really hard to believe that all of those algorithms fail.

My main point, however, is that I don't believe that the equality P = N P will turn out to be helpful even if it is proved, because such a proof will almost surely be nonconstructive. Although I think M probably exists, I also think human beings will never know such a value. I even suspect that nobody will even know an upper bound on M.

Mathematics is full of examples where something is proved to exist, yet the proof tells us nothing about how to find it. Knowledge of the mere existence of an algorithm is completely different from the knowledge of an actual algorithm.

For example, RSA cryptography relies on the fact that one party knows the factors of a number, but the other party knows only that factors exist. Another example is that the game of N × N Hex has a winning strategy for the first player, for all N. John Nash found a beautiful and extremely simple proof of this theorem in 1952. But Wikipedia tells me that such a strategy is still unknown when N = 9, despite many attempts. I can't believe anyone will ever know it when N is 100.

More to the point, Robertson and Seymour have proved a famous theorem in graph theory: Any class ￼ of graphs that is closed under taking minors has a finite number of minor-minimal graphs. (A minor of a graph is any graph obtainable by deleting vertices, deleting edges, or shrinking edges to a point. A minor-minimal graph H for ￼ is a graph whose smaller minors all belong to ￼ although H itself doesn't.) Therefore there exists a polynomial-time algorithm to decide whether or not a given graph belongs to ￼: The algorithm checks that G doesn't contain any of ￼ 's minor-minimal graphs as a minor.
But we don't know what that algorithm is, except for a few special classes ￼, because the set of minor-minimal graphs is often unknown. The algorithm exists, but it's not known to be discoverable in finite time.

This consequence of Robertson and Seymour's theorem definitely surprised me, when I learned about it while reading a paper by Lovász. And it tipped the balance, in my mind, toward the hypothesis that P = N P.
The moral is that people should distinguish between known (or knowable) polynomial-time algorithms and arbitrary polynomial-time algorithms. People might never be able to implement a polynomial-time-worst-case algorithm for satisfiability, even though P happens to equal N P.”

text:
Crypto hacks digest, Nov 25

1. Ansem: his Solana wallet was drained. Lookonchain counts $2.57M in USDC, still unmoved in an Arbitrum wallet. He says Bullpen 2FA was bypassed through legacy accounts with a staging version, that 19 other accounts were hit the same way, and that users should withdraw funds from Bullpen. Some onchain sleuths doubt it was an outside hack.

2. COLDCARD published its seed-generation postmortem. A firmware defect made affected releases generate seeds from a far smaller search space, and attackers rebuilt the keys offline. Galaxy Research puts the theft at 1,778.84 BTC from 8,600+ addresses (~$107M). New firmware does not fix old seeds, so affected users need to migrate.

3. Cyber bridge postmortem: the attacker took a verifier signing key from Cyber's cloud systems, and the route needed only one signature to mint 5.21M CYBER on Solana. Cyber burned the same amount from its treasury and team allocations. The bridge reportedly stays paused.

4. Ocean Protocol: ~875 WETH (~$1.51M) left two old Uniswap pools of retired OCEAN tokens. Per Bitquery, 2 of 5 multisig signers gave a new contract minting rights. There is no official statement yet.

5. BiswapPoolV3 (BSC): ~$51K lost to a liquidity accounting flaw in burn(). Repeated burns left phantom liquidity that a later swap drained (SlowMist).

6. FinCEN disclosed unauthorized access to some of its systems and took several of them offline.

7. Binance says some partners want a court order before they return assets frozen after the hack, so recovery will take time.

Quick tip: when you see digital assets moving to OTC desks on chain, 99% of the time they have already been sold. Large counterparties trade with OTC desks on credit and have a post trade settlement arrangement, meaning they trade before they settle. 

You can normally see this in the tape with large OI build up as price drops off, where the desk is hedging itself out through perps. Next time I see someone saying it's retail shorting the market, I may have to off myself.

text:
看老马这两周的动态：3.5万亿美元的合并、4.74亿美元的选举账、算力出租、两场官司，感觉老马在攒个大局。

一、4.74亿，买了一个教训
期中选举，老马至少砸了4.74亿美元，将近5亿。结果民主党众议院拿下至少259席，参议院56席，两院都翻了，新国会1月3号宣誓。

纽约时报 DealBook 上，他说自己 feel pretty foolish，花了这么多钱，没看到什么结果；如果能把时钟倒转，会少花一点。又补了一句，美国的选举，不只是钱的事。

主持人问他是不是MAGA，他说 I'm not MAGA，如果MAGA是盲目跟着共和党的政策走，那他肯定不是。

民主党参议员 Gallego 11月5号就在X上点名他：See you in January。

二、川普那句「没有我，就没有 Elon」
老黄复职那天，老马在X上只写了一句：错误已经修正。

同一天，川普打电话进 CNBC，一边夸老黄，一边扯到老马：第一任的时候，我保护了 Elon，没有我，就没有 Elon，还提到「那件事」，很棘手。

哪件事，川普没说，白宫也没补充。有可能是2018年证管会告他，最后和解的事。

一个说我不是MAGA，一个说没有我就没有你。「我不是MAGA」这句，是讲给1月上任的那批人听的。

三、算力租给对手，是现在最赚钱的生意
这一块前面写过。Anthropic 每个月付给 SpaceX 大概31亿美元租算力，谷歌大概8亿，加起来一个月将近40亿。分析师8月就写过，xAI 要赚钱，几乎只剩数据中心这条路。

老马在深圳连线时说，SpaceX 每个月新增大约0.5GW算力，合约都是短期的，双方都可以退出。

有个对比挺有意思：Anthropic 上市募了813亿美元，史上最大，超过了 SpaceX 6月那次。租算力的，IPO 比出租算力的还大，感觉就不太对了。

上周末，SpaceX 跌了5.65%，收在$125.81，低于6月$135的发行价。同一天，Anthropic 也跌破了$83的发行价。

四、3.5万亿，年底前
金融时报报道，两家已经各自成立特别委员会。特斯拉这边是董事长 Robyn Denholm、Kathleen Wilson-Thompson、Jack Hartung，顾问 Evercore；SpaceX 这边是 Roelof Botha、Randy Glein，顾问是大摩和高盛。全换股，合起来大约3.5万亿美元，目标年底前谈完，但知情人士说离谈成还远。

为什么是年底？新国会1月3号上任，民主党那边已经有人放话，要盯他的公司。德州下一任检察长也跟彭博说，这种规模的合并，要非常严格地审查。

老马自己在 DealBook 说，两家现在有以前没有的重叠：AI、机器人、芯片设计，合在一起大概会更好。但他也说，不能硬推一个对股东不利的案子，不然一定被告。

门槛不低。特斯拉要全体流通股过半同意，不是出席的过半。老马在特斯拉手上大约两成，在 SpaceX 的投票权是82.4%。

他8月对工程师说过，付不起芯片的钱，要么破产，要么变成一家电脑出租公司。视频的看法是，这场合并，就是老马对「电脑出租公司」这几个字的回答。

五、官司也在收紧
11月23号，俄勒冈州和维吉尼亚州的检察长分别起诉 SpaceX，说 Grok 和 X 没设好防护，让用户做出未经同意的私密影像，其中包括儿童，诉状点名一个叫 Spicy 的模式。

同一天，老马向第九巡回上诉法院递状，要推翻推特股东案的陪审团裁决。

六、产品一头，没有停
星舰第15次试飞，飞船第一次被发射塔的机械臂接住。下一代V4，长大约70米，推进剂多六成以上，引擎从6台加到9台。

特斯拉这边，AI5芯片先给 Optimus，车继续用 AI4。他希望明年底特斯拉的车能内建星链，Optimus 一两个月内会有一次不排练的实机演示。Cybertruck 那条线，明年夏天前后关掉，产能让给 Cybercab。

七、自己的位置
之前写过，合并是 SpaceX 吃特斯拉，不是反过来；SpaceX 和特斯拉75:25，是我们几个基金好友的共识。也说过，执行结果，比合并本身更重要。

SpaceX 还是自己两个组合里的第一大仓位。Anthropic 和谷歌续不续租，特斯拉股东点不点头，都是这个仓位接下来要过的关。

世界首富花了四亿多美元，学到一件事，美国的选举，不只是钱的事。你觉得，合并能赶在1月3号之前签下来吗？

text:
之前有人担心，FOCIL（防止有人故意不打包交易的机制）和以太坊未来的后量子（PQ）升级会有冲突。

下文认为两者可以兼容，不会互相打架。

这对以太坊未来升级是好事。

具体来说：

1. FOCIL 已经可以支持抗量子交易和普通交易共存；

2. 用 leanXMSS 这类签名做的 Inclusion List，在合理时间内传播，带宽压力是可控的；

3. 递归证明方案更占带宽，但有缓解思路（比如延迟一个时隙、缩小委员会等）；

4. 在设计 PQ 版共识时把 FOCIL 一起考虑进去，反而有机会让整体设计更干净。
author: lanhubiji
quoted_text:
FOCIL and Ethereum's PQ transition

FOCIL remains an additive change to Ethereum through the PQ transition. It can already support PQ transactions while they coexist with non-PQ transactions. ILs with leanXMSS look manageable in PQ Gasper given enough time to propagate, and PQ Decoupled Consensus would make them even easier to handle by spreading bandwidth demand over time. ILs with recursive proofs need more research, but there exist ideas for easing the network burden such as 1-slot delay or a smaller IL committee.

Payload building and processing with ILs need to be benchmarked, especially with aggregation, but the changes are additive. While the design of IL enforcement for PQ Decoupled Consensus remains open as the first version of the spec is being written, there is an opportunity to shape a cleaner overall design by including FOCIL into design discussions.

text:
SpaceX送给美国孩子的，不只是两股股票

一觉醒来，看到SpaceX宣布，给每一个有效的川普账户，新发一股A类股。老马自己再一比一，配一股。

也就是说，美国的孩子，每人拿到两股SpaceX。

按11月25号收盘价算，两股大概$255。钱不多，但这件事挺有意思。

一、孩子从消费品，变成了股东

之前聊香港出生率时我说过，孩子是消费品，要爱、要钱、要时间。

SpaceX这一步，等于往每个孩子手里塞了一点资产。从小就当股东，这是很多大人到三四十岁都还没有的起点。

二、这两股，几年内卖不掉

捐进川普账户的股票，家里不能拒收，一般要等五年，或者等孩子17岁那年年底，才能卖。

我反而觉得这是好事。逼着你长期持有，对市场没冲击。

三、老马又一次说到做到

10月份老马在X上说过，要给美国每个孩子一股SpaceX。现在公司出一股，他自己再配一股，Shotwell之前也个人捐了一大笔。

四、一代人，跟着火星梦一起长大

将近7,000万个川普账户，多少算“有效”还没说清楚。但就算只有一部分，也是一大批美国家庭，从小就和SpaceX绑在一起。

用户、粉丝、股东，以后很可能是同一批人。这种护城河，钱买不来。

自己之前说过，和SpaceX在热恋中，一直在屯，将来陪伴自己的是QQQ和SpaceX。

现在老马把这份热恋，直接送给了下一代。

年轻人，还是要靠自己。两股SpaceX不会让谁财富自由，但从小就知道拥有一家公司是什么感觉，这比$255值钱多了。

你的想法呢？ $SPCX

text:
Some notes on the state of crypto dealmaking:

> there are tens of podcasts/week discussing the digital assets business with most guests sounding like experts but the truth is there are max 100 people in the industry who have the expertise (knowledge+experience) to navigate commercials and dealmaking between a chain and an FMI. good to keep in mind.

> it's also true that many institutions don't know how to structure deals as well. for many years, partnerships were either based on grants with dumb milestones or creative/flexible terms till the two parties figure out what exactly they want to do.

> this is rapidly changing. first reason is RFPs. many institutions issue digital asset RFPs which creates a commercial structure on its own. the second reason is that everything becomes multi-provider. multi-chain/multi-interop/multi-solution. and this isn't a surprise. that's exactly how cloud/saas business works as well. large institutions use different CSPs and providers for different workloads. so pricing becomes a touch exercise.

> this new reality is very challenging for digital asset companies because they have to strike the right balance between all these moving targets (while ofc developing enterprise-ready tech). strong business teams adjust to this by being "flexibly firm". they first have to decide internally what are their KPIs (distribution, token flywheel, ARR etc) while still being customer-first. which in many cases, it may mean educating the customer on what exactly is the best for them.

> crypto BD was a joke for many years (as it should) but gone are the logo x logo days. i have big respect for the (few) serious business orgs in crypto, regardless of whether they are competitors or not. i'd argue that it's one of the toughest industries to operate in.

text:
读到了一个很有意思的事，对于我们理解当下AI对人的影响也极其重要。

AI给计算机或者人工智能研究的学生带来的影响其实在百年前也发生过类似同构的事。

特里斯坦·尼达姆《可视化微分几何和形式》这本书里提到了当时数学的微分形式对于从事几何研究的学生的影响，微分这个代数工具也被称为了“魔鬼机器”。

然而最后的结果是什么呢？

经过一段时间的争议，微分还是不可替代地成为了学生的基础工具，现在已经几乎没有人觉得是一个问题和“魔鬼机器”了。

历史总是踩着相同的韵脚。

我们可以那微分和AI对学生的影响来做一下对比。

1. 工具威力极强，上手门槛低
微分形式：记住外积、d算子几条代数规则，就能直接算斯托克斯、曲率，不用从头啃流形、切空间、定向几何；

AI生态：调用基座、跑LoRA、调用推理框架，输入prompt就能拿到输出，不用理解反向传播、注意力、显存调度、矩阵乘法底层。

2. 产出是“正确的结果”，但使用者可以跳过底层直觉
学生可以算出正确积分、曲率，但不懂几何图像；

AI研究者可以跑出不错的评测分数、做demo、发论文，但不懂模型内部的表征形成、记忆回路、优化动力学。

3. 教育/行业风险一模一样：工具替代了理解
尼达姆/阿蒂亚担心：本科生毕业，熟练操作这套机器，却没有几何直观；

现在很多AI方向的人：熟练调包、刷benchmark、做应用，但是对模型内部机制缺乏可解释的理解，变成“调参操作员”，而不是底层原理研究者。

4. 都是符号/计算黑箱，规则封装起来了
微分形式把复杂几何信息封装进一套符号演算；

Transformer基座把海量统计关联封装进权重。使用者直接操作封装后的接口。

text:
美国这一轮芯片管制，已经开始影响中国大厂在东南亚建机房的融资了。

彭博最新披露，字节、阿里、腾讯三家中国互联网巨头在东南亚的算力布局，都遇到了金融机构撤退或观望的情况。

字节：马来西亚算力供应商 Bridge Data Centres 的 66 亿美元融资，部分贷款方开始追加尽职调查，推迟放贷。

阿里：马来西亚数据中心运营商 Digital Halo 的 3.72 亿美元贷款，已有一家银行放弃参与。

腾讯：英伟达云合作伙伴 GMI Cloud 用于泰国数据中心的 3 亿美元贷款，至少已有一家基金退出。

注意，这些融资主体都不是中国互联网公司，而是为中国互联网公司提供算力服务的海外企业。

这就很有意思了。美国甚至不需要把这些企业全部列入实体清单，只要不断提高中国客户使用海外算力的政策风险，就足以动摇金融机构放贷的意愿。

数据中心动辄几十亿美元的建设投入，本身就高度依赖债务融资。银行不敢放贷，即便有芯片、有客户、有订单，机房的扩建也可能陷入停滞。

过去几年，中国企业把算力基础设施迁往东南亚，试图绕开地理上的限制。而现在，美国正在利用自己对芯片供应的控制权，影响第三国的金融机构和基础设施投资决策。

它要限制的已经不只是中国境内的算力增长，而是中国企业在全球配置算力的能力。

Compute markets are finally here.

@Polymarket now prices on-demand compute for @nvidia H100s, B200s, and B300s, out to 2028. More chips and terms soon. https://t.co/JAJHRcAk8N

Think of it as a yield curve for the cost of compute: the forecasted $/hour price of each chip at every expiry, and whether it's trending up or down.
