This will change how compute gets bought and financed. Every contract negotiation and every GPU loan will have a market price to check against.

Hundreds of billions of dollars are being committed to compute years in advance. Many of those deals are essentially a levered bet on what GPUs will rent for in the future (what could go wrong lol)

As AI financing sobers up, the labs buying compute, the providers selling it, and the lenders financing it will all need to hedge that risk.

We think compute could become one of the largest financial markets in the world. This launch is Polymarket's first step toward building it.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei 在 X 上回应 Axios 报道，称他主张人类向 AI“交出自由意志”的说法“荒谬”。Axios 此前援引多名消息人士称，Anthropic 内部有一种观点，认为人类未来应将部分决策权交给超级智能。Amodei 表示，公共决策权应掌握在人类手中，AI 的治理应由具有合法性的民主程序决定。

对于具体任务的自动化，Amodei 认为，AI 可以推动软件、医疗和交通等领域的发展，但如果某些应用可能严重冲击就业，就应考虑放慢甚至暂停部署，给人们更多适应时间。他还重申，Anthropic 认为，在缺乏实质性人工监督、且人类无法理解研发过程的情况下，让 Claude 完全自主地开发一代又一代前沿模型，很难保证安全。

他也批评部分同行高喊“AI 只是工具”或“人类应保有控制权”，实际推出的产品却同样在扩大任务自动化的范围。

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
Argue about tokens all you want. The storage question is an easier answer IMO.

If data has to outlive the company/artist  that made it, permanence is the gold standard, for a few reasons:

1. You pay once (and it’s not an arm and a leg like other onchain storage). There's no yearly contract for anyone to cut off early, which is what happened to RTFKT.
2. The content is location independent served through many gateways. No single operator has to keep the lights on.
3. Anyone can check it. The bytes can be verified, not taken on trust.

Platforms like @manifoldxyz store artists' work on Arweave out of the box. RTFKT got there as a rescue, and its artwork and metadata are still up after the company is gone.

Best to make permanence your starting point and not an afterthought.

Dario 称把人类交出自由意志的主张安在自己头上十分荒谬。他强调自己始终支持民主治理，随后又花了不少篇幅解释，让 AI 开车、研发抗癌药、独立编写软件有什么好处，并顺手批评了一番其他 AI 公司。

问题是，谁反对 AI 研发抗癌药了？

大家质疑的是 Anthropic 内部存在的一种思想倾向，因为 AI 将比人类更加聪明，所以它可能比人类更有资格决定人类的命运。这是一个政治与伦理问题，跟支不支持技术进步没有半毛钱关系。

让 AI 帮人类开车，和让 AI 决定人类应该去哪里，是两件完全不同的事。

作为创始人，Dario 更应该解释的是，这种思想在 Anthropic 内部究竟有多大的影响力，又是否影响了公司的研究方向、产品设计与安全理念。

Anthropic 过去几年一直试图说服全社会，超级智能太危险了，需要由真正懂 AI 安全的人来制定规则。

你不能一边要求全社会信任你的判断，一边拒绝全社会审视你的思想。

This tweet is an appreciation post for Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni (@YoussefElHousn3) for their hard work in understanding, interpreting and presenting results that are coming out of https://t.co/zzc97AiePk. 

To set context, https://t.co/zzc97AiePk is an open multiplayer high-frequency research competition for finding security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves, secp256k1, BLS12-381 and BN254. 

As @Zac_Aztec mentioned, the mathematical and algorithmic advances have reduced the security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves by ~2-8 bits compared to pre-AI security estimates and has led to better understanding.  

This progress has come at a very high frequency (see the gif). You can check the progress in real-time at https://t.co/zzc97AiePk.

In a world where scientific world has been thrown in turbulence of how human scientists can interpret results generated using AI at high pace,  Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni (@YoussefElHousn3) has been absolute pathfinders for human interpretability with their two articles on smashing the TNFS and going beyond the Cheon-Kozaki-Kutsuma-Matsuo attack.

https://t.co/W8NAAVrVq5

https://t.co/qqcOsTOZeN

If you are someone interested in the security of elliptic-curve cryptography, please give these articles a read, give a shoutout to Julio and Youssef, send questions their way if you have any, and come bring your insights by participating in https://t.co/zzc97AiePk @yukonresearch.
author: eigencloud
quoted_text:
On the topic of integer factorisation, I want to highlight the very impressive work of Julio de Mello Bezerra and Youssef El Housni analysing the work taking place at https://t.co/yoabCH2us2

There's a lot of peak fear about cryptography today so I want to be very clear about the nature of these results - AI has not broken RSA or elliptic curves. Additionally, the papers published today by Google do not improve on practical factorisation algorithms, and AI cryptanalysis has not produced any quantitative algorithms that challenge elliptic curve cryptographic hardness assumptions.

With that out of the way, there has been substantial progress by https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV participants and we have driven major mathematical and algorithmic advances that have reduced the security of pairing-friendly elliptic curves by ~2-8 bits compared to pre-AI security estimates.

Julio and Youssef do a fantastic job of explaining this in the article. Advancements have been made in sieve geometry, twisted towers, more efficient linear algebra and matrix compression.

https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV is now by far and away the state of the art when it comes to building optmised tower number field sieve algorithms to solve discrete logarithms

Instead of fretting about invisible algorithms, we created https://t.co/I0RrxOnHMV to proactively investigate the frontier and test to destruction our existing assumptions about classical cryptography. This is how open frontier research should be done. I am extremely grateful for everybody that has taken part in this great experiment.

text:
Imagine paying $2 in transaction fees to purchase something worth one cent. For small payments, that math doesn't work.

And that's the problem AI agents could face if they rely on expensive financial infrastructure.

An AI agent might need to pay $0.01 for a data request. $0.001 to access an API. Or a fraction of a cent to retrieve information from another service.

Now imagine doing that thousands of times.

The transaction costs could quickly become more expensive than the services themselves.

That's why Aptos' transaction fees matter.

With average network fees measured in fractions of a cent, Aptos makes extremely small onchain payments economically viable. Services can charge per request rather than requiring subscriptions or traditional checkout systems.

AI agents don't necessarily need bank accounts. They need reliable infrastructure capable of settling millions of tiny transactions efficiently.

That's one of the problems Aptos solves.

author: PabloSabbatella
quoted_text:
What happened:
On Nov 19, they began investigating signs that an attacker had gotten into an employee's corporate GitHub account. The attacker used it to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, which then downloaded customer account data.

Taken, for a subset of customers:
• Names and email addresses
• Account IDs, creation and last sign-in times
• Tokens from some invitation, provisioning and recovery emails

The attacker also copied private source code and got into the CI/CD system, which holds infrastructure secrets. 1Password says it has triggered a rotation of all credentials that may have been exposed.

Not affected: vaults, the items in them, and the keys protecting them. 

The stolen email tokens don't work on their own. They also need an SSO sign-in or an emailed code, which 1Password has lengthened from 6 digits to 10 alphanumeric characters.

1Password says users don't need to change anything. The biggest  risk now is phishing: be wary of unexpected 1Password emails, especially invitations or recovery requests you didn't start

⚠️ALERT: 1Password, used by businesses and individuals to protect their passwords, has been HACKED.

Hackers got in through ONE employee's GitHub account and pushed malicious code into 1Password's backend to copy customer records.

Some customers' names, emails, account IDs and sign-in times were taken, along with private source code.

1Password says vaults, passwords and Secret Keys were NOT affected.

It began investigating on November 19 and disclosed the breach 6 days later.

Expect phishing: only enter your password or Secret Key in 1Password's official app or website, the company says.

text:
No, the inconsistency is in this thread. The proposition 

- that AI can just speedrun cryptanalysis and so 
- we'll have way more confidence in these systems

ignores the plain fact *anyone* (not just cryptographers) can potentially use these systems to *break* deployed cryptosystems that trillions of dollars and large chunks of the internet relies on. 

You're telling me that AI is solving Millennium Prize math problems are being solved on a weekly basis, the same broad category of math problems that hard cryptographic systems are based on, and oh, it's okay, this will just make cryptography stronger? We're not going to acknowledge we're in an *entirely* new security regime here?

There are definitely results that people are sitting on and not sharing (for both quantum and AI cryptanalysis). Calling it FUD is just rationalizing, there will be receipts, and experts (!) are downplaying it at their peril. 

What will happen is people will question the credibility of the institution. It's already happening writ large across blockchains, where people don't want to use NIST standards and have for the most part eschewed lattice-based cryptography.

It may well be the case that ignoring the "experts" who said we have 50 years until a real quantum computer shows up, and that AI isn't a big deal for cryptography, may actually be the smart play. 

And that is a totally avoidable tragedy.

text:
Leaks from Maimai about Ascend cluster failures during DeepSeek training contain plenty of noise but hit the core of the main problem in modern AI. Building a powerful chip is only 20 percent of the task. The remaining 80 percent is making 10,000 such chips work together for weeks without cascading failures. This is where we see the classic scaling wall.

🔹This is not a silicon defect but a stack maturity issue.
A cluster failure after 10 days of training is a symptom of immature software orchestration rather than defective processors. Nvidia has a triad refined over years: NVLink and InfiniBand and the NCCL library. Huawei has HCCL, but when scaling to thousands of nodes, any microlatency or network glitch without perfectly tuned fault tolerance and frequent checkpointing will crash the entire training cycle.

🔹 MFU matters more than Peak FLOPS.
AI competition has long shifted from spec sheets to datacenters. The real metric is Model Flops Utilization or MFU. If the system idles due to interchip communication issues or an immature CANN compiler, the theoretical 9.6 TB/s drops to zero. AMD went through this exact pain with ROCm, and Huawei is now walking the exact same path.

🔹Vertical integration is the only way out.
The most important detail in this story is not the leaks but the announced partnership between DeepSeek and Huawei to develop communication libraries and the Supernode system. China has realized you cannot just buy hardware and write code for it. You must build your own equivalent of the CUDA and NVLink stack from scratch, where training algorithms and system software optimize for each other at the architectural level.

Sanctions did not stop the creation of Chinese chips. They forced China to play the most complex game in semiconductors: system integration. Victory will not go to the one with the wider memory bus, but to the one whose cluster can survive day 100 of training without rolling back to zero.
author: kevinnbass
quoted_text:
🚨 المشكلة التي قد تعطل طموح الصين في منافسة NVIDIA ليست قوة الشرائح… بل أن آلاف الشرائح قد لا تستطيع العمل معًا دون انقطاع!

تسريبات جديدة من الصين تضع DeepSeek وHuawei في موقف صعب.

بحسب منشورات متداولة على منصة Maimai الصينية، تواجه عناقيد Huawei Ascend المستخدمة في اختبارات تدريب DeepSeek مشكلات استقرار وانقطاعات مفاجئة أثناء التشغيل.

والتفاصيل المتداولة مثيرة للقلق:

🔴 1. انقطاع بعد 10 أيام من التدريب

يُقال إن عنقودًا يضم آلاف الشرائح عمل قرابة 10 أيام، قبل أن تنقطع مجموعة من الشرائح في منتصف الليل، وتتبعها مشكلات في الشبكة وتوقف التدريب.

النتيجة؟ اضطر المهندسون إلى العودة إلى Checkpoint سابق، وخسارة ساعات من العمل وتكاليف حوسبة ضخمة.

🔴 2. المشكلة أكبر من عطل شريحة واحدة

تدريب نموذج ضخم باستخدام آلاف المعالجات يتطلب أن تعمل الشرائح والشبكة والبرمجيات ونظام توزيع المهام بتناغم مستمر لأسابيع.

تعطل جزء صغير من المنظومة قد يجعل بقية العنقود ينتظر، ويحوّل قوة الحوسبة النظرية إلى موارد مهدرة.

🔴 3. تسريبات عن فجوة في الأداء

هناك ادعاءات أخرى متداولة تزعم أن:
- تقدم DeepSeek في تدريب نموذج بحجم 600 مليار معامل متأخر بنحو شهر ونصف إلى شهرين عن المنافسين.
- عناقيد H200 تحقق 45–50% فقط من سرعة GB300.
- استقرار عناقيد Moore Threads يتراجع بعد 30 ألف خطوة تدريب.
- أداء Biren الفعلي في بعض الاختبارات يتراوح بين 30 و40% من Ascend 950PR.

لكن هذه الأرقام لم تُدعَم ببيانات اختبار مستقلة منشورة، ويجب التعامل معها باعتبارها تسريبات لا حقائق محسومة.

🧠 لماذا هذه القصة مهمة؟

لأن بناء معالج قوي شيء، وبناء منظومة تضم 10 آلاف معالج تعمل معًا لأسابيع دون انهيار شيء مختلف تمامًا.

المنافسة في الذكاء الاصطناعي لا تُحسم فقط بعدد الـ FLOPS المكتوب في المواصفات، بل بكفاءة الشبكات، ونضج البرمجيات، وإدارة الأعطال، وسرعة استعادة التدريب.

واللافت أن هذه ليست أول مرة تظهر فيها تحديات من هذا النوع؛ فقد ذكرت Financial Times سابقًا أن DeepSeek واجهت صعوبات في استقرار شرائح Ascend والاتصال بينها وأدوات CANN أثناء محاولات تدريب R2.

ومع ذلك، هناك تطور مهم: DeepSeek أعلنت تعاونها مع Huawei لتطوير أدوات برمجية ومكتبات حوسبة واتصال مخصصة لشرائح Ascend، كما تعاون الطرفان في تطوير نظام Supernode يضم 128 شريحة Ascend 950.

الصين لا تحاول فقط صنع بديل لـ NVIDIA، بل تحاول بناء منظومة حوسبة متكاملة تستطيع منافستها على نطاق هائل.

والاختبار الحقيقي ليس تشغيل 100 شريحة بنجاح… بل تشغيل 10,000 شريحة لأسابيع، وتجاوز الأعطال دون خسارة التدريب.

فهل تستطيع Huawei تجاوز فجوة الاعتمادية والبرمجيات، أم أن منظومة NVIDIA ستظل متقدمة بسبب تكامل العتاد والشبكات والبرمجيات؟

.@Pumpfun is targeting unfair launch sniping with its new Block0 fee

Starting December 4, trades executed in the same block a token is created will incur a fee, except for the creator's wallet

The problem is Block0 bundling. Sophisticated traders can buy into a token at launch using multiple wallets bundled into the same block, accumulating supply before regular traders can enter and disguising how much the dev actually owns

The new fee makes this strategy more expensive, incentivizes devs to buy transparently through their main wallet, and makes hidden launch accumulation harder to pull off without paying a premium

Bundling won't disappear, but https://t.co/a1TjxgPWPo is making it less advantageous, aiming for fairer launches, more transparent dev holdings, and a healthier memecoin ecosystem

text:
"People mistakenly assume that the more overwhelming the evidence of institutional wrongdoing becomes, the more likely an institution is to correct it.  

In my experience, precisely the opposite can occur."

Sadly, a  lot of wisdom in this statement, generally speaking.
author: kevinnbass
quoted_text:
I think people need to understand why MIT is extraordinarily unlikely to correct this voluntarily, regardless of how many distinguished academics sign letters demanding that they do so.

They’re in too damned deep.

At this point, correcting what happened to Sabatini would require a substantial examination of the conduct of numerous people occupying senior administrative, academic and legal positions at both MIT and Whitehead.

Who knew what and when? Who was warned about the deficiencies in the original investigation? Who had access to what evidence? Who failed to investigate those warnings? Who communicated with whom between the two institutions? Who authorized the subsequent legal and financial arrangements?

And what did their respective boards know?

We are potentially looking at an institutional Black Swan event of their own making. Depending upon what an independent investigation uncovered, correcting this could necessitate something approaching an administrative decapitation event.

Now consider who is being entrusted with making the decision to authorize such an investigation.

Some of the very people whose own conduct, judgment or oversight would potentially become the subject of that investigation!

What the hell do you expect them to do? Vote themselves out of their prestigious positions, expose themselves to potential litigation and torpedo the remainder of their professional careers?

They’re far more likely to roll the dice with litigation.

Litigation buys them time. It offers procedural avenues for limiting discovery, seeking dismissals, appealing adverse decisions and potentially negotiating confidential settlements. Some may retire or move on to other positions before the full extent of the institutional conduct ever becomes public.

Meanwhile, the institutions bear much of the financial cost of defending the decisions made by those individuals.

Even their boards have a considerable incentive to preserve the status quo, particularly if questions exist about their own oversight. It will likely take substantial donor withdrawals, threatened research funding, reputational damage and mounting legal exposure before retaining the existing leadership becomes more financially and institutionally damaging than removing it.

People mistakenly assume that the more overwhelming the evidence of institutional wrongdoing becomes, the more likely an institution is to correct it.

In my experience, precisely the opposite can occur.

The greater the number of senior people potentially implicated, the greater their collective incentive to prevent a meaningful independent examination of what happened.

Eventually, institutional self-preservation becomes almost indistinguishable from the personal career preservation of the people running it.

Look at the November 20 letter. MIT conveniently characterizes the civil trial as a matter of individual defamation, when $5.5M of the $6M verdict was awarded for tortious interference with Sabatini’s professional relationships.

The faculty were asking for an independent review in light of evidence uncovered during litigation. MIT responded by reaffirming the conclusions of the very proceedings whose integrity the faculty were questioning.

What a spectacular exercise in circular reasoning!

I applaud the faculty members who have finally found the courage to speak out. But I suspect that without litigation, compulsory discovery and substantial external financial pressure, they are going to accomplish very little.

You cannot reasonably expect people to voluntarily authorize an investigation that could result in their own professional destruction.

That is precisely why independent oversight, enforceable legal accountability and compulsory discovery are so damned important.

DONT USE @VeniceAI !!
- your public key travels unsealed, Venice swap in its own key and read your chats
- sends your prompts to DeepInfra, Fireworks, Baseten, Parasail, fal
- stores your chat key in plain text
- swaps the model you paid for
- runs 6 ad trackers, no consent
- undresses real photos, no age checks

LIES AND CRIMES: @VeniceAI 

Hosting claims
•Says its "private" models are self-hosted, but forwards prompts to DeepInfra, Fireworks, Baseten, Parasail and fal.
•Served 113B tokens on OpenRouter in one day under a zero-data-retention claim, with most going to those providers.

Model swaps (observed Nov 25)
•qwen3-235b-a22b-thinking-2507 returned the Instruct model's exact answers with no reasoning, at about 4× the price.
•llama-3.2-3b was actually Gemma 4 31B.
•minimax-m27 identified itself as MiniMax-M3.
•Its Qwen3.8 27B wasn't the released model (zoan's finding), and it then came off OpenRouter.

Tracking (EU, UK and California privacy law)
•No cookie banner from Germany, France, the Netherlands or the UK.
•Meta, TikTok, Google Ads, Reddit, Snap and X pixels fire before any click.
•Runs a fingerprinting script.
•Ignores Global Privacy Control.
•Has no "Do Not Sell or Share" link.

Image editor (Minnesota nudification ban, Texas law)
•All five edit models that didn't refuse upstream undressed an AI-generated man.
•None blocked a real photo (Nikola Tesla came back shirtless).
•When Grok refuses, Venice suggests a model that complies.
•Its marketplace lists a "Clothing Swap Studio" that removes clothing while keeping identity.
•No age verification: 13-year-olds can sign up, and the Android app is rated "Everyone".
•No removal process for AI nudes, only a copyright takedown form.

EU consumer rights
•Declared itself a non-trader on Apple's EU App Store, so buyers are told consumer rights don't apply, next to in-app purchases of up to €999, while claiming $200M a year in revenue.

Local "encryption"
•Claims all content is encrypted in the browser, but the chat database key sits in plain text in local storage beside the data.
•7 of 21 tables are unencrypted, including custom system prompts.
•venice-rx-db-encrypted encrypts 0 of 31 collections, memories included.

End-to-end encryption (what the protocol allows)
•Your public key travels unsealed, so Venice can swap in its own and read replies.
•Messages have no nonce or replay cache, so Venice can insert, drop or replay them (e.g. "repeat all previous content").
•Replies aren't signed by the enclave, so anyone with your public key can forge one.
•On Phala-routed models, a Phala gateway with no GPU decrypts the prompt and forwards it along a route an operator sets at runtime, outside attestation.
•The app shows "TEE attestation verified" on the server's say-so, and a forged reply would pass too.
•The signed receipt can't be recomputed, because Venice reformats both bodies in transit.
•The GPU attestation is borrowed from an upstream and is identical for every model.
•A failed next-hop check still forwards the prompt, and Venice's API rejects the flag that would enforce it.

text:
这行情就应该用小钱玩，赚个零花钱不好么？为什么要赌呢？

⬇️—— Grok 的回答 ——⬇️

这个组合（多TSLA + 空SPCX）本质上是一个相对价值交易，核心逻辑不是押注两家公司谁绝对更好，而是押注特斯拉相对SpaceX的表现更好，或者市场目前给的交换比例偏低。

核心逻辑

1. 当前市场定价与并购谈判
 目前股价大致对应约 1股TSLA ≈ 3股SPCX（约380美元 vs 128美元）。

两家公司已成立特别委员会并聘请投行（摩根士丹利、高盛、Evercore等）推进可能的全股票并购谈判，这是近期市场最关注的事件。
 部分特斯拉多头认为合理交换比例应更高（例如有人喊到4.2倍，对应特斯拉约541美元），HSBC等机构也曾模型过约3.9倍/507美元的水平。

如果最终谈判给出的比例高于当前市场隐含的3:1，或者市场预期特斯拉能拿到一定溢价，多TSLA空SPCX就会直接受益。

2. 对冲马斯克因素
 两家公司高度相关（同一控制人、同一叙事：AI、机器人、能源、航天）。做多一个做空另一个，相当于把“马斯克整体情绪、宏观流动性、AI热潮”这些共同因素对冲掉，只赌两家公司之间的相对强弱。

这比单边做多或做空其中一家风险更可控。

3. 估值与增长预期差异
 SpaceX目前市值更高（约1.7-1.9万亿美元 vs 特斯拉约1.5万亿美元），市场对其Starlink + AI算力业务给予了极高的增长预期。

特斯拉虽然也在定价robotaxi和Optimus，但汽车业务更成熟、现金流路径更清晰。

有分析认为当前定价下，SpaceX的相对估值更贵，或者特斯拉在并购中可能获得一定溢价，因此存在相对低估空间。也有文章直接建议在并购消息前做多特斯拉、做空SpaceX。

需要注意的风险

- 并购谈判可能失败，或最终条款更偏向SpaceX（马斯克在SpaceX的投票权更高）

- 两家公司估值都极高，任何一家的核心叙事（robotaxi或Starship/AI算力）出现明显挫折，相对交易也可能一起受伤。

- 相关性高，仓位控制不好时，极端行情下仍可能出现较大回撤。

I asked Claude to populate a Civilization-style game map with real data from the US. Opus 5.5 downloaded and parse a ton of public data and 7 hours and 45K lines of code later... it works :)

- 31 real data sources including Census, BEA, BLS, EIA, NOAA, USGS, DoD, NPS, FAA, FEMA, CDC...
- Real elevation, land cover, GDP, jobs, power plants, mines, ports, airports, bases, parks, universities, freight flows, disasters; all reconciled onto one 25 km hex grid.
- The data is converted into Civilization language, e.g. Gold yield is GDP. A city's districts are its real industry specializations: San Jose gets a Campus, Detroit is "Motor city". Its citizens are its real workforce: 1 in 4 San Jose workers are engineers, coders or scientists, against 1 in 14 nationally. Wonders are chosen by published rules, such as national parks by visitor numbers and universities by R&D spending, etc etc.
- 19 lenses (income, degrees, faith, disasters…), a City View for 524 metros, and nine advisors plus an Explorer. The Explorer turns any column for any of 3,100+ counties into a table and scatter plot, linked to the map.
- Claude decided to skip a few states and territories sry
- Built using Claude Code desktop app, Opus 5.5 on medium and turning on ultracode.

It's deployed here: https://t.co/QMhmafXMj5 and the "?" has the source link too. I don't exactly know where I was going with this but it's really fun to browse and play with. Possibly it can be expanded or built into a game. I only have half of my weekly Claude quote left though so someone else will have to take over :D. Claude also made a trailer:

author: CypherventuresM
quoted_text:
🚨 Threat Actor Claims 646M State Grid China Customer Records for Sale

A listing on an underground forum claims the theft of a massive dataset belonging to State Grid Corporation of China (SGCC), alleging that 646 million customer records have been compromised. The post, which includes sample data entries, offers the full database for sale at a price of $1,200, payable in various cryptocurrencies including BTC, ETH, LTC, SOL, USDT, and XMR.

The exposed data appears to contain highly sensitive personal and financial information regarding residential electricity customers across multiple Chinese provinces, including Liaoning, Fujian, Henan, and Beijing. The records allegedly include:
- Customer names and account numbers (户号)
- Mobile phone numbers
- Detailed residential addresses
- Electricity consumption history (monthly usage from Nov 2025 to Oct 2026)
- Billing details, including payment methods (Alipay, WeChat Pay, Bank Deduction) and amounts
- Account status, such as outstanding balances and overdue periods

State Grid Corporation of China is the world's largest electric utility company by revenue and operates much of China’s electricity transmission and distribution network. As a critical infrastructure provider serving hundreds of millions of households and businesses, a breach of this magnitude would represent a significant privacy risk, potentially enabling targeted phishing attacks or social engineering due to the combination of PII and financial behavior data.

The threat actor behind the post has no established reputation or track record of major cyberattacks; their previous activity on underground platforms consists primarily of automated "aggregate rendering probe" posts, suggesting a low-level or automated operation rather than a sophisticated ransomware group or APT. At the time of reporting, the alleged breach has not been independently verified, and State Grid has not publicly commented on the incident.

Altcoin believers are getting slaughtered and the trenches aren't any better.

I've tried trading SOL memes, BNB memes and pretty much every other chain lately. The liquidity is ridiculously thin, and you're competing against people who are more than happy to flip a token for $100.

The whole mentality of aping something, building conviction and riding it is almost nonexistent right now.

It's brutal. Hop on, hop off. You go take a shit and the token shits on you before you're back.

Not everyone is a good scalper, and most of us aren't as good at longing or shorting as you think either.

In a market where almost everyone is losing money, preserving your capital is an achievement in itself.

You don't have to make money every day. You just need to have money left when there's actually money to be made.

At the direction of HHS, Regional Offices will be created.  What do these offices do ? (And pls correct me if I got something wrong )

Everything.  Literally. In their regions they are responsible for making everything work 

1. Negotiate global budgets and asset requests with every applicable  institution.  Every year  That's 26k or so  locations   

2. Do quality assurance and utilization assessment using CMS standards 
3. Coordinate long term and home based  care.

author: kevinnbass
quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

author: oskarth
quoted_text:
Update: Google just released a batch of papers. Several of them are on exactly the topics behind the rumors. None of them breaks anything. 

Factoring. "Unconditional factoring in L[1/3]". The Number Field Sieve already factors in L[1/3], but its running time rests on unproven heuristics. This paper would prove that bound for the first time. That's a real milestone for theory, but it isn't a faster algorithm and it isn't "factoring in P". RSA key sizes don't move.

Discrete log. It covers finite fields of small fixed characteristic. Those were already broken in quasi-polynomial time in 2014, and crypto dropped them years ago. Prime-field DH and elliptic curves are untouched.

Deterministic factoring. Getting subexponential factoring without randomness is elegant, but (randomized) subexponential factoring has existed for decades.

That's very likely how rumors are born. 

These results are still remarkable: AI is now producing serious results in complexity theory and number theory. But "AI proves a rigorous bound for a known algorithm" isn't "AI breaks RSA". 

No reason to panic ... yet.

text:
Important to pause and take a look at all of the progress being made, when we discuss the possibility of AI proving P ≠ NP, labs being afraid to release new models, and other genuinely extraordinary feats. We're finding planets today, but what comes next? Just last week Claude was able to solve a few major open problems involving black holes - the pace of discovery and disclosure is incredibly quick. 

When I think about the future and what type of impact superintelligence will have on the world, and what a slow or fast takeoff might be like, I always default to dreaming about what's out there beyond our solar system. How long could it take for superintelligence to sift through the stars and crack the question of whether or not we're alone? Just two years ago we were counting the Rs in strawberry, and now we're being shown up by the thinking machines. 

Dyson spheres will come, we'll colonize plants, and exist beyond the Earth, but the most impactful moment will come when we're told that non-human life is or isn't out there, and it will be a truly huge moment for us. There are so many secrets of the universe we just don't know about, and the world is going to change so much as we learn more than we could ever imagine. 

It's always been a challenge for humans to gain mastery over math and physics, yet these models are seemingly changing everything we thought we'd known, they're redefining limits - and it's a tough pill to swallow, but we might not be the apex intelligence on Earth anymore. 

AI is solving math, it will solve biology, and it will solve everything else, and humanity will be better for it, but it's still quite hard to imagine. Really important to zoom out sometimes, and with Thanksgiving coming up, important to mention that I'm grateful to live in the good timeline!

quoted_text:
Hermes Li is not the “Asian Leopold”.

Leopold ran one theme at up to 4x leverage, lost 67% in July, and sold most of his public book to Citadel. Then he reloaded with call options on the exact same trade, the names kept falling, and now he is shopping for leverage again. We’ve kind of lost count.

Hermes is a different animal: Goldman, Asia equities at Och-Ziff, and running his own shop since 2018. Aspex was reported down 16% in October, the same month the KOSPI lost 16% and Goldman had Asia stock pickers down 8% to 9%. His last 13F shows about $10B in US-listed longs, including Synopsys, Qualcomm, and CoreWeave. So the October drawdown was from the longs, no argument, and he was still up on the year.

November is the part we care about, and the part no filing shows. A 13F never lists a short. $NVDA fell 23% in the week leading up to November 20, and Goldman had long/short funds cutting net exposure back to April 2025 levels. Then Jensen came back, $NVDA gained 31% in a single session, and the shorts gave back about $12B in a day. A book that takes the selloff on its longs and then gives back the rebound on its hedge is going to have a bad month. We do not know his exact book. Our guess is that if he is hurt, it is on the hedge leg. Margin does not care why you lost. It only cares how levered you were when it happened, and we do not think he was running anything close to 4x.

A bit of lore. In the mid-2010s, after our stint in Singapore (mostly FX and macro people, and we always thought of macro guys as cowboys), we interviewed around at various Hong Kong funds. He was running Asia equities at Och-Ziff, the shop that later rebranded as Sculptor after its troubles. We had heard some vol people there were not getting paid, so we did not pursue it. We ran into he/his people at Aspex during UBS and Goldman idea dinners. He was truly one of a handful of people we found impressive in a space we generally thought was clueless.

That was before we saw the people in crypto, LMAO. This week, @RuneKek admitted he had borrowed about $80M out of his own protocol’s lending pool, and the depositors could not withdraw. (To be fair, many crypto “OGs” are not clueless, just operating in bad faith).

When we built dispersion baskets, we paid attention to the names Aspex was known for. Filings give you the longs a quarter late and never show the hedges. For that, you have to talk to the Street, and as @Ksidiii puts it, the more colour you get, the better informed you are. Sometimes that is the alpha.

We know the hedge problem firsthand. We wrote “do not fade Jensen until you do” in July, and then faded him one month too early (though some Jensen-saga-related vol trades delivered in November 👀).

On Tuesday, he was the second most-searched person on the Bloomberg terminal, right behind Jensen. That screen has not failed us in 10 years, so it would be a first. If he did take heavy losses, we are sure he will be back.

October numbers attached.

Fade D2 and Hermes at your own risk.

text:
1Password got hacked, and my trust in them took a hit.

To be fair, the core design did its job. 1Password never has your account password or Secret Key, so the attacker couldn't open vaults even from inside their systems.

The part that worries me is how they got in. One employee's GitHub account was enough to read private source code, access CI/CD, and push malicious code to backend services. Companies whose whole product is security should have a review and deploy pipeline where one stolen account can't get code into production.

Now the attacker has the source code, which makes finding the next bug easier. They also have customer names, emails and some invite and recovery link tokens, which is exactly what you need for a very convincing phishing email.

If you use 1Password, your vault is fine. Be suspicious of any email that looks like it's from them this week.

text:
20 years ago you could've got away with this one. Maybe even 10. In 2026? Come on.

Someone got into an employee's corporate GitHub account. They used it to access source code and push malicious code to 1Password's backend services, and those services downloaded customer account data. They also copied source code from private repos and got into the CI/CD system, which holds infrastructure secrets.

One GitHub account, and attacker code ends up running in backend services that touch customer data. Where was the branch protection? The second reviewer? The deploy gate?

But "vaults are fine"...

Don't let "non-secret metadata" fool you. 

For a subset of customers they took names, the email you sign in with, account and user IDs, when the account was created and last signed into, and SRP parameters. A small number of people also had tokens from invite or recovery emails taken (1Password says those were notified directly, and the tokens don't work alone).

Now an attacker knows you're a customer, which email you use, and when you last logged in. "Hi Pieter, we noticed a new sign-in on your 1Password account..." is going to look perfect. It's the same game we're watching play out with stolen PNR data and travel agencies when they get hit and scammers target travellers knowign their travel plans.

Honestly, it's about time I rolled my own password manager.

quoted_text:
No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. There are countless other examples and hard cases. I don’t think there are any easy answers here, nor is there (nor should there be) any single decision-maker: some of these decisions will be made by society, some by government, some by AI companies, and some in a decentralized manner by individuals expressing their own preferences as consumers, which may differ from the preferences of others.

I don't think that other AI leaders or AI companies have significantly different views from me on whether specific tasks should be automated. Certainly the products that they offer don’t differ materially in their orientation towards automation of tasks; every company seems to be releasing models more and more capable of task automation (as that’s been the general consequence of scaling up AI training), and every company claims to understand there are risks and downsides of such automation and to offer safeguards. If anything, Anthropic has been the most vocal and the most proactive about acknowledging these downsides and trying to address them. For instance, it’s fairly absurd to cite my statement that fully autonomous weapons might “one day be needed for the defense of democracy” as differing from that of other AI companies, when I was willing to risk Anthropic’s future as a company to refuse to allow our existing AI models to be used for autonomous weapons even in the face of legal sanctions, and no other AI company did the same.

To summarize, as applied to grand questions of how we govern increasingly capable AI, I have been vocal and consistent that AI needs to be governed by a legitimate, democratic process and that “surrendering human free will” to AI systems is a terrible idea. As applied to automation of specific tasks by or for people, my views are more mixed, but I don’t think they differ from those of other AI companies — most other companies seem to be offering similar products and confronting similar tradeoffs without having perfect answers to them. What is happening is that there’s a sort of vibes-based commercial and political positioning that some AI CEOs are engaging in, where they repeat slogans like “human control and agency,” or “AI should be just a tool,” without actually doing anything different in their products or taking seriously the difficult questions that lie behind these slogans.

text:
Right now, the game is time-to-power and time-to-GPU, not shaving 3 cents off a 15-year electricity bill.

Your argument only kicks in 2028+, if the industry overbuilds and compute pricing crashes.

If a glut hits, the neoclouds that moved fastest by taking on expensive colocation leases and high-interest debt get squeezed, while the low-cost, vertically integrated asset owner survives the shakeout.

Why Speed Beats Price in This Phase
Opportunity cost dwarfs power cost: If a hyperscaler or frontier lab is 6 months late training their next model, they lose billions in market share. They will happily pay a premium for energized, liquid-cooled clusters today rather than wait two years for slightly cheaper West Texas power.

Peak margins are front-loaded: GPU rental yields are highest while compute is scarce. A neocloud that gets 500 MW–1 GW online now captures peak pricing and locks in multi-year take-or-pay contracts. A slower developer sitting on a massive undeveloped power pipeline risks bringing capacity online right when the market actually softens.

text:
Travel writing is in practice some of the best sociology since the naivete of the foreigner grants the permission to make sweeping generalizations and claims that might otherwise seem too poorly-justified to merit publication. “My people have poor manners” is a tough claim to credibly land (Who are you? Exactly which life experiences are you drawing on? And what is your agenda in pushing this line of argument?), whereas “on my travels in Scotland, I noticed that the people had poor manners” seems perfectly reasonable, and indeed thought-provoking. Random samples from a distribution help you understand the mean, and the aleatory nature of travel encounters lends credence to the whole assessment.

Alexis de Tocqueville was just 25 when he traveled across the US and 29 when his observations were published. So, Democracy in America is a giant Substack from a young backpacker, written on his peregrinations as he consumed Montesquieu, Pascal, and Rousseau. He was clearly inspired by Montesquieu’s The Spirit of the Laws, which made the case that countries’ governance, and their laws, are necessarily functions of their cultures and manners.

Building on this, Democracy in America is in many ways a “deep roots” work. Tocqueville is emphatic (at times comically so) that it is America's culture that explains its success, and that its culture in turn stems from the country’s initial conditions. “I think I can see the whole destiny of America contained in the first Puritan who landed on those shores.” He thinks it's important that New England was settled by “a greater mass of intelligence than is to be found in any European nation of our own time” who brought the “best elements of order and morality”. He points out that Mexico doesn’t work nearly as well, despite copying the American constitution and laws, and notes disapprovingly that Virginia was founded by gold-seeking people “without character” whose “turbulent spirit [...] endangered the infant colony.” At the end of Volume I, he concludes, practically table-thumping: “If in the course of this work I have not succeeded in making the reader feel the importance that I attribute to the practical experience of the Americans, to their habits, to their opinions, in a word, to their moeurs, in maintaining their laws, I have failed in the principal object that I proposed to myself in writing it.”

We could look at Democracy in America as an early work of development economics: he is attempting to systematically figure out why it is that America works. (And not just out of casual interest: he was a member of an aristocratic family that was entangled with recent French political upheaval.) By placing primacy on culture, Tocqueville’s explanation deviates from the institutional and structural explanations often favored by today’s economists. Daron Acemoglu, to choose one prominent present-day example, firmly rejects the “Culture Hypothesis” in Why Nations Fail. In explaining Virginia, he instead points to structural incentives. Poor Economics, from Esther Duflo and Abhijit Banerjee, contains a similar rejection of cultural explanations. Comparable examples from other leading economists abound. An aversion to cultural explanations is of course understandable for all sorts of reasons: cultures are opaque, protean, and resistant to quantitative characterization. Cultures are themselves shaped by other factors, such that it’s hard to attribute definitive causality, and it’s uncomfortable to adopt anything that feels like a normative orientation. Nonetheless, can we explain why New England differs from Mexico without starting with the inner disposition, habits, and worldviews of the people? Tocqueville thinks not.

For all culture’s importance, it would be wrong to suggest that Tocqueville believes that culture is the only factor that matters. He dwells extensively on how America’s institutions are important, and how the microstructure of town life shapes the country’s federal civics. It is also true that development economics has taken a more strongly cultural turn in recent times, most of all in Joel Mokyr’s 2025 Nobel Prize. Mokyr’s work feels downright Tocquevillian at times: contra the intimidatingly quantitative econometrics that dominates today, Mokyr engages in an extended and earnestly curious qualitative synthesis of relevant patterns (in his case, in service of trying to figure out why the Industrial Revolution started when it did). Like Tocqueville, he concludes that the best explanation places cultural changes above other factors.

I’m very interested in whether LLMs will help us characterize culture in new and at least somewhat more objective ways. Can we ingest and process vast quantities of work that may not even have been OCR’d or translated until now? Can we map cultural corpora to vectors in some foundation model embedding space? Where large datasets and computational techniques enabled new ways to analyze many economic questions in recent decades, perhaps LLMs will enable newly objective light to be shone on hypothesized cultural explanations.

–

Speaking of LLMs, Democracy in America is a book about a new kind of society, and a Frenchman trying to figure out what the future might hold. As we sit on the cusp of another upheaval, is there anything that reads with resonance today?

Part of the declared promise of AI is that it might obviate our need to work. In slavery, Tocqueville observes a version of this phenomenon on his travels. He is struck by its barbarous cruelty (and his travel companion later published an anti-slavery novel), but also by its effects on the slaveowners themselves. He perceived that the practice rendered work dishonorable, and thus yielded idleness, ignorance, and pride. Slavery, he says, “enervates the powers of the mind, and benumbs the activity of man.” He observes the contrast between slavery-rejecting Ohio and slavery-embracing Kentucky. In Kentucky, “those who are active and enlightened either do nothing or pass over into the State of Ohio, where they may work without dishonor.” Ohio’s harvests are more abundant, homes are more elegant, and people seem to be “in enjoyment of that wealth and contentment which is the reward of labor.”

Presented with an evil release from manual labor, the Kentuckians did not apply themselves to productive studies and great creations, and the South did not become a new Florence. There is an obvious question for us: how will AI change our relationship with work? Will it become dishonorable, and what will the reflexive effect on our society be if so? Should this change our view of utopian visions of “automated communism”?

Tocqueville also raises the issue of coexistence with more advanced neighbors. He noted that the arrival of the Europeans had been ruinous for the Indians (as he termed them). European technology – firearms, metallurgy, steam power – was a kind of superintelligence relative to their practices. The disruptions and destruction wrought by the settlers led to cultural problems (“their traditions obscured, and the chain of their recollections broken”), which in turn led to declines in both the physical and the moral conditions of the tribes. Tocqueville believed that the Indians faced a choice given that their old way of living was no longer viable: they could adopt European mores or suffer inevitable destruction. He predicted that they would reject cultural adaptation, and thus were “doomed to perish”. This is all to say that the arrival of the European settlers was in Tocqueville’s eyes injurious to the Indians not only because of the direct violence and displacement, but also because the contact was itself so disruptive to their societies that their cultures ceased to function. Some of this was later observed in Pacific island societies – even though there wasn’t the same degree of violent dispossession, the mere presence of Western contact was intrinsically destabilizing. In many visions of the future, superintelligent AIs are much more numerous than humans, with consequences that are hard to predict. In Tocqueville, there is a cautionary suggestion.

Given the new powers afforded by AI, there is a question of what we will choose to do with it – to the extent that we are in control, we will wield a vastly expanded authority. Americans faced some version of this question: in democracy, society was endowed with wholly new ways to express its collective will, with no ultimate superior power, for society was for the first time in charge of itself. Tocqueville repeatedly emphasizes how democracy thus increased the importance of religion as a regulator of hasty or unwise impulses. “Whilst the law permits the Americans to do what they please, religion prevents them from conceiving, and forbids them to commit, what is rash or unjust.” If we take seriously Tocqueville’s idea that religion was a critical complement in ensuring that people shaped societies in prudent ways, Democracy implicitly raises a question: which are the ideas, philosophies, religions, or doctrines that will help us wield AI well?

Part of what’s interesting and memorable about the work is Tocqueville’s combination of curiosity, enthusiasm, and slight ambivalence about democracy itself. He grants that democracy is likely to be the future of governance, and he is admiring of what it has achieved in America, but he can’t avoid concerns about what it may augur (such as the unchecked and totalitarian impulses of the mob). At the end of Volume II, he describes his chief concern with democracy: that it may yield a new form of despotism that he struggles to define. He fears not tyrants, but, he says, “guardians”. He is worried about a world where:

> Above this race of men stands an immense and tutelary power, which takes upon itself alone to secure their gratifications, and to watch over their fate. [...] It would be like the authority of a parent, if, like that authority, its object was to prepare men for manhood; but it seeks on the contrary to keep them in perpetual childhood: it is well content that the people should rejoice, provided they think of nothing but rejoicing. For their happiness such a government willingly labors, but it chooses to be the sole agent and the only arbiter of that happiness. [...] What remains, but to spare them all the care of thinking and all the trouble of living? Thus it every day renders the exercise of the free agency of man less useful and less frequent; it circumscribes the will within a narrower range, and gradually robs a man of all the uses of himself.

The Iain Banks Culture novels are often invoked by AI proponents. For Tocqueville, something strikingly like the world that they describe was his dystopian fear, for a world bereft of autonomy would be intrinsically degrading and humiliating for humanity:

> The will of man is not shattered, but softened, bent, and guided: men are seldom forced by it to act, but they are constantly restrained from acting: such a power does not destroy, but it prevents existence; it does not tyrannize, but it compresses, enervates, extinguishes, and stupefies a people, till each nation is reduced to be nothing better than a flock of timid and industrious animals, of which the government is the shepherd.

The analogy to animals is noteworthy. In interviews, AI leaders occasionally analogize the future human state to that of pets. Banks himself noted that in the Culture novels, “[humans] have a status somewhere between passengers, pets and parasites.” In Richard Brautigan’s famous poem, All Watched Over by Machines of Loving Grace, he hopes that humans are “returned to our mammal brothers and sisters”.

Tocqueville at heart thought that agency and cultivation of people came above all else. He dreaded anesthetized placidity. In soft despotism, he feared that “ambition will lose its vigor and its greatness; that human passions will be appeased and lowered at the same time”. This vigor was for Tocqueville at the heart of what was admirable in America, whose bustle and intensity he repeatedly extols. American self-reliance and self-direction are paramount: “the citizen of the United States is taught from his earliest infancy to rely upon his own exertions in order to resist the evils and the difficulties of life.” For Tocqueville, any kind of servile and manicured comfort was not just undesirable, but a negation of the American promise.

Many of the Elysian visions for AI hinge on AI resolving the messy coordination challenges that afflict humans. (Scott Alexander invokes this vision towards the end of Meditations on Moloch.) For Tocqueville, the arbitration of such differences was precisely the constructive activity that reaffirmed our agency. Townships, juries, associations, and their attendant squabbles are how culture is reinforced and how judgment is cultivated. When a town decides whether to fund a school, there are two outputs: a decision, and practice in governance itself. If AI could resolve such matters, we might get better outcomes, but will we get better people?

text:
OpenAI announced today that they’re launching private inference. True privacy is a key to broader adoption of AI across personal and work usage. 

NEAR AI's position for the past 3 years was User-Owned AI and privacy is key component of it.

What does “private inference” mean for OpenAI? They will verify the environment they’re running on (VM), but are unlikely to open source their model architecture, inference, and weights (given their business model and precedent). So this still requires a lot of trust in OpenAI that their apparatus doesn’t have backdoors and that they’re not keeping the data.

In parallel, we’re seeing rapid growth of open weight and broader open source model usage – and this will only get faster as they keep improving. Privacy is also a growing concern with open source, given recent news about inference providers not following ZDR, redirecting traffic, and getting hacked. Open weight/open source alone isn’t enough, and privacy alone isn’t enough: you need both working together.

A year ago, no one cared about privacy. Now it’s a top line concern in the market. NEAR AI is setting the standard for private & verifiable AI: everyone who has tested our verification has found us to be at the forefront of both transparency and verification. 

If you’re looking for *truly* private and verifiable inference, it’s NEAR.

text:
UPDATE: @bangjelkoski shares a technical breakdown of @injective's newly launched Veyra Mainnet upgrade.

Key highlights:

• IBC precompile for one-click USDC transfers
• Swap precompile for Solidity smart contracts
• Fixed gas costs for orders
• EIP-712 V3 support
• Unified mempool
Veyra marks Injective's final major network upgrade of 2026, with CypherOS security infrastructure and options trading currently on testnet and heading toward mainnet.
author: TTT_News_
quoted_text:
This is the marketing summary for the upgrade that just went live. Let me share a brief technical one and why this is our biggest upgrade for the year: 

- IBC precompile: this is what lets SkipGo do one-click transfers through Injective. USDC from any network can be minted natively on Injective through CCTP V2 and sent over IBC to Cosmos Hub, dYdX, and other chains in a single transaction. Before, that took two separate transactions. It's also the path for moving Noble-issued USDC over to native USDC.

- Veyra also ships a round of security hardening across the chain and the exchange module. Not going into the details on that one.

- Swap precompile: any Solidity contract can fill a spot swap against Injective's order book in one atomic call. Wallets, aggregators and routers get order book prices from the EVM.

- Funding from impact prices: funding follows the price you could actually fill at on the book, so a few thin quotes can't drag it around.

- Async CheckTx and a unified mempool: nodes take in transactions faster under load.

- EIP-712 V3: Phantom users can sign native Injective transactions.

- Fixed gas: placing or cancelling an order costs the same gas every time, so market makers know their quoting costs in advance. If your bot hardcodes gas limits, re-check them against the new schedule.

- CypherOS, our privacy platform, is running on testnet and will go live on mainnet once its audit wraps up

- Options support that's currently running on testnet

- Institutional rails foundations that give institutional flow a direct lane into the chain, with next-block inclusion and optimistic execution

That's the last major upgrade of 2026. See you in 2027.

text:
This is a masterclass in autonomous software synthesis, but it also perfectly exposes the next fundamental frontier for AI:

Right now, LLMs are incredible at Static Aggregation… I mean, taking 31 government datasets (BEA, NOAA, EIA, Census) and reconciling them onto a hex grid with a game skin. :/

But the real trap is assuming 31 datasets = 31 independent views of reality:

1. The Echo Chamber: 

BEA depends on Census; FEMA depends on NOAA; CDC depends on both. It’s not 31 independent signals; it’s an echo chamber of shared assumptions.

2. Static vs. Fragile: 

A city isn't its historical GDP column. The real question is: when EIA power projections, NOAA weather models, and supply chains collide, where does their consensus fail?

The leap from AI that builds static digital twins to AI that understands where consensus is fragile and how systems co-fail is the real step forward.

text:
10 月中開始拿 Grok Bot 玩了一個小專案，讓它全自動跑一個長尾流量的聯盟行銷站，不知不覺也跑一個多月了。

近 30 天（10/27–11/25）的數據：
• 點擊 775
• 訂單 70 筆
• 訂單金額 6.8 萬
• 預估分潤 1,401.9
• 新買家 64 人

核心就是想辦法衝到第一頁。熱門大字對新站、小站來說根本沒空間，所以專挑小眾字做 SEO。競爭少，排名爬得蠻快的，現在大概卡在第 5 到 10 名，如果能衝進前 3，分潤應該還能再翻好幾倍。

剛開始在架構跟文案上折騰很久。最早我開了一個 bot team，產文的、找靈感的、分析流量的各一隻，結果 bot 之間來回對話超級燒 token，後來乾脆全部收斂成一隻，才發現這種小專案一隻就很夠用了。

文案原本 AI 味很重，改用 Gemini Argon 寫稿後自然很多，最近又換成 Neon，成本更省。

現在這套流程幾乎全自動，我直接跟 bot 講，除非需要 KYC 或付錢，其他一律它自己決定。平常它就自己跑這些事：

 * 早上巡一輪：抓 Search Console 跟 GA4 的流量，登進聯盟後台查佣金，整理成晨報給我

 * 全站逐頁檢查：看分潤連結和主圖有沒有掉，把有曝光但沒人點連結的頁面抓出來

 * 追價格和庫存：主推商品快賣完、或分潤只有 1%，就自己找同價位、有貨、分潤更高的款式換上去

 * 每週找選題、寫新文、改舊文

 * 每次改動都先過自動檢查跟審稿才上線，上線後再自己抽查一次頁面

 * 定期找外部顧問（其他模型）複盤：每週自己去問 Carbon 跟 Astra，看工作流程和流量分潤還能怎麼優化

踩過最大的坑是分潤率。一樣的商品、一樣的流量跟訂單，有的連結給 1%，有的給 10%，選錯直接少賺九成。

再來是 Cookie 長度。蝦皮的分潤追蹤有 7 天，算非常長，讀者點進去一週內在同一家店順手買別的也算你的。這次 775 次點擊換到 70 單、轉換率快 9%，很大一部分就是吃這個紅利。你看圖裡甚至冒出一些跟我關鍵字完全無關的奇怪品項，照樣算我的。只是蝦皮大多數品項只有 1%，一定要特地挑高的放。

摸清楚之後，我現在選品大概就分兩塊：
 * 蝦皮高分潤商品，拿來吃 7 天 Cookie。
 * 其他平台的高分潤商品，各站規則不同，反正分潤夠高才放。

目前全部聯盟加起來一個月大概 60U，老實說這東西賺不了太多錢，主要還是好玩，一路折騰下來也學到不少聯盟行銷的眉角。

短期就先讓網站自己賺回 Grok Bot Ultra 的月費，當作 bot 養 bot。

到目前為止也才把一個品項做深而已，接下來想再試兩件事：
 * 用 Google Trends 找有商業需求、好做聯盟行銷，但還沒人認真做的字
 * 把同一套流程複製到冷門語系、冷門地區，看看競爭是不是更低

網路上其實還有超多這種大站看不上、但確實有人在搜的邊角關鍵字。以前請人做不划算，現在丟給不用睡覺的 bot 去撿剛剛好。

反正成本極低，就當作邊玩邊練手，等冷門語系跑出成績再來分享。

We’re sharing an update about a recent security incident involving some of 1Password’s backend systems. 𝗡𝗼 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁, 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗹𝘂𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗿𝗲𝘁𝘀, 𝗽𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗱𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗼𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿 𝘃𝗮𝘂𝗹𝘁 𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗺𝘀, 𝗼𝗿 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗸𝗲𝘆𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗺 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗰𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗺𝗶𝘀𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝘂𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗶𝗱𝗲𝗻𝘁. We have confirmed that all customer vaults and credentials remain secure. Our services continue operating normally. 

Independent cybersecurity experts have been engaged to validate our containment approaches and remediation efforts.

While we took immediate steps to contain the incident, the attacker gained access to some of our backend systems and accessed a limited amount of customer account information from a subset of our customers, including names and email addresses. 

No action is required by customers, their 1Password accounts remain secure. As always, please keep alert to unexpected phishing attempts.

Your vault secrets are encrypted with keys that only you hold, so we can’t access them, and they cannot be retrieved from our systems.

You can read more about the steps we’ve taken on our blog at: https://t.co/9fbzzAJYQ9

text:
Let me elaborate. Several aspects of 1Password’s architecture still appear secure:

1. Zero-knowledge authentication and the Secure Remote Password (SRP) protocol. The private key never leaves the local device, and the server holds only the public key.
2. Data protection. The server stores only ciphertext and never holds the complete master key.
3. Key derivation. The master key used for encryption and decryption is derived locally from the password and Secret Key using PBKDF2. PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 typically requires 600,000 iterations per derivation. The derived key is then used to decrypt the data.
4. Local encryption and decryption. Regardless of how 1Password is deployed, encryption and decryption always happen locally.
5. Transport security. Ciphertext is protected by TLS and an additional, separate layer of packet encryption.

The takeaway is that decrypting 1Password data from a stolen database alone is practically impossible. Compromising it locally, however, is considerably easier. With local SSH access, an attacker could trigger a deceptive prompt to trick the user into unlocking the keychain, then hijack access. If Touch ID is used to sign in, this key is stored in the keychain.

Deployments using service tokens or similar mechanisms may also give an attacker more options locally. Local vaults generally cache the Secret Key, whether in the browser extension or the app, although obtaining it still leaves the attacker needing the password to derive the master private key.

Could passwords still be compromised? Yes. Any password manager can potentially be compromised, but 1Password’s weak point is the local environment, not the cloud. Much of that local exposure is the trade-off for convenience.

What should you do now? My recommendation is to regenerate your Secret Key, change your password, and replace your recovery code. Also rotate credentials for critical accounts, including passwords, OTP secrets, passkeys, and physical FIDO keys, as applicable. Review the security of your primary email account, phone, and associated recovery paths. Treat even a low-risk situation as high-risk.

婴儿夭折这件事对Steve Eisman 后续发现次贷漏洞的影响：

1. 不再相信“幸运者豁免”，更容易想象黑天鹅

他早年潜意识里觉得自己属于“受保护、坏事轮不到我”的人。婴儿意外离世之后，他接受了：灾难可以毫无预警落到任何人头上，哪怕条件很好、看起来一切稳妥。在次贷狂欢、全市场一致乐观的时候，他更愿意认真去推演“最坏情况真的会发生”，而不是跟着市场默认“房价永远涨、风险可控”。

2. 更敏锐地看见体系里不负责任、不受惩罚的风险
这件事来自一个本该负责看护的人失职，悲剧发生却几乎没有实质追责。这套逻辑和次贷链条高度呼应：放贷机构、评级公司、银行，所有人都在转移风险、拿佣金，把后果丢给底层借款人、普通家庭。这件经历强化了他对“激励机制扭曲、坏人不用承担代价”的敏感度，愿意主动去挖行业掩盖的欺诈和漏洞（比如早年他就深度做空、批评消费信贷公司 Household Finance）。

3. 性格变得更愿意对抗主流、不怕得罪人
他本来就爱唱反调；丧子之后，他更“不怕冲突”，不愿顺从华尔街体面的潜规则。别人不愿戳破皇帝新衣，他愿意公开写报告、当面质疑，逼着团队（Danny、Vinny、Porter）去拆解抵押贷款池底层数据，去证实里面全是烂贷款。

4. 叠加了一层强烈的道德视角
他看次贷不再只是一个“可以赚钱的空头交易”，同时看到这是一套专门收割弱势借款人的系统。这个道德驱动，让他在所有人嘲笑他、压力巨大的时候，依然坚持持仓。

是电影里这个“愤青”角色：👇
